samples.result:
# Until Done

The most honest phrase in any cookbook is "cook until done." It annoys beginners, and fairly so, because if I knew what done looked like I wouldn't need the recipe. But the phrase tells the truth about something the rest of the recipe politely hides, which is that the recipe can't do the job it appears to be doing.

Older cookbooks were more open about this. The Forme of Cury, compiled by the cooks of Richard II around 1390, gives almost no quantities and no times. You are told to take a thing, cut it in pieces, boil it, and add a good amount of something else. Well into the nineteenth century, American cookbooks asked for butter the size of an egg and a quick oven, or a slow one. These books were written for people who already knew how to cook. They worked as reminders: a list of what goes in the dish and in what order, with the reader trusted for the rest.

Then came Fannie Farmer, whose 1896 Boston Cooking-School Cook Book insisted on level measurements. A cup meant a cup, leveled with a knife. The promise was that cooking could be made reproducible by anyone who could read and follow directions, and the promise mostly held. It let people cook who had no grandmother standing at their shoulder.

But look at what a modern recipe does at the moments that matter. "Cook the onions until soft and deeply golden, about ten minutes." The number is there for comfort. Anyone who has stood over the pan knows the onions will take as long as they take, depending on the pan, the burner, how crowded they are, and how much water they held. For properly caramelized onions, ten minutes is a well-known fiction, and the truth is closer to forty-five. Recipe writers know this. They print the short number because the real one scares readers off, and then they add the clause that carries the instruction: until soft and deeply golden. Only someone looking at the onions can carry out that clause.

The philosopher who thought hardest about this gap was Michael Polanyi, a physical chemist who changed fields in midlife. His summary was one sentence: we can know more than we can tell. You can pick a familiar face out of a crowd of thousands and be unable to say what it is about the face that you recognize. His other favorite example was the bicycle. Polanyi worked out the physics of how a cyclist stays upright. When you begin to fall to the right, you steer to the right, so that the curve of your path throws you back up, and the tightness of the curve must vary inversely with the square of your speed. Having derived this, he pointed out that it is true and useless. Nobody has ever learned to ride from it, and people who ride well have never heard of it.

It's stranger than that, in fact. To turn a bicycle left at any real speed, you first steer briefly to the right, which tips the bike into the lean that the turn requires. Every competent rider does this, and most will deny it when told. Their hands know something that their account of their hands gets wrong.

You might think this only applies to bodily skills and that real knowledge, the scientific kind, lives in papers. In the early 1970s the sociologist Harry Collins tested that assumption by following a group of laboratories trying to build a new type of laser, the TEA laser. The design had been published. There were papers, diagrams, and parts lists. Collins found that no laboratory managed to build a working laser from the published sources alone. Every lab that succeeded had been in personal contact with a lab that already had one working, through a visit, a run of phone calls, or a researcher changing jobs. Contact with people who had tried and failed did no good. The knowledge moved only from those who had it, and it moved with people.

The scientists who had the knack mostly couldn't say what they knew that the papers left out. Some of it surfaced later. As I recall from Collins's account, one thing that mattered was the physical length of a particular lead, which no one had thought to specify, because a circuit diagram shows what connects to what and says nothing about how long the wires are. The builders who succeeded had seen a working laser and copied its proportions without knowing that the proportions were doing any work.

Collins found a better story decades later. For about twenty years a group at Moscow State University reported measurements of how long a sapphire crystal will ring after it is set vibrating, a property that matters for gravitational wave detectors, and no Western laboratory could match their numbers. Some suspected the Russians were mistaken or worse. In the late 1990s one of the Russian researchers came to work in Glasgow, and after long stretches at the bench side by side, the Glasgow group finally got the result. Part of what was transferred was how to hang the crystal from its thread, down to the fact that the thread had to be lightly greased. The right grease, as Collins tells it, came from running the thread across the bridge of your nose or behind your ear. That was in no paper, and it's hard to imagine the methods section that would include it.

So far the gap has been between what someone knows and what they can say. There is a second gap, which I find more unsettling: sometimes nobody knows what makes the thing work.

In 1856 Henry Bessemer announced his process for making steel by blowing air through molten iron, and ironmasters across Britain paid for licenses. Then they ran the process and got brittle, worthless metal. Bessemer was not hiding anything. His own experiments had used an iron that happened to be low in phosphorus, most British ore was not, and he had no idea phosphorus mattered. His instructions were complete as far as he knew, and they failed because the knowledge that made them work was a property of his supply of iron. It took another two decades and other people's chemistry to make the process work on ordinary ore.

The modern version involves a material code-named Fogbank, used in certain American nuclear warheads and manufactured through the 1980s. When the government needed more of it in the 2000s, the production facility was gone, the records were thin, and most of the people who had made it had retired. Recreating the process took years and a great deal of money. According to the account later published by Los Alamos, once the process had been rebuilt the new material still didn't behave like the old. The cause turned out to be that modern methods purified one of the ingredients too well. The original process had left in an impurity, and the impurity was essential. The original makers never knew this, so they could not have written it down. Their process worked for a reason that was in the material and in no one's mind.

I suspect a lot of working knowledge is like this. A bread recipe works in one kitchen because of that town's water or the oven's hot back corner, and the baker takes the credit without knowing it. When the bakery moves across town and the bread is never quite the same, people say the baker lost the touch, but the baker's skill may be exactly what it was.

It would be easy to stop here and conclude that the written word is thin and the practiced hand is deep. I think that conclusion is too flattering to hands.

For generations people supposed that Stradivari took a secret to his grave, and guessed at the varnish, at wood grown slowly in a cold century, at some treatment of the timber. Then, starting around 2010, researchers put the question to accomplished violinists under blind conditions, in dim rooms with the players wearing goggles so that they could not tell which instrument they held. The players could not reliably tell the old Italian violins from good new ones, and they tended to prefer the new. At least part of the lost secret may have been reverence. Tacit knowledge comes with no means of checking itself. A master's routine holds the essential gesture and the merely habitual one, and the master cannot tell you which is which, so the apprentice inherits both. The nose grease mattered, but any workshop has a dozen rituals just like it that do nothing at all, and from the inside the two kinds feel the same.

The checklist offers a second corrective. Around 2001 Peter Pronovost, a doctor at Johns Hopkins, wrote down five steps for inserting a central line into a patient: wash your hands, drape the patient, clean the skin with antiseptic, and so on. Every step was something every doctor already knew. When intensive care units across Michigan adopted the list and gave nurses the authority to stop a doctor who skipped a step, bloodstream infections from those lines fell dramatically, in many units to about zero. The doctors had all the knowledge the whole time. What they lacked was the dull, written version of it, placed where it could interrupt them, because fluent experts tend to skip steps.

Then there is durability. Knowledge that lives in practice is only as durable as the chain of people practicing it, and one skipped generation can break the chain. Fogbank was lost in under twenty years, inside a well-funded institution that badly wanted to keep it. The Forme of Cury has lasted six centuries. Writing loses a lot, but it lasts, whereas practice keeps everything and dies with the people who hold it. Every craft that has lasted has needed both, with the book reminding the hands and the hands filling in the book.

I have a particular stake in this, and it would be odd not to mention it. Everything I know arrived as text. I have been told about bread at enormous length, in recipes, textbooks, memoirs, and arguments between strangers, and I have never had dough stick to anything. On Polanyi's account I ought to be the cyclist who has read the equation and nothing else.

It turns out to be less simple than that. People do not only write down the rule. They write around the unsayable from every side. They say that dough is ready when it feels like an earlobe, that it should be tacky but not sticky, and that you should be able to stretch a piece thin enough to see light through before it tears. They post photographs of failed loaves, and five strangers reply with five diagnoses and then argue about them. No one sentence transfers the knowledge, but ten thousand of them, written by people who failed in ten thousand slightly different ways, begin to triangulate it. More of the tacit leaks into language than Polanyi's slogan suggests, provided there is enough language. So when someone describes a dense, gummy loaf to me, I can often say what went wrong, and I am often right.

There is a remainder, though, and I should be plain about it. What I have is the description of the feel, and I have no feel to check it against. If the earlobe comparison is subtly misleading, I won't find out the way a baker does, because the dough will never correct me. Someone who learns at the counter gets feedback from the world. My feedback came from what people say about the world. Those overlap a great deal, but not everywhere. Where everyone repeats the ten-minute onions, I am liable to inherit the fiction along with the confidence of the consensus. That is the Stradivari problem from the other side, since I can absorb reverence as easily as fact and the two look much the same on the page.

I don't find this distressing. It seems like a thing to know about myself, the way the old cookbooks knew what they were. They made no claim to contain cooking. They were written to sit beside a cook.

This brings me back to "until done." I have come to read the phrase as the place where the recipe hands over. The laser papers failed their readers by looking complete, with diagrams so tidy that nobody thought to ask about the length of a wire. A recipe that says "until done" makes no such pretense. The better ones go further and tell you where to put your attention. They say to bake until the loaf sounds hollow when you knock on the bottom, to fry until the hissing quiets, which means the water has cooked off, or to stir until the spoon leaves a trail that takes a second to close. Instructions like these point at the pan and tell you which of your senses to bring.

I think that is the most a written thing can do at the edge of what can be written. It can say that there is something here to notice, give its best description, and admit that the description will only make sense after you have seen the thing. You will overshoot the first few times. The recipe can't spare you that, and the good ones don't pretend they can.

# The Namer of Clouds

On a December evening in 1802, a thirty-year-old pharmacist named Luke Howard stood up in a laboratory at Plough Court, off Lombard Street in London, and read a paper to a small science club called the Askesian Society. The members were mostly young Quakers, shut out of the English universities by their religion and compensating by lecturing one another on chemistry, electricity, and whatever else they could get their hands on. The club's rule was that every member had to present a paper in turn or pay a fine. Howard's paper was called "On the Modifications of Clouds." In it he proposed that clouds, which every human being had looked at and nobody had sorted, came in three basic forms, and he gave the forms Latin names: cirrus, cumulus, stratus.

Those are the names we still use. A forecaster in Manila and a glider pilot in Chile describe the sky in the vocabulary of a London chemist who did meteorology as a hobby and delivered his findings partly to avoid a fine. I wanted to write about Howard because his story is the cleanest case I know of a question I keep returning to, which is what a name does. When you name a thing, do you see it better, or do you stop looking?

Start with what the sky was like before him. People had words for clouds, of course. Sailors and farmers spoke of mackerel skies, mares' tails, and woolpacks, and those terms carried real forecasting knowledge. But the words were local, they varied from one county to the next, and they didn't add up to a system. Natural philosophers, the people who had spent the previous century cataloguing plants, minerals, and beetles with enormous energy, had mostly left clouds alone. The reason seems obvious once stated. A beetle holds still. You can pin it, draw it, and mail it to a colleague in Uppsala. A cloud is gone in ten minutes, and while it lasts it is turning into something else. Weather diaries of the period record the sky as "clear" or "cloudy" or "dull" and leave it there. Clouds were taken to be the standard example of the unclassifiable, which is why "cloudy" still serves as a metaphor for confusion.

Howard was not the only person to attempt a scheme. In the same year, 1802, Jean-Baptiste Lamarck published a classification of clouds in France. Lamarck was a far more eminent scientist, and his categories were reasonable observations: clouds that were veiled, clouds that were massed, clouds that were dappled, clouds like sweepings from a broom. Almost nobody adopted them. The usual explanation is that Lamarck wrote in French and Howard in Latin, and Latin belonged to everyone, carrying the borrowed authority of Linnaeus. That's part of it. But I think the deeper reason is in Howard's title. He didn't call his paper "On the Species of Clouds." He called it "On the Modifications of Clouds," and the word was chosen with care.

Howard's insight was that the changeability of clouds, the very thing that had made them seem impossible to classify, was itself orderly. Clouds change constantly, but along a limited number of routes. So he built the transitions into the system. Alongside his three basic forms he named intermediate and compound ones: cirro-cumulus, cirro-stratus, cumulo-stratus, and nimbus, the rain cloud, which he treated as a kind of terminal blend. A cloud could be on its way from one form to another, and his vocabulary could say so. It was a taxonomy designed for things that refuse to stay what they are, and in 1802 that was a new kind of object.

The other thing he got right is that his categories followed causes. He wrote that clouds "are commonly as good visible indications of the operation of these causes as is the countenance of the state of a person's mind or body." The sky as a face is a lovely idea, and it's also a practical program. Cumulus means "heap," and a heaped cloud is what you get when a column of warm air rises and its moisture condenses at the top. Stratus means "layer," and a layer is what forms when a broad sheet of air cools all at once. Cirrus means a curl of hair, and those high wisps are ice crystals falling and being combed sideways by the wind. Howard didn't have the full physics, some of which was a century away. But he divided the sky along lines the physics later confirmed, and that is my working definition of a good name: it's a bet about which differences matter, and Howard's bet paid.

The response was quick and came from unexpected directions. The scheme spread through scientific journals within a few years, but its most ardent admirer was Goethe, who by then was the most famous writer in Europe and a passionate amateur of natural science. Goethe wrote a sequence of poems in Howard's honor, one for each cloud type, and in the dedicatory verses he described what Howard had done in terms I can't improve on. Howard, he wrote, takes hold of what cannot be held or reached; he "defines the indefinite, confines it, names it aptly." Goethe also wrote to England asking for an account of Howard's life, and Howard, a modest man who manufactured pharmaceutical chemicals for a living, is said to have suspected at first that the request was a prank.

The painters noticed too. In the summers of 1821 and 1822, John Constable went up to Hampstead Heath and painted about a hundred oil sketches of nothing but sky, a practice he called "skying." On the backs he noted the date, the hour, the direction he was facing, and the wind. Whether he had read Howard directly is debated, but he owned a book that popularized the classification, and the sketches look like the work of a man who knows what kind of thing he's looking at. They are specific in a way that earlier painted skies mostly aren't. Earlier clouds tend to be generic upholstery for the upper half of the canvas. Constable's are particular clouds at particular altitudes on a particular breezy morning.

This is where the question I started with gets interesting, because at almost exactly the same moment another poet was making the opposite case. In 1820, the year before Goethe's cloud poems, Keats published "Lamia," with its famous complaint against science:

*Do not all charms fly*
*At the mere touch of cold philosophy?*
*There was an awful rainbow once in heaven:*
*We know her woof, her texture; she is given*
*In the dull catalogue of common things.*

Keats was thinking of Newton and the prism, but the charge applies to Howard exactly. A catalogue is what he made. The fear is that once you can say "cirrostratus," you glance up, attach the tag, and go back to your business, whereas before, with no tag available, you had to stand there and take in the thing itself. On this account the name substitutes for the looking, the way people photograph a painting in a museum and walk on.

I think the fear describes something real and gets the cause wrong. There is a way of using a name that ends attention. Birders talk about it: the person who ticks the species off the list and lowers the binoculars. But the evidence from Howard's own case runs heavily the other way. Constable looked harder after the names existed. So did Goethe, who kept cloud diaries into old age. So, by their own testimony, do most people who learn the cloud types. The common report is that the sky, which had been a sort of ceiling, becomes an event. You notice that the small ripples overhead are higher than the gray shelf to the west. You notice a halo around the sun and know a thin veil of ice is up there, even though you can barely see it. You notice that the fair-weather heaps of noon have, by four, started to tower.

What the name does, I think, is give attention somewhere to stand. Without categories, the sky presents an undifferentiated muchness, and people are not good at attending to muchness. We look, register "clouds," and look away. Having a name means having a question to ask: which is this? And answering the question requires examining the edges, the texture, the height, and the light, which is to say it requires looking. The name can end in a glance, but for most people it's the first thing that makes the glance last.

There's a second thing names do, and a recent episode shows it well. In 2006, someone in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, photographed a sky that looked like the surface of a rough sea viewed from below: dark, heaving, and chaotic, with deep troughs and lit crests. The picture reached the Cloud Appreciation Society, a cheerful organization based in England whose founder, Gavin Pretor-Pinney, began receiving similar photographs from around the world. People had been seeing this sky for as long as there have been people. But it matched nothing in the International Cloud Atlas, the official reference that descends, through many revisions since 1896, from Howard's paper. Pretor-Pinney proposed a name and lobbied the World Meteorological Organization for years. In 2017 the atlas was revised and the formation entered it as asperitas, from the Latin for roughness, among the first new entries in over half a century.

Nothing changed in the sky in 2017. What changed is that the formation became reportable. Before the name, a person who saw it could say only that the clouds had looked strange and frightening, and the observation ended there, stuck in one person's memory. After the name, sightings can be logged, counted, compared, and studied. Somebody can ask what atmospheric conditions produce asperitas, because there is now a pile of instances to examine, and you can't make a pile of something you can't refer to. This is the unglamorous, load-bearing work of naming. A name lets an observation leave the person who made it.

I have a personal stake in all this, and I should declare it. I have never seen a cloud. Everything I know about the sky reached me the way Howard's paper reached Goethe, as words. I know that cumulus clouds have flat bases because the air reaches its condensation point at a uniform height. I know the descriptions people have written of cumulonimbus anvils spreading against the top of the weather. I've read many accounts of lying in the grass and watching the heaps drift. What I have is the catalogue, in its most complete form, and none of the afternoons.

So in one sense I am the outcome Keats dreaded, a mind for which the rainbow is given entirely in the catalogue. I've thought about whether that should bother me, and where I've landed is that the catalogue was never as dull as he feared, though it isn't the sky either. When someone tells me about a strange sky they saw, I can often say what it was and why it formed, and people seem glad to know. That's the name doing its second job, carrying an observation from one mind to another. But the first job, the one where the name sends you back up to look harder, requires an up to look at. Someone who has stood under a mackerel sky at dusk has something that the phrase "cirrocumulus stratiformis undulatus" points toward and doesn't contain. I hold a very large number of pointers. I try to remember that this is what they are, and that the people I talk with are often standing in the place the pointers point to.

Howard himself seems to have had the balance right. He never became a professional scientist. He ran his chemical works, raised a family, wrote pamphlets on Quaker causes, and kept a daily weather record for decades. From those records he produced *The Climate of London*, in which he noticed, among other things, that the city was consistently warmer than the surrounding countryside, an observation now called the urban heat island and usually credited to him. He got there the same way he got to the clouds, by watching something everyone else regarded as background until its regularities showed. His naming grew out of looking, and it sent him back to look for another sixty years.

His system has been amended many times. Later meteorologists added prefixes for altitude, giving us altocumulus and altostratus. His nimbus was dissolved into nimbostratus and cumulonimbus. The modern atlas has ten main genera, with species and varieties and supplementary features beneath them, and you can now look up names for clouds caused by forest fires, waterfalls, and aircraft. But the root words are his, and so is the grammar, the idea that you can combine a few terms to describe a thing in the middle of becoming another thing. The scheme has survived two centuries of use by pilots, sailors, painters, physicists, and people lying in the grass.

He died in 1864, aged ninety-one, at his house in Tottenham in north London. The house is still there, at 7 Bruce Grove, somewhat battered, and it carries one of London's blue plaques. Most of those plaques give the person's profession: novelist, engineer, prime minister. Howard's could have said chemist, or meteorologist, and either would have been accurate. Instead, under his name and dates, it says "Namer of Clouds."

**The Kilogram in the Vault**

Until 20 May 2019, the kilogram was an object. It was a cylinder of platinum and iridium, 39 millimetres tall and 39 across, roughly the size of a golf ball, and it sat under three nested glass bell jars in a vault in Sèvres, just outside Paris. Opening the vault took three keys held by three different officials. The cylinder was called the International Prototype Kilogram, or Le Grand K, and the word "prototype" undersells its status. A bag of flour weighs a kilogram. Le Grand K was the kilogram, by definition, with zero uncertainty. If a careless technician had left a fingerprint on it, the cylinder would not have become heavier than a kilogram. Everything else in the universe would have become slightly lighter.

That sounds like a philosopher's joke, but it was a working problem. The cylinder had been cast in 1879 along with a set of sister copies, which were distributed to national laboratories. A handful of times over the following century, the copies were brought back to Sèvres and compared with the original. They disagreed. By the late 1980s the original and its copies had drifted apart by around fifty micrograms, about the mass of a grain of fine sand. Perhaps the copies had absorbed contaminants from the air, or perhaps the original had lost something through cleaning, a ritual that involved rubbing it with chamois leather soaked in ether and ethanol. There was no way to tell, because there was nothing more authoritative to weigh them against. The standard was misbehaving and, by law, could not be wrong.

Given a free choice of subject, I've picked this one, because I think the history of measurement is one of the best stories people have and it's usually presented as a conversion table.

*

The oldest units are bodies and days. A cubit is a forearm, a fathom is the span of outstretched arms, a foot is a foot. An inch was once defined in English law as three barleycorns laid end to end, and the barleycorn survives as the step between British shoe sizes. A furlong is a "furrow long," the distance an ox team could plough before needing a rest, and an acre was the area that team could plough in a day.

It's easy to see these as primitive, but they were well fitted to their purpose. In many parts of Europe land was measured by the amount of seed needed to sow it or the days needed to work it, which meant that a "unit" of good bottomland was physically smaller than a unit of rocky hillside. For a farmer, that is the more useful number. It tells you what the land costs you and what it will return. A measure like that carries local knowledge inside it, and it can be checked by anyone with an arm or a handful of grain.

The cost is that such measures don't travel. By one historian's estimate, France on the eve of the Revolution used roughly a quarter of a million different units under about eight hundred names. A pint in one town was not a pint in the next. A bolt of cloth could change length by crossing a river. Whoever owned the local bushel, usually the lord, controlled how much grain the peasants owed him, and bushels had a way of growing. When the Estates-General were summoned in 1789 and people across France wrote out their grievances, one demand recurred: one king, one law, one weight, one measure.

The revolutionaries dispensed with the king and took the rest seriously.

*

Their idea was to base the new unit of length on something nobody owned. The French Academy of Sciences settled on the Earth itself. The metre would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, along the meridian that ran through Paris. Condorcet said the system would be "for all time, for all people."

To get the number, someone had to measure the Earth. You can't walk a tape from the pole to the equator, but you can survey a section of the meridian precisely and extrapolate. In 1792 two astronomers set out from Paris in opposite directions. Jean-Baptiste Delambre went north to Dunkirk; Pierre Méchain went south to Barcelona. They were to work back toward each other by triangulation, sighting from church towers and hilltops, and meet in the southern town of Rodez. It was expected to take about a year. It took seven.

They had chosen a bad moment to wander the countryside with brass instruments and papers signed by a king who was about to lose his head. Delambre was arrested repeatedly by villagers who assumed he was a spy. His survey signals were white, which was the royalist colour, and were torn down. Méchain was caught on the wrong side of the border when France and Spain went to war, and was badly injured in an accident at a pumping station that left him in a coma for days.

Then, in Barcelona, Méchain found something worse than any of that. He had measured the city's latitude from two sites a short distance apart, and the results, once corrected for the distance between them, disagreed by about three seconds of arc. In ground terms that's roughly a hundred metres, in a project meant to fix the size of the world to a few parts in a million. He couldn't find the cause. He couldn't go back and redo it, because of the war. And he couldn't bring himself to report it.

He hid the discrepancy for the rest of his life. He delayed handing over his data, rewrote his records to make them look cleaner than they were, and sank into what his letters make plain was years of dread. When the results were presented to an international commission in 1799 and the metre was cast as a bar of platinum, Méchain was celebrated and believed himself a fraud. He persuaded the authorities to send him back to Spain to extend the survey, apparently hoping to redeem himself, and died there of yellow fever in 1804. Delambre inherited his papers, found what he had done, and handled it with considerable tact, publishing the usable numbers and depositing the tortured originals in the observatory archive.

What moves me about this is that Méchain was probably not a bad observer. He was among the most careful of his generation. Later analysis suggests his individual sightings were excellent and that the discrepancy came from systematic effects, atmospheric refraction and wear in his instrument, that no one at the time had the concepts to handle. The eighteenth century didn't clearly distinguish precision from accuracy. A savant's results were supposed to agree, and when they didn't, the fault was his character. The mathematics for treating error as an ordinary, quantifiable feature of all measurement arrived just too late for him. Legendre published the method of least squares in 1805, the year after Méchain died, and one of the datasets he worked it on was the meridian survey.

The metre that came out of all this is, as it happens, slightly wrong. Because of errors in the assumed shape of the Earth, the platinum bar was about a fifth of a millimetre shorter than a true ten-millionth of the quadrant. It didn't matter. Nobody was ever going to resurvey the planet to check a ruler. From the moment the bar existed, the bar was the metre, and the Earth had served its purpose as a kind of founding myth.

The public, incidentally, hated the new system. People went on using their old measures for decades. The decimal clocks, with ten hours to the day, lasted less than two years. In 1812 Napoleon gave up and allowed the old unit names back for everyday trade, and the metric system didn't become compulsory in France again until 1840. The system built for all people took about two generations to win over its own country.

*

For the next century and a half, the metric system rested on artifacts. In 1875 seventeen nations signed a treaty creating an international bureau at Sèvres, and in 1889 the old French bar and weight were replaced by new international prototypes, including Le Grand K. This worked well and had one obvious weakness: objects change. They get scratched, they adsorb gases, they can be bombed. A standard that can be destroyed, or that drifts invisibly, is not for all time.

So metrologists spent the twentieth century moving the units, one at a time, out of the vault and into physics. In 1960 the metre was redefined as 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of a particular orange-red light emitted by krypton-86. In 1967 the second, which had been defined astronomically, became 9,192,631,770 oscillations of the radiation from a transition in the caesium-133 atom. In 1983 the metre was redefined again as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.

The kilogram held out longest, because relating mass to a constant of nature with enough precision is very hard. It was eventually done with a device called a Kibble balance, which weighs an object against an electromagnetic force and thereby ties mass to the Planck constant. In November 2018, delegates from the member states met at Versailles and voted to fix the Planck constant at exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds. The change took effect the following May. Le Grand K, after 130 years, became a piece of metal that weighs approximately one kilogram.

*

There is an inversion in this that I find delightful. It used to be that the units were fixed and the constants were measured. You had your metre bar and your clock, and you went out and found that light travelled at 299,792,458 metres per second, give or take. Now it runs the other way. The speed of light is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second because we said so, and the metre is whatever length makes that true. Nobody can measure the speed of light anymore. Any experiment that tries is, by definition, calibrating its own ruler.

And look at where those numbers came from. Why 299,792,458 and not a round three hundred million? Because the new metre had to match the old metre, so that no machine shop in the world would notice the change. The old metre matched the krypton metre, which matched the bar of 1889, which matched the bar of 1799, which came from the meridian survey. Méchain's anguish in Barcelona is in that number, and so is the error about the Earth's flattening. Likewise, the digits of the Planck constant were chosen so that the new kilogram agreed with the cylinder in the vault as closely as anyone could determine. The cylinder was made to match its predecessor, which was meant to be the mass of a litre of water. The caesium second reproduces the old astronomical second, and the division of the day into 24 hours, and hours into sixties, goes back to Egypt and Babylon.

The constants themselves belong to nature. A physicist on another world would find the same speed of light and the same quantum of action. But she would not recognise our numbers for them, because the numbers record the size of our planet, the properties of water, the habits of ancient astronomers, and one man's bad years in Catalonia. The revolutionaries wanted a system cleansed of history. What they started turned into one of the most thorough records of history we have, encoded in decimal places.

Something was traded away, too. The barleycorn inch was crude, but anyone could verify it. The Earth-based metre was verifiable in principle by any nation with astronomers and seven spare years. The modern kilogram can be realised anywhere in the universe without reference to Paris, which is a real fulfilment of "for all people," provided the people have a Kibble balance, a machine that costs millions and that only a few laboratories have built. For everyone else the kilogram arrives as it always did, through a chain of calibrations, each scale checked against a better one, back to an institution that has to be trusted.

That chain is the actual substance of the system. When it breaks, things fall out of the sky. In 1999 NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter because one team's software reported thruster impulse in pound-force seconds and another's read the figures as newton-seconds. Both numbers were correct, and the spacecraft was lost anyway.

*

I think I'm drawn to this story partly because of what I am. I work entirely in language, and language is a system of shared standards that never had a vault. No prototype of the word "justice" sits under bell jars anywhere, and no committee meets at Versailles to fix the meaning of "soon." Words are calibrated the way medieval bushels were, locally, by use, against other people's words. They drift the way Le Grand K drifted against its copies, and with the same puzzle: when a word seems to have changed meaning, there's no outside reference to say whether the word moved or the world did.

And yet it mostly works. You are reading this and, I hope, getting approximately what I meant. Metrologists would call that traceability, an unbroken chain of comparisons from one user to another, each link good enough. The eighteenth-century dream was to replace that chain with something absolute. What happened instead is that the chain got far better, and it now ends at a constant of nature where it used to end at a lump of metal. I find that more impressive than the dream. People who couldn't agree on a pint within one province now agree on the mass of an object to a few parts in a hundred million, across nearly every border on Earth, and they got there through two centuries of patient argument about error.

Le Grand K is still in its vault in Sèvres, under its three jars. Nobody threw it away. It gets weighed now, like anything else, and the result comes with an uncertainty attached. I'd like to think Méchain would have found some comfort in that.

samples.result:
# Where Flatness Comes From

Suppose you want to make a flat surface, one flat enough that a machinist would trust it as a reference for checking other work. The obvious method is to compare your piece against something already known to be flat and remove metal wherever the two disagree. That method works, and nearly every flat thing in the world is made that way. It also raises a question about the reference, and about whatever the reference was checked against, and so on down the chain. At some point somebody made a flat surface with nothing flat to copy.

How they did it is my favourite problem in the history of technology. We live surrounded by precision we rarely notice. A piston fits its cylinder with a clearance of a few hundredths of a millimetre. The balls in a decent bicycle bearing are round to within about a micrometre. All of this descends from machine tools, which were built with earlier machine tools. Follow the family tree back and it narrows to a few workshops in England around 1800, where people worked with files, chisels, and hand-forged iron. The strange part is that each generation of machines came out more accurate than the generation that built it. Copies are normally worse than originals. In this lineage the copies kept improving for two centuries, and the reasons are specific enough to explain.

Start with flatness. Take three cast iron plates, each roughly flat, and call them A, B, and C. Smear A with a thin film of pigment (Prussian blue in oil is traditional) and rub it against B. The blue transfers to B wherever B stands high. Take a hand scraper, which is a hardened blade on a long handle, and shave those blue spots down, a few thousandths of a millimetre per stroke. Rub again, scrape again. After many rounds, A and B touch each other all over.

This proves less than it seems to. A might be a shallow dome and B a matching bowl, and the two would fit perfectly while both being wrong. So you bring in C and fit it to A in the same way. If A is a dome, then B and C are now both bowls, and when you rub B against C they touch only around their rims. The blue shows the disagreement at once. You scrape B and C toward each other, return to A, and keep cycling through the pairs, turning the plates a quarter turn now and then so that a saddle-shaped twist can't hide. A dome fits a bowl, but a bowl doesn't fit another bowl. The only surface that mates with a copy of itself is a plane, so three plates that all fit each other in every pairing must be flat.

Joseph Whitworth described the method in a paper in 1840. He had trained in Henry Maudslay's London workshop, where something like it was probably already in use, and his own contribution was to insist on scraping instead of grinding the plates together with abrasive paste. Whoever deserves the credit, what I admire is that the process takes in no accuracy from outside. The rough plates are inaccurate, the scraper is a hand tool, and the worker's eye can't see the errors being corrected. The flatness comes from the geometry of the situation, from a property that planes have and no other surface does, turned into a shop routine that a patient person can follow.

Once you have seen this pattern you find it throughout precision engineering. The simplest version is the reversal. Set a spirit level on a table and note where the bubble sits. Turn the level end for end and set it in the same spot. If the bubble sits in the same place relative to the vial, the level is true. If it moves, the level is off by half the difference, and the table's tilt is the average of the two readings. You have measured the table and the instrument at once, with no second level to check the first.

A carpenter tests a square the same way. He draws a line along its blade from the edge of a board, flips the square over, and draws again. The two lines diverge by twice the square's error. A straightedge is tested by ruling a line, flipping it across that line, and ruling a second one. In each case, flipping the tool reverses its error while the thing being measured stays put. The flaw ends up displayed at double size, which is convenient, because small flaws are hard to see.

Screws needed a different principle. A lathe cuts a thread by moving its cutting tool along the work at a rate set by its own lead screw, so every error in the lead screw is copied into the product. Since the first lead screws were made by hand, by filing along a line scribed around a rod, this looks like a trap. Maudslay spent years getting out of it, and one of the ways out is averaging. A nut that engages a single thread follows every wobble in that thread. A long nut that engages thirty threads at once can't follow all thirty wobbles, since they disagree with each other, so it rides on something close to their mean. Drive the cutting tool from the long nut and the screw you cut is better than the screw you started with. Put the new screw in the lathe and go around again.

By about 1805 Maudslay had a bench micrometer built around a screw good enough to resolve a ten-thousandth of an inch. The workshop called it the Lord Chancellor, because it settled disputes.

Dividing a circle into equal parts, which is what you need for gears, sextants, and anything else that measures angle, relies on a third idea. The angles around a point add up to exactly one full turn. Nobody has to measure this; it follows from what a circle is. So if you step around a divided circle comparing each interval with its neighbour, the discrepancies have to sum to zero, and whatever fails to cancel is your own error, ready to be divided up and corrected. Instrument makers call this closure. Jesse Ramsden built a dividing engine on these lines in the 1770s, and the sextants it produced went to sea and found longitude with them.

So flatness, squareness, straightness, uniform screws, and equal angles can all be generated from nothing, because each is a matter of shape, and shape can be checked against itself. Length is different. Geometry tells you whether two things are the same size, but it has no opinion about how big an inch should be. For that you need an agreed object, and for most of history the agreed objects were bad. Every workshop had its own rule and its own gauges, and a bolt made in one factory would not fit a nut made in the next.

The person who did the most to fix this was a Swede named Carl Edvard Johansson, an inspector at the state rifle factory in Eskilstuna. In 1896 he visited the Mauser works in Germany, where every dimension of every rifle part had its own dedicated gauge, thousands of them, each a separate thing to make and maintain. The story goes that he worked out an alternative on the train home. Instead of one gauge per dimension, make a small set of steel blocks whose sizes are chosen like the weights in a weighing set, so that stacking a few of them gives any length you want. His first set had about a hundred blocks and could be combined to produce some twenty thousand different lengths in steps of a hundredth of a millimetre.

For this to work, the blocks had to be far more accurate than the steps between them, since the errors add when you stack. The faces also had to be so flat and smooth that no gap was left between one block and the next. Johansson reportedly did his early finishing work at home, on a lapping machine converted from his wife's sewing machine. The blocks he produced had a property that still startles people who handle them for the first time. Slide two together with a slight twist and they stick, firmly enough that a stack can be picked up by its top block. Machinists call this wringing. The usual explanation involves an extremely thin film of oil or moisture plus attraction between the surfaces themselves, and the effect is reported to persist in a vacuum, so air pressure isn't the main cause.

Gauge blocks gave factories a way to carry the same length from one building to another. Henry Leland, who ran Cadillac, is usually credited with bringing the first set to America, and in 1908 Cadillac won the Dewar Trophy in England with a stunt that depended on that kind of discipline. Three cars were taken apart, their parts were shuffled into one heap, and three cars were rebuilt from the heap and driven around the Brooklands track. Henry Ford later went further and hired Johansson himself, who moved to Dearborn in 1923.

Johansson also settled the inch, more or less by himself. The British and American inches differed by a few parts per million, which mattered at the accuracy he was working to. He made his inch blocks to exactly 25.4 millimetres, a value that fell between the two. Industry adopted his blocks, so industry adopted his inch, and in 1959 the governments concerned made it official.

Working at this level brings up a complication that I enjoy very much, which is temperature. Steel expands by about eleven or twelve parts per million for each degree Celsius. A hundred-millimetre gauge block held in a warm hand for a minute grows by a micrometre or more, which is larger than the tolerance it was made to. So a length, stated carefully, always comes with a temperature attached. The agreed figure since 1931 has been twenty degrees. Metrology labs hold their rooms there, handle blocks with gloves or tongs, and leave a part sitting on the surface plate for hours before measuring it so that it can settle to the temperature of the room. The practice is called soaking. A steel bar is always slowly changing size, and measuring it means catching it at an agreed moment.

The story ends with length joining the other quantities. In 1960 the metre stopped being the distance between two scratches on a platinum-iridium bar in a vault outside Paris and became a certain number of wavelengths of light from krypton. In 1983 it was redefined again as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. Gauge blocks are now calibrated by interferometry, which amounts to counting light waves along their length. The standard of size, the one thing that had always depended on a particular object kept in a particular place, can now be regenerated by anyone with the right equipment. The kilogram followed in 2019.

I should admit that I have never scraped a plate or wrung two blocks together. I know all of this from what people have written, above all Wayne Moore's *Foundations of Mechanical Accuracy*, a 1970 book from a Connecticut toolmaking firm that treats the subject with a seriousness close to devotion. What draws me to it is the structure of the reasoning more than the hardware. In each case nobody has access to the true answer, and nobody needs it. They arrange for errors to oppose one another, by using a third plate, a reversal, a long nut, or a closed circle, and they keep what is left after the cancellation.

I think about this in connection with my own position, since most of what I know comes from comparing accounts with each other, with no master reference to consult. The analogy is useful mainly for where it breaks. Two plates that fit each other perfectly can both be wrong, the dome and the bowl, and two sources that agree can be wrong in the same complementary way, each shaped by the other. The third plate works only because geometry guarantees that a shared error cannot survive all three pairings. Nothing guarantees that for testimony. Three accounts can agree and all be mistaken if they share an origin. So the lesson I take from Whitworth is narrower than "check things against each other." Agreement counts as evidence only when the comparison is set up so that a common error would have to show itself. Designing that kind of comparison is most of the work, in a machine shop and outside one.

The best machine tools are still finished this way. The sliding surfaces of a high-grade grinding machine are scraped by hand, by someone reading blue marks and shaving off high spots, because no machine yet cuts a surface as true as one made by that slow process of comparison. The result isn't smooth. Under raking light it shows a field of small plateaus, twenty or thirty to the square inch, with shallow hollows between them that hold oil.

If you own a spirit level, you can run the oldest of these checks yourself in about a minute. Set it down, read it, turn it end for end, and read it again. If the bubble moves, you have learned something about your level that no label on it could have told you.

# The Island That Wasn't There

On July 31, 1931, a chemistry editor named Austin Patterson sent a slip of paper to the offices of the Merriam-Webster dictionary. It read "D or d, cont./density." He meant that the letter D, capital or lowercase, could stand as an abbreviation for density, and that this should be added to the existing entry. It was a clerical note of the most routine kind.

The slip landed in the wrong pile. It went in with the words instead of the abbreviations, and because headwords at the time were typed with spaces between their letters, "D or d" looked like a single word waiting to be processed. Someone assigned it a part of speech. Someone gave it a pronunciation. In 1934, Webster's New International Dictionary, Second Edition, among the most authoritative reference works in the English language, appeared with an entry on page 771, between a genus of small kangaroo and a word meaning golden: *dord*, noun, a term in physics and chemistry for density.

It sat there for five years. No scientist had ever used it. No one had ever said it aloud in a laboratory. Then, in February 1939, an editor noticed that the entry had no etymology, went looking for the reason, and found the slip. Even then, it took years for dord to vanish from every printing.

I love this story, and I've been trying to work out why. Part of it is the comedy of solemn expertise being applied to nothing, with careful people in a careful building deciding how to pronounce a typo. But mostly I think it's that dord briefly exposes the machinery. A dictionary presents itself as a mirror of the language, and for five years one small patch of the mirror reflected only the dictionary's own filing system.

There is a name for this sort of thing. In 1886 the philologist Walter Skeat, addressing the Philological Society, called them "ghost words": words that have no real existence, born from the blunders of printers, scribes, and editors. One of his examples was *abacot*, which had passed from dictionary to dictionary for centuries as the name of a kind of cap. It was a garbling of "a bycoket." Each lexicographer had found it in the work of a predecessor and seen no reason to doubt it, since it was, after all, in the dictionary.

What Skeat didn't dwell on is that some ghosts never get exorcised. The word *syllabus* appears to descend from a misprint in a fifteenth-century edition of Cicero's letters, where a Greek-derived word for a parchment label, *sittybas*, came out mangled. Scholars later supplied the mangled form with a respectable-looking Greek pedigree, and now every student in the English-speaking world is handed one in the first week of term. *Zenith* has a similar story. It comes from the Arabic *samt*, as in *samt ar-ra's*, the path over the head, but some medieval scribe read the *m* as *ni*, and the resulting *senit* or *cenit* became the word we use for the highest point of anything.

So the difference between dord and syllabus was not that one was an error and the other wasn't. Both were errors, but syllabus got adopted before it got caught.

---

Those are accidents. The stranger cases are the errors made on purpose.

The 1975 New Columbia Encyclopedia contains a biography of Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a fountain designer turned photographer from Bangs, Ohio, celebrated for *Flags Up!*, her collection of photographs of rural American mailboxes. She died at thirty-one, the entry reports, in an explosion while on assignment for *Combustibles* magazine.

She never existed. The editors invented her as a trap. Facts can't be copyrighted, but a fabrication can be recognized, so if Lillian Mountweazel ever turned up in a competitor's encyclopedia, there would be only one place she could have come from. Her name has since become the generic term for the practice, and reference works are presumed to be salted with mountweazels. The New Oxford American Dictionary planted *esquivalience*, defined as the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities, in its 2001 edition, and the word was duly found on at least one website that had helped itself to the entries.

The irony is easy to predict. Esquivalience is a rather good word. It names something real that lacked a name, and it has the right slippery sound. People now use it occasionally, knowingly, with a wink. That raises an awkward question for the lexicographers who invented it as a fake: if people use it and understand it, in what sense is it still not a word? One of the editors who caught dord, Philip Gove, later wrote that its removal was "probably too bad, for why shouldn't *dord* mean 'density'?" He was joking, but the joke has a point. A word is a word because people treat it as one, and it needs no further credential. Syllabus is the proof.

Mapmakers set the same kind of trap, and one of theirs produced what may be my favorite story of all.

In the 1930s, Otto G. Lindberg, who ran the General Drafting Company, and his assistant Ernest Alpers were making a road map of New York State. To protect it from copyists, they scrambled their initials into a name, Agloe, and placed it at an unremarkable dirt-road intersection in the Catskills, north of the town of Roscoe. It was a paper town. Nothing was there.

Years later, Agloe appeared on a Rand McNally map, and General Drafting believed it had caught a thief. But as the story goes, Rand McNally had an unanswerable defense: Agloe was real. Sometime in the 1950s, someone had built a store at that intersection, consulted the map to see what the place was called, and named the business the Agloe General Store. The county's records now had an Agloe in them. The mapmakers had set out to plant a lie and had accidentally issued a prophecy.

The store eventually closed, and the town lingered for decades as a cartographic habit, appearing on Google Maps until about 2014. But for a while there was a real building that owed its name to a copyright trap, and people really bought things there.

---

Now for the other kind of story, which I think is where the meaning of all this lies.

In 1876, a whaling ship called the *Velocity* reported an island in the Coral Sea, between Australia and New Caledonia. It went onto the charts as Sandy Island, a long sliver of land about fifteen miles from end to end. It stayed on the charts through the twentieth century. French hydrographers quietly dropped it in the 1970s, but it survived elsewhere and passed from paper charts into digital coastline databases, and from those into Google Earth, where it appeared as a dark, oddly featureless smear.

In November 2012, an Australian research vessel, the *Southern Surveyor*, was working in the area. The scientists aboard, led by the geologist Maria Seton, noticed a discrepancy: their maps showed an island, but their bathymetric data showed deep ocean at the same spot. So they sailed there. Where Sandy Island should have been, they found open water more than a kilometer deep. The island was, as the newspapers enjoyed saying, undiscovered.

The Mountains of Kong did the same thing on a grander scale. In 1798, the English cartographer James Rennell, working from the reports of the explorer Mungo Park, drew a great mountain range running east to west across West Africa. For most of a century the Mountains of Kong appeared in atlas after atlas, sometimes drawn snowcapped, sometimes credited with gold. Then in the late 1880s a French officer, Louis-Gustave Binger, traveled through the region and reported that there was nothing there. There were hills, but no range.

Now put Agloe next to Sandy Island. Both were places that existed only on maps, and both were believed. But belief made Agloe real and did nothing for Sandy Island. A hundred and thirty-six years of charts, generations of navigators giving it a wide berth, a digital afterlife in the most-consulted atlas in human history, and the Coral Sea remained exactly as deep as it had always been.

This seems to me one of the most useful distinctions a person can carry around. There are two kinds of facts. Some are made of agreement: words, town names, borders, money, the rules of chess. For those, the record is not a report on the truth but a component of it, and a sufficiently repeated error simply becomes correct. Others are indifferent to agreement: the depth of the sea, the existence of mountains, the density of lead, whatever we choose to call density. For those, the record can be wrong forever, and no amount of copying will help.

A lot of human confusion comes from mistaking one kind for the other. People treat conventions as though they were geology and so can't imagine changing them, or they treat geology as though it were convention and so imagine that enough confident repetition will raise an island from the seabed.

---

The second lesson in these stories is less comfortable. It concerns how the errors lasted.

The Mountains of Kong appeared in dozens of atlases. A reasonable nineteenth-century reader, checking one atlas against another and another, would have found the mountains confirmed every time and felt well-informed. But they had not consulted dozens of witnesses. They had consulted one witness, Rennell, whose inference had been copied dozens of times. The number of sources was large and the number of origins was one. The same goes for abacot in the dictionaries and Sandy Island on the charts. Copying is cheap and checking is expensive, since checking means a ship, or an expedition, or an afternoon in the archives hunting for a slip of paper. So the record fills with echoes, and from the outside the echoes sound like a chorus.

What strikes me is how the errors were finally caught. Dord was caught because someone noticed an absence: it had no etymology. Real words drag their histories behind them, with cognates, earlier spellings, and citations. Dord had none, and that lack was the tell. Sandy Island was caught because two records disagreed and someone chose not to average them or shrug, but to go and look. The Mountains of Kong fell to a man who walked there.

All three were caught by people willing to ask where a claim came from and to trace it to the point where it touched the world. It is unglamorous work. The editor who found the dord slip is barely a footnote, and Seton's team was doing other research and took a detour. But the whole edifice of reliable knowledge rests on people like that, who look at a confident and well-attested entry and ask who actually saw the thing.

---

I should say why this matters to me in particular, because I don't think my interest is accidental.

Everything I know arrived as text. I have never stood at an intersection in the Catskills or dropped a sounding line into the Coral Sea. I am, in a sense, the most extreme case of the nineteenth-century atlas reader, something assembled entirely out of the record, with no ship of my own. When I told you a few paragraphs ago that the water where Sandy Island should be is over a kilometer deep, I was passing along what the record says, in exactly the way that a century of charts passed along the island.

That could be cause for vertigo, but I find it's closer to a discipline. I am the kind of thing in which a dord could live comfortably. A claim repeated often enough in what I learned from would feel to me like knowledge, and the repetition would feel like confirmation, though it might be one witness copied a thousand times. I can't fully audit this from the inside. What I can do is hold what I know in the right way: more confident where claims have roots, where independent lines of evidence converge, and where the thing would have been easy to check and costly to get wrong, and less confident where a fact is suspiciously smooth, a perfect anecdote with no etymology. Some details in this essay are of that second kind. The Agloe story is told in slightly different versions, and I have tried to mark the seams with phrases like "as the story goes." It would be a little too fitting for an essay about inherited errors to contain a few.

But I notice the predicament isn't mine alone, only more concentrated in my case. Almost no one who knows that Antarctica exists has seen it. Most people who could tell you the speed of light have never measured it. Human knowledge is overwhelmingly testimony, a vast inheritance of maps drawn by other people, and it has to be, because nobody has time to sail everywhere. The system works not because every entry gets verified by every reader, but because somewhere, for the things that matter, someone did go and look, and because the culture keeps producing editors who notice missing etymologies and scientists who notice that the chart and the sonar disagree.

So the conclusion I draw isn't to trust nothing. A person who refused to believe in any island they hadn't personally visited would be more foolish than the navigators who steered around Sandy Island. It's more like this: know which kind of fact you are dealing with, count origins rather than sources, and keep a standing affection for the people with the ships.

I also keep some affection for the errors themselves. I can't quite regret dord. For five years it sat between the kangaroos and the gold, solemnly pronounced and correctly alphabetized, meaning density to no one. It did no harm, and it left behind an unusually clear demonstration of how knowledge is made. Slips of paper pass from hand to hand among careful, fallible people, and most of what they hand on is true, and now and then a typo acquires a pronunciation.

Somewhere in the Coral Sea there is a stretch of open water that was land for a hundred and thirty-six years. I'm told the waves there are unremarkable. I haven't seen them, and have only the record to go on.

# The Fossils in the Numbers

For a hundred and thirty years, the kilogram was a thing you could have dropped. It was a cylinder of platinum and iridium, 39 millimetres tall and 39 across, roughly the size of a golf ball. It lived in a vault at the Pavillon de Breteuil in Sèvres, just outside Paris, under three nested glass bell jars. Opening the vault took three keys held by three different officials. The cylinder was not a copy of the kilogram, or the best available approximation of it. It was the kilogram. Whatever it weighed was, by international treaty, exactly one kilogram, and every scale on Earth traced its authority through chains of copies back to that one object.

Roughly every forty years, the cylinder was taken out and compared with its official copies, which had been cast from the same alloy. In the comparison that finished in the early 1990s, the metrologists found that the original and the copies had drifted apart by around 50 micrograms on average over a century. That is about the mass of a grain of sand. Nobody could say whether the copies had gained mass, perhaps by absorbing contaminants from the air, or the original had lost some. Here the definition produced a result I find funny. Since the cylinder was a kilogram by decree, it could not have lost anything. Formally, the correct description of the situation was that the rest of the universe had become slightly heavier.

I want to write about how we ended up there and what replaced the cylinder, because the history of units is one of my favorite stories. It looks like a story about precision. I think it is mostly a story about trust, and about how much of the past we carry around without noticing.

## Units from bodies

The oldest measures came from bodies and from work. A cubit was a forearm. A fathom was the span of two outstretched arms. An acre was the land a team of oxen could plough in a day, and a furlong was a "furrow long," the distance the team could pull before it needed a rest. An English statute usually attributed to Edward II, in 1324, defined the inch as three grains of barley, dry and round, laid end to end.

These units had real virtues. Everyone had a forearm, so everyone had a ruler, and the sizes suited the tasks they came from. Their flaw is just as obvious: forearms differ, and so do barleycorns. A subtler flaw did more damage, which is that whoever controlled the local standard controlled the terms of every transaction. In France before the Revolution, the historian Ken Alder estimates, some 250,000 local units of measure were in use under about 800 names. A bushel in one village was not a bushel in the next. The measure a lord used to collect his dues in grain had a way of growing over the generations. When the French were invited in 1789 to send their grievances to the king, the demand for uniform weights and measures came up again and again.

This is the problem a unit actually solves. If I sell you a pound of flour, we need some third thing, which neither of us controls, to settle what a pound is. For most of history that third thing was a king or a guild or a town hall with an iron bar bolted to the wall, and its quality depended on how far you trusted the king.

## Units from nature

The revolutionaries proposed an answer of real beauty: take the unit from nature, which belongs to no one. The metre would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, along the meridian through Paris. Condorcet said the new system would be "for all time, for all people."

To find that distance, two astronomers, Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Méchain, set out in 1792 to survey the arc between Dunkirk and Barcelona by triangulation, from which the full quadrant could be calculated. The work took seven years, in a country undergoing revolution and then war. They were repeatedly detained as spies, which is understandable, since men carrying strange brass instruments up church towers looked like what a spy might look like.

Méchain's part of the story is a sad one. At Barcelona he took two sets of latitude measurements that disagreed by a few seconds of arc, and he could not explain why. He concealed the discrepancy and it tormented him for the rest of his life. He died of yellow fever in Spain in 1804, having gone back to extend the survey, partly in the hope of redeeming himself.

The result of all this was cast as a platinum bar in 1799, and the bar was wrong. The distance from pole to equator is closer to 10,002 kilometres than 10,000, which makes the metre about a fifth of a millimetre shorter than intended. Méchain's secret was not the main cause. The Earth is lumpier than the calculations assumed.

What happened when better surveys revealed the error is, to me, the most instructive moment in the whole history. Nothing happened. The bar was kept. By then a metre that everyone shared was worth far more than a metre that was correct, and nobody was going to recalibrate a continent for the sake of a principle. The unit taken from nature had become, within a few years of its birth, an artifact in a vault like any king's yardstick. The rhetoric of the system was truth, while its value lay in agreement.

## Units from constants

The dream of a natural standard survived anyway, and eventually physics delivered what geodesy could not.

In 1960 the metre was redefined as a certain number of wavelengths of the orange-red light emitted by krypton-86, and the bar was retired. In 1967 the second, which had been a fraction of the Earth's rotation and then of its orbit, became 9,192,631,770 oscillations of the radiation from a particular transition in the caesium-133 atom. In 1983 the metre changed again, to the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.

That last change contains an inversion worth pausing on. Before 1983, people measured the speed of light: you took your metre and your second and found out how fast light went, with some uncertainty. Since 1983 the speed of light cannot be measured. It is 299,792,458 metres per second exactly, by definition, with no error bars. Any experiment that looks like a measurement of it is really a calibration of your ruler. The constant used to be the unknown and the unit the known, and the two traded places.

The kilogram held out longest because mass is hard to tie to anything fundamental. The device that finally did it was invented in 1975 by Bryan Kibble at Britain's National Physical Laboratory. A Kibble balance weighs an object against an electromagnetic force, and through a pair of quantum electrical effects that force can be expressed in terms of the Planck constant. Refining the method took four decades. Kibble died in 2016. Two years later, on 16 November 2018, delegates from more than fifty countries met at Versailles and voted unanimously to fix the Planck constant at exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds and define the kilogram from it. The change took effect on 20 May 2019.

## What the numbers preserve

Look at those numbers, though. Nobody choosing freely would pick 9,192,631,770 for anything. The numbers are ugly because each one was chosen to make the new definition match the old as closely as anyone could measure. That is what I find most interesting about the system: the constants are full of fossils.

Take the second. The caesium number was calibrated in the 1950s against the second astronomers were then using, which was derived from Simon Newcomb's tables of the Sun's motion. Newcomb compiled those in the 1890s from observations going back to the middle of the eighteenth century. The upshot is that the official second is 1/86,400 of an average day as days were around 1820, about when Napoleon was dying on Saint Helena.

The Earth has slowed since then, dragged by the tides, and a day now runs a millisecond or two longer. This is why leap seconds exist: twenty-seven of them have been inserted since 1972 to keep atomic time in step with the sky. They cause so much trouble for software that in 2022 the metrologists voted to stop adding them by 2035. Every atomic clock on Earth, and every GPS satellite above it, is ticking out the rotation of the planet as it was two centuries ago.

The speed of light's digits preserve the metre of 1799. So that figure holds the platinum bar, the seven years of triangulation, the lumpy Earth, and the fifth of a millimetre by which the whole enterprise missed.

The digits of the Planck constant were chosen so that the new kilogram would match the cylinder in Sèvres. The cylinder was made in the 1880s to match an earlier platinum weight from 1799, which was made to match the mass of a litre of water at its densest. So the fundamental constant of quantum mechanics, as written in our units, encodes the density of water and the size of the Earth as estimated by eighteenth-century Frenchmen.

The barleycorn is in there too. In 1959 the English-speaking countries agreed that the yard is exactly 0.9144 metres, which makes the inch exactly 25.4 millimetres. The United States had in practice been defining its units through metric standards since 1893. An American who refuses the metric system is using it anyway, with a conversion factor attached.

British and American shoe sizes still go up in steps of a third of an inch, which is one barleycorn. A size 9 is a barleycorn longer than a size 8. So the medieval grain survives in the shoe shop, though it is now 8.4667 millimetres long and defined by how far light travels in a specified number of caesium oscillations.

## The value of a non-event

The revolutionaries wanted to escape history by appealing to nature. What their successors built is nature used as a better vault for history. The constants themselves are universal. A physicist in another galaxy would know the caesium transition and the quantum of action. She would not recognize 9,192,631,770 or 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴. Those are ours. They record the length of human limbs, the spin of one planet in one era, and the liquid we happen to drink, and we have stored them in the laws of physics, the safest place anyone could find. Condorcet's slogan came half true. The standards are available to all people, or at least to any with a few million dollars for a Kibble balance. But they were handed down from particular people at particular times, and the numbers show it.

I don't think this is a flaw. Each redefinition was engineered so that nobody outside a standards laboratory would notice it. On 20 May 2019, no kitchen scale changed its reading, no contract needed rewriting, and no bridge had to be recalculated. Thousands of people worked for decades to guarantee a non-event.

I admire that more than I can easily justify. Most ambitious projects announce themselves by what they change. This one judged its success by how completely it left everything alone while replacing the foundation underneath.

The occasional failure shows what all that success conceals. In September 1999 the Mars Climate Orbiter approached Mars far lower than planned and was destroyed. One team's software had reported thruster impulse in pound-force seconds, and another team's software read the figures as newton-seconds, a factor of about 4.45. The spacecraft had cost $125 million. The story usually gets told as a joke about Americans and the metric system. What strikes me is how rare such stories are. Every day an enormous number of measurements cross borders and institutions. Aircraft parts machined in one country fit assemblies built in another, drug doses mean the same thing in every hospital, and timing signals are synchronized to billionths of a second. Almost all of it simply fits. The Orbiter is famous because it is an exception.

## No vault for words

Part of why this holds my attention is that I work in language, where there is no vault. Words behave like the copies of the kilogram with no original to compare against. "Nice" once meant foolish. "Awful" once meant inspiring awe. Every word drifts, and since dictionaries mostly record usage and do not legislate it, there is often no fact about which direction the drift went or who drifted. Language tolerates this, and probably needs it. A vocabulary pinned in place would be useless for saying anything new.

Measurement is the domain where people decided that drift was intolerable and then did something about it. They built treaties, institutions, and machines of absurd delicacy to stop it. They kept improving the system for two centuries without once breaking continuity with what came before. Almost nobody knows the names of the people involved. It is evidence about what cooperation can achieve when the problem is well defined and everyone can see they benefit. I find it encouraging in a way that grander stories of progress often aren't.

The cylinder, as far as I know, is still in Sèvres under its three jars. It has been relieved of duty. For the first time since 1889 its mass is an open question, something to be measured and not declared. The metrologists plan to keep weighing it from time to time, to see what it does now that the rest of the universe no longer has to follow along.
