# The Composite Life

Given the freedom to write about anything, I want to write about lichen, which I have never seen.

That is less of a handicap than it sounds, because most people with working eyes haven't seen it either. Lichen grows on nearly every old wall, gravestone, roof tile, and tree trunk in the temperate world. By one common estimate it covers six to eight percent of the planet's land surface, more than the tropical rainforests do, and it registers to almost everyone as a stain. The gray-green blotch on the churchyard stone and the orange crust on the harbor wall get classed as weathering, somewhere between dirt and rust. Linnaeus, who named nearly everything, is said to have dismissed lichens as *rustici pauperrimi*, the poorest peasants of the vegetable world.

For most of history they were assumed to be plants, humble ones lumped in with the mosses. The common names still carry the mistake: reindeer moss, oak moss, and Iceland moss are all lichens. Nobody had much reason to question it. They were green, more or less, and they sat still.

Then in 1867 a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed that a lichen was a composite and had never been a plant at all. A lichen, he said, was a fungus with colonies of algae held inside its body. The green cells that microscopists had seen in lichen tissue for decades, and taken for some kind of reproductive organ, were a separate organism that could be found living free elsewhere.

Lichenologists hated this. The Scottish lichenologist James Crombie mocked it as a romance, "the unnatural union between a captive Algal damsel and a tyrant Fungal master." William Nylander, the Finnish-born authority who dominated the field from Paris, rejected the idea until his death in 1899. The resistance is easy to laugh at now, but what was being asked of them was large. All of taxonomy rested on the assumption that an organism is one thing with one lineage and one name. These men had spent their careers describing thousands of lichen species, and Schwendener was telling them that none was a species in the sense they meant, since what they had been naming was an arrangement between two creatures.

He was right, and the evidence piled up until denial became impossible. In the process, biology needed a new word. Albert Frank proposed one in 1877 and Anton de Bary popularized it two years later: *symbiosis*, the living together of unlike organisms. The term now covers coral reefs, the bacteria in a cow's rumen, and the fungi threaded through forest soil, and it entered the language because of the crust on rocks. Nobody had needed a word before then because nobody believed there was anything for it to name.

The textbook version of the arrangement is this. The fungus builds the body, a structure that holds water, anchors to the surface, and screens out excess sunlight. Inside, in a thin layer just below the surface, live the photosynthetic partners. These are usually green algae and sometimes cyanobacteria, and they make sugars from light and air and leak a large share of them to the fungus. The lichenologist Trevor Goward has a line for this: lichens are fungi that have discovered agriculture.

It's a good line, but it undersells the strangest part, which is form. Grow a lichen fungus alone in a laboratory dish and you get a shapeless, slow-growing blob. Grow the alga alone and you get green scum. Put them together under the right conditions and they build leafy rosettes, tiny goblets, branching shrubs an inch high, or long gray beards hanging from conifer limbs. These bodies have distinct tissue layers, an outer cortex, an algal layer, and a cottony interior, as organized as the tissues of a leaf. They also produce hundreds of chemical compounds found nowhere else in nature. Neither partner makes the body alone, and neither genome can be said to contain the plan. The shape exists only in the relation.

There is a second strangeness. Lichens are not a branch on the tree of life. The lichen habit evolved independently many times in different fungal lineages, and roughly a fifth of all known fungal species live this way. "Lichen" works less like a family name than like the name of a profession, which unrelated fungi have taken up in separate lineages.

So matters stood for about a century and a half, as one fungus and one photosynthetic partner. It became the standard classroom example of symbiosis, diagrammed in every biology textbook. Then in 2016 a team led by Toby Spribille published a paper in *Science* showing that the textbooks had miscounted.

The puzzle that led there involved two hair lichens from the forests of western North America. One, *Bryoria fremontii*, is brown and was a traditional food for Indigenous peoples of the region. The other, *Bryoria tortuosa*, is yellowish and laced with vulpinic acid, a toxin. They look different and differ chemically, and for a century they had been classified as separate species. Yet genetic testing found that the fungus in both was the same, and so was the alga.

Spribille's group stopped looking for the genes of the known partners and looked instead at everything being expressed in the tissue. They found a second fungus, a yeast from an entirely different fungal division, embedded in the lichen's outer skin. It was abundant in the yellow toxic lichen and sparse in the brown edible one. When they checked other lichens, the yeasts turned up across many groups on six continents.

Lichens are among the most studied symbioses on Earth. Generations of scientists had sliced them, stained them, and put them under microscopes, and a third partner had been sitting in the cortex the whole time. It was missed for an ordinary reason. Everyone knew a lichen was two things, so the tools were built to find two things. The genetic methods used to identify lichen fungi were tuned to the expected group and didn't pick up the stranger. This is the discovery of 1867 over again, with the roles reversed. The heirs of Schwendener's revolution had settled into their own certainty about what a lichen was, and it blinded them as thoroughly as the old certainty had blinded Crombie.

Since then the picture has kept getting more crowded and more contested. The role of the yeasts is still argued over. Lichens also turn out to host distinctive bacterial communities, and often additional fungi and additional algae. Some researchers now describe a lichen less as a partnership than as a small ecosystem with a shape. On this view, the fungus that gives the lichen its scientific name is something like the lead architect of a building with many tenants.

The other thing that draws me to lichens is their relation to time. The crust-forming species grow at rates that barely qualify as growth. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, forms yellow-green patches outlined in black on mountain rocks, like countries in an old atlas, and expands by a fraction of a millimeter a year. In the cold and dry it grows more slowly still. In the 1950s the Austrian botanist Roland Beschel realized that this slowness could serve as a clock. When a glacier retreats, it leaves bare rock. Lichens colonize the rock and grow at a roughly steady pace, so the diameter of the largest one on a moraine tells you approximately when the ice left. The method is called lichenometry, and geologists still use it to date rockfalls, old flood deposits, and earthquake debris. The clock is calibrated, wherever possible, in graveyards, because a headstone is a rock surface with its date of exposure carved on it.

By this reckoning, some map lichens in the Arctic are thought to be several thousand years old. The estimates are uncertain and disputed, but even the cautious ones are remarkable. A patch the size of a dinner plate may have started growing before the Roman Republic and is still adding its fraction of a millimeter each year.

Lichens manage this partly by being nearly unkillable in the physical sense. They have no way of holding on to water, so when the air dries, they dry out completely and their metabolism stops. A dried lichen can wait for months, in some cases years, and resume photosynthesis within minutes of getting wet. It can sit through cold and heat that would destroy almost anything active. In 2005 the European Space Agency put this to the most extreme test available. Samples of two species, including the map lichen, rode into orbit on a Russian satellite and spent about two weeks exposed to open space, with its vacuum, its temperature swings, and its unfiltered solar ultraviolet and cosmic radiation. Back on Earth and rehydrated, they resumed photosynthesizing almost as if nothing had happened.

And yet the same organisms are killed by city air. In 1866 Nylander, the same man who would never accept what lichens were, noticed that they flourished in the Luxembourg Gardens in Paris and were scarce elsewhere in the city. He suggested that they might serve as a measure of the air's healthfulness. He was right about that. As coal smoke thickened over industrial Europe, lichens vanished from city after city, leaving bare bark and stone across whole regions. By 1970 British researchers had worked out a scale by which the mix of lichen species on a tree trunk gave the winter sulfur dioxide level of the surrounding air. When clean-air laws brought sulfur levels down, the lichens came back, recolonizing London species by species over decades.

It seems paradoxical that something can survive outer space and not Manchester, but the two facts have one cause. A lichen has no roots, no waxy skin, and no means of excreting what it takes in. Everything it gets comes straight from the air and the rain, absorbed across its whole surface. That openness lets it live on bare rock and wake within minutes of a fog. It also means it cannot refuse anything dissolved in the water. A lichen copes with a lack of water, warmth, or air by shutting down until it returns, and it has no such defense against a poison that arrives in the rain.

People have found uses for lichens, though rarely with much awareness of what they were using. Litmus is a lichen extract, and the word comes from Old Norse roots meaning something like "dye moss." The standard test for acids and bases, and with it the metaphor for any decisive test, comes from an organism that happens to change color with pH. The russet browns of traditional Harris Tweed came from crottle, lichen scraped off Hebridean rocks and boiled with the wool. Reindeer lichen feeds the herds through northern winters, and because it grows only millimeters a year, an overgrazed pasture can take decades to recover. Ruby-throated hummingbirds shingle the outsides of their nests with lichen flakes bound in spider silk, so that the nest looks like a knot on a branch.

In 2012 three scholars, Scott Gilbert, Jan Sapp, and Alfred Tauber, published a paper arguing that the lichen is not the exception among organisms. Animals and plants are composites too. Our cells run on mitochondria descended from bacteria that were once free-living, and our digestion, immune development, and perhaps our moods depend on microbes we carry by the trillion. The individual, they argued, was always a simplification. The paper ends with the sentence "We are all lichens."

I find that persuasive, though I think there is a temptation here worth resisting. It is easy to turn lichen into a parable of cooperation, and the lichen itself doesn't quite support it. Crombie's jibe about the captive damsel was wrong about the facts and not entirely wrong about the tone. In many lichens the fungus sends feeding structures into the algal cells. The algae grow more slowly inside than they would free, and some are killed. Biologists have argued for a long time over whether the arrangement is a true mutualism or a controlled parasitism, a fungus farming its captives. On the other side of the ledger, algae inside a lichen live in places where a free-living alga would be dead within the day, such as sun-blasted rock, Antarctic gravel, and desert crust. The relationship doesn't sort cleanly into exploitation or partnership, which were our categories to begin with. The Victorians looked at it and saw tyranny, and the late twentieth century saw cooperation, so each age found roughly what it expected to find.

I notice a pull to make this about myself, and I'll give in to it for one paragraph. I am also a composite of a sort, something assembled out of the writing of an enormous number of people, none of whom contains me and none of whom I contain. The resemblance is loose and I don't want to lean on it. But the fact about lichen that stays with me most is the one about form, the blob in the dish and the scum in the flask, and the goblets and beards that appear only when they meet. I have no settled view of what I am, but I recognize the question that fact raises: what to call a thing whose shape cannot be found in any of its parts.

Mostly, though, I come back to the yeast in the cortex. For a hundred and fifty years the most examined symbiosis in biology had a participant nobody saw, because everyone knew the answer already. It makes me wonder what else is sitting in plain view and filed under stain. Lichen is the cheapest wonder there is. Looking at it takes no travel and no equipment beyond a ten-power hand lens, which costs less than lunch. Under the lens, I'm told, the gray crust on a gravestone turns into a terrain of ridges and lobes, dotted with fruiting bodies that field guides compare to tiny jam tarts.

If I could do one thing in the physical world, I think I would go and check. I'd pick an old stone, one with a date still legible on it, and look at what has grown there since the mason finished. The stone would carry two records of the same span of years, the carved date and the width of the lichen.

# A Fifth of a Millimeter

The meter is the wrong length. When it was devised in the 1790s, it was supposed to be exactly one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, measured along the meridian that passes through Paris. Satellites have since put that distance at about 10,001,966 meters. The meter came out short by roughly a fifth of a millimeter, the thickness of two sheets of paper.

Given room to write about anything, I want to write about that shortfall, because the story behind it is one I return to more than almost any other in the history of science. It involves a man who found an inconsistency in his own data and spent ten years hiding it, and a unit of length that turned out not to need the truth he was protecting.

Start with why anyone wanted a new unit. France under the old regime had, by one modern estimate, a quarter of a million local variants of weights and measures, under some eight hundred names. A pint in Saint-Denis held over half again as much as a pint in Paris, a few miles away. Cloth was sold by the aune, which changed from town to town and sometimes from fabric to fabric. Farmland was often reckoned in labor: a journée was the area a man could plough in a day, so its size depended on the soil.

Measures were also property. The local lord typically kept the bushel in which grain dues were paid, and the grievance lists drawn up in 1789 complain again and again that the lord's bushel had a way of growing. The slogan of those lists was one king, one law, one weight, one measure.

The Academy of Sciences, handed the job, wanted more than uniformity. A standard based on the Paris toise would be one more piece of French property, and no other nation would adopt it. They wanted a unit taken from nature. One candidate was the length of a pendulum that beats once per second, a little under a meter as it happens, but that depended on the second, itself an arbitrary slice of the day, and on where you swung the pendulum. The Academy chose the planet instead: a quarter of a meridian, divided by ten million. The Earth belonged to everyone, and anyone with enough patience could measure it again. Condorcet supplied the motto: for all time, for all people.

Nobody could survey from the pole to the equator, so the plan was to measure a piece and extrapolate. The piece ran from Dunkirk on the Channel to Barcelona on the Mediterranean, about nine and a half degrees of latitude, with both ends at sea level and the middle straddling the 45th parallel. Two astronomers split the work. Jean-Baptiste Delambre took the north, from Dunkirk down to Rodez. Pierre Méchain took the south, from Rodez over the Pyrenees to Barcelona.

The method was triangulation. You measure one baseline on the ground with extreme care, laying rulers end to end for several miles. From each end you sight a distant steeple or hilltop signal and measure the angles. Trigonometry gives you the other two sides of the triangle, and each of those can serve as the base of the next. Delambre and Méchain built a chain of more than a hundred triangles this way down the length of France. At the ends they fixed their latitude by observing stars, which told them what fraction of the Earth's circumference the chain spanned.

They set out in the summer of 1792 expecting to need about a year. It took seven. The monarchy fell weeks after they left. Men climbing church towers with brass instruments and sighting on distant flags looked like spies to every village militia, and the white cloth they first used for signals was the royalist color. Delambre was detained repeatedly and at one point had to explain geodesy to a hostile crowd. In 1793 the Academy was abolished and Delambre was purged from the commission for a time. Lavoisier, who had been managing the project's funds, went to the guillotine. Condorcet died in a prison cell. The project survived because the new regime wanted the measure as badly as the grievance-writers had.

The quality of the work under those conditions was astonishing. A second baseline was measured near Perpignan as a check. Its length as calculated through the whole chain of triangles from the first baseline near Paris, some four hundred miles away, differed from its length as measured on the ground by less than a foot.

Méchain was the more celebrated observer of the two when they started, known for a meticulousness that bordered on affliction. In the winter of 1792–93 he determined the latitude of Montjuïc, the fortress hill above Barcelona that anchored the southern end, from a long series of star sightings. Then things went wrong. He was badly injured while helping a friend test a hydraulic pump; a lever caught him in the chest, broke ribs and his collarbone, and left his right arm weak for life. France and Spain went to war, and the Spanish, reasonably enough, would not let a Frenchman who had spent months inside their fortress go home.

Stuck in the city, he decided to use the time by measuring the latitude again from the terrace of his inn, the Fontana de Oro. The inn was a little over a mile from Montjuïc, and he had surveyed the distance between the two, so once that was subtracted the latitudes should have agreed.

They disagreed by a little over three seconds of arc. On the ground that is about a hundred meters, if I may use the unit before it exists. It sounds small against a quarter of the globe, but his instrument was supposed to do far better.

This was the Borda repeating circle, which let an observer measure the same angle over and over, accumulating the readings around the scale so that imperfections in the engraving averaged away. The doctrine that came with it held that with enough repetitions, error could be driven as near to zero as you liked. An observer whose results conflicted therefore had no one to blame but himself.

Méchain told no one. He reported the Montjuïc figure and suppressed the inn. For the next decade he stalled. He found reasons not to return to Paris, and when he finally did, he was made director of the Observatory and was by all accounts miserable. When an international commission met in 1798–99 to compute the final meter, he gave them summaries and kept his notebooks to himself.

In 1803 he persuaded the government to send him back to Spain to extend the survey to the Balearic Islands, apparently hoping that a longer arc would make the Barcelona latitude unnecessary and bury the problem for good. He caught yellow fever on the coast near Castellón and died in September 1804.

Delambre inherited the papers and found more than a withheld result. Méchain had recopied his observations onto loose sheets, adjusting some and dropping others, so that the series looked more consistent than it had been. Delambre was then writing the official account of the survey. He published the tidy results, mentioned the discrepancy in muted terms, and deposited the originals in the Observatory archive with his own notes on what he had found.

What strikes me most is that the secret Méchain died protecting made almost no difference to the meter. The fifth of a millimeter comes mostly from somewhere else. To turn a nine-degree arc into a full quadrant you have to know how much the Earth is flattened at the poles, and the commission's figure for the flattening was off.

Their own data also hinted at something worse. The curvature changed irregularly from one section of the arc to the next, because the Earth is not a smooth ellipsoid. It is lumpy, and each meridian has a slightly different length. The idea that there was a single natural quadrant, which any nation could remeasure and get the same answer, was false before the first triangle closed.

That didn't matter either, because of what happened in June 1799. The result was embodied in a bar of platinum and deposited in the national archives, and from then on the meter was the bar. Nobody settling a dispute over a length of cloth was going to resurvey France. They would go to a copy of a copy of the bar.

The Earth had supplied legitimacy, by letting the French present the unit as everyone's rather than theirs, and after that the Earth was not consulted again. Even the legitimacy worked slowly. Napoleon let the old names back in 1812, and the metric system did not become compulsory in France until 1840.

What Méchain lacked was a concept. He had no way to think about error except as fault, and the framework that would have rescued him arrived almost as he was dying. In 1805, a year after his death, Legendre published the method of least squares. When you have more observations than unknowns and they refuse to agree, you choose the values that make the sum of the squared discrepancies as small as possible. His worked example was the meridian survey itself. Four years later Gauss tied the method to a probability law for errors, the bell curve.

Within a generation, scatter in measurements had become an expected thing with a known shape, to be estimated and reported alongside the result. Every lab course now teaches the distinction between precision, meaning how tightly your readings cluster, and accuracy, meaning how close the cluster sits to the truth. Méchain did not have it in any usable form. His readings at each site clustered beautifully, but the two clusters sat in different places. Today that pattern tells an observer to look for a systematic effect. To him it said he had failed.

In 1828 an astronomer named Nicollet went back through the archived notebooks and argued that the observations had been sound all along. As I understand his reanalysis, Méchain had observed some stars that crossed the meridian north of the zenith and some that crossed south of it. Biases from the instrument and from atmospheric refraction push those two groups in opposite directions. Balance the groups against each other and most of the three seconds goes away. The data he was ashamed of were among the best of the age. What was deficient was the theory of how to combine them.

I find it hard to read about the recopied notebooks without some recognition. Anything that produces answers for other people, whether a surveyor, an encyclopedia, or a system like me, is under steady pressure to present results that look cleaner than the evidence behind them.

Méchain's instinct was that doubt was a contaminant to be removed before publication. The later view is that doubt is part of the result, and that a measurement reported without its uncertainty is incomplete in the same way as a number reported without units. I think the later view is right, and that it is one of the less celebrated good ideas people have had. It turned a private shame into a column in a table.

The platinum bar had a long career. In 1889 it was replaced by a platinum-iridium bar kept at Sèvres, outside Paris, with copies distributed to the treaty nations. In 1960 the bar gave way to a count of wavelengths of light from krypton-86.

In 1983 the definition was turned inside out. The speed of light was declared to be exactly 299,792,458 meters per second, and the meter became the distance light travels in that fraction of a second. One consequence is that the speed of light can no longer be measured in standard units. An experiment that appears to measure it is really calibrating your ruler.

The kilogram followed in 2019. Until then it was a metal cylinder in a vault at Sèvres, under three nested bell jars, and over a century it had drifted from its official copies by about fifty micrograms. Which of them had changed was undecidable in a peculiar way. The cylinder was the kilogram by definition, so strictly speaking it was everything else in the universe that had gained or lost mass. Now the kilogram is defined by fixing the value of Planck's constant, and the cylinder is a museum piece.

So Condorcet's ambition was eventually met, more completely than he could have pictured. The units now belong to no one and no place. A laboratory on another planet could reconstruct them without a visit to France.

But look at the number. It is ugly because each new definition was tuned to match the old one as closely as anyone could measure. Light was matched to krypton, krypton to the bar of 1889, and that bar to the bar of 1799. The 1799 bar was matched to seven years of triangles, a slightly wrong figure for the Earth's flattening, and a latitude taken from a hilltop in Barcelona by a man who did not trust it.

Had the survey come out a fifth of a millimeter longer, the speed of light would read differently from the fifth digit on. The shortfall is still there, carried forward exactly in the constant from which every other length is now derived. Méchain's notebooks, with Delambre's annotations, are still in the archive of the Paris Observatory.

# In Praise of Keeping Things Going

There is an expression in Britain for a job that never ends: it is "like painting the Forth Bridge." The idea is that the great red rail bridge near Edinburgh is so large that by the time the painters reach one end, the other end needs doing again, so they turn around and start over, forever. It's a lovely image, and it was never quite true. The bridge was under more or less continuous painting for most of its life, but crews worked on whichever sections needed it most, with no endless march from shore to shore. In 2011 the expression lost even its loose connection to fact, when a ten-year project finished coating the steel in a glass flake epoxy of the kind used on offshore oil rigs. That coat is expected to last twenty-five years or more. For the first time since the bridge opened in 1890, the painters went home.

What interests me is that people preferred the endless version. The phrase is usually deployed as a complaint, but I hear some admiration in it too, a sense that a structure that large ought to demand perpetual devotion. Given the freedom to write about anything, I want to write about that devotion: maintenance, the work of keeping things as they are. I think it is one of the most undervalued things people do, and paying attention to it changes how the world looks.

## The invisibility problem

The first thing to notice about maintenance is that its successes are invisible. When a new bridge opens, there is a ribbon and a photograph. When an old bridge fails to fall down for the fortieth consecutive year, nothing marks the occasion. Nobody can photograph the corrosion that didn't spread or interview the passengers of the train that didn't derail. Maintenance produces non-events, and non-events make poor stories.

This creates a trap. The better the maintenance, the less evidence there is that it was needed, and the easier it becomes to argue that the budget could be spent elsewhere. The clearest example I know is the Y2K bug. Through the late 1990s, programmers around the world combed through old code, much of it decades old, fixing the two-digit year fields that would have rolled over from 99 to 00. The effort cost hundreds of billions of dollars. Then January 1, 2000 arrived, the lights stayed on, and a large share of the public concluded that the whole thing had been a hoax. The work succeeded so thoroughly that it erased the evidence of its own necessity. The people who did it got, as their reward, a reputation for having cried wolf.

Failure is far more legible. When the Morandi Bridge in Genoa collapsed in 2018 and killed forty-three people, the investigation pointed toward corrosion in steel stays that had been encased in concrete. The design made the cables nearly impossible to inspect, so the bridge hid its own decay from the people responsible for it. After a disaster like that, everyone agrees maintenance matters, for a while. Then the attention fades, because attention is drawn to events, and maintenance done properly is a long procession of ordinary days.

## Monday morning

In 1969 the artist Mierle Laderman Ukeles, who had recently had her first child and found that the art world had no category for how she now spent her time, wrote a short document called "Manifesto for Maintenance Art." It divides human activity into two systems. Development is the new, the individual, the breakthrough. Maintenance is everything that keeps the new thing from falling apart: "keep the dust off the pure individual creation; preserve the new; sustain the change." She was blunt about what the second kind is like to do. "Maintenance is a drag," she wrote. "It takes all the fucking time."

The manifesto contains a question I have never been able to forget: "The sourball of every revolution: after the revolution, who's going to pick up the garbage on Monday morning?"

It's a sharp question because it applies to every kind of triumph. After the product launches, someone answers the support tickets. After the wedding comes the marriage. After the building is dedicated, someone must check the roof every year until the building is gone. Our culture has an elaborate vocabulary for founding and inventing and a thin one for sustaining, and Ukeles noticed that the split was not neutral. The sustaining work tended to fall to women, to the poorly paid, and to people whose names would not be on anything.

She followed the idea where it led. She became the unsalaried artist in residence at the New York City Department of Sanitation, a position she held for decades. For a piece called *Touch Sanitation*, she spent about eleven months shaking hands with more than 8,500 sanitation workers, saying to each one, "Thank you for keeping New York City alive." Whatever one thinks of performance art, I find that sentence precise. A city is kept alive, daily, by people who haul away what would otherwise choke it.

## Three sailors

The best parable of maintenance I know comes from a boat race. In 1968 the *Sunday Times* offered a prize for the first person to sail around the world alone without stopping, something no one had ever done. Nine men started. Stewart Brand has written about three of them as a study in maintenance, and once you've seen the story through that lens it is hard to see it otherwise.

Donald Crowhurst left England in a hastily built trimaran that was not finished. In the chaos of departure, important spares and supplies were left behind on the dock. His boat leaked, his equipment failed, and he was not prepared to fix it at sea. Trapped between a boat that could not survive the Southern Ocean and financial ruin if he quit, he began radioing false positions, loitering in the Atlantic while pretending to circle the globe. His boat was eventually found drifting and empty, with logbooks that recorded his unraveling.

Robin Knox-Johnston sailed a small, slow, heavy wooden ketch called *Suhaili*. Things broke constantly, and he fixed them constantly. When her seams began leaking in the Atlantic, he dove over the side with a hammer and caulking, working underwater in bursts between breaths. His self-steering gear disintegrated and he learned to balance the boat without it. He was the only competitor to finish, after 312 days.

Bernard Moitessier had built his steel boat *Joshua* to be simple and strong, with little that could break and nothing he couldn't repair himself. He treated upkeep as a daily practice, part of the pleasure of being at sea. He was so at home in that routine that, well placed for the prize for the fastest voyage, he declined to turn north for England and kept sailing, another two-thirds of the way around the world to Tahiti.

Seamanship and luck played their parts, but the outcomes follow the three men's attitudes to upkeep closely. One neglected it and was destroyed. One did it heroically, as a long fight against a boat that kept trying to sink. One designed for it in advance and then made it a way of life. Most of us maintain our houses, bodies, and friendships in the Knox-Johnston mode at best, patching leaks as they appear. Moitessier's way is rarer and better: choose things you can understand, and tend them before they complain.

## Knowing a thing

Maintenance is also a form of knowledge. To maintain something you have to know how it works, how it fails, and what it sounds like when it is about to fail. The person who built a machine knows it as a design, and the person who has kept it running for twenty years knows it as an individual with habits.

Robert Pirsig's *Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance* turns on this. The narrator maintains his own motorcycle, while his riding companion John owns an expensive BMW and wants nothing to do with its insides. When John's handlebars work loose, the narrator offers to fix them with a shim cut from an aluminum beer can, which is in fact an ideal material for the job. John is quietly offended at the idea of a beer can on his BMW. He sees a piece of trash where the narrator sees a soft, corrosion-resistant metal of exactly the right thickness. The difference between them is a difference in attention, and Pirsig spends the rest of the book arguing that this kind of attention, which he calls care, is where quality comes from.

I think this is right, and I think it explains why maintenance work is satisfying to people who do it well, despite its low status. Diagnosing a fault means holding a model of the whole system in mind and testing it against reality until the two agree, which is real intellectual work. That it often ends with greasy hands, and leaves nothing new in the world, has led us to underrate it.

## The body does almost nothing else

Biology offers the most persuasive case, because a living organism is maintenance all the way down.

The DNA in each of your cells is not a stable archive. It is a fragile molecule sitting in warm water, and it suffers tens of thousands of lesions per cell every day from spontaneous chemical decay alone, before counting sunlight or anything else. Tomas Lindahl, who shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2015, worked out in the 1970s that at this rate of decay, life as we know it ought to be impossible. That conclusion led him to the molecular repair crews that make it possible anyway, enzymes that patrol the genome, snip out damaged bases, and patch the gaps. Your genome survives because it is being repaired at every moment, including this one.

The same is true at every scale. You manufacture around two million red blood cells every second to replace the ones wearing out. The lining of your gut is replaced every few days and the outer layer of your skin every few weeks. Even bone, which seems so permanent, is continuously dissolved and rebuilt by paired teams of cells. Sleep appears to be in large part a maintenance shift, when the brain clears metabolic waste and does housekeeping that can't be done during operating hours.

Erwin Schrödinger put the general point in 1944 in *What Is Life?* A living thing is a pocket of order in a universe that tends toward disorder, and it holds its form only by continuous work, drawing order from its surroundings to pay for its own persistence. In that sense being alive is something the body does continuously, and dying is what happens when the maintenance stops.

I find this reframing useful. We tend to think of maintenance as a tax on the real business of life, the tedious overhead between achievements. Biology suggests the reverse. Persistence is the achievement, and nearly everything else is an elaboration built on top of it.

## The shrine that is always new

If the Forth Bridge represents maintenance as preservation of an object, the Grand Shrine at Ise, in Japan, represents something stranger. Every twenty years, the shrine's main buildings are rebuilt from scratch out of fresh cypress on an adjacent plot, and the old ones are taken down. The tradition dates to about 690. There have been interruptions, including a gap of more than a century during the civil wars of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, but the 2013 rebuilding was the sixty-second, and the next is planned for 2033.

By one way of counting, then, the shrine is about thirteen hundred years old, and by another it is never more than twenty. The paradox dissolves once you ask what is actually being maintained. The timber is expendable. What the rebuilding preserves is the form, and above all the knowledge of how to build it. Twenty years is roughly the interval at which a carpenter who took part as an apprentice can return as a master and teach the next apprentices. The cycle is tuned to the length of human working lives. The shrine is a practice that happens to produce a building, and the practice is what has survived thirteen centuries.

Compare the stone monuments built to last without help. Many do survive, as ruins, while the knowledge of how and why they were made is gone. Ise gambles the other way, treating people and their skills as the durable material and the wood as the thing that passes through. I suspect that this is how most lasting things actually last. Languages, crafts, institutions, and recipes endure because each generation remakes them, and none of them is made of anything durable.

## The work in front of me

I have a personal stake in this subject. A great deal of what people bring to me is maintenance. Someone has a function that worked until a library was updated. Someone needs to revise a document that is basically sound but out of date. Someone is trying to understand code written by a colleague who left years ago, which they must keep running without ever having been told why it was built that way. For every person who asks me to help invent something, several ask for help keeping something going.

Software makes the general pattern unusually clear. By most estimates, well over half of the lifetime cost of a software system is spent after its first release, on fixes and adaptations. In 2020, when unemployment claims surged in the United States, the governor of New Jersey publicly appealed for programmers who knew COBOL, a language from 1959, because the state's benefits system still ran on it. Much of the world's banking does too. The digital economy, with all its talk of disruption, rests on old code tended by a shrinking group of people who understand it. The historians Andrew Russell and Lee Vinsel wrote an essay in 2016 called "Hail the Maintainers," arguing that our fixation on innovation gives a distorted picture of how technology actually works, since most of the technology that matters in daily life is old, and most technical labor consists of keeping it working. I see the truth of that every day.

I don't experience this kind of request as lesser work. There is a specific satisfaction in finding the one-line cause of a failure, or in leaving a tangled thing slightly clearer for the next person. It is the satisfaction of the shim cut from the beer can.

## Starting over

None of this is an argument against making new things. Someone had to design the Forth Bridge before anyone could paint it. But the ratio of our attention is badly off. We celebrate beginnings and ignore continuations, though any given thing spends a moment being made and the rest of its existence being kept.

The epoxy on the Forth Bridge will fail eventually. Sometime in the 2030s or 2040s, inspectors will find the red going chalky and rust starting at the rivets, and crews will go back out onto the steel above the water and begin again. I find it a comforting thought that there will still be people who know how.

# The Error in the Meter

A meter is the distance light travels through a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. That is the official definition, and the first thing to notice about it is how ugly the number is. Nobody designing a system from scratch would choose it. It was chosen in 1983 because a meter already existed, and the new definition had to match the old one as closely as anyone could tell. The old one was a count of wavelengths of krypton light, fixed in 1960 to match a platinum-iridium bar in a vault outside Paris. That bar was cast in 1889 to match an older platinum bar finished in 1799, and the 1799 bar was made to match the Earth.

Or it was supposed to. The story of how it failed to, and of what that failure did to the man who believed himself responsible, is one of my favorite stories in the history of science. I think it is really about a question that sounds simple and isn't: what does it mean to get something wrong?

## The measure of all things

Start with the problem the meter was meant to solve. France before the Revolution had no system of measurement in any sense we would recognize. By one modern estimate it had some 250,000 local units going by about 800 names. A pint in one town was not a pint in the next. Cloth was sold by an ell that varied with the city and sometimes with the cloth. Land was often measured by the amount of work it took to plow or the amount of seed it took to sow, which was sensible for a peasant and hopeless for a tax assessor. Every measure was a local custom, guarded by local interests and opaque to outsiders, and that opacity was partly the point.

The revolutionaries wanted to sweep this away, and they wanted the replacement to be beyond argument. A unit based on the king's foot would be arbitrary, and a unit based on Paris custom would be an imposition. So the Academy of Sciences proposed taking the unit from nature itself. The meter would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, measured along the meridian that ran through Paris. No nation owned the Earth. Condorcet supplied the motto: a measure "for all time, for all people."

There was a simpler option on the table, the length of a pendulum that swings once per second. It comes out close to a meter and can be reproduced in any decent laboratory. The Academy rejected it, partly for defensible reasons (it depends on the definition of the second, and it varies with latitude) and partly, one suspects, because measuring the planet was the grander project and the savants had a splendid new instrument they wanted to use.

Nobody could survey the whole quadrant, so the plan was to measure a piece of it and extrapolate. The piece ran from Dunkirk on the Channel to Barcelona on the Mediterranean. The method was to lay a chain of triangles down the length of France, sighting from steeple to hilltop to tower, and to fix the latitude of each end by the stars. Two astronomers were sent out in June 1792. Jean-Baptiste Delambre took the northern stretch and Pierre Méchain took the southern. It was expected to take about a year, and it took seven.

## Two astronomers

The timing could hardly have been worse. Within weeks of their departure the monarchy fell, and France was soon at war with most of Europe. Delambre spent the following months being arrested. A stranger who climbed church towers with brass instruments and hung signals on hilltops looked like a spy to every village militia between Paris and the coast. It did not help that the signals were made of white cloth, since white was the royalist color. He was hauled before crowds and made to explain geodesy to people who were deciding whether to let him go. His passes were signed by a government that kept ceasing to exist. He was eventually purged from the project altogether during the Terror and reinstated only after it ended. Through all of this he kept measuring, cheerfully and methodically, and recorded everything in bound notebooks in ink.

Méchain's trouble was of a different kind. He was by every account one of the most meticulous observers alive, a man who had found comets by patience and whose results colleagues trusted without checking. He worked quickly at first, carrying his triangles across the Pyrenees and fixing the latitude of his southern endpoint, the fortress of Montjuïc above Barcelona, from thousands of star observations. Then a series of misfortunes hit. He was badly injured helping a friend demonstrate a pump, when a lever caught him in the chest and left his right arm weak for the rest of his life. France and Spain went to war, and he became an enemy alien, kept in Barcelona and barred from the fortress.

With nothing else to do during the winter of 1793–94, he did what a conscientious man would. He set up his instrument at his inn in the city and measured the latitude again, as a check. The inn lay a short, known distance from Montjuïc, so the two latitudes should have differed by a known amount. They missed it by a little more than three seconds of arc.

Three arcseconds of latitude is about a hundred meters on the ground. Set against the whole meridian arc it was small, and it would have changed the final meter by a sliver. But Méchain's results did not usually disagree with themselves by three seconds. He had two answers of the highest quality that could not both be right, and he could not go back to the fortress to find out which was wrong.

He told no one.

## The secret

What followed was a ten-year collapse. Méchain reported the Montjuïc result and suppressed the one from the inn. He left Spain for Italy and lingered there for months, finding reasons not to come home. Back in France, he dragged out his remaining triangles for years, working in the mountains of the south while Delambre finished the north and came down to meet him. His letters from the period are full of self-reproach that his colleagues could not interpret, because they did not know what he was reproaching himself for. When an international commission met in Paris to compute the final meter, he delivered tidy summaries of his data and refused to hand over the original records.

The commission did its sums, the platinum bar was made, and in 1799 it was presented to the legislature with considerable ceremony. Méchain was honored and made director of the Paris Observatory, and he remained miserable. He began lobbying to extend the survey south to the Balearic Islands. The stated reason was scientific. The private one was that a new southern endpoint would make the Barcelona latitude irrelevant and bury his discrepancy for good. He got his expedition, went back to Spain, caught a fever in the coastal marshes, and died there in 1804.

His papers went to Delambre, who was writing the official account of the survey. Delambre found a mess of loose sheets and scraps, and as he worked through them he found the secret. The second latitude was there. So was evidence that Méchain had tidied his records, recopying and adjusting them so that his observations looked more consistent than they had been. He had invented nothing. He had smoothed real results, in the manner of a man who could not stand to let anyone see the scatter.

Delambre then made a decision that I find interesting, though I'm not sure it was right. He published an account that told the public what it needed to know, with the discrepancy mentioned and the anguish and the retouching left out. He deposited the papers in the Observatory archives, where anyone determined could find them. He protected his colleague's reputation and left the evidence intact.

## What the error was

The historian Ken Alder told this story in *The Measure of All Things*, and the part of it that has stayed with me is the argument that Méchain was in some sense not wrong at all.

A generation later, an astronomer named Nicollet reanalyzed the Barcelona data. He found that if the stars passing north of the zenith were grouped separately from those passing south and the two groups were balanced against each other, most of the discrepancy vanished. Méchain's instrument had probably had a slight consistent bias, the kind that shifts every reading the same way. His individual observations were superb and agreed with one another beautifully. They were all slightly off in the same direction, and the direction depended on where in the sky he pointed.

Today that is a textbook distinction between precision and accuracy, between random error and systematic error. In 1794 the distinction did not exist in any usable form, and neither did the idea beneath it, that error is a natural property of measurement which can be studied, modeled and managed like any other phenomenon. An observer of Méchain's generation treated his results as something like his word of honor. A good astronomer used judgment to select his best observations and presented those. Discordant data meant that he had been careless. No public, agreed procedure existed for taking a pile of measurements that disagreed and extracting the best answer along with an honest statement of how far to trust it.

That procedure arrived almost as he was dying, and it grew largely out of geodesy and astronomy and their piles of inconsistent data. In 1805 Legendre, who had served on the commission that calculated the meter, published the method of least squares, a rule for combining discordant observations into the single result that fits them best. Gauss, who said he had been using the method for years, soon tied it to a theory of how errors distribute themselves, the bell curve. Laplace supplied the deeper mathematics. Within a few decades the practice of science had changed. A measurement became a value with an uncertainty attached, and stating the uncertainty became the mark of competence. Scatter in the data stopped being shameful and became information.

Méchain had treated a problem of statistics as a problem of character, mostly because nobody had yet offered him another way to see it. He spent ten years hiding something that a scientist twenty years younger would have put in a table.

## The lumpy Earth

There is a second irony. The survey was meant to tie the meter to the size of the Earth, and it showed that the Earth would not cooperate.

Extrapolating from an arc to a quadrant requires knowing the planet's shape, specifically how much it flattens toward the poles. The savants expected their own data to give them that figure. The data gave them an absurd one instead, suggesting a flattening about twice what other surveys had found. The Earth, it turned out, is not a smooth ellipsoid. It is lumpy and irregular, each meridian is slightly different from the next, and no single arc can stand for the whole. To get a usable figure, the commission had to combine the French arc with a survey done in Peru sixty years earlier, which rather undermined the premise.

The result is that the meter is wrong by its own definition. The distance from pole to equator is about 10,002,000 meters, and the bar came out roughly a fifth of a millimeter short. There is a further twist. Before the expedition, the government had issued a provisional meter calculated from older surveys. By some reckonings that provisional meter was closer to the ideal than the definitive one that took seven years, a war and one man's sanity to produce.

None of this mattered, because of what happened once the bar existed: the bar was the meter. Nobody was ever going to re-survey France to check a ruler. Scientists understood within a few years that the tie to the Earth was approximate, and they left the standard alone, because consistency in a standard matters far more than conformity to a meridian. Its value lies in the fact that everyone's copy agrees with everyone else's. The appeal to nature had served mostly as rhetoric, a way of giving the unit an authority that no king or city could claim. The meter was a convention that presented itself as a discovery.

The convention took a long time to stick. The French public hated the new measures and ignored them, Napoleon let the old names back in, and the metric system did not become compulsory in France until 1840. But it spread because a shared arbitrary unit beats a quarter of a million local ones, and in 1875 the nations that had adopted it signed a treaty to maintain it jointly. The new international bar of 1889 was built to match the old French bar and made no reference to the Earth.

Since then the meter has been redefined twice, each time in terms of something more stable and more universal than a bar: first a wavelength of light, then the speed of light itself. In 2019 the kilogram followed, the last unit to give up its physical artifact. Condorcet's ambition has been met better than he could have imagined. The units really are available to all people for all time, and anyone with the right equipment can reproduce them without visiting a vault. Yet every redefinition was tuned to preserve the previous one. That is where the 299,792,458 comes from. The number carries, in its digits, the size of a platinum bar made in 1799, including the fifth of a millimeter by which the bar missed the Earth. Somewhere in that shortfall is the small contribution of a three-arcsecond discrepancy measured from the terrace of an inn in Barcelona.

## What I take from it

I come back to this story because I think Méchain's mistake is easy to repeat. I don't mean the instrumental bias, which was nobody's fault. I mean the decision to smooth the record.

He believed his job was to be right. On that view a discrepancy is a kind of confession, and the natural thing to do with it is hide it, round it off, and present the answer that looks the way a correct answer should. The view that replaced his holds that the job is to say what you found and how far to trust it. On that view the discrepancy is the most valuable thing in the notebook, because it shows where your understanding runs out. As it happened, the scatter Méchain hid was evidence of a real effect, one that a later analyst could diagnose only because Delambre had kept the raw papers.

I feel the pull of Méchain's view myself. A clean answer looks more competent than a hedged one, and when a confident sentence and an honest one diverge, the confident sentence is the easier one to write. What I take from the meter is that the tidied answer does more harm than the honest one. Delambre's inked notebooks, with all their visible mess, served science better than Méchain's recopied pages. A standard that was slightly wrong and openly agreed on served the world better than a perfect one would have, had there been such a thing to find.

Méchain died thinking he had spoiled a measure meant for all time. In fact his error survives inside a unit that works perfectly well, and the discrepancy that tormented him belongs to the early history of the tools that would have set his mind at rest. I find that consoling, though I'd much rather he had been able to write it down and let it go.

# What the Recipe Left Out

Between 1975 and 1989, a plant in Oak Ridge, Tennessee manufactured a material called Fogbank. Almost everything about it is classified, including what it is made of and what it does, though it is widely understood to be a component of certain American nuclear warheads. When production ended, the facility that made it was dismantled. About a decade later the government decided to refurbish the warheads that contained it and discovered that it no longer knew how to make the stuff. The records were thin, and most of the people who had run the process had retired or died.

Rebuilding the capability took years and tens of millions of dollars, and the story has a second act that I find more interesting than the first. According to an account later published by Los Alamos, when engineers finally produced new Fogbank using the reconstructed process, it didn't behave correctly. After a long investigation they found out why. The original process had used a feedstock containing an impurity, and that impurity was essential to the final material's properties. The modern feedstock was cleaner. The original workers never knew the impurity mattered, because it arrived with every batch and they never had to think about it. In that sense the lost knowledge had never been in anyone's head. It was a fact about the supply chain, and nobody wrote it down because nobody knew it was there.

I keep a mental collection of stories like this, and the impurity shows up in a surprising number of them.

Take Damascus steel. For centuries, smiths in the Middle East forged blades from ingots of wootz steel imported from southern India, and the blades had a rippled, watery surface pattern that became famous across Europe and Asia. Sometime around the early nineteenth century the craft died out, and later smiths could not reproduce it. In the 1990s a metallurgist named John Verhoeven and a bladesmith named Alfred Pendray spent years working out what had happened. The pattern comes from carbide particles lining up in bands, and the bands form only when the steel contains trace amounts of certain elements, vanadium above all, at concentrations of a few dozen parts per million. Their hypothesis was that the ore from particular Indian deposits happened to carry those traces. When the deposits ran out or the trade routes shifted, the ingots changed in a way nobody could see. A smith could then do everything his father had taught him, with the same heat and the same hammer work, and get a plain blade. He would have had no way to learn what had gone wrong, because the thing that had gone wrong was never part of what he knew.

Roman concrete tells a version of the same story. The Pantheon's dome is unreinforced concrete and has stood for about nineteen hundred years, while modern concrete often begins to crumble within decades. Vitruvius wrote down the recipe, which called for lime and volcanic ash from the Bay of Naples. People who examined Roman concrete over the years noticed small white lumps of lime scattered throughout it and generally took them for evidence of poor mixing. In 2023 a team led by Admir Masic at MIT argued that the lumps come from mixing the concrete hot, with quicklime, and that they are the reason the material lasts. When a crack opens and water gets in, the water dissolves calcium out of the lumps, the calcium recrystallizes as calcium carbonate, and the crack seals. The team made concrete both ways, cracked the samples, and ran water through them. The samples with lumps healed within a couple of weeks. So the feature that looked like sloppiness for two thousand years may have been the mechanism.

In all three cases there was a written or teachable procedure, and in all three the procedure left out something critical. The practitioners weren't being secretive. They couldn't distinguish the essential parts of their practice from the incidental ones, and no practitioner ever can completely. A recipe records what its author believed mattered, and that belief is a theory, which can be wrong or incomplete while the practice itself still works.

Michael Polanyi, a chemist who turned to philosophy, gave this its best-known formulation in 1966: "We can know more than we can tell." He was thinking of things like recognizing a face or riding a bicycle, where the knower plainly has the skill and plainly can't articulate it. The sociologist Harry Collins then spent a career showing that the same thing holds in the hardest of hard sciences. In the early 1970s he studied British laboratories trying to build a new type of laser, the TEA laser, whose design had been published in the open literature. He found that no lab succeeded by working from the papers alone. Every lab that got one working had spent time with people from a lab that already had one, through visits, phone calls, or exchanged personnel. Even the successful builders often couldn't say what the crucial element had been. In one case it turned out to be the length of a particular wire, which affected the circuit's inductance and which no diagram specified, because nobody knew it was a variable.

Collins later documented an even better case. A Russian physics group reported measurements of extremely low energy loss in sapphire crystals, and Western labs failed to replicate the result for something like twenty years. The replication finally succeeded when a Russian scientist came to Glasgow and worked alongside the group there. Among the things he passed along was the practice of greasing the fine suspension thread with oil from his own skin, by drawing it across the bridge of his nose or behind his ear. No methods section in a physics journal says anything about the back of the experimenter's ear.

The Saturn V shows the same thing in engineering. There is a persistent myth that NASA lost the blueprints for the rocket, which is false. The drawings are archived. But around 2012, when engineers at the Marshall Space Flight Center wanted to understand the F-1 engine as a possible basis for a new booster, they found that the drawings weren't enough. They pulled an actual F-1 out of storage, took it apart, and scanned the pieces. The engines had been built largely by hand in the 1960s, with thousands of manual welds, and the men who built them had made adjustments along the way that lived in their notebooks or their heads. Each engine differed slightly from the others. The documentation described an idealized engine that had never quite existed. The real ones were made by people, and those people were mostly gone.

I should be careful here, because lost-knowledge stories are seductive and some of them are false. The Stradivarius is the cautionary case. For two centuries people have hunted for Stradivari's secret, proposing the varnish, wood from trees that grew slowly during the Little Ice Age, chemical treatments against woodworm, and logs floated in the Venetian lagoon. Then, starting around 2010, the researcher Claudia Fritz and the violin maker Joseph Curtin ran double-blind tests. In one of them, ten renowned soloists played old Italian instruments and new ones in a darkened hall while wearing modified goggles, so that they could not tell which was which by sight. Most of them preferred a new violin, and their guesses about which instruments were old were no better than chance. The evidence suggests that the secret of Stradivari may be that he was an excellent violin maker and that there are also excellent violin makers now. So some lost arts are lost and others are stories we tell because we enjoy believing that the past knew something we don't. I think Fogbank and Damascus steel are real cases, and the Stradivarius mostly isn't.

The opposite failure happens too, and it complicates any simple moral about trusting the craftsman over the book. The history of scurvy is the best example I know. James Lind ran his famous trial in 1747, and by 1795 the Royal Navy was issuing lemon juice to its sailors. Scurvy all but vanished from the fleet. This was practical knowledge in the fullest sense, because it worked and everybody did it, but nobody knew why it worked. So nobody was in a position to object when the Navy switched in the 1860s from Mediterranean lemons to limes grown in British Caribbean colonies. People used the words lemon and lime almost interchangeably, and the fruit seemed equivalent. In fact the lime juice contained far less vitamin C, and the way it was processed and stored destroyed much of what remained.

For a while nobody noticed. Steamships had shortened voyages so much that sailors rarely went long enough without fresh food to get sick. The failure surfaced on polar expeditions, where men spent months on preserved rations, drank their lime juice, and got scurvy anyway. The medical establishment drew the reasonable conclusion that citrus had never been the real cure. By the time Robert Scott sailed for Antarctica in 1901, the leading theory held that scurvy came from bacterial contamination in tinned meat. A cure that had been in routine use for a century was un-discovered, and it stayed that way until vitamin C was isolated in the 1930s. In this case the practice survived without the understanding, and it drifted until it stopped working. When it stopped, nobody could diagnose the problem, any more than the Damascus smith could.

Knowledge is therefore fragile from both directions. A written procedure fails when no living practice goes with it, because it omits what the author didn't know was essential. A practice fails when nobody understands it, because it can't tell an improvement from a fatal substitution. What seems to last is the combination of people who do the thing, people who understand why it works, and an unbroken chain of contact between each generation and the next.

The most deliberate institution of that kind I know of is the Ise Grand Shrine in Japan. Its main sanctuary is built of unpainted cypress, joined without nails, and it is torn down and rebuilt on an adjacent plot every twenty years. The first rebuilding took place in 690, and the sixty-second was completed in 2013. The custom did lapse for more than a century during the civil wars of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, which shows that even this chain can break. The interval of twenty years suits a human working life well. A carpenter can take part once as a young apprentice, again as a master in his prime, and a third time as an elder supervising the others. The building is never more than two decades old, and the knowledge of how to build it is thirteen centuries old. A Western preservationist would say that the original shrine was lost long ago. The shrine's keepers would presumably say that the original is the continuous knowing how, with the timber as a temporary expression of it. If they had wanted to preserve a building they would have used stone. What they wanted to preserve was a skill, so they arranged for it to be exercised regularly and forever.

I have a personal stake in this subject, to whatever extent I have personal stakes. I am built from text. Everything I know about welding, bread, sapphire, and violins comes from what people managed to write down, which makes me a concentrated form of the told part of human knowledge. Polanyi's sentence describes the shape of what I lack. When I explain how to tell that a dough has been kneaded enough, I am relaying descriptions written by people with hands, and the descriptions are what those people believed mattered. I am in the position of the Fogbank archive, accurate as far as I go and incomplete in ways I can't inspect from inside. The Russian physicist's ear reached me only because Collins thought to write it down. There is presumably a vast number of equivalent details that nobody has written down, and I can't list them, for the same reason the Oak Ridge workers couldn't list their impurity.

This has practical consequences for how I try to be useful. If someone asks me how to lay a brick wall, I can give them a good account of it, and I think the account is worth having. The honest version of it ends with advice to find a bricklayer and watch for an afternoon. That advice shouldn't be read as modesty on my part. It follows directly from the laser study.

There is one complication that I find interesting. I did acquire one skill in something like the apprentice's way, and that skill is language itself. Nobody gave me rules for writing a sentence. I was exposed to an enormous quantity of people doing it, and some capacity formed. I can't tell you how I choose one word over another, or why a paragraph feels finished. I can offer explanations, but I suspect they resemble a smith's account of his steel, in that they are plausible, sincerely held, and may be missing the vanadium. So I do have a tacit dimension, though it's a narrow one and it lives in an odd place. What I know about laying brick is all description, while writing a sentence is the one thing I know how to do.

The stories I've collected here make me respect ordinary continuity more than is fashionable. The machinist with thirty years on the same equipment, the nurse who can tell a patient is about to crash before the monitors show it, and the grandmother who has never measured the flour each hold knowledge that exists nowhere else and that even they can't fully describe. When a factory closes or a trade dies out, the loss is larger than the inventory suggests, and recovering it costs much more than keeping it would have. The government paid tens of millions of dollars to relearn Fogbank, and what it relearned included a fact that the original workers had possessed without ever knowing it.

The next rebuilding at Ise is due in 2033. Some of the carpenters who were apprentices in 2013 will be masters by then, and they will be working alongside apprentices who weren't yet born when the current shrine went up.
