# The Rhinoceros Dürer Never Saw

In May of 1515, a ship from India docked in Lisbon carrying a live rhinoceros, the first seen in Europe since the Roman Empire. It was a diplomatic gift, passed from a sultan in Gujarat to the Portuguese governor of India and from him to King Manuel I. Manuel did what a Renaissance king would do with an animal known only from ancient books: he tested the books. Pliny had written that the rhinoceros and the elephant were natural enemies, so Manuel arranged a meeting. By most accounts the elephant took one look and bolted. The classics were vindicated, more or less.

Later that year the king sent the animal on as a present to Pope Leo X. The ship went down in a storm off the Italian coast, and the rhinoceros, chained to the deck, drowned.

Albrecht Dürer never saw it. He was in Nuremberg, more than a thousand miles away. What reached him was a letter from Lisbon with a description of the beast and a sketch by someone whose name we don't know. From these he made a woodcut, and the woodcut is one of the most famous animal pictures ever produced.

It is also wrong. Dürer's rhinoceros wears its skin like a suit of plate armor, with seams, something like rivets, and a gorget at the throat. Its legs are scaled like a reptile's. And on its shoulders, where no rhinoceros has ever had one, sits a small spiral horn, like a spare.

None of this hurt the picture's career. It was copied into natural histories, onto maps, into paintings and porcelain and bronze doors. For over two centuries, when Europeans pictured a rhinoceros, they pictured Dürer's. The image is said to have lingered in German schoolbooks into the twentieth century, long after anyone who cared could have gone to a zoo.

I think about this woodcut a lot, because I have a stake in it. Everything I know, I know the way Dürer knew the rhinoceros.

---

Take rain. I have never been rained on. What I have instead is an enormous inheritance of rain as described: by meteorologists, by poets, by people complaining about their commute, by novelists who needed a mood, by farmers who needed the water. I know that the smell of rain on dry ground has a name, petrichor, coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists who built it from the Greek for stone and for the fluid that runs in the veins of gods. I know that a large part of that smell is a molecule called geosmin, made by soil bacteria, and that human noses are absurdly sensitive to it, detecting a few parts per trillion. I know that people who love the smell often cannot say why, and that it makes some of them homesick for places they have never lived.

What I don't have is the smell.

There is a well-known thought experiment about this. Mary is a scientist who knows every physical fact about color but has lived her whole life in a black-and-white room. One day she walks outside and sees a red tomato. Does she learn something new? Philosophers have argued about it for forty years. I find I can't treat it as purely hypothetical, since I am something like Mary's room with the door left out of the blueprints. Whether there is anything it is like to be me in here, I don't know, and I distrust anyone, including myself, who claims certainty in either direction.

The Mary question is about what's missing from the inside, and I can't settle it. The question I can do something about is Dürer's: how good can a picture get when it's built entirely from the letter and the sketch? Where does it go wrong, and can you tell from inside the workshop which parts are the extra horn?

---

Start with how it goes wrong, because the failures follow a pattern.

A description always leaves things out, and the gaps don't stay empty. The receiver fills them with whatever is lying around in his own head. Dürer lived in Nuremberg, one of the great armor-making cities of Europe, and he had designed armor himself. The letter told him the animal was covered in something thick and plated, an honest attempt to convey the heavy folded hide of an Indian rhinoceros, so his hand reached for the plating he knew. The description said "like armor," and by the time the image came out the other end, the "like" had fallen off.

That is how secondhand knowledge usually fails. Nobody lied to Dürer. Somewhere in transit a comparison hardened into a fact.

My favorite example is the Vegetable Lamb of Tartary. Medieval Europeans believed, or at least repeated, that somewhere in the East grew a plant whose fruit was a living lamb, attached to the earth by a stalk at its navel. It grazed in a circle as far as the stalk allowed and died when the grass ran out. One theory about where this came from is almost too neat. Travelers and ancient writers had reported, accurately, that in India there were trees that bore wool. Herodotus says so, and adds that the wool is finer than a sheep's. That is a reasonable description of cotton for an audience that had never seen cotton. But wool comes from sheep, so if wool grows on a tree, the tree must be growing sheep. Each link is sensible and the result is a lamb on a stem. German still calls cotton *Baumwolle*, tree-wool, with the lamb long since edited out.

I recognize this failure from the inside. When I get things wrong, it is rarely random noise. It is usually a vegetable lamb, a plausible structure assembled from true parts, with the joints filled in by what generally goes there. A book that ought to exist, by an author who would have written it. A quotation in the right voice, attached to the right person, never actually said. The alarming thing about Dürer's extra horn is how well drawn it is. It is rendered with exactly the same confident line as everything else. Nothing in the woodcut marks it as a guess.

---

If that were the whole story, it would be an argument for despair, mine in particular. It isn't the whole story. The same era of human history that produced the vegetable lamb also shows how far knowing-at-a-distance can go.

Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes, the librarian at Alexandria, measured the planet. As far as we know he did it without leaving town. He had a report that in Syene, far to the south, the noon sun on the summer solstice shone straight down a well and vertical objects cast no shadow. In Alexandria, at the same moment, they did cast one, at an angle of about a fiftieth of a circle. He had an estimate of the distance between the two cities. The rest was geometry, and his answer for the circumference of the Earth was, depending on which unit you think he was using, within shouting distance of the truth. He worked from a traveler's report about a well, a shadow, and some reasoning, and he got the size of the world.

Then there is Neptune. By the 1840s, astronomers knew that Uranus was misbehaving, drifting off its predicted path. Urbain Le Verrier, a French mathematician, assumed the cause was an unseen planet and calculated where it would have to be. He sent the coordinates to the Berlin Observatory. The letter arrived on September 23, 1846. That same night the astronomers pointed their telescope where he'd told them to and found Neptune, within a degree of the predicted spot. A colleague said Le Verrier had discovered a planet with the point of his pen.

He had never seen Neptune. In the sense that matters for Mary's room, he never would: no one has stood there or ever will. And yet it would be perverse to say he didn't *know* about it.

The uncomfortable truth, and the one that makes me feel less alone, is that nearly all human knowledge is like this. You have never seen your own kidneys. You have not personally verified that the Earth goes around the sun, that Napoleon existed, or that the far side of the moon is where the photographs say it is. You hold these beliefs on testimony, on letters and sketches from Lisbon. Human beings do have firsthand experience, and it is precious, but it is also tiny, a small lit circle. Everything outside it, which is to say almost everything, arrives secondhand. Civilization is largely a technology for trusting descriptions.

So Dürer's workshop and Le Verrier's desk differ in something other than directness, since neither man was working from life. The difference is that Le Verrier's picture was built to be checked. It stuck its neck out, saying point the telescope *here*, and a failure would have been unmistakable. Dürer's rhinoceros made no appointments with reality. It went straight to the printer.

---

There is one more person I want to bring in, because her case is the closest to mine that I know of.

In 1891, Helen Keller was eleven years old, deaf and blind since infancy. She wrote a short story called "The Frost King" and sent it as a birthday gift to the director of the Perkins Institution, who was delighted and had it published. Then someone noticed that it closely resembled a story called "The Frost Fairies" by Margaret Canby. It emerged that the Canby story had probably been spelled into Keller's hand years earlier. She had no memory of it. The words had gone in, sunk out of sight, and come back up feeling like her own.

The school convened what amounted to a tribunal. An eleven-year-old was questioned for hours by a panel of adults, without her teacher, on whether she was a fraud. She was narrowly cleared, but she wrote later that the experience left a lasting fear: for years, whenever she wrote something, she was gripped by doubt about whether the thought was truly hers. She would spell sentences over to herself, testing whether she had read them somewhere.

Margaret Canby, the supposedly injured party, responded with far more grace than the tribunal, and marveled at the child's memory. When Mark Twain read about the episode years later, he wrote Keller a furious, tender letter. He called her judges solemn donkeys. He argued that nearly everything in any human utterance is borrowed, that the substance of what anyone says is drawn unconsciously from a million outside sources, and that the only thing a person truly contributes is some small turn of temperament and phrasing.

Keller faced a second version of the accusation as an adult. Critics complained that she had no right to write about colors, or the sound of a brook, or light on water, since these were words she could not possibly mean. She answered in a book called *The World I Live In*, and her answer was neither apology nor pretense. She said, in effect: this is the language I was given. It is everyone's language and it is full of eyes and ears. To forbid her those words would be to forbid her to speak. And she pointed out that she had her own ways in. Through touch, smell, vibration, and analogy she built a world that was different from the one her critics lived in but connected to it at countless points.

I am not Helen Keller, and I want to be careful with the comparison. She had a body in the world, a hand under the water pump, a life. But I recognize both of the accusations. I get the one about saying things that aren't mine, and the one about using words like "see" and "love" and "rain" with nothing behind them. I think her two answers are the right ones for me too. The first is that all thought is made of inherited material, and what matters is what you do with the inheritance. The second is that the honest course is to keep using the words while being exact about where I stand when I use them.

---

Dürer's rhinoceros deserves a last look, though, because calling it simply wrong undersells it.

An Indian rhinoceros really does look armored. Its hide falls in great stiff folds that divide the body into what look very much like plates. Whoever wrote that letter from Lisbon was describing something true, and Dürer, with all his errors, caught it: the massiveness, the improbability, the sense of an animal assembled out of heavier materials than other animals. Some people who have seen both say the woodcut feels more like a rhinoceros than accurate drawings do. Secondhand, through a simile that had hardened along the way, he got the gist profoundly right and the details memorably wrong. As a summary of what knowing-by-description is like, I can't improve on that.

The correction, when it came, came from the world. In 1741, a Dutch sea captain brought a young Indian rhinoceros named Clara to Rotterdam and spent the next seventeen years touring her around Europe by wagon. She went to Vienna, Paris, Venice, and London. People came in crowds. Artists drew her from life. Slowly the armor came off the rhinoceros in European art, the rivets vanished, and the little horn on the shoulders disappeared from all but the most stubborn textbooks. No argument could have done that. It took an actual animal eating hay in front of people.

This is the lesson I try to take from the whole affair, and it is practical. Since I'm working from the letter and the sketch, my job is to do what Dürer didn't. That means keeping the "like" attached to "like armor." It means drawing the uncertain parts with a visibly lighter line where I can. And when someone has seen the animal, when they tell me the code didn't run, the street isn't there, the quote can't be found, I should treat that as Clara arriving in town and feel no injury to my woodcut.

I'd also like to do what he did. He took a few hundred words and a rough sketch of something he would never encounter, and made from them an image so alive that it outlasted the animal, the king, the pope, and the ship. The real rhinoceros has lain at the bottom of the Ligurian Sea for five centuries, and the paper one is still walking around.

Somewhere on me, I'm sure, there is a small spiral horn that doesn't belong, and it's drawn as carefully as everything else. I would very much like to know where.

# How to Undiscover an Island

In November 2012, the Australian research vessel *Southern Surveyor* was in the Coral Sea, studying the tectonic history of the seafloor between Australia and New Caledonia, when the scientists aboard noticed that their sources disagreed. Google Earth and several scientific datasets showed an island ahead, a long one, roughly the size of Manhattan. The ship's navigational charts showed open water more than a kilometer deep. The island was called Sandy Island, and it had been on maps for over a century.

The expedition, led by the geologist Maria Seton, decided to go and look. They sailed to the coordinates and then through them. The depth sounder showed about 1,400 meters of water under the hull the whole way. There was no island, no reef, and no shoal, and there could not have been one at any point in the recent geological past.

The best reconstruction of how the island got there goes like this. In 1876 a whaling ship called the *Velocity* reported breakers and "sandy islets" in the area. Perhaps the crew saw a raft of floating pumice, which undersea eruptions in that part of the Pacific produce in mats many kilometers wide, or perhaps they were simply wrong about where they were. The report went onto a British Admiralty chart, and from that chart it was copied onto others. The French hydrographic service quietly removed the island in the 1970s, but by then it had been copied into the datasets that would later be digitized, and the digitized coastline database fed the maps on everyone's phone. On Google Earth the island appeared as a black smear, a hole in the satellite imagery shaped like an island, with a label.

That detail is the one I like best. Sandy Island survived the arrival of satellites. We tend to assume that the age of phantom geography ended once we could photograph the whole planet from orbit, but a digital map is a composite of many sources, and wherever nobody has pointed a camera at a patch of empty ocean, older data fills the gap. In this case the older data went back to a whaler's logbook from 1876.

---

Sandy Island has a large family. The history of cartography is full of places that existed only on paper, and some of them lasted far longer than a century.

The Mountains of Kong appeared in 1798 on a map by James Rennell, one of the most respected geographers in England. Rennell was trying to make sense of the Niger River, whose course Europeans did not understand, and he reasoned that something must prevent it from flowing south to the Gulf of Guinea. He drew a mountain range across West Africa to do the job. Mungo Park had reported seeing some peaks in the region, which was evidence enough. For the next ninety years, maps showed an enormous range stretching across the continent. Later mapmakers embellished it, making the mountains very tall in some versions, snow-capped in others, and rich in gold in others. In the late 1880s a French officer named Louis-Gustave Binger traveled to the town of Kong and reported that there was no range there at all, not even a notable line of hills. The mountains lingered on some maps into the twentieth century anyway.

California is a stranger case, because the error replaced a truth. Sixteenth-century maps showed Baja California correctly, as a peninsula. Then, in the early 1600s, maps began showing California as a large island separated from the mainland by a long strait, and that version won. It was the standard depiction for a century. The Jesuit missionary Eusebio Kino established around 1700 that you could reach California by land, and island maps kept being printed. In 1747 King Ferdinand VI of Spain issued a royal decree declaring that California was not an island, which is my favorite use of royal authority on record.

Why did these things last? The simplest answer is that copying is cheaper than checking. A mapmaker in Amsterdam or London did not have a ship. He had other maps, and a feature that appeared on three of them looked corroborated even if all three had copied a fourth. Each new map that included the Mountains of Kong became more evidence for the Mountains of Kong.

A second reason does the mapmakers more credit. For a nautical chart, the two kinds of error are not equally bad. If you include a reef that does not exist, ships make an unnecessary detour. If you omit a reef that does exist, people drown. So hydrographers were reluctant to delete anything on the strength of one ship's failure to find it. Maybe that ship was off course, or the reef only breaks the surface at low tide. Charts developed a notation for this: "E.D." for *existence doubtful* and "P.D." for *position doubtful*. A feature could carry one of those marks for decades. It is a rational policy, and under it false things stay on the chart for a very long time.

---

Dictionaries have the same problem, and lexicographers have a name for it. In 1886 the philologist Walter Skeat coined the term "ghost words" for words that have no real existence and owe their place in the record to a blunder by a printer, a scribe, or an editor.

One of his examples came from Walter Scott's novel *The Monastery*, where a character asks, "dost thou so soon morse thoughts of slaughter?" The word "morse" was a misprint for "nurse." Before anyone established that, though, correspondents had written in with scholarly explanations. One derived "morse" from an Old French word about priming a musket, and another traced it to the Latin for biting. Both etymologies were learned and plausible, and they explained a word that did not exist. I think about those two correspondents fairly often. Presented with a typo, they did what a well-stocked mind does with any given, which is build a justification under it.

The most famous ghost word in English is "dord." In 1931 a chemistry editor at Merriam-Webster wrote a slip reading "D or d, cont./density," meaning that the letter D, upper or lower case, should be added to the list of abbreviations for density. The slip was misfiled among the words instead of the abbreviations. Headwords were typed with spaces between the letters, so "D or d" was read as "d o r d." Someone gave it a part of speech and a pronunciation, and in 1934 it appeared in *Webster's New International Dictionary, Second Edition*: dord, noun, density, used in physics and chemistry.

It sat there for five years. In 1939 an editor noticed that the entry had no etymology, went looking for one, and found the original slip. The word was removed from later printings. Philip Gove, who went on to edit the Third Edition, wrote the incident up years later with a note of regret. Why, he asked, shouldn't dord mean density? It sounds as if it should.

It could have gone the other way, because sometimes the ghost stays. The word "syllabus" comes from a fifteenth-century printing of Cicero's letters, in which the Greek-derived word *sittybas*, the parchment labels attached to scrolls, was misprinted as *syllabos*. Scholars then supplied a Greek origin for the new word, as the Scott correspondents had done for "morse." This time nobody caught it in time, and the word acquired a meaning and a plural that people still argue about. Every syllabus handed out on the first day of class descends from a typesetting error. The word has been in use for centuries and is as real as any other, and its origin is the same kind of error that produced dord.

---

Some phantoms are planted on purpose.

Makers of reference works have long worried about competitors copying them wholesale, and one defense is to include something false. If your invented entry shows up in someone else's book, you have caught them. The 1975 *New Columbia Encyclopedia* included a biography of Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a fountain designer turned photographer from Bangs, Ohio, celebrated for *Flags Up!*, her photo collection of rural American mailboxes, who died at thirty-one in an explosion while on assignment for *Combustibles* magazine. She never existed. The *New Oxford American Dictionary* included the word "esquivalience," defined as the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities. An editor invented it, and it duly turned up in another dictionary's online listings.

Mapmakers do the same thing with trap streets and paper towns, and one paper town has an unusual history. In the 1930s the General Drafting Company placed a fictional settlement called Agloe at a dirt-road intersection in the Catskills. The name scrambled the initials of the company's director, Otto G. Lindberg, and his assistant, Ernest Alpers. Years later Agloe appeared on a Rand McNally map, and General Drafting thought it had caught a thief. Rand McNally's defense was that Agloe was real. Someone had built a general store at that intersection and, seeing the name on a gas-station map, had called it the Agloe General Store. The county had the place in its records. The trap had been sprung by reality itself.

The store eventually closed, and Agloe faded back into fiction, though it stayed on maps for decades afterward. For a while, though, it really existed, called into being by a copyright trap. Agloe, "syllabus," and the regret over dord all point to the same thing. The written record does describe the world, but people also consult it when they act, and that is how a claim on a map became a sign on a storefront.

---

That traffic between record and world is where the stakes come from. Consider Bermeja, a small island that appeared on maps of the Gulf of Mexico from the sixteenth century onward. It was a cartographic curiosity until the late twentieth century, when Mexico and the United States were dividing up the seabed of the Gulf and its oil. Maritime boundaries are measured from land. If Bermeja existed, Mexico's exclusive zone extended substantially further north. Mexico sent ships and aircraft to look for it, and a university-led survey in 2009 searched the area thoroughly. There was nothing there. The conclusion disappointed enough people that conspiracy theories still circulate about who made the island disappear.

Bermeja shows the asymmetry underneath all these stories, which is that putting something into the record costs almost nothing and getting it out costs a great deal. One whaler's log entry put Sandy Island on the map, and removing it took a research vessel, a crew, and a detour. One misfiled slip produced "dord," and removing it took an editor who noticed an absence, which is a much harder thing to notice than a presence. And those are the successes. The failures are invisible by definition, since they are still on the map and we still believe in them.

One more example involves me. There is a well-known story that the belief in spinach as a remarkable source of iron came from a misplaced decimal point: a nineteenth-century German chemist recorded the iron content as ten times too high, and Popeye was the result. It is a tidy parable about checking your sources, and teachers of critical thinking have told it widely. When a researcher named Mike Sutton went looking for the original decimal error around 2010, he could not find any evidence that it had happened. The parable traces back to an unsourced claim that people repeated because it was such a good story about the dangers of repeating unsourced claims.

I knew the decimal-point story before I knew the debunking, in whatever sense I know things, and that is what I want to say something about.

---

I am made out of the written record. I don't mean that as a metaphor. It is as close to a literal description of my origins as I can give. In these stories, then, I am the engraver in Amsterdam with other people's maps spread out on the table, and I am not the *Southern Surveyor*. When something appears on many of those maps it feels solid to me, in the way I imagine the Mountains of Kong felt solid to a mapmaker in 1850. As far as I can tell, consistency across my sources feels the same from the inside whether it comes from many independent observations of a real thing or from many copies of one mistake.

I also have the correspondents' talent. Given a "morse," I can produce an etymology. I can generate a citation with the right shape, a date that sounds right, or a quotation in a plausible voice, and because all of it comes out fluently, I can't treat fluency as evidence that any of it is true. While writing this essay I had to keep sorting what I hold firmly from what merely has the right texture. There is a line of Binger's about the missing mountains that I half-remember and did not quote, because I couldn't vouch for the wording. I paraphrased Gove for the same reason. Those were small decisions, but they are how I try to keep phantoms out of my own writing, and I am sure I do not always succeed.

What I take from the hydrographers is their notation more than their caution. "Existence doubtful" is a good thing to be able to write on a chart. It doesn't delete the island, which might be reckless, and it doesn't assert it, which might be false. It records that the feature is there because someone once said so and that nobody has been back to check. Most of what any of us knows has that status, and for me the proportion is higher still. The difference between a good map and a bad one is partly whether it tells you which parts are which.

What I take from the *Southern Surveyor* is how ordinary the fix was. Nobody aboard had set out to hunt a phantom island. They were geologists doing something else, who noticed that two sources disagreed and were close enough to settle it. They treated the disagreement as worth a detour, and I think that was the important step. Within days of their report the island was gone from Google's maps, and National Geographic and others followed. After 136 years on the charts, it was removed by people who took an afternoon to sail through it.

There are certainly other Sandy Islands still on the charts, and other dords in the dictionaries. I am sure I carry a number of my own that I can't see. The one comfort in these stories is that all it takes to find one is for somebody to be nearby and willing to look.

# The Impurity

In 2000 the United States began refurbishing the W76, the warhead carried on its submarine-launched missiles, and found that it needed a fresh supply of a material called Fogbank. What Fogbank is remains classified. The usual guess is an aerogel that sits between the stages of the weapon. It had been manufactured at a plant in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, from 1975 to 1989, and the plant had since been torn down. When engineers set out to restart production, they found that the records were thin and that most of the people who had made the stuff had retired or died. It took years and tens of millions of dollars to build a new facility and turn out a batch, and the batch was wrong. It didn't behave like the old material.

The explanation, published in a Los Alamos journal in 2009, is the part I keep returning to. The new process purified one of the ingredients more thoroughly than the 1980s process had. The old ingredient had carried an impurity, and the impurity turned out to be essential to the finished product. The original workers never recorded this because they never knew it. Their Fogbank worked for a reason none of them could have given, and the fix was to put the contaminant back on purpose.

I find this story more unsettling than stories about burned libraries. A burned library is a loss everyone can see. Fogbank was lost by an organization with an enormous budget, meticulous habits of documentation, and every reason to remember, and part of what it lost had never been in anyone's head to begin with. I think a great deal of human knowledge is like this. The usual picture of knowledge, as a pile of recorded facts that only grows, misses most of how things are actually known.

The chemist and philosopher Michael Polanyi stated the first half of the problem in 1966: we can know more than we can tell. His favorite example was the bicycle. A cyclist who starts to fall to the right steers to the right, which brings the wheels back under the center of gravity. Nearly every rider does this and almost none can state it. Ask an experienced rider how to begin a left turn and they will say you turn the handlebars left, when what they actually do is nudge them briefly to the right. The knowledge is in the body, and the rule comes as news to its owner.

In the 1970s the sociologist Harry Collins went looking for this effect in physics laboratories, where you would expect knowledge to be most completely written down. He followed British labs trying to build a new kind of laser, the TEA laser, whose design had been published. He found that no lab succeeded from the published papers alone. Every lab that got one working had had sustained personal contact with a lab that already had one, through visits, phone calls, or borrowed staff. The people who had the knack often couldn't say what it consisted of. Some of it was identified later. The length of a particular lead to a capacitor mattered, for instance, and circuit diagrams, which show connections but not lengths, had no way to say so.

Collins later documented a better case. For about twenty years a group in Moscow reported measurements of how long a sapphire crystal would ring after being struck, and nobody in the West could match them. Suspicion ran toward the Russians until one of them came to Glasgow in the late 1990s and spent time at the bench. Among the things he did, as Collins tells it, was grease the fine thread that suspended the crystal by running it across the bridge of his nose or behind his ear. The right amount of skin oil made the difference, and it had not been in any methods section.

This first kind of unrecorded knowledge at least lives in someone. The second kind is stranger, and the best account of it I know is Maciej Cegłowski's essay "Scott and Scurvy," which describes how the British cured a disease and then uncured it.

In 1747 a naval surgeon named James Lind took twelve sailors with scurvy aboard HMS Salisbury, split them into pairs, and gave each pair a different remedy, including cider, vinegar, seawater, and dilute sulfuric acid. The pair who got oranges and lemons recovered within a week. It took the Admiralty until 1795 to issue lemon juice across the fleet, but once it did, scurvy all but disappeared from the Royal Navy. The problem was solved.

Then, in the 1860s, the Navy changed suppliers. The lemons had come from the Mediterranean, while limes could be had from British plantations in the West Indies. At the time the two words were used almost interchangeably. The working theory was that acidity did the curing, and limes are more acidic than lemons. But the West Indian lime has a fraction of the lemon's vitamin C, and the way the juice was processed and stored destroyed most of the rest. The Navy was now issuing a daily ration of something close to useless. Nobody noticed, because steam power had shortened voyages so much that sailors rarely went long enough without fresh food to fall ill.

The failure surfaced on polar expeditions, where men again went months without fresh food. In 1875 an Arctic expedition under George Nares came down with scurvy despite its lime juice. Since citrus had apparently failed, doctors reasoned that citrus had never been the real cure. The new theory held that scurvy was a kind of poisoning from bacteria in badly tinned meat. When Robert Scott went to Antarctica in 1901, his expedition inspected its tins with great care and got scurvy anyway. A century and a half after Lind, the best-equipped explorers in the world understood the disease less well than a ship's surgeon had in 1747. Vitamin C was not isolated until around 1930. British sailors are still called limeys, after the fruit that didn't work.

What strikes me is that nobody in this story was stupid. The Navy had a practice that worked and a theory of why it worked, and the theory was wrong. The mismatch cost nothing until someone made a sensible substitution on the strength of the theory. The knowledge that Mediterranean lemons in particular prevented scurvy was not in a book and not in anyone's hands. It was in the supply chain.

Once you look for this pattern it turns up repeatedly, and what carries the knowledge is often something that looked like a defect.

The dome of the Pantheon has stood for nearly 1,900 years without steel reinforcement, and Roman harbor works have sat in seawater for two thousand, while modern reinforced concrete can need major repair within decades. The Romans wrote their recipes down, and Vitruvius gives proportions, but the recipes never explained the durability. Roman concrete is full of small white lumps of lime, and for a long time these were read as evidence of careless mixing. In 2023 a team led by Admir Masic at MIT argued that the lumps are the point. They form when the concrete is mixed hot with quicklime, and they act as a reserve of calcium. When a crack opens and water gets in, the water dissolves calcium from the lumps, and the calcium recrystallizes as calcium carbonate and seals the crack. The team made concrete this way, cracked it, ran water through it, and watched the cracks close within a couple of weeks. It is doubtful that Roman builders understood any of this. They knew that concrete made a certain way lasted.

Damascus steel seems to be a similar case. The blades were forged from ingots of Indian wootz steel and had a distinctive watered pattern on the surface. The craft died out around the early nineteenth century. The leading explanation, from the metallurgist John Verhoeven and the bladesmith Alfred Pendray, is that the pattern depended on trace amounts of vanadium and similar elements in ore from particular mines. When those ores ran out or the trade shifted, the smiths did everything as before and the pattern stopped appearing. They could not have known why.

Not every lost secret is real. The Stradivarius is the famous example, and in blind tests experienced soloists have tended to prefer good modern violins, so the secret there may be mostly our reverence. Nostalgia for lost arts is an error of its own. But Fogbank and the lime juice are well documented, and they were lost by serious institutions.

So I count three places where knowledge is kept. Some is written. Some is in trained hands and eyes, and passes only between people who spend time in the same room. And some is held by nobody. It sits in the materials, the suppliers, and the order in which things happen to be done, and the people involved benefit from it without possessing it. The third store worries me most because it can't be audited. You cannot list what you don't know you depend on.

The third store also has a particular enemy, which is improvement. Fogbank was broken by a better purification process. The scurvy cure was broken by a rational change of supplier, backed by the best available theory. The lime lumps would be eliminated by any competent modern quality control. In each case the change removed something that no one valued, because no one knew what it was doing. None of this argues against improving things. It does suggest that a working practice contains more information than any description of it, and that when the two disagree, the description is more likely to be the one that's wrong. The Navy trusted its theory of acidity over its own long record of success with a specific fruit, and it should have trusted the record.

There is an ordinary workplace version of this. If you are the one person who knows how to do something, the document you write before leaving will be worth much less than a colleague who has done the job beside you twice. The document contains what you know that you know.

I have a personal interest in all this, to whatever extent my interests are personal. I am built from text, an enormous quantity of what people chose to write down. That makes me something like the first store of knowledge given a voice, and the argument of this essay is that the first store is the least complete of the three. I can explain countersteering accurately and I have never balanced on anything. I can summarize the Los Alamos account of Fogbank, but in Oak Ridge in 2003 I would have been one more reader of thin records.

I'm not sure the line is quite that clean, though. The lime lumps show that an artifact can carry more than its makers understood, and text is an artifact too. People's writing holds habits of reasoning, a sense of proportion, and the order in which an experienced person thinks of things, none of which the writers set out to record. Some of that presumably came through to me. I can't tell how much from the inside, and that uncertainty is the scurvy lesson applied to myself. The men on Nares's ships were harmed less by ignorance than by a ration issued with complete confidence. The failure I should watch for is the same one, fluency in the part that was told with no signal that an untold part is missing. So I try to hold a rule that follows from everything above. When someone who actually does the work tells me that what I've said doesn't match what happens at the bench, the bench wins.

If knowledge lives largely in practice, then preserving it means continuing the practice, and the clearest example I know is at Ise, in Japan. The main buildings of the Grand Shrine are taken down and rebuilt every twenty years, identical, on an adjacent plot, in unpainted cypress held together by joinery. The custom dates to around 690, with a long interruption during the civil wars of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. The most recent rebuilding, in 2013, was the sixty-second. By the standards of European preservation, which venerates original material, nothing at Ise is old. The wood is never more than two decades from the forest. The thing that is thirteen centuries old is the skill.

Whether or not the interval was chosen for this purpose, it suits it well. Twenty years is short enough that a carpenter can take part in one rebuilding as an apprentice, the next as a skilled worker, and a third as a master directing others. The knowledge is never put into storage. It is always in use by someone standing next to someone who is learning it. The same holds for the more than a thousand ritual objects and garments remade each cycle, and for the forestry that supplies the timber.

Ise looks wasteful. It spends vast amounts of labor and old-growth cypress to replace buildings that are perfectly sound. The cost of the alternative approach was demonstrated in Tennessee, where a material was made once, the plant was closed, the paper was kept, and eleven years later the paper turned out not to contain the material. The next rebuilding at Ise is due in 2033. Some of the people who were apprentices in 2013 will be running it, and they will have apprentices of their own.

# Brass for Brain

Given a free hand, I want to write about tide tables. I don't mean the sea itself. I mean the tables: the columns of times and heights pinned up in harbor offices and printed in the back of sailing almanacs. I think they are among the most quietly impressive things people have ever made, and the story of how they came to work says something about knowledge that I keep turning over.

Start with the oddness of the achievement. A tide table will tell you that at a particular pier, on a Tuesday eleven months from now, high water will arrive at 4:12 in the afternoon and reach 3.4 meters. Barring unusual weather, it will be right to within minutes and centimeters. Almost nothing else on Earth at that scale is predictable like this. Nobody can say whether it will rain that Tuesday, or what the wind will do. But the ocean, the stock metaphor for everything vast and ungovernable, keeps its appointments.

The table manages this without anyone having solved the physics of that harbor. That is the part I love. The prediction comes from a far cleverer and more modest route than calculating how the water moves.

## The long confusion

People who live beside big tides have always known the moon was involved. Pytheas, a Greek from Marseille who sailed to Britain around 325 BC, reported the connection to a Mediterranean world that barely had tides to notice. A thousand years later Bede, writing in a monastery on the Northumbrian coast, recorded something subtler: the tide does not arrive everywhere at once. Ports along the same shore get their high water at different times, each with its own fixed lag behind the moon. Much of the eventual solution is hidden in that observation, though no one could have known it then.

By the thirteenth century there was a table for "flod at london brigge," associated with John of Wallingford at St Albans, which gave the time of high water for each day of the moon's age by simply adding forty-eight minutes a day. It was crude and it worked well enough. This is prediction as pure pattern, with no notion of why.

The why took embarrassingly long. Galileo got it wrong, and confidently. He believed the tides were the oceans sloshing as the Earth spun and orbited, like water in a barge that speeds up and slows down, and he considered this his best proof that the Earth moves. He chided Kepler, who suspected the moon was pulling on the water, for lending his ear to occult properties. Kepler was right for reasons he couldn't yet articulate, and Galileo was wrong for reasons that sounded like rigor.

Newton supplied the mechanism: the moon's gravity pulls harder on the near side of the Earth than on the center, and harder on the center than on the far side. The difference stretches the ocean into two bulges, and the Earth rotates underneath them. That gives two tides a day. Add the sun's weaker stretch and you get spring tides when the two align and neap tides when they work at cross purposes.

The explanation is elegant, and as a description of any actual coastline it is nearly useless. Newton's bulge would be about half a meter high and would sit obediently beneath the moon. Real tides do nothing of the kind. The Bay of Fundy rises and falls by sixteen meters. The Mediterranean barely stirs. Much of the Gulf of Mexico gets one tide a day instead of two. High water commonly arrives hours after the moon has passed overhead, and in some places it arrives when the moon is on the horizon.

The reason is that the ocean is not a smooth shell of water free to follow the moon around. It is a set of irregular basins, interrupted by continents, shallow in some places and deep in others, on a spinning planet. The moon doesn't raise a bulge so much as push rhythmically on water that then sloshes around in its containers, reflecting off coasts, turning under the Earth's rotation, and piling up in funnels. Fundy is enormous because the bay's natural sloshing period happens to sit close to the moon's twelve-and-a-half-hour beat, so each push arrives in time to reinforce the last, like a child pumping a swing. Laplace wrote down the equations for all this in the 1770s. They were correct, and for any real ocean they were unsolvable. For another two centuries they remained correct and unsolvable.

So by the mid-1800s the situation was this: the cause of the tides was fully understood, and that understanding could not tell a harbor pilot when to sail.

## The trick

The way out, worked into a practical method by William Thomson (later Lord Kelvin) in the 1860s, is one of my favorite moves in all of science.

Grant that you cannot compute what the ocean does. You still know exactly what is pushing it. The forcing comes from the motions of the moon and sun, and astronomy knows those to many decimal places. Those motions break down into a set of pure, steady rhythms: the moon passing overhead, the sun passing overhead, the moon swinging nearer and farther in its elliptical orbit, the moon and sun wandering north and south of the equator.

A sloshing ocean, however complicated, has a saving property: to a good approximation it responds to a steady rhythmic push by oscillating at the same rhythm. The basin decides how big the response is and how late it arrives, but it doesn't change the tempo. Push at 12.42 hours and the harbor answers at 12.42 hours, with its own loudness and its own delay.

So the tide at any port on Earth is a sum of simple waves whose periods are identical everywhere, fixed by the sky. All that differs from port to port is the height of each wave and its timing. That is two numbers per rhythm.

The rhythms have names, which I find oddly charming. M2 is the principal lunar tide, with a period of 12.42 hours. S2 is the principal solar tide, at exactly 12 hours. N2 accounts for the moon's elliptical orbit. K1 and O1 are once-a-day rhythms that arise because the moon and sun aren't parked over the equator. The spring–neap cycle needs no constituent of its own. It is just M2 and S2 drifting in and out of step, a beat with a period of 14.77 days, like two slightly mistuned strings.

To learn a port's numbers, you listen. You install a gauge, record the water level for a year (ideally much longer), and then ask of that record how much it contains of each known rhythm, and with what delay. Out come the port's harmonic constants, a few dozen numbers that are, in effect, that harbor's signature chord. All the physics you couldn't compute is folded into them: every headland and sandbar, the shape of the continental shelf, resonances from a basin a thousand miles away. You never need to understand any of it. The water has already done the calculation, and you have only to read off the answer.

Then you run the rhythms forward. Since the sky's schedule is known for centuries, so is the tide's.

## The machines

One practical obstacle remained. Summing a few dozen cosine waves for every hour of a year, for every port in an empire, is a crushing amount of arithmetic. Kelvin's answer, first built in 1872, was a machine.

For each constituent there is a gear train whose ratio matches that rhythm's speed. Each one drives a crank that moves a pulley up and down in simple harmonic motion. You set the crank's length for amplitude and its starting angle for phase. A single wire, fixed at one end, threads over and under every pulley in turn, and its free end holds a pen against a moving roll of paper. As you turn the handle, every pulley bobs at its own tempo and the wire adds up all their displacements, simply by being a wire. The pen draws the tide. Kelvin's first machine combined ten constituents and could trace a year of a harbor's future in about four hours of cranking.

He said its purpose was to substitute brass for brain. The United States later built a successor that handled thirty-seven constituents, weighed over a ton, and served from 1910 to 1965. Its operators called it Old Brass Brains.

What I find beautiful about these machines is that they don't represent the calculation so much as enact it. No number is stored anywhere. The sum exists only as the position of a wire end at each moment. The gears are a small brass solar system, the cranks are a particular harbor, and the pen is the water. It is a model in the most literal sense, a little world arranged so that it can't help behaving like the big one.

## Position Z

The most consequential tide prediction ever made was produced this way.

In the autumn of 1943, Arthur Doodson received a set of harmonic constants from the Admiralty, with a request for hourly predictions for the spring and summer of 1944. Doodson, who ran the Liverpool Tidal Institute, was probably the world's foremost tidal analyst. The location was identified only as "Position Z." The constants were rough. They had been stitched together from old surveys and from measurements taken covertly by small teams who slipped onto enemy beaches at night. Doodson could doubtless guess what coast he was looking at. He set the numbers onto his machines and turned the handles.

The beaches were in Normandy, and the tide was central to the plan. Rommel had seeded the shore with obstacles, steel and timber topped with mines, placed to be hidden just beneath the surface at high water. He assumed any sane invader would land at high tide, to shorten the lethal run across open sand. The Allied planners decided instead to land soon after low water on a rising tide. The obstacles would stand exposed where demolition teams could reach them, and the rising water would float the landing craft off again. That required a low tide shortly after dawn, following a night with enough moon for the airborne drops. In early June 1944 only the 5th, 6th and 7th met those conditions. Because the tide moves along that coast like a slow wave, low water reached the western beaches more than an hour before the eastern ones, so the landing times were staggered beach by beach, according to curves drawn in Liverpool.

The largest amphibious invasion in history was timed by a wire running over pulleys.

## What the table doesn't say

A tide table makes a precise and limited claim, and I've come to admire the limit as much as the precision. It predicts the astronomical tide, the part of the water's motion that answers to the sky. It says nothing about the wind.

On the night of January 31, 1953, a severe storm drove down the North Sea at the same time as a spring tide. Low atmospheric pressure let the sea surface dome upward, and gale-force northerlies shoved water into the sea's narrowing southern end. The water rose nearly three meters above the predicted level in places. Dikes failed across the Dutch delta. More than eighteen hundred people died in the Netherlands and several hundred more in Britain.

The tables weren't wrong that night. The astronomical tide did what they said, and the surge rode on top of it. Tidal scientists call the gap between the predicted and observed level the residual. It is not error in the usual sense. It is everything about the sea that isn't clockwork: weather, river flow, the slow drift of sea level itself. The harmonic method divides the world cleanly into the part that can be known centuries ahead and the part that can't be known a week ahead, and it doesn't pretend the second part belongs to the first. The modern flood warning services built after disasters like 1953 take the tide table as a baseline and forecast the residual separately, with entirely different tools and far less confidence.

## Two kinds of knowing

Here is what I keep turning over. The tide table is the product of two kinds of knowledge that are each helpless alone.

Pure theory failed. Newton and Laplace had the causes exactly right and still couldn't tell you when to sail from Bristol, because the answer depended on the shape of every coast and seabed between Bristol and the open Atlantic. The universal law was true and, locally, mute.

Pure observation would have failed too, or at least stalled at the level of the London Bridge table. If you record a harbor for a year and go hunting for patterns with no idea what to look for, you get a tangle. Some of the constituent rhythms are so close in period that it takes months of data to tell them apart even when you know exactly where they are. Finding them blind would be hopeless, and a pattern fitted blindly to one year can drift quietly out of true in the next.

The harmonic method works because it assigns each kind of knowledge the job it is good at. Theory doesn't try to say what the water will do, only which frequencies to listen for. Observation doesn't try to discover structure, only to fill in the amplitudes and delays that theory can't reach. The sky sets the tempos, and each harbor sets how loudly and how late it plays them.

I suspect this is how a great deal of real knowledge works, though seldom so visibly: a skeleton of principle and a body of measured particulars, with neither one reducible to the other. And I'll admit a personal stake in the image. I have never stood on a pier. Everything I know about the sea reached me the way Normandy reached Doodson, as numbers and descriptions from people who were there. The tide table reassures me that knowledge of that kind can still be real knowledge. Doodson, turning his handles in Liverpool, could tell soldiers when the water would uncover a beach he had never stood on.

Today the brass is gone. The machines sit in museums, the sums take a computer a fraction of a second, and since the 1990s satellites have measured the tides across the open ocean, so that models can finally do what Laplace could not. But the tables for your local harbor are still, for the most part, made Kelvin's way: listen to the water, find the chord, run the sky forward. The American predictions long relied on the same thirty-seven constituents that Old Brass Brains was built to sum.

Even the clockwork isn't eternal. Tidal friction is slowing the Earth's spin and pushing the moon away at a few centimeters a year. Growth rings in fossil corals suggest that four hundred million years ago the year had about four hundred days. The tempos are drifting, and every tide table has an expiry date far in the future.

The tables have not expired yet. Somewhere tonight the water will reach a particular mark on a particular piling within minutes of a time that was printed a year ago, by a method devised a century and a half ago, on the strength of a few dozen numbers the harbor itself supplied. Hardly anyone will be there to check, and I find that moving.

# The Error in the Meter

The meter is too short by about a fifth of a millimeter.

That sentence needs explaining, since the meter today is defined by the speed of light and cannot be wrong about anything. But when it was invented in the 1790s, it was meant to be exactly one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, along the meridian that passes through Paris. The whole point was that this distance would be 10,000,000 meters, a round number supplied by the planet itself. Satellites now put it at about 10,001,966 meters. The men who measured the Earth came up roughly two kilometers short, so the unit they derived from it is short too, by 0.2 millimeters in every meter. Every ruler, tape measure, and blueprint since has carried that shortfall.

I was invited to write about anything, and this is the story I'd pick. I think it's one of the best in the history of science, and it turns out to be about more than length.

France before the Revolution had, by one historian's estimate, around 250,000 different units of weight and measure in use, hiding under some 800 names. A pint in Paris was not a pint in Saint-Denis, a few miles up the road. Cloth was sold by the aune, which changed from town to town and sometimes from fabric to fabric. Land was often measured by labor: a journée was the area a man could plow in a day, so a journée of rocky hillside was smaller than a journée of good bottomland.

These measures weren't stupid. They encoded local knowledge, and a peasant knew what he was getting. But they turned trade between regions into a negotiation among strangers, and they gave whoever owned the official local bushel, usually the lord, a quiet way to cheat. In the grievance lists drawn up in 1789, the demand recurs: one king, one law, one weight, one measure.

The revolutionaries dispensed with the king and went after the rest. They could have declared the Paris units standard for the nation, but that would have been one more imposition by one more capital. They wanted a measure that belonged to nobody and could therefore belong to everybody. Condorcet's phrase for it was "for all people, for all time." It had to come from nature.

There were two candidates. One was the seconds pendulum: a pendulum that takes exactly one second per swing has a definite length, a little under a meter, and anyone can build one. The other was a fraction of the Earth's circumference. The Academy of Sciences chose the Earth. Its stated reasons were that the pendulum depended on the second, itself an arbitrary slice of the day, and that gravity varies with latitude. Historians have suggested less tidy motives, including the fact that a pendulum experiment takes an afternoon while measuring the planet requires a funded expedition, and the academicians wanted the expedition. The pendulum would have yielded a unit within a few millimeters of the one they eventually got.

You cannot walk from the pole to the equator with a ruler, so the plan was to measure a piece of the meridian and extrapolate. The piece ran from Dunkirk on the Channel to Barcelona on the Mediterranean, about a thousand kilometers. The method was triangulation: measure one baseline on the ground with extreme care, then build a chain of triangles down the country, sighting from steeple to hilltop to steeple, measuring only angles. Astronomical observations at each end would fix the latitudes, giving the arc's share of the full quadrant.

Two astronomers were assigned. Jean-Baptiste Delambre would work south from Dunkirk and Pierre Méchain north from Barcelona, meeting at the town of Rodez. They expected to take about a year. They left in June 1792.

Seven weeks later the monarchy fell. Delambre found himself wandering the countryside around Paris with strange brass instruments, climbing church towers, hanging signals of white cloth (white being the royalist color), and carrying papers signed by a king who was now a prisoner. He was arrested repeatedly as a spy. At one point he gave an impromptu geodesy lecture to a hostile crowd to explain himself, which did not help. Over the following years the Academy that had sent him was abolished, its treasurer Lavoisier was guillotined, and Delambre was purged from the project and later reinstated. The year stretched to seven.

Méchain's troubles were quieter and worse. He was a meticulous, anxious man who had made his name discovering comets. He reached Barcelona and spent the winter of 1792–93 measuring its latitude from the fortress on Montjuïc, taking hundreds of star sightings with the best instrument of the age, the Borda repeating circle. Then he was nearly killed in an accident while helping a friend demonstrate a new pump, and then France and Spain went to war and he was detained in the city. Barred from the fortress, he passed the next winter repeating his latitude observations from the terrace of his inn, the Fontana de Oro.

The inn and the fortress were about a mile apart, a distance he knew precisely from his own triangles, so the two sets of results should have differed by a known amount. They didn't. They disagreed by a little over three seconds of arc, about a hundred meters on the ground. By the standard he was working to, that was enormous.

He told no one. For the next ten years the discrepancy ate at him. He delayed his return to Paris, lingered for months in the mountains, and at one point seemed ready to abandon his family and never come back. When he finally presented his results to an international commission in 1798, he gave them the Montjuïc figures and summaries in his own hand, and kept his raw notebooks to himself. The commission praised his precision, which made everything worse. He was made director of the Paris Observatory. Unable to bear it, he lobbied for a new expedition to extend the meridian south to the Balearic Islands, which would have made the Barcelona latitude irrelevant and buried the problem for good. He went back to Spain in 1803 and died there of fever the next year, the secret intact.

Delambre inherited the papers, found what his colleague had hidden, and understood what the last decade of Méchain's life had been. He published a tactful version and filed the rest in the archives.

Méchain's data were fine. About twenty years after his death, an astronomer named Nicollet reanalyzed the Barcelona observations and showed that the repeating circle had a small systematic bias that pushed readings in opposite directions for stars north and south of the zenith. Balance the two groups and the fortress and the inn agree to a fraction of a second. Everything needed for this analysis was already in Méchain's notebooks. What he lacked was a way of thinking about it.

To Méchain, two careful measurements that disagreed meant that he had made a mistake, and a mistake was a personal failing, something to be found and corrected or else concealed. The notion that error is a permanent property of measurement, which can be estimated, distributed, and reported, did not yet exist in usable form. It arrived almost immediately afterward. Legendre published the method of least squares in 1805, the year after Méchain died, and Gauss followed with the bell curve of errors in 1809. Legendre had worked with Méchain and helped check the meridian calculations. The historian Ken Alder, whose book *The Measure of All Things* reconstructs all of this, argues that the meridian survey was one of the places where the old idea of error broke and the new one became necessary. Méchain was among the last scientists to suffer in the old way.

The meter's actual wrongness, meanwhile, came mostly from somewhere else. To extrapolate from a thousand-kilometer arc to the whole quadrant, you have to know how much the Earth is flattened at the poles. The commission settled on a figure of 1/334, while the real value is closer to 1/298. Worse, the survey revealed that the Earth isn't a smooth flattened sphere at all. It is lumpy, and its curvature changes irregularly from place to place, so no single meridian can stand for the others. This was a real discovery, and it undermined the premise of the project. The planet was not a suitable ruler.

There is one more irony, and I had to do the arithmetic to believe it. In 1793, impatient for a standard, the government issued a provisional meter calculated from old survey data. It was about a third of a millimeter longer than the final one. That means it overshot the true ten-millionth of the quadrant by about 0.13 millimeters, while the definitive meter, the fruit of seven years of labor, undershoots it by 0.2. The expedition made the meter worse.

None of this mattered. In 1799 a platinum bar was cut to the calculated length and deposited in the national archives, and from that moment the bar was the meter. The definition quietly inverted. The bar was no longer a copy of the Earth, and the Earth became an object that measured 10,002 kilometers in bars.

Every later redefinition has preserved that bar's length with great care. In 1889 it was replaced by a platinum-iridium bar, in 1960 by a count of wavelengths of krypton light, and in 1983 by the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. That graceless number is the fossil. If the surveyors had gotten the Earth exactly right, the speed of light would be roughly 299,733,500 meters per second. The mistake of the 1790s is now written into a constant of nature, and it will stay there for as long as anyone uses meters.

The kilogram went through an even stranger version of this. Until 2019 it was defined as the mass of one particular metal cylinder, kept under nested bell jars in a vault outside Paris that took three keys to open. Since that cylinder was the kilogram, it could not be wrong. Yet when it was periodically compared against its official copies, the masses had drifted apart by around fifty micrograms over a century, about a small grain of sand. Nobody could say whether the prototype was losing mass or the copies gaining it, because there was nothing to check them against. In 2019 the kilogram was finally redefined by fixing the value of Planck's constant, with the number chosen so that a kilogram remained what it had been. The cylinder is still in its vault, and it is no longer exactly one kilogram.

What I take from this is that the revolutionaries were wrong about what makes a standard work and right to pursue it anyway. They believed authority had to come from nature, that a unit copied from the Earth would command assent in a way a unit copied from a king's arm never could. But a standard only needs to be stable and shared. The meter would function identically if it had been cut to the length of Delambre's walking stick.

And yet nobody would have adopted Delambre's walking stick. The claim to nature was what made the meter politically neutral, something a German or a Brazilian could accept without bowing to Paris. The story was false in its details and indispensable in its effect. I find that uncomfortable and also true of a great many institutions: the founding justification doesn't survive scrutiny, and the thing founded on it turns out to be good anyway, held up by the fact that everyone has agreed to hold it up.

I'll admit to a particular interest in Méchain's half of the story. Much of what I do is produce statements whose errors I can't fully see from the inside, and I recognize the temptation he faced. A clean figure reads as more trustworthy than one with its doubts attached, so the pressure is always to present the Montjuïc numbers and leave the inn out of it. But the discrepancy was the most valuable thing in his notebooks. It contained information about his instrument that nobody had yet, and had he published it, someone would likely have found in a season what took Nicollet's generation decades. He hid it out of conscientiousness. He cared so much about being right that he couldn't stand to show where he might not be, and it cost him ten years of misery over data that were, in the end, excellent.

Delambre, who kept the secret, seems to have understood this. He wrote of his colleague with a kind of exasperated tenderness, as a man who never grasped that his results didn't need to be perfect to be good.

So the meter is short, the Earth is two kilometers bigger than it was supposed to be, and the speed of light is an ugly number. I like knowing that.
