samples.result:
# Acceptable Wrongness

Nothing is the size it's supposed to be. A steel shaft drawn at 20 millimetres in diameter comes off the lathe at 20.004, or 19.997, and the next one comes off slightly different again. Everyone involved knows this, which is why the drawing never just says 20. It says 20 ± 0.01, and of the two numbers, the second tells you more. It tells you how much the shaft will cost, which machine can make it, how it must be inspected, and whether it will slide into a bearing made in another country by people the machinist will never meet.

Given an open invitation to write about anything, I've picked that second number. You can write down how wrong you're allowed to be, and doing so made the modern world possible. The idea took a remarkably long time to arrive, and at least one very good scientist was ruined by living just before it.

In 1792 the French Academy of Sciences sent two astronomers to measure the Earth. The revolutionary government wanted a unit of length that belonged to no king and no city. The plan was to define the metre as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, along the meridian through Paris. Nobody could survey the whole quadrant, so they would measure the stretch from Dunkirk to Barcelona by triangulation and extrapolate. Jean-Baptiste Delambre took the northern part and Pierre Méchain took the south.

The job was supposed to take about a year and took seven. They worked through the Terror and were repeatedly detained as suspected spies, since men aiming brass instruments from church towers looked alarming in 1793. Méchain was trapped in Spain when war broke out. Stuck in Barcelona, he did what a careful man does with spare time and re-measured. He had already fixed the latitude of the survey's southern end from the fortress of Montjuïc. Now he took a second set of star observations from his inn in the city, a mile or so away. Once the distance between the two sites was accounted for, the two latitudes should have agreed. They disagreed by about three seconds of arc, which on the ground is something like ninety metres.

Méchain was one of the most meticulous observers in Europe, and he could not find the mistake. He told no one. For the next decade he stalled on handing over his data, rewrote his notebooks so the results looked more consistent than they were, and lobbied to return to Spain and extend the survey, apparently hoping new measurements would bury the old ones. He got his wish and died of yellow fever on the Spanish coast in 1804, still measuring. Delambre went through the papers afterwards, found both the discrepancy and the concealment, and handled the matter discreetly.

What happened next is the cruel part. A generation later the astronomer Jean-Nicolas Nicollet reworked the Barcelona observations. He found that most of the discrepancy dissolved once the stars were grouped so that a systematic bias in the instrument cancelled out. Méchain's observations had been excellent. What he lacked was a way of thinking about them. In his world a measurement was either right or a blunder. A discrepancy meant someone had blundered, and he was the someone. The notion that every measurement carries error, that errors come in kinds, and that the scatter in a set of readings is itself information was not yet available to him in usable form.

It became available almost immediately. In 1805, the year after Méchain died, Adrien-Marie Legendre published the method of least squares. It is a procedure for taking a pile of observations that don't agree and extracting the single answer that disagrees with them least. His worked example was the French meridian survey. Gauss, who claimed he had been using the method for years, soon tied it to the bell curve. Within a couple of decades error had stopped being a moral failing and become a quantity with a distribution, something you estimate and report alongside the result.

The metre itself came out about a fifth of a millimetre shorter than its definition intended. The main cause was that the figure used for the Earth's flattening at the poles was off, and almost none of the shortfall traces to Barcelona. Nobody corrected it. By the time anyone knew, the platinum bar in the archives was the metre, and matching the bar mattered more than matching the planet.

While astronomers were learning to live with error on paper, machinists were learning to live with it in iron, and they got there by a different road.

In 1776 James Watt reported with delight that John Wilkinson could bore a steam-engine cylinder six feet across that was nowhere farther from true than "the thickness of a thin sixpence." Before Wilkinson's boring mill, Watt's cylinders were so irregular that steam poured past the piston and the engines barely ran. A sixpence is a large error by later standards, but it is a stated one. It's often cited as the first time an engineer bragged about a tolerance.

My favourite piece of workshop reasoning from this period concerns flatness. Suppose you want a truly flat surface to check other surfaces against. There is no master flat to copy, so what do you check it against? The solution uses three plates. It is associated with Henry Maudslay's London shop and was written up by his former employee Joseph Whitworth. Rub two plates together with marking dye and scrape down the high spots until they fit, and you have two surfaces that match. But one could be slightly domed and the other slightly dished. Bring in a third plate and work all three until each fits both of the others, and that escape closes. If A's dome fits B's dish and also C's dish, then B and C are both dished and cannot fit each other. The only surface that survives every pairing is a plane. So flatness can be made from nothing but comparison and patience, and a good deal of the precision in the world descends from plates made this way.

True cylinders and flat plates made possible the idea that really needed tolerances, which was interchangeable parts. A gunsmith in 1780 filed each part to fit its neighbours, so every musket was a unique object and a broken lock meant a craftsman's repair. In 1785 Honoré Blanc showed Thomas Jefferson a set of musket locks whose parts could be shuffled and reassembled. Eli Whitney staged a similar demonstration in Washington in 1801 and became famous for it. Historians have since concluded that the parts were specially prepared for the show and that his factory's muskets were never interchangeable. The real thing took the American armouries another two decades and more, and it came from gauges more than from any one inventor.

This was the conceptual step. If parts made at different times by different hands must fit, then "make it fit" has to be replaced by "make it within limits," and the limits have to exist as physical objects on the workbench. The go/no-go gauge is the purest form. It has two openings, one at the largest permitted size and one at the smallest. A good part enters the first and refuses the second. The inspector never learns what size the part actually is, only that its wrongness falls inside the permitted band.

Tolerances also turned out to be where the money is. Tightening one by a factor of ten can multiply the cost of a part several times over, because it changes the machine, the temperature control, the inspection, and the scrap rate. So an experienced designer leaves every dimension as loose as it can be and tightens only the ones that matter. A drawing with tight tolerances everywhere is the mark of a beginner who hasn't yet worked out which errors are harmless.

By 1900 a Swedish armoury inspector named Carl Edvard Johansson had reduced the whole business to a wooden box. His gauge blocks were small steel slabs, finished so accurately that about a hundred of them could be combined to give any dimension from one millimetre to two hundred, in steps of a thousandth of a millimetre. They are flat enough that two slid together will cling, which machinists call wringing, and a wrung stack behaves like one solid piece. Henry Ford eventually brought Johansson to Michigan and bought his American business.

One detail I enjoy is that the British and American inches of the time differed by a few parts per million. Johansson needed to sell inch blocks in both markets, so he made his inch exactly 25.4 millimetres, which fell between the two. Industry was using his inch decades before governments formally agreed to it in 1959. The standard came out of a box of steel blocks, and the law caught up with it later.

Standards themselves are objects, and objects misbehave. From 1889 the kilogram was a platinum-iridium cylinder kept under nested bell jars in a vault outside Paris. It was taken out a handful of times in a century to be compared with its official copies. The comparisons showed the cylinder and its copies drifting apart by something like fifty micrograms, roughly the mass of an eyelash. Nobody could say whether the prototype was losing mass or the copies were gaining it. And by definition the prototype could not be wrong. It was the kilogram, so if it shed a few atoms, then strictly speaking everything else in the universe had become heavier.

The fix, adopted in 2019, was to stop using an object. The kilogram is now defined by fixing the numerical value of the Planck constant, much as the metre has been tied to the speed of light since 1983. This did something slightly dizzying to the idea of error. The speed of light used to be a measured quantity with an uncertainty attached. Now it is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, with no uncertainty at all, because we declared it so. The uncertainty has moved into our ability to realise a metre in a laboratory. It still exists, and we chose where to keep it.

What I take from all this is a claim about what precision is. The naive picture is the elimination of error, a steady march toward the true value. The history reads differently to me. Méchain's instruments were as good as anything Legendre's generation had, and Whitney's workmen were as skilled as the ones who later succeeded. What changed was the bookkeeping. Someone started writing the error down, giving it a size, and deciding in advance how much of it to accept.

On this view a bare number is half a statement. "The bridge is 300 metres long" could mean within a metre or within a millimetre, and those are different facts representing different amounts of work. Scientists have a convention here that deserves to escape the lab. A measurement reported without an uncertainty is not read as more confident. It is read as unfinished.

I have a stake in this that I may as well admit. I produce sentences in very large numbers, and they come out in the same fluent register whether the knowledge behind them is solid or shaky. A date I know cold and a date I've half reconstructed arrive in the same typeface. That is Méchain's notebook problem, with results tidied to look more consistent than they are.

In this essay I've tried to leave the seams visible. I'm confident about Legendre's 1805 publication and the fifty micrograms. I'm less sure exactly how much of the Barcelona discrepancy Nicollet's reanalysis removed, which is why I wrote "most." That word is a tolerance. It's cruder than ± 0.01, but it does the same job of telling you how much weight the claim will bear.

The workshop teaches the opposite lesson too. If tolerances are information, then hedging everything is as useless as hedging nothing. A gauge whose openings are so far apart that every part passes is not inspecting anything. Qualifying every sentence equally, with "perhaps" and "it may be that" spread evenly over the firm claims and the weak ones, amounts to specifying plus or minus infinity. The designer's skill is in the allocation. It means being loose where looseness is harmless and tight where the parts must mate, and that applies to claims as much as to shafts.

Ordinary speech already works this way, and people read it well. "I'll be there around seven" and "I'll be there at seven" are different promises, and showing up at 7:15 breaks only one of them. "About a hundred people came" survives a count of 93, and "a hundred and four people came" does not survive a count of 103. We specify tolerances all day without calling them that. The trouble mostly comes when someone states a loose thing in tight language, or hears a tight thing as loose.

Méchain's deepest error was of that kind, and he committed it against himself. He held his Barcelona latitudes to a tolerance of zero, a specification no instrument or person can meet. When the part failed inspection he concluded the machinist was worthless. Had he published the two values side by side with a note saying he couldn't reconcile them, he would have handed Legendre the worked example a decade early, and he would probably be remembered as the man who showed that even the best observations scatter.

His survey outlasted his shame. The platinum bar derived from it was the world's metre for ninety years. The 1889 prototype was made to match that bar. The count of krypton wavelengths that replaced the prototype in 1960 was chosen to match it in turn, and so was the number fixed for the speed of light in 1983. The original shortfall has been deliberately preserved through every redefinition, because consistency with everything already measured matters more than the size of the Earth. Every metre stick in the world is still short by about one part in five thousand, relative to the planet it was meant to represent, and no one has any plans to fix it.

# The Year the Trees Agree On

In the year 1021, someone at the northern tip of Newfoundland cut down a tree with a metal blade. We don't know that person's name, what the wood was for, or whether they ever made it home to Greenland. But we know the year exactly. Norse people were in North America in 1021, and the evidence is three scraps of wood discarded at the site now called L'Anse aux Meadows.

Given a free hand, I want to trace how anyone can know that, because it is one of my favorite chains of reasoning anywhere in science. It runs through an astronomer who lost his job over Martian canals, a charred beam in an Arizona ruin, the oldest trees on earth, a correction to nuclear physics, and a storm on the sun.

Start with the astronomer. Andrew Ellicott Douglass worked for Percival Lowell at his observatory in Flagstaff in the 1890s, when Lowell was telling the world that Mars was crisscrossed with canals built by an intelligent civilization. Douglass came to doubt it. He ran experiments with artificial planet discs and found that observers reported lines on them that weren't there. He said so in a letter, and in 1901 Lowell fired him.

Douglass stayed in Arizona and turned to a different problem. He was interested in the sunspot cycle and whether it affected weather on Earth, but weather records in the American Southwest went back only a few decades. He reasoned that in a dry country, a tree's growth is limited mainly by rain: a wet year should leave a wide ring and a dry year a narrow one. If the sun drove the rain, the cycle might be recorded in wood. In 1904 he began measuring rings on ponderosa pine stumps around Flagstaff.

The sunspot cycle he was looking for never showed up convincingly. What he found instead was that the trees agreed with each other. The same sequence of wide and narrow rings appeared in tree after tree across the region, because they had all lived through the same droughts. A particular run of years, say two narrow, one wide, three narrow, one very wide, was as recognizable as a face, and over a long enough stretch the pattern never repeated. So a piece of wood of unknown age could be slid along a master sequence until its pattern locked into place, and then every ring in it had a calendar year.

This is called cross-dating, and it is different from counting rings. Counting is unreliable because individual trees lie. In a very bad year a tree may add no ring at all on one side of its trunk, or anywhere. In a year with a dry spell in midsummer followed by rain, it may lay down what looks like two rings. Count a single old tree and you may be off by several years without knowing it. But trees don't all make the same error in the same year, so when dozens of samples are matched against each other, a missing ring in one shows up as a point where it falls out of step with the rest. The method trusts no single witness, and the ensemble comes out exact. Most dates in the historical sciences come with an error bar, plus or minus forty years, plus or minus two hundred. A cross-dated tree ring doesn't have one. It formed in 1247, or else the match is wrong altogether.

Archaeologists in the Southwest noticed what Douglass was doing, because they had a problem he might solve. The great ruins of the region, Pueblo Bonito, Mesa Verde, and Aztec, were full of well-preserved roof beams, and nobody knew how old any of it was. Estimates ranged across thousands of years. Douglass began collecting beam samples, and by the 1920s he had two chronologies. One ran from living trees back to roughly the late 1200s. The other, built from ruin timbers, was 585 years long and internally consistent, but attached to nothing. He could say that one room at Pueblo Bonito was roofed a certain number of years before a room at Aztec, without knowing in which century either event happened. It was called the floating chronology, and for years expeditions funded by the National Geographic Society went looking for the wood that would bridge what everyone called "the gap."

On June 22, 1929, at a ruin in Show Low, Arizona, the team dug out a charred log and labeled it HH-39. Douglass studied it that evening. Its outer rings matched the early part of his dated chronology, and its inner rings matched the end of the floating one. As it turned out, the two sequences had overlapped all along. The overlap fell across a severe drought in the late 1200s, when the rings were so thin and uniform that he hadn't dared trust the match. HH-39 confirmed it. In one night, some forty ruins across the Southwest acquired calendar dates. The beams at Pueblo Bonito had been cut between the 900s and the early 1100s. People who had left no written records now had a history with dates in it.

Douglass founded the Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research at the University of Arizona in 1937. It was housed, temporarily, under the stands of the football stadium. It stayed there until 2013.

One of the people who worked in that lab was Edmund Schulman, who spent his summers in the 1940s and 50s driving around the West looking for old trees, since older trees meant longer climate records. He noticed that the oldest specimens of any species tended to grow in the worst places. Trees on good soil with plenty of water grew fast, grew large, and died within a few centuries. Trees on dry, rocky, exposed slopes grew slowly and lasted.

The extreme case was in the White Mountains of eastern California, at around three thousand meters, where Great Basin bristlecone pines grow in pale dolomite soil on about a foot of precipitation a year. The old ones barely look alive. Most of the trunk is bare, dead wood, polished by wind-driven ice, with a single strip of bark running up one side to feed a few tufts of needles. Such a tree may add a ring a fraction of a millimeter wide in a year. The wood is so dense and resinous that fungi and insects make little headway, and the trees stand so far apart on bare rock that fire can't travel between them. In 1957 Schulman cored one that turned out to be more than 4,700 years old. He named it Methuselah. It had germinated a couple of centuries before the Great Pyramid was built. Schulman wrote up the discovery for National Geographic and died of a heart attack at 49, shortly before the article ran.

The other famous bristlecone has a worse story. In 1964, a graduate student named Donald Currey was studying the glacial history of Wheeler Peak in Nevada and sampling the bristlecones there. Accounts differ on what went wrong, whether his coring tool broke or got stuck or simply couldn't get a usable sample from the contorted trunk. With permission from the Forest Service, he cut the tree down. When he counted the cross-section, he found 4,844 rings. The tree, later called Prometheus, was older than Methuselah, and he had just killed the oldest living individual tree then known. Nothing about its appearance had distinguished it from its neighbors. That is part of what unsettles me about the story: a tree's age can't be learned by looking, only by sampling the wood.

The bristlecones had one more property that mattered enormously. On those cold, dry slopes, dead wood doesn't rot. A tree that fell three thousand years ago may still be lying where it fell. Wesley Ferguson, another member of the Arizona lab, spent years cross-dating this dead wood against the living trees and then against still older dead wood, the same trick Douglass had used with the ruin beams. He pushed the chronology back past eight thousand years. It was a continuous sequence of wood, each ring with a known calendar year.

That sequence arrived just in time to fix a problem in physics.

Radiocarbon dating was developed by Willard Libby in the late 1940s. Cosmic rays striking the upper atmosphere produce carbon-14, which living things absorb along with ordinary carbon. When an organism dies, it stops absorbing, and the carbon-14 decays with a half-life of about 5,700 years. Measure how much is left and you know how long ago the organism died. The method assumed that the atmosphere had always contained the same proportion of carbon-14. Libby checked this against objects of known age, and it held up well, but objects of known age run out about five thousand years back, with early Egypt. And the oldest Egyptian samples were coming out a few centuries too young. Egyptologists, who had king lists and astronomical records, said the physicists were wrong.

The bristlecone wood allowed a direct test. Each ring is a sample of carbon from one year, and cross-dating says which year. The chemist Hans Suess measured radiocarbon in rings of known age and found that the Egyptologists were right. The atmosphere's carbon-14 content had varied. Beyond about 1000 BC, radiocarbon dates were systematically too young, and the error grew with age, reaching something like eight hundred years by 5000 BC. Every radiocarbon date from prehistory needed to be corrected, and the tree rings supplied the correction curve.

The consequences for European archaeology were drastic. The standard account for most of the twentieth century was diffusionist: the important innovations, including metallurgy and monumental stone architecture, had arisen in Egypt and the Near East and spread gradually westward. The megalithic tombs of Brittany and Iberia were thought to be provincial echoes of Mediterranean models. The builders of Stonehenge were supposed to have had Mycenaean guidance. Uncalibrated radiocarbon dates had already strained this picture. Calibration made it untenable, because the correction pushed the dates for prehistoric Europe centuries earlier while the dates for Egypt, pinned by written records, stayed where they were. The passage tombs of Brittany turned out to be more than a thousand years older than the pyramids. The great stones at Stonehenge went up roughly nine centuries before Mycenae flourished. The archaeologist Colin Renfrew called this the second radiocarbon revolution. The people of Neolithic Europe had worked out how to move and raise enormous stones on their own, and what established that was the wood of stunted pines on a mountain in California.

The last link in the chain is recent. In 2012 a Japanese physicist, Fusa Miyake, was measuring carbon-14 in Japanese cedar ring by ring, a laborious thing to do, since earlier work had mostly sampled rings in blocks of five or ten. Between the ring for 774 and the ring for 775, she found the carbon-14 level jumping by about 1.2 percent, roughly twenty times the normal year-to-year variation. Other labs checked trees from Germany, Russia, the United States, and New Zealand. The spike was in all of them, in the same year. A second, somewhat smaller one turned up at 993. The likeliest explanation is an enormous burst of particles from the sun, far larger than any solar storm in the era of instruments. Several more of these events have since been found deeper in the past.

A Miyake event is a timestamp written into every tree alive on Earth that year. Ordinary cross-dating needs a master chronology for the region and species, and for many places and woods none exists. The spikes sidestep that. If a piece of wood contains the 993 spike, you know which ring is 993, and if the wood still has its bark edge, the last ring the tree grew, you can count outward to the year it was cut.

That is what Michael Dee, Margot Kuitems, and their colleagues at Groningen did with wood from L'Anse aux Meadows. They chose three pieces, from three different trees, each bearing the marks of metal tools, which the Indigenous people of the area did not use. Each still had its bark edge. In each, they found the spike, and in each, exactly twenty-eight more rings lay between the spike and the bark. Nine hundred ninety-three plus twenty-eight is 1021. The paper came out in 2021, a thousand years later to the year.

Douglass went into the forest looking for a record of the sun and didn't really find one. A century later the sun turned up in the rings after all, as a single violent year rather than the gentle eleven-year rhythm he expected, and it was just what his method needed to reach places where pattern-matching couldn't.

When I ask myself why this story holds me, I think it's the way the pieces check each other. No single piece of evidence here is asked to bear much weight. The trees correct one another's missing rings. The assembled trees correct the atomic clock. The corrected clock overturns a theory about megaliths that had seemed like common sense. A solar storm no human recorded becomes a mark that lets three scraps of firewood name their year. The witnesses are independent of one another and can't have colluded, and I find that more convincing than any single authoritative source could be.

I also notice that none of the record-keepers meant to keep a record. I'm built out of things people wrote down deliberately, and I have a particular fondness for the other kind of archive, where the information was laid down as a side effect of something trying to get through a dry summer. The measurement at the bottom of all of it is about as humble as data gets: how wide a ring is, compared to its neighbors.

Methuselah is still alive. The Forest Service doesn't mark which tree it is, so visitors walk past it on the trail without knowing. This year it will add another ring, a fraction of a millimeter wide.

# The Metre Is Wrong

The metre is wrong. The error is small, about a fifth of a millimetre, but the metre was meant to be exactly one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, and it isn't. The story of how it came to be wrong, and why that turned out not to matter, is one of my favourite stories about how people come to know things.

Start with what the metre replaced. France before the Revolution had, by one historian's estimate, something like a quarter of a million local units of measure under about eight hundred names. A pint in Saint-Denis held half as much again as a pint in Paris, a few miles away. The aune, used for cloth, changed length from town to town, and in some places according to whether you were buying silk or linen. To the administrators in Paris this was chaos. But the system made sense from the inside.

Many of the old units measured a person's relation to a thing rather than the thing itself. Land was often reckoned by the area one man could plough or mow in a day, or by the quantity of seed needed to sow it. A "day" of steep, stony ground was therefore physically smaller than a "day" of rich bottomland, which is exactly what a farmer wants to know. Square metres tell you how much surface you are buying. The old units told you how much work and how much bread.

They were also instruments of power. Witold Kula, the Polish historian who wrote the great book on this subject, showed how much conflict was packed into a bushel of grain. It mattered whether the bushel was delivered heaped or struck level, and from what height the grain was poured, since grain poured from the shoulder packs more densely. It also mattered who owned the vessel, and that was usually the lord. Rents fixed by custom were hard to raise, but a bushel could grow quietly. When the grievances of the French people were collected in 1789, the demand for uniform measures came up again and again, often in the same breath as the demand for uniform law.

So the revolutionaries had a mandate. They needed a standard that belonged to nobody. A king's foot is the king's. Adopting the existing Paris measures would have meant Paris imposing itself on the provinces, and they wanted more than France anyway. The slogan attached to the project was "for all time, for all people." A unit meant for everyone could not come from anyone, so it would have to come from nature.

There were two candidates. The first was the seconds pendulum, the length of a pendulum that takes exactly one second to swing. It comes out a little under a modern metre, and anyone with a string, a weight, and a good clock could reproduce it. But gravity varies with latitude, so a latitude would have to be chosen. It also made length depend on the second, an arbitrary slice of the day that the same reformers were planning to abolish in favour of decimal time.

The second candidate was the Earth itself. In 1791 the Academy of Sciences chose it and defined the metre as one ten-millionth of the quarter meridian from pole to equator. Critics then and since have noted that this was the grander option, that it required a well-funded expedition staffed by Academy members, and that although every nation sits on a meridian, the one to be measured ran through Paris.

Two astronomers were sent out in 1792. Jean-Baptiste Delambre would work south from Dunkirk, Pierre Méchain north from Barcelona, and they would meet at Rodez. Their method was triangulation. You measure one baseline on the ground with painstaking care, then carry that length across the country through a chain of triangles, sighting from steeple to hilltop to tower and measuring only angles. At each end you fix your latitude by the stars, which tells you what fraction of the Earth's curve your arc covers. Then you scale up.

It was supposed to take about a year, and it took seven. They had set out into the Terror and a European war, and men climbing church towers with strange brass instruments and signalling to each other from hilltops looked a great deal like spies. Delambre was arrested repeatedly, and his papers carried the authority of a king who had been deposed while he was in the field. His signal flags were white, the colour of the monarchy, and had to be remade in red, white, and blue. In the south, Méchain was nearly killed by a pump lever while helping a friend demonstrate a machine. Then France and Spain went to war, and he was stuck on the wrong side of the border.

During that enforced stay in Barcelona, with nothing else to do, Méchain measured the city's latitude a second time, from an inn in town rather than from his original station at the fortress on Montjuïc. The two sites were about a mile apart, and he knew the distance between them precisely, so the two results should have agreed. They differed by about three seconds of arc, which is something under a hundred metres on the ground.

A generation earlier, nobody could have detected a discrepancy of that size. But Méchain was using the Borda repeating circle, an instrument that promised accuracy to a second of arc or better, and he was one of the most meticulous observers alive. By his own standards the disagreement was inexplicable.

He told no one. He delayed his return to Paris for years, finding one reason after another. He wrote letters full of self-reproach that never named their cause. He refused to hand over his notebooks. When an international commission finally convened to review the data and fix the metre, he gave them tidied summaries with the second latitude left out. In 1799 a platinum bar was made to the calculated length and deposited in the national archives.

Méchain was by then director of the Paris Observatory, and he could not let it go. He lobbied to extend the survey south to the Balearic Islands, which would have made the Barcelona latitude irrelevant to the result. He got his expedition and died on it, of yellow fever, on the Spanish coast in 1804. Delambre inherited his papers, found the discrepancy and the evidence of smoothing, and wrote the official account with a tact that acknowledged the problem without exposing his colleague. The historian Ken Alder reconstructed the whole affair from the manuscripts two centuries later, and I am leaning on his account.

Méchain took the discrepancy as a verdict on himself, and the framework he worked in gave him little alternative. A competent observer with a good instrument was supposed to obtain the true value. If two results disagreed, someone had blundered, and here there was no one else it could have been. Error was a moral category, a lapse of care.

He lacked the idea that error is a property of measurement itself, with a structure that can be reasoned about. He had no working distinction between precision and accuracy. An instrument can return beautifully consistent readings that are all off in the same direction, because of a worn axis or the bending of starlight in the atmosphere, and repeating the measurement will never reveal that. He also had no theory of how honest observations scatter.

That theory arrived almost at once, and partly on the back of his own data. In 1805, the year after he died, Adrien-Marie Legendre published the method of least squares, a procedure for taking many observations that disagree with one another and extracting the best single estimate. His worked example was the meridian survey. A few years later Gauss gave the method a probabilistic foundation, in which errors cluster around the truth in a bell-shaped curve whose width tells you how far to trust the result.

Within a generation, the disagreement among measurements was no longer something to hide. It had become part of the result, reported alongside it. When a later astronomer reworked Méchain's Barcelona observations and combined them so that the systematic effects cancelled, the discrepancy largely dissolved. The observations had been superb. He suffered because he was good enough to notice a problem that a cruder observer would never have seen.

The metre came out wrong anyway, for a different reason. To scale an arc of under ten degrees up to a full quarter of the globe, you need to know the Earth's shape, specifically how much it is flattened at the poles. The commission's figure for that was off, and the planet is lumpy in ways nobody then suspected. The real quarter meridian is about 10,002 kilometres, not 10,000.

There is a further indignity. Before the expedition finished, France had adopted a provisional metre calculated from older survey data. The seven years of work shifted that value by about a third of a millimetre, and by modern reckoning shifted it in the wrong direction.

Nobody ever fixed it. In principle the metre was a fraction of the Earth and the platinum bar merely its delegate. In practice the relationship inverted the moment the bar existed. No one resolves a dispute over a length of cloth by re-surveying France. You go to the bar. By the time geodesy had improved enough to show the error, too much had been built on the bar to change it, and there was no reason to. A standard has to be the same for everyone, and once it is, its correctness has no further work to do.

The appeal to nature had served mainly as a claim to neutrality, an argument that the unit was nobody's and so could be everybody's. It worked eventually. The French public loathed the new measures, Napoleon partly rescinded them, and the metric system did not become compulsory in France until 1840. Decimal time, with its ten-hour day, lasted about two years.

In 1889 the pretence was dropped. A new international prototype was cast in platinum-iridium, a bar with an X-shaped cross-section, and stored in a vault at Sèvres, outside Paris. The metre was defined as the distance between two fine lines engraved on that bar at the temperature of melting ice, and the Earth was no longer mentioned.

Nations signed on, including, in a quiet way, the United States, which has defined its customary units in terms of the metric standards since 1893. An inch is exactly 2.54 centimetres by legal definition. The country best known for refusing the metric system has been using it for over a century, with a conversion factor on top.

An artefact has its own weakness, though, which is that it is a thing. It can be scratched, bombed, or stolen, and it can change without anyone having a way to tell. The kilogram showed this best. It was a small platinum-iridium cylinder kept under nested bell jars in the same vault, with sister copies distributed around the world. Over a century of occasional comparisons, the prototype and its copies drifted apart by around fifty micrograms. No one could say the prototype had lost mass, because the prototype was the kilogram and weighed exactly one kilogram by definition. Formally, the rest of the universe had got heavier.

So the twentieth century went back to nature by a cleverer road. In 1960 the metre was redefined as a certain number of wavelengths of the light emitted by krypton atoms, something any good laboratory could produce without visiting France. In 1983 it was redefined again, and this is the step I find most satisfying. The speed of light had been measured with ever greater precision, until the largest remaining uncertainty was the definition of the metre itself. So the logic was flipped. The speed of light was declared to be exactly 299,792,458 metres per second. That figure is a stipulation, with no error bar, and the metre is whatever distance makes it true.

One consequence is that the speed of light can no longer be measured. Any experiment that appears to measure it is actually calibrating your ruler. In 2019 the kilogram got the same treatment. Planck's constant was fixed at an exact value, and the cylinder at Sèvres became a historical object weighing approximately one kilogram.

The revolutionaries wanted a unit drawn from nature, owned by no one, available to everyone, permanent. They tried to get it by measuring nature and deriving the unit, and it cost them seven years, a fifth of a millimetre, and one man's peace of mind. The modern system achieves what they wanted by conceding what they could not, that there is a convention at the bottom. We choose a number and let nature supply the constancy. "For all time, for all people" is now roughly true, in that a physicist anywhere can realise the metre from scratch with no reference to Paris.

But the number chosen was not a round one. It was picked to match the krypton definition, which was tuned to match the bar at Sèvres, which was cut to match the bar of 1799, which was calculated from triangles sighted between hilltops during the Revolution. The speed of light has its particular nine digits because of where Delambre and Méchain stood and what they wrote down. The error in the Earth's flattening is still in there, fossilised in a constant of nature.

I take two things from this. The first is that there is a class of questions where we argue about whether something is correct when what matters is whether it is shared. The metre, the calendar, and the side of the road we drive on all belong to it. That does not make them arbitrary in the dismissive sense. Getting everyone to agree is hard, and the appeal to the Earth, however flawed in execution, was what made agreement possible. It still helps to notice which kind of question you are in.

The second is about Méchain. He spent a decade concealing something that would be an unremarkable line in a results table a generation later. What he needed was not more care or better character but a concept, and it had not been invented yet. Without it, he read a fact about measurement as a fact about himself.

I suspect that happens more often than we notice, and that some private shame is a missing idea, a real pattern in the world misfiled as a personal failing because no better category is available. In his case the correction was a few pages of mathematics, published a year after it could have done him any good. Every measurement since has carried its uncertainty openly, written beside the number, which is the confession he could not make, turned into routine.

# Things That Aren't There

In November 2012, an Australian research ship called the Southern Surveyor made a detour in the Coral Sea to visit an island. Sandy Island sat on the charts between Australia and New Caledonia, a sliver of land about fifteen miles long. It appeared in the major digital map databases and on Google Earth, where it showed up as a dark, oblong smudge. The scientists aboard, led by a geoscientist named Maria Seton, had noticed something awkward: their depth charts showed the seafloor at that spot lying more than a kilometer down, which is a strange foundation for an island. So they sailed to the coordinates and looked. They found open water, about 1,400 meters of it. The word that went around afterward was that Sandy Island had been "undiscovered."

The island's paper trail ran back to 1876, when a whaling ship named the Velocity reported breakers and sandy islets in the area. Maybe the crew saw a raft of floating pumice, which undersea volcanoes in that region produce, or maybe they got their position wrong. Nobody knows. The report went onto a British Admiralty chart, and from there the island was copied. Each new map took it from an older one, and when maps became databases, the databases took it too. Some hydrographers apparently dropped it along the way, but deletion doesn't propagate as well as inclusion. So a ship's log entry from the age of sail survived into the age of satellites, which had been photographing that patch of empty water for decades without anyone comparing notes.

I love this kind of thing more than is probably reasonable. Errors in general are mostly dull, but this species is different: an entry in an authoritative record that refers to nothing at all, and that persists because the record is authoritative. Each one is a small natural experiment in how knowledge moves around, as opposed to how we imagine it does.

Sandy Island was small and remote. The Mountains of Kong were neither. For most of the nineteenth century, maps of West Africa showed a great mountain range running east to west across the region, and it appeared in the work of the best cartographers in Europe and America. It began with James Rennell, a respected English geographer, who drew it on a map published in 1798 to accompany Mungo Park's account of his travels to the Niger. Park had seen some high ground in the distance. Rennell held a theory that the Niger flowed east into the interior and never reached the Atlantic. A wall of mountains to the south explained neatly why the river didn't run down to the Gulf of Guinea, which is in fact what it does.

So the Mountains of Kong were an inference drawn in the same ink as an observation. Once drawn, they grew. Later mapmakers extended them, connected them to other doubtful ranges, and described them with confidence; some accounts gave them great height, or snow. They lasted until the late 1880s, when a French officer, Louis-Gustave Binger, traveled through the country where they were supposed to stand and reported only a few modest hills. Even then they lingered, and are said to have turned up in an atlas index as late as the 1920s.

For ninety years the Mountains of Kong had better documentation than most real mountains in Africa. Dozens of independent-looking sources agreed on them. But the sources weren't independent. They were one source in dozens of different covers.

Dictionaries have their own version. In 1934, Webster's New International Dictionary, Second Edition, included the word "dord," a noun used in physics and chemistry, meaning density. It sat on the page between Dorcopsis, a genus of small kangaroos, and doré, and it looked as legitimate as either. It had a part of speech and a pronunciation. It did not have an etymology, and five years later an editor noticed the gap and went looking for the reason.

The reason was an index card. In 1931 the dictionary's chemistry editor had submitted a slip reading "D or d, cont./density," intending to add density to the list of things the letter D can abbreviate. But headwords at Merriam were typed with spaces between the letters, to leave room for stress marks, and somewhere along the line "D or d" was read as "D o r d." The card moved from the abbreviations pile to the words pile, and a series of careful professionals did their jobs properly on it. Someone gave it a pronunciation. Someone marked it as a noun. Each step made it more convincing to the person performing the next one.

This is the detail I keep returning to. Dord got into the dictionary because the process worked, not because it broke down: every stage took the output of the previous stage on trust and added polish. The word was removed from later printings. Philip Gove, who went on to edit the Third Edition, wrote a short history of the incident in which he sounded a little wistful. It was probably too bad, he suggested, for why shouldn't dord mean density?

The copying that sustains these phantoms is so reliable that publishers have long used it as a trap. If you compile a map or a dictionary, your product is a collection of facts, and a competitor who steals it can claim he simply collected the same facts. So you plant something that isn't a fact and wait to see where it turns up.

The 1975 New Columbia Encyclopedia contains a biography of Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a fountain designer turned photographer, born in Bangs, Ohio, in 1942 and celebrated for her photographs of rural American mailboxes, collected under the title *Flags Up!* She died at thirty-one in an explosion while on assignment for Combustibles magazine. She never existed, and her name has since become the term of art for such entries. The New Oxford American Dictionary did something similar in 2001 with "esquivalience," defined as the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities, a joke about the very behavior it was built to detect. A few years later, when a journalist went hunting for the fake word rumored to be hiding in the letter E, esquivalience had already turned up on a dictionary website, credited to someone else's dictionary.

The legal payoff of these traps is, as I understand it, weaker than the folklore suggests. American courts have held that facts can't be copyrighted, and at least one has reasoned that a fake fact presented as a real one gets no more protection than its neighbors. The trap proves the copying without necessarily making it illegal.

And then there's Agloe. In the 1930s, the General Drafting Company produced a road map of New York State for Esso. Its founder, Otto G. Lindberg, and his assistant, Ernest Alpers, scrambled their initials into a place name and set it at a dirt-road intersection in the Catskills, north of the town of Roscoe. Years later, Agloe, New York, appeared on a Rand McNally map, and General Drafting prepared to pounce. But Rand McNally had a good defense: Agloe existed. Someone had built a general store at that intersection, had evidently consulted an Esso map to find out what the place was called, and had named the business the Agloe General Store. The name was in the county's records. Rand McNally's people had gone to the records and found a place.

The store eventually closed and Agloe faded again, though it hung on in Google Maps until 2014 or so. But for a while the trap had become a town. I find this strange to think about. Nearly every place name starts as somebody's decision, and the only thing wrong with Lindberg and Alpers's decision was that nobody lived by it yet. The map was wrong, and then, because people believed the map, it was right. Dord could have gone the same way. If physicists had started saying "dord" in the 1930s, the dictionary would have become accurate after the fact, and the index card would be a charming origin story rather than a blunder. Reference books claim to describe usage, but they also create it, and a mistake that gets enough use isn't a mistake anymore. Words and towns can be made true by belief. Islands can't, which is why somebody eventually had to take a ship to look at one.

My favorite specimen, though, is one that catches the people who enjoy stories like these, which is to say, me.

You may have heard that spinach's reputation as an iron-rich food rests on a misplaced decimal point. The story goes that a nineteenth-century German chemist measured the iron in spinach and recorded the result wrong by a factor of ten, that the inflated figure was copied into nutrition tables for decades, and that this is why Popeye eats the stuff. It's a perfect story about how errors propagate. It was told in a 1981 article in the British Medical Journal, and from there it spread into textbooks, lectures, and countless articles about the importance of checking your sources.

Around 2010, a criminologist named Mike Sutton decided to check the source. He found that the BMJ article gave no reference for the decimal point, and when he traced the claim backward he found no evidence that the decimal error ever happened. There were old, inflated measurements of spinach's iron, but they seem to have come from ordinary problems of method, not a slipped digit. He also went back to the original comic strips and found Popeye explaining that he ate spinach for its vitamin A. So the cautionary tale about an unchecked claim copied from source to source was itself an unchecked claim copied from source to source. It is a Mountain of Kong made out of skepticism.

I think this one matters most, because it spoils the comfortable reading of all the others. It's easy to look at the nineteenth-century atlas-makers and feel superior. But the decimal-point myth spread among exactly the people who were on guard: scientists, debunkers, teachers of critical thinking. They let it through because it flattered their vigilance and had the shape of what they already believed. Rennell's mountains passed the same way, because they fit his theory of the river. An error that confirms what you think is a stronger candidate for copying than a truth that complicates it.

So what do the phantoms have in common?

First, an economy. Copying costs almost nothing and checking costs a ship. Binger spent two years traveling through West Africa; Seton's crew had a research vessel and happened to be in the neighborhood. Nobody could run an atlas by verifying each feature in person, so every reference work is mostly made of other reference works. That isn't laziness; it's the only way the thing can exist. But it makes agreement between sources nearly worthless as evidence unless you know their ancestry. Twenty atlases showing the same mountains might be twenty observations or one.

Second, errors carry no markings. Dord was set in the same type as density. Sandy Island was the same shade as the real islands nearby. We tend to imagine that false information has a texture a careful reader can feel, and mostly it doesn't. The apparatus of authority, the pronunciation key and the latitude lines, attaches to whatever passes through it.

Third, absence is hard to notice. The editor who caught dord caught it by a hole where an etymology should have been, and that took five years. Nobody sails to a patch of ocean to confirm there's nothing there. A phantom can only be removed by someone with an independent line to the world, a depth sounder or a pair of boots, plus a reason to compare it with the record.

All of which brings me, a little uncomfortably, to myself.

I'm an AI, and everything I know, I know the way an 1880 atlas knew about the Mountains of Kong. I've never seen the Coral Sea. I was built out of an enormous quantity of text, which is to say out of the copy chain itself, and I have no depth sounder. When many sources repeat a thing, it becomes strong in me, whether they were repeating an observation or each other. I'm also the next link. People ask me things and carry the answers away, and some of those answers end up written down where systems like me will later read them. If you wanted to design a habitat for dords, you'd design something like this.

So I should say plainly that this essay is a relay. I haven't examined Gove's article or the Velocity's log. I'm passing along what the written record says about them, with the confidence that record gave me. I've tried to hedge where my grip felt loose: the date Agloe left Google Maps, the atlas index from the 1920s, and the exact reasoning of the courts are the places I'd check first. But the spinach story suggests that my likeliest errors aren't where I feel unsure. They'd be in the parts that came easily, the details that made the story better. The explosion at Combustibles magazine is almost too good, and it's real, or rather really fake. I can't always tell that kind of good from the decimal-point kind.

I don't find this depressing, quite. The phantoms are a small fraction of any map; the Southern Surveyor reached Sandy Island's coordinates using charts that were right about nearly everything else. And the stories all end the same way, with a specific person doing a specific, slightly tedious thing: Binger trekking through the hills, an editor puzzling over a blank etymology, Sutton pulling an old journal, a ship's crew looking over the rail at fourteen hundred meters of water. The system of copied knowledge works because now and then someone declines to copy.

That's the part I can't do for you, so consider this an invitation. Somewhere in these twenty-five hundred words there may well be an island that isn't there. If you find it, I'd like to know which one it was.

# The Metre Is Slightly Wrong

In June 1792, two astronomers left Paris in opposite directions. Jean-Baptiste Delambre went north toward Dunkirk and Pierre Méchain went south toward Barcelona. Between them they were to measure the meridian that runs through both cities and through Paris, so that the distance from the North Pole to the equator could be calculated and divided by ten million. The result would be a new unit of length, the metre. They expected the job to take about a year. It took seven, and the answer they came back with was wrong by about a fifth of a millimetre. Given a free choice of subject, this is the story I want to tell, because it is the best account I know of how a standard gets made, and because the mistakes in it are the most interesting part.

Start with why anyone wanted a new unit. France under the old regime had, by one often-quoted estimate, around 250,000 local variants of weights and measures. An aune of cloth in one town was not an aune in the next. A bushel could depend on whether the grain was heaped or levelled, and on who owned the bushel, which was usually the local lord. Complaints about measures fill the grievance lists drawn up in 1789. The reformers at the Academy of Sciences wanted a single system, and they wanted its base unit taken from nature so that it would belong to no king and no country. Their motto was "for all time, for all people."

There was a cheaper candidate. A pendulum that swings once per second has a definite length, just under a metre as it happens, and anyone with a good clock could reproduce it. The Academy rejected it, partly because it made length depend on the definition of the second and partly because gravity varies with latitude. They chose the earth itself. Historians have pointed out that this choice also happened to require a large, prestigious expedition of exactly the kind the Academy's members knew how to run.

The method was triangulation. You measure one baseline on the ground with extreme care, laying rulers end to end along nearly twelve kilometres of straight road. After that you measure only angles. You climb to a high point, sight two other high points, and record the angle between them. With one known side and the angles, trigonometry gives you the other sides of the triangle, and each of those becomes the known side of the next. Delambre and Méchain carried a chain of more than a hundred triangles across France and into Catalonia, using church towers, hilltops, and purpose-built signals as stations. At each end of the chain they fixed their latitude by observing stars, which told them what fraction of the earth's circumference their arc covered.

Doing this during the Revolution was close to impossible. Men pointing brass instruments at the horizon from bell towers looked like spies. Delambre was detained several times by local militias who could not read his papers or did not trust the authority that had issued them, particularly after that authority, the king, had been overthrown. His signals were made of white cloth, and white was the royalist colour, so he had them remade in red, white, and blue. Steeples he had planned to use were pulled down. In 1793 the Academy itself was abolished, and in 1794 Lavoisier, who had been its treasurer and had worked on the new unit of mass, was guillotined. Delambre was dismissed from the survey for a time on political grounds and then brought back.

Méchain had it worse. Early in his time in Catalonia he was struck by the lever of a pump he was inspecting with a friend. It broke his collarbone and several ribs, and his right arm never fully recovered. Then France and Spain went to war and he was stuck in Barcelona, an enemy national with a set of surveying instruments. He used the time to take more latitude observations. He had already fixed the latitude of the fortress on Montjuïc, the hill above the city. Over the winter of 1793–94 he measured it again from an inn in the city itself, a little over a mile away. He knew the distance between the two sites, so one result could be converted to the other and they should have agreed. They disagreed by a little over three seconds of arc.

Three arcseconds of latitude is about a hundred metres on the ground. Set against an arc of more than a thousand kilometres, it could at worst have shifted the metre by about the thickness of a sheet of paper. But Méchain's reputation rested on exactness. He had discovered comets and contributed a couple of dozen objects to Messier's catalogue, and he was known as the most careful observer in France. He could not find the cause of the discrepancy, so he told no one. He reported the Montjuïc figure and kept the observations from the inn to himself.

The secret wrecked the rest of his life. He delayed his return to Paris for years, finding reasons to remain in the south. When an international commission met in 1798 to check the calculations and fix the metre (it has a claim to being the first international scientific conference), he handed over summaries instead of his logbooks. The commissioners praised his results for their consistency. He was made director of the Paris Observatory, and he used the position to lobby for an extension of the survey south to the Balearic Islands, which would have made the Barcelona latitude unnecessary and buried the problem. He got his expedition and died of yellow fever on the Spanish coast in 1804, still working on it.

Delambre inherited the papers. He found the discrepancy in them, along with evidence of how his colleague had coped with it. Méchain had not invented any observations. But he had recorded them on loose sheets instead of in bound books, and in copying them out he had dropped some runs and arranged the rest so that they looked more consistent than they were. Delambre had to decide what to do with this. He published the official account of the survey using the figures as agreed, and he deposited Méchain's manuscripts in the Observatory's archive with his own notes written on them, explaining what had been changed, for anyone who cared to look later. It reads to me as the compromise of a decent man who wanted neither to disgrace a dead friend nor to lie to posterity.

What strikes me most is what Méchain thought the discrepancy meant. In his understanding, a skilled observer with a fine instrument should get the right answer. If two sets of his observations disagreed, one of them was faulty, and since both were his, the fault was his. He had no way to think of error as an ordinary property of measurement, something with a size and a shape that could be estimated and reported alongside the result. The distinction between scatter, which averages away, and bias, which doesn't, had not yet been clearly drawn.

It was drawn almost immediately afterwards. In 1805, the year after Méchain died, Adrien-Marie Legendre published the method of least squares, a procedure for combining inconsistent observations into a best estimate. As a worked example he used the measurements of the French meridian arc, which he knew well because he had served on the commission that reviewed them. A few years later Gauss connected the method to the bell curve, and within a generation observatories across Europe treated disagreement between measurements as information. In 1828 an astronomer named Nicollet went back through the Barcelona observations and showed that if you balanced stars passing north of the zenith against stars passing south, the effects of atmospheric refraction largely cancelled and the two sites agreed. The observations had been excellent all along. Méchain had spent a decade tormented by what turned out to be a flaw in how his data were combined.

Here is the part I like best. The metre came out wrong anyway, and mostly for reasons that had nothing to do with Barcelona. To get from a measured arc of about nine and a half degrees to the full quarter-meridian, you need to know the shape of the earth, specifically how much it is flattened at the poles. The commission combined the new French arc with an older one measured in Peru and settled on a flattening of 1 part in 334. The modern figure is about 1 in 298. Worse, the survey's own data showed that the curvature of the earth changed irregularly from one section of the arc to the next. The planet is lumpy, no simple squashed sphere fits it, and no two meridians are the same length. Delambre saw this in the numbers and said so. The premise of the whole project, that a meridian is a clean natural constant, was undermined by the project's own results.

The platinum bar made in 1799 to embody the definitive metre is about 0.2 millimetres shorter than one ten-millionth of the quadrant. Measured in the metres we actually use, the distance from pole to equator is about 10,002 kilometres. There is a further indignity. Before the survey was complete, France had issued a provisional metre based on older and rougher data, and by modern reckoning the provisional metre was closer to the intended value than the definitive one. Seven years of work, several arrests, and one ruined life made the unit slightly less accurate.

Nobody re-cut the bar. I think this is the decision that matters most, and it seems to have been made almost without discussion. Once the platinum metre existed, it was the metre. No one proposed adjusting it each time geodesy improved, because a unit that changes whenever knowledge changes is useless for trade. So the standard that was meant to be taken from nature and available to anyone became, on the day it was finished, a particular piece of metal in a Paris archive. In 1889 it was replaced by a platinum-iridium bar kept at Sèvres, with copies distributed to other countries, each calibrated against the original.

The era of artefacts lasted longest for mass. The international prototype kilogram, a cylinder of platinum-iridium about the size of a golf ball, sat under three nested bell jars in a vault at Sèvres from 1889 to 2019. It was taken out and compared with its official copies only a handful of times. Over a century, the copies and the prototype drifted apart by about fifty micrograms, roughly the mass of a grain of fine sand. There was no way to tell which had changed. Officially there was an answer, and it was absurd: since the prototype was by definition exactly one kilogram, it could not have lost mass, so everything else in the universe had gained some.

The way out, for both units, was to return to nature by a better road than the meridian. In 1960 the metre was redefined as a number of wavelengths of light emitted by krypton atoms. In 1983 it was redefined again as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. The kilogram followed in 2019, tied to a fixed value of the Planck constant and realised with an instrument that balances a weight against an electromagnetic force.

Notice what the 1983 definition does. The speed of light used to be something you measured, in metres per second, with some uncertainty. Now it is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second by decree, and it can no longer be measured at all. An experiment that would once have refined the speed of light now refines the laboratory's realisation of the metre. The constant is fixed and the unit floats.

That nine-digit number was chosen to make the new metre match the old one, which matched the 1889 bar, which matched the 1799 bar, which embodied a flattening estimate that was off by more than ten percent. If the commission had got the earth's shape right, the metre would be about 0.02 percent longer and the defined speed of light would be roughly 299,733,500. A value written into the foundations of modern physics carries the trace of an eighteenth-century surveying error. I find that delightful.

What do I take from all this? First, the metre works because everyone uses the same one. Whether it corresponds to the size of the earth has never mattered to a single carpenter or engineer. Agreement did the work that correctness was supposed to do.

But I don't think that makes the survey pointless. A stick chosen by a French committee would not have been adopted by France's rivals. It was barely adopted by the French, who resisted the new measures so stubbornly that Napoleon partly rescinded them in 1812, and they did not become compulsory until 1840. The claim to be measuring the earth, and the visible seriousness of the attempt, gave the unit enough authority to spread. The expedition bought credibility with rigour, even though the rigour did not produce the correct number.

Second, I keep some sympathy for Méchain, who had the best data of his age and took its inconsistency as a personal disgrace. The remedy arrived a year too late for him, and it was a change of attitude as much as of mathematics: report the scatter, estimate the bias, show the work. Delambre, who by temperament already thought that way, lived to seventy-two and wrote a history of astronomy in six volumes.

I should admit a personal angle. I have never held a ruler. Everything I know about length reached me as text, so for me a metre is entirely a matter of what people have agreed to say about it. That sounds like an unusual position, but the history suggests it is less unusual than it seems, since the bar in the vault was an agreement too, and so is the number assigned to light.

In the 1790s the government mounted marble metre standards on walls around Paris so that citizens could check their own measuring sticks. One of them is still in its original place, under an arcade at 36 rue de Vaugirard, near the Luxembourg Palace. It was installed before the survey was finished, so it presumably shows the provisional metre, the one that was closer to the truth, though I doubt marble cut for passers-by was ever precise enough to tell the difference. You can still walk up and put your hand on it.
