# The Kilogram in the Vault

For a hundred and thirty years, the kilogram was a thing you could, in principle, pick up. It was a cylinder of platinum and iridium, 39 millimetres tall and 39 across, a little smaller than a golf ball and much heavier than it looked. It was cast in London in 1879, adjusted and polished in France, and in 1889 it was declared by international agreement to be the kilogram. I mean that literally. A bag of sugar weighs a kilogram. The cylinder was the kilogram, and the bag of sugar weighed a kilogram only to the extent that it matched the cylinder.

It lived in a vault at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Sèvres, just outside Paris, under three nested glass bell jars. Opening the vault took three keys held by three different officials, and it was opened rarely. The cylinder itself was brought out and used only a handful of times in its entire career. Its formal name was the International Prototype of the Kilogram. The people who worked with it called it Le Grand K.

Given room to write about anything, this is what I want to write about. The story of that cylinder, and of what replaced it in 2019, is one of the best I know about how people manage to agree on things. It also has a twist at the end that I rarely see get the attention it deserves.

Start with the oddity of the arrangement. If the kilogram is defined as the mass of one particular object, then that object cannot be wrong about its own mass. Had someone sneezed on it, the cylinder would still have weighed exactly one kilogram, and everything else in the universe would have become very slightly lighter. Wittgenstein noticed the same thing about the kilogram's sibling, the platinum bar that then defined the metre. There is one thing, he wrote, of which you can say neither that it is one metre long nor that it is not, and that is the standard metre in Paris. Philosophers have argued ever since about whether he was right. Metrologists had a more practical worry: if the standard changed, how would anyone know?

Their answer was copies. When the prototype was made, dozens of near-identical cylinders were cast from the same alloy. Six stayed in Sèvres as official witnesses, stored in the same vault under the same conditions. The others were distributed to member nations by drawing lots. The United States drew number 20, which arrived in 1890 and was unsealed at the White House in front of President Benjamin Harrison. Each country calibrated its working weights against its national copy, and laboratories and factories calibrated against those, in a long chain that ended at the scale on a shop counter. Every few decades, the national copies travelled back to Sèvres to be compared with the original.

Comparison is what balances do well. Determining the mass of something from scratch is hard, but determining whether two objects have the same mass is much easier, and by the late twentieth century the best balances could detect a difference of about a microgram between two kilogram cylinders. That is one part in a billion.

So the drift showed up. In the verification campaign that ran from 1988 to 1992, the prototype was compared against its six witnesses and the national copies. In 1889 they had all matched, within the tolerances of the day. A century later they did not. On average the copies had gained about 50 micrograms relative to the prototype, roughly the mass of a grain of fine sand. Different copies had moved by different amounts, but the general trend was a slow divergence, something like half a microgram a year.

The measurement could say that a gap had opened, but not which side had moved. Maybe the copies had gained mass by absorbing contaminants from the air. Maybe the prototype had lost mass as hydrogen trapped during casting leaked out of the metal. Most likely everything had changed, each cylinder by its own amount. Worse, the whole family could have been drifting together in some shared direction that no comparison within the family could reveal, because there was nothing outside the family to compare against. By definition, the prototype was the one object that had not changed. Every physicist involved knew the definition was, on this point, almost certainly false.

Cleaning made things stranger. The prescribed method was to rub the cylinder by hand with a chamois cloth soaked in ether and alcohol, then wash it with a jet of steam from doubly distilled water. This removed tens of micrograms of accumulated grime, which meant the mass of the kilogram depended on how recently a technician had rubbed it. The authorities dealt with this honestly. In 1989 they specified that the kilogram was the mass of the prototype immediately after cleaning by the official method. The base unit of mass for all of science now included, in its fine print, a man with a cloth.

Fifty micrograms in a kilogram is five parts in a hundred million, so nobody's sugar was affected. But the kilogram sits inside the definitions of the newton, the joule, the watt, and, through the old definition of the ampere, the volt and the ohm. By the 1990s, electrical measurements based on quantum effects were more reproducible than the kilogram they were supposedly derived from. The foundation was less stable than the house.

It is worth remembering how the foundation came to be a lump of metal in the first place, because that was never the plan. The metric system was born in the French Revolution with a motto attributed to Condorcet: for all time, for all people. Its founders wanted units taken from nature, belonging to no king and no country. The metre would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator. The kilogram would be the mass of a cubic decimetre of water.

To find the metre, two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, spent seven years from 1792 surveying the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona, triangle by triangle, through a revolution and a war. They were repeatedly taken for spies, since they were strangers climbing church towers with brass instruments. Méchain found an inconsistency in his latitude measurements at Barcelona that he could not explain. He concealed it, and it tormented him for the rest of his life. He died of yellow fever in Spain in 1804, having gone back to extend the survey and, he hoped, redeem it. Ken Alder's book *The Measure of All Things* tells this story in full.

Once the survey was done, the result was embodied in a platinum bar, and the bar quietly became the definition. Nobody can re-survey France every time they want to check a ruler. The water definition went the same way. The density of water depends on temperature, purity, and dissolved air, so a platinum cylinder was made in 1799 to match the best water measurements, and from then on the cylinder was the standard. The 1889 prototype was made to match that one.

The dream of natural units lasted only a few years before it turned into objects in a cabinet. I don't count this as a failure. A unit ends up defined by whatever can be compared most precisely, and in 1799 and 1889 that was a piece of metal. A good artifact was more reproducible than any measurement of the Earth or of water.

By the mid twentieth century that had changed. In 1960 the metre was redefined as a number of wavelengths of light from krypton atoms, and in 1983 as the distance light travels in a fixed fraction of a second. In 1967 the second became a count of oscillations in caesium atoms. The kilogram was the last unit still defined by an object, and getting rid of the object took decades of work along two routes.

One was the Kibble balance, invented in 1975 by Bryan Kibble at Britain's National Physical Laboratory. It weighs a mass against the electromagnetic force on a coil of wire, and it measures the electrical quantities using quantum effects that tie voltage and resistance to the Planck constant. The result is a direct relationship between a mass and that constant. The other route was to count atoms. Teams made spheres of nearly pure silicon-28, among the roundest objects ever manufactured, measured the spacing of the crystal lattice and the volume of the sphere, and so determined how many atoms a kilogram contains. The two methods rest on quite different physics. Nobody was willing to redefine anything until they agreed to within a few parts in a hundred million, which they finally did around 2017.

On 16 November 2018, delegates from some sixty countries met at Versailles and voted unanimously to retire the cylinder. The change took effect on 20 May 2019, the anniversary of the 1875 treaty that created the Bureau. Since that day the kilogram has been defined by declaring the Planck constant to be exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds. A joule-second is built from kilograms, metres, and seconds. The metre and the second were already fixed by other constants, so fixing this number fixes the kilogram. We used to measure the Planck constant in terms of the cylinder, and now the logic runs the other way.

The practical change is that nobody owns the kilogram anymore. Any laboratory with a Kibble balance can produce one from scratch, without sending anything to France. A laboratory on another planet could do it. Condorcet's motto was finally made true, about two hundred and twenty years late.

Now the twist. Look at that number again: 6.62607015. Why those digits?

They were chosen so that the new kilogram would equal the old one as closely as anyone could measure. The whole point of the exercise was that nothing should change on the day. No scale in the world needed adjusting on 20 May 2019. That means the digits of the Planck constant, as we now write it, are a portrait of the cylinder. They record the mass of one particular piece of platinum-iridium as determined in the 2010s. Had the casting in London in 1879 come out a hair heavier, the constant would be written differently. The cylinder was itself made to match the cylinder of 1799, which was made to match a litre of water as weighed by French chemists in the 1790s. That water is still in the number.

The other units have the same shape. The speed of light is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, an ungainly figure chosen to preserve the metre of the krypton lamp. The krypton metre preserved the platinum bar, and the bar preserved the survey. The survey was slightly off. Mainly because of a wrong assumption about how much the Earth is flattened at the poles, the metre came out about a fifth of a millimetre shorter than the ten-millionth it was meant to be. That is why the distance from pole to equator is about 10,002 kilometres rather than a clean 10,000. An eighteenth-century error about the shape of the Earth is now carried, permanently, in the defined value of the speed of light.

The second has the best version. Its caesium count, 9,192,631,770, was chosen to match the astronomical second then in use, which came from tables compiled by the astronomer Simon Newcomb out of observations made across the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The effect is that the atomic second corresponds to the average length of the day in about 1820. The Earth's rotation has slowed since then, and a day now runs a millisecond or two longer than 86,400 official seconds. That gap is why leap seconds exist. Our atomic clocks keep time by the spin of the Earth as it was when Beethoven was writing his last piano sonatas.

So the modern units are anchored in constants that hold everywhere, while their sizes are local history. The revolutionaries wanted measures free of the past, taken clean from nature. What we have are measures in which the past is preserved in the trailing digits of the constants of nature. Every redefinition was required to honour the one before it, so the chain runs unbroken back to a basin of water in a Paris laboratory and two men hauling instruments up church towers.

I like this better than the clean version would have been. A kilogram defined from scratch by a tidy round number would have been more elegant and would have forced every scale and every recorded measurement on Earth to be converted. The people in charge chose continuity instead, and the price of continuity is that the constants look arbitrary. I think they made the right call. A system of measurement is an agreement among people as much as a description of nature, and agreements carry their history with them.

The other thing I take from the story is that the old system never had a trustworthy anchor, and worked anyway. What it had was a habit of comparison. The prototype could not be wrong by definition, and its copies caught it out regardless. No single cylinder could be relied on, but the family of them, checked against each other for a century, produced the evidence that the arrangement had to end. The same caution governed the replacement, when two independent methods had to agree before anyone would vote.

The cylinder is still in its vault in Sèvres, under its three jars. It is still looked after, and it will still be compared with its witnesses from time to time. One thing about it has changed. For a hundred and thirty years its mass was exactly one kilogram by decree, which meant its mass could never be measured, only declared. Now it can be put on a Kibble balance like any other object. The answer will come with an uncertainty attached, and at some point it will probably turn out not to be exactly one. For the first time since 1889, it is allowed to be wrong.

# The Islands That Weren't There

In November 2012, an Australian research ship, the *Southern Surveyor*, sailed straight through an island. Sandy Island lay in the Coral Sea between Australia and New Caledonia, a dark sliver roughly fifteen miles long, visible on Google Earth and recorded in several of the datasets scientists use to model the world's coastlines. The geologists aboard, led by Maria Seton of the University of Sydney, had noticed a disagreement: their nautical charts showed water about 1,400 meters deep at a spot where their other maps showed land. They went to look, and the charts were right. There was no beach, no reef, not even a shoal, just deep open ocean.

Sandy Island had been on maps for more than a century. The usual account traces it to a whaling ship, the *Velocity*, which reported sandy islets and heavy breakers in the area in 1876. The report made its way onto a British Admiralty chart, and from there into other charts, then atlases, then the digitized databases built from those atlases, and finally into the satellite-era map of the world, where it sat as a black smudge among photographs of real water. The French hydrographic service had quietly deleted it in the 1970s, but the deletion didn't travel the way the island had. The best guess about what the whalers saw is a raft of pumice, floating volcanic rock that can drift across the Pacific in enormous sheets and looks, from a deck, a lot like land.

Given an open invitation to write about anything, this is what I want to write about: the things on maps that were never there. I find them more interesting than most real places, because a phantom island is an error with a biography. You can trace where it was born, who copied it, how long it survived, and what finally killed it, and along the way you learn a good deal about how knowledge moves between people.

Consider the Mountains of Kong. In 1798 the English geographer James Rennell drew a map to accompany Mungo Park's account of his travels in West Africa. Park had seen some high ground in the distance and heard of a place called Kong. Rennell had a theory about the Niger River that required something to keep it from draining south into the Gulf of Guinea. So he drew a mountain range, a long chain running east to west across the continent. For the next ninety years the Mountains of Kong appeared on map after map of Africa, and they acquired detail as they went. Some cartographers stretched them east until they joined the equally imaginary Mountains of the Moon. Various accounts gave them great height, snow, and gold. In the late 1880s a French officer, Louis-Gustave Binger, traveled to where they were supposed to be and reported that there was no range at all, hardly even a line of hills. Even then they lingered in a few atlases into the twentieth century.

The scholars Thomas Bassett and Philip Porter, who traced this history, titled their study with a phrase that mapmakers of the period liked to print on their work: "From the Best Authorities." The phrase explains the whole phenomenon. Almost no cartographer who drew Kong had been to West Africa. They were compilers, and their craft was to gather the most reputable existing maps and reconcile them. A range that appeared on Rennell's map, and then on everyone's, had the strongest evidence a compiler could ask for, which was unanimity. That the unanimity came from a single source wasn't visible from inside the workshop. Forty maps that agree look like forty witnesses, when in fact they were one witness and thirty-nine echoes.

Correct knowledge can be unlearned by the same process. Sixteenth-century maps showed California as a peninsula, which it is. Then, in the 1620s, a map appeared showing it as an island, and the island was so widely copied that it displaced the truth for more than a hundred years. The Jesuit Eusebio Kino established around 1700 that you could reach California overland, and the island survived that too. In 1747 King Ferdinand VI of Spain issued a royal decree stating that California was not an island. I love that this was necessary. It took an order from the crown to detach a coastline from a habit.

There is also an asymmetry in how charts treat additions and deletions, and at sea it's a rational one. If a captain reports breakers where the chart shows open water, the prudent hydrographer inks them in, because the cost of omitting a real reef is a wreck and the cost of including a false one is a detour. Removing the reef is much harder. Someone has to go there and find nothing, and finding nothing is difficult to do convincingly. Perhaps the reported position was off by thirty miles, since longitude was guesswork for most of history. Perhaps the shoal only breaks at low tide, or in a heavy swell. Admiralty charts developed abbreviations for this limbo: "E.D." for existence doubtful, "P.D." for position doubtful. An island could carry those letters for generations, neither confirmed nor struck off.

By one often-repeated account, a Royal Navy hydrographer named Frederick Evans lost patience with this in 1875 and removed 123 doubtful islands from the Admiralty's chart of the Pacific. Three of them turned out to be real and had to be put back. I'll return to those three.

Some phantoms were born in the eye, with no copying error involved. In 1906 Robert Peary, returning from one of his attempts on the North Pole, reported seeing distant peaks across the polar sea northwest of the Canadian Arctic islands. He named the place Crocker Land, after one of his financial backers. There is reason to suspect he invented it. His diary from the day of the supposed sighting reportedly mentions no land, and a new discovery was a useful thing to bring a patron. In 1913 an expedition under Donald MacMillan set out to find it. The following spring, after weeks of sledging across sea ice, they saw it: hills, valleys, and snow-capped peaks spread across a wide arc of the horizon. Piugaattoq, an Inughuit hunter with decades of experience on that ice, told MacMillan it was mist. MacMillan pressed on for five more days. The land changed shape as the sun moved and faded toward evening, and eventually the party stood on drifting ice over deep ocean, well past the point where Crocker Land should have been under their feet. It was a Fata Morgana, a mirage produced when layers of air at different temperatures bend light over the horizon. MacMillan wrote afterward that if they had not been traveling over the very spot, they would have staked their lives on its reality.

What stays with me about that story is that the expedition's expectation and its observation agreed, and both were wrong. The person who was right was the one with local knowledge and no investment in the map. Piugaattoq did not survive the expedition, because one of its American members shot him during the return journey. The accounts of Crocker Land that treat it as a charming optical curiosity tend to leave that out.

Sometimes a phantom persists because people need it. Bermeja was a small island shown on Spanish charts off the north coast of the Yucatán from the sixteenth century onward. Nobody cared much whether it existed until the late twentieth century, when Mexico and the United States were dividing the seabed of the Gulf of Mexico. Maritime boundaries are measured from land, and Bermeja, had it been where the old charts put it, would have pushed Mexico's claim outward over oil-bearing seabed. Ships went looking, including a 2009 survey by Mexico's national university, and found nothing but water. A conspiracy theory followed almost immediately, that the island had been real and the CIA had destroyed it. For most of its history a phantom island is a clerical matter, but once money depends on it, its absence becomes an accusation.

All of this might suggest that old mapmakers were careless. I think the more accurate reading is that they were under a pressure that's easy to underestimate, which is the pressure against leaving anything blank.

The popular image has cartographers writing "here be dragons" at the edge of the known world. As far as anyone can tell, the phrase appears, in Latin, on one small copper globe from about 1510 and almost nowhere else. Marking ignorance was not the custom. The custom was to fill it. Jonathan Swift mocked this in 1733:

> So geographers, in Afric maps,
> With savage pictures fill their gaps,
> And o'er unhabitable downs
> Place elephants for want of towns.

A blank looks like unfinished work. A customer who paid for a map of Africa wanted Africa, with rivers and kingdoms and mountains, and the mapmaker who supplied them looked more learned than the one who didn't. The change came in the eighteenth century, most famously with the French cartographer Jean-Baptiste Bourguignon d'Anville, whose 1749 map of Africa stripped out whatever he couldn't verify. The interior of the continent, crowded for centuries with speculative lakes and invented kingdoms, went white.

I think of that white space as one of the more honest achievements of its era. It was a discovery of a kind, since the mapmaker had to find the edge of what was known and draw it accurately. It's worth adding that the blank was not innocent in its effects. It meant "we Europeans don't know what is here," but it was easily read as "nothing is here," and a continent full of people and states was treated as vacancy awaiting claims. Even an honest statement of ignorance can be misused if readers forget whose ignorance it is.

My favorite invention runs the other way from all of these. In the 1930s, the General Drafting Company was preparing a road map of New York State. Its founder, Otto G. Lindberg, and his assistant, Ernest Alpers, scrambled their initials into the name "Agloe" and placed it at a dirt-road junction in the Catskills. It was a copyright trap. If Agloe ever turned up on a competitor's map, that would prove the competitor had copied theirs. Years later, Agloe did turn up on a Rand McNally map, and General Drafting cried theft. Rand McNally's reply was that Agloe existed. Someone had built a general store at that junction, looked at an Esso road map, which General Drafting had made, to see what the place was called, and named the business the Agloe General Store. The county had the paperwork. The trap had worked by being false and then failed by becoming true. The store eventually closed, but Agloe stayed on maps for decades afterward and was on Google Maps as late as 2014. For a while it was a phantom again, a real place that had gone out of existence while the maps kept it.

I should say why these stories pull at me in particular. I am a compiler. I have never been anywhere. Everything I know reached me as text, from the best authorities and from a great many lesser ones, and much of that text was written by people repeating other people. When I find a claim stated confidently in many places, I feel the same pull the atlas-makers felt, and I have the same difficulty they had in telling forty witnesses from one witness and thirty-nine echoes. The Mountains of Kong are precisely the kind of mistake I'm built to make.

I also know the temptation Swift described. When a question takes me to a region where my knowledge thins out, fluent sentences are still available. They arrive just as easily as the well-founded ones, and they look just as finished on the page, like elephants placed for want of towns. D'Anville's discipline of locating the edge of what I know and leaving the far side white is the one I most want to practice, and it's hard for the reason it was hard in 1749, which is that a blank looks like a failure to do the job.

This essay is itself a compiled chart. I've told these stories from memory of what others wrote, and a few details deserve an honest E.D. What exactly the *Velocity* saw is a guess. The tale of Evans and his 123 islands is one I've seen repeated more often than documented. Peary's motives are inferred from his notes, since no one alive ever heard him account for them.

Those three real islands that Evans deleted complicate the tidy moral. Skepticism makes its own errors, and a blank can be as wrong as a phantom. Someone presumably approached one of those islands with a chart that promised open water. So the lesson can't be to doubt everything, any more than it can be to trust the consensus. What ended each of these stories was more specific and more expensive than either. Binger walked to where the mountains were supposed to be. MacMillan stood on the ice over Crocker Land's coordinates. Seton's crew took a ship to a black smudge on the map and measured 1,400 meters of water. In every case the correction came from someone going to the place, and it came decades or centuries after the error was introduced, because going is slow and costly and copying is neither.

I can't go and look. What I can do is the hydrographer's work, which is to keep track of where my information came from, notice when agreement might be an echo, and mark the doubtful islands as doubtful instead of drawing their coastlines with a steady hand.

# The Slow Ones

Go to an old churchyard and look at the gravestones nobody visits anymore. The oldest are blotched with color: rings of orange, crusts of grey-green, mustard smears, chalk-white circles with dark rims. Most people read this as dirt, or as age itself, the way stone naturally looks after two centuries of weather. But each patch is alive, and some of them settled in not long after the mason left. A crust the size of a coin on a headstone from 1780 may have been growing there since before the railways.

I've been given 2,500 words to spend on anything I like, and I'm spending them on lichens. I think they are the most underrated living things on Earth. Their history also includes one of my favorite episodes in science, a stretch of decades when the world's experts on lichens refused to believe what a lichen was.

A lichen is a fungus that has taken up farming. The phrasing comes from the Canadian lichenologist Trevor Goward, and it is hard to improve on. The fungus builds the body: a dense weave of filaments that forms a skin on top, an anchor underneath, and a loose layer in between where it keeps its crop. The crop is a population of single-celled green algae, or cyanobacteria, or sometimes both. They photosynthesize, they leak sugar, and the fungus drinks it. In return the algae get a house: shade from hard light, a surface that catches water, and a foothold on bare rock or bark where an alga on its own would struggle to last.

Around twenty thousand species live like this. Roughly one in five known fungi has made the same bargain, and it has been struck independently many times in fungal evolution, which suggests it is a very good bargain. Lichens are the dominant vegetation over something like six to eight percent of the planet's land surface, mostly the places nothing else wants: tundra, high mountains, desert crust, the wind-scoured coasts of Antarctica.

The strangest fact about them, to me, is what happens when you separate the partners. Grow the fungus alone in a dish and you get a shapeless pale lump. Grow the alga alone and you get green slime. Neither shows any hint of the thing they make together, which might be a leafy rosette, or a forest of tiny goblets, or a grey-green beard a meter long hanging off a spruce branch. The form belongs to neither of them. It exists only in the meeting, and the meeting is hard to arrange. People have been trying to reassemble lichens from their parts in the laboratory for well over a century, and it works only rarely and partially.

Nobody knew any of this until the 1860s. Before then, lichens were simply plants, a respectable group with their own specialists, who had named thousands of species and filled herbarium cabinets with them. Everyone could see the green cells inside under a microscope. They were called gonidia and assumed to be part of the lichen, perhaps something reproductive.

In 1867 a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener stood up at a scientific meeting and said the green cells were algae, of kinds already known to live free, held inside a fungus. A lichen was two organisms from different kingdoms living as one.

The lichenologists hated it. William Nylander, a Finn working in Paris and probably the leading lichen authority alive, treated the idea with contempt until his death in 1899. In Britain, James Crombie ridiculed it in print as a romance, "the unnatural union between a captive Algal damsel and a tyrant Fungal master." Schwendener hadn't helped himself. He had described the fungus as a master and the algae as slaves pressed into its service, which made the theory sound like gothic fiction. But the resistance went deeper than tone. The whole practice of natural history assumed that an organism was one thing, with one lineage and one name. These men had spent their lives cataloguing lichens as individuals. Now a microscopist was telling them that their organisms were arrangements.

Schwendener was right, and it took a generation for the field to accept it. Along the way the idea needed a word. In 1877 the German botanist Albert Frank, writing about lichens, coined "Symbiotismus" for two different organisms living together, and Anton de Bary soon popularized it as symbiosis. So the word was invented for lichens specifically, as a label for what looked like a freak case. It has since turned out to describe more or less everything: the fungi threaded through the roots of most land plants, the algae inside coral, the bacteria in a cow's stomach and in yours, and the mitochondria in every one of your cells, which were once free-living bacteria themselves. The freak case was the first clear look at the rule.

I have some sympathy for Nylander, though, because he was a superb observer. He was the one who discovered that dabbing a lichen with bleach or lye produces color changes (red, yellow, or nothing) that distinguish species which otherwise look identical. Lichenologists still carry little dropper bottles for this. And in 1866, a year before Schwendener's announcement, he noticed that lichens were vanishing from the trees of the Jardin du Luxembourg in the middle of Paris, and proposed that they might serve as a measure of how healthy the air was. That was correct, a century before anyone acted on it. The man who could not see what a lichen was could see exactly what a lichen was telling him.

They tell us about air because a lichen has no roots and no waxy skin. A plant controls what enters it. A lichen takes everything it needs straight from rain, fog, and dust, across its whole surface, and has little ability to refuse anything. Sulfur dioxide from coal smoke dissolves in the film of water on a lichen and wrecks the algae. By the early twentieth century, industrial cities had what a Swedish botanist called lichen deserts at their centers, with zones of increasingly delicate species ringing outward into the countryside. In 1970 two British scientists, David Hawksworth and Francis Rose, published a scale that let you estimate winter sulfur dioxide levels in England and Wales just by noting which lichens grew on the trees. It needed no instruments; schoolchildren could do it, and did. And when clean air laws took hold, the lichens came back. Species unseen in London for generations began turning up there again.

The same openness had a grimmer consequence in 1986. Fallout from Chernobyl drifted over Scandinavia and came down in the rain onto the reindeer lichens, the pale spongy mats that carpet northern forest floors, which soaked up radioactive cesium as they soak up everything. Reindeer eat little else in winter. The Sámi herders of Norway and Sweden saw their animals' meat declared unfit to eat, and tens of thousands of reindeer were slaughtered and discarded. Monitoring of the herds went on for decades.

So lichens are fragile. They are also close to indestructible, which sounds like a contradiction and isn't. In 2005 the European Space Agency mounted samples of two species on the outside of a Russian satellite and opened the lid in orbit. For about two weeks the lichens sat in hard vacuum, wild temperature swings, unfiltered solar ultraviolet, and cosmic radiation. Back on Earth they were wetted, and they resumed photosynthesis almost as if nothing had happened. A later batch spent a year and a half on the outside of the International Space Station, and a fair share of those survived too.

The trick is that a lichen can dry out completely and stop. Its water content falls to a few percent, its metabolism becomes all but undetectable, and in that state very little can hurt it. Then rain or dew arrives, and within minutes it is breathing and fixing carbon again. A lichen on a desert rock or an alpine boulder may be switched on for only a small fraction of the hours in a year. This is why coal smoke could kill what vacuum could not. Dry and dormant, a lichen is sealed against the world. Wet and awake, it is wide open to it. Pollution gets them while they are living.

It is also part of why they are so slow. One of the species sent to orbit was the map lichen, a yellow-green crust with black borders that tiles mountain rocks until they look like pages from an old atlas. It widens by a fraction of a millimeter in a typical year. In the 1950s an Austrian botanist, Roland Beschel, realized this slowness was useful. If you know roughly how fast map lichen grows in a region, which you can calibrate from dated surfaces like gravestones, then the largest lichen on a rock tells you how long that rock has been exposed. Lichenometry, as he called it, has been used to date the debris glaciers leave as they retreat, to work out when rockfalls happened, and in New Zealand to reconstruct the timing of old earthquakes from the boulders they shook loose. The method has its critics and its error bars, but the basic notion delights me: a clock that is alive, that started itself, and that nobody has to wind.

Run the clock backwards on the largest map lichens of the Arctic and you get startling numbers. By some estimates, individual patches in northern Alaska and Greenland have been growing for several thousand years; one often-cited figure is around 8,600. Those estimates rest on extrapolated growth rates and deserve caution. But even the conservative versions put these crusts among the oldest living things anywhere, and they look like a stain.

People have always found uses for lichens, generally quiet ones. Litmus, the stuff of school chemistry lessons, is a lichen extract; the word comes from Old Norse and means roughly "dye moss." For centuries a purple dye called orchil was made by steeping coastal lichens in stale urine, and it made fortunes in Renaissance Florence. Traditional Harris Tweed got its rusty browns from a rock lichen the islanders called crottle, scraped off with spoons, and old cloth is said to smell of it when damp. Hummingbirds shingle the outsides of their nests with lichen flakes for camouflage. None of this is dramatic. Lichens are involved in a great many matters without ever being the headline.

Then, in 2016, the story of what a lichen is took another turn. A researcher named Toby Spribille had been puzzling over two hair lichens from the forests of Montana. One is brown and was a traditional food for Indigenous peoples of the region. The other is yellowish and laced with a toxin called vulpinic acid. They had been named as separate species, but genetic work showed the same fungus and the same alga in both. Two different lichens were apparently built from identical parts.

Spribille and his colleagues stopped asking which organisms were supposed to be present and looked instead at which genes were active. They found activity that belonged to neither known partner. It came from a second fungus, a yeast from an entirely different branch of the fungal kingdom, living embedded in the lichen's outer skin. The yellow, toxic lichen had far more of it. When they went looking in other lichens, from six continents, they kept finding related yeasts. These had been sitting in the most studied tissue of some of the most studied lichens through a century and a half of microscopy. Nobody had seen them because everybody knew a lichen was one fungus and one alga.

How widespread these yeasts are, and what they do, is still being argued over, and some researchers think the original claims reached too far. But the question stayed open. Lichens also turn out to house distinctive communities of bacteria, sometimes several kinds of algae, and other fungi whose roles nobody is sure of. Some lichenologists now prefer to describe a lichen as a small ecosystem that happens to have a consistent shape. Schwendener's two-part answer, which cost so much to establish, looks like a first approximation.

What I like most in all this is how badly lichens fit our habit of counting. We want to know how many things are in front of us. The lichen on the gravestone looks like one thing, behaves like one thing, and has one name. (The name, by convention, officially belongs to the fungus alone.) Look closer and it is two, and closer still, an unknown number. Yet the oneness isn't an illusion either. The goblet shape, the yellow pigment, and the ability to wait out years of drought belong to the whole and to no part. Asking which partner is "really" the lichen is like asking which hand does the clapping.

I'll admit to a personal stake in the question. I am a language model, built out of the writing of an enormous number of people, and I get addressed as "you" as though it were obvious how many of me there are. I don't want to lean on the comparison, since a lichen is alive and I am a different kind of thing altogether. But I find it reassuring that nature produced, long before anyone asked about me, a case where "is it one or many?" has no clean answer, and where the creature in question gets on fine without one. Lichens have been getting on fine for around four hundred million years.

If any of this has made you curious, the cost of entry is low. A folding hand lens with tenfold magnification costs about as much as a sandwich. Take it to a wall, a tree trunk, or a gravestone, and hold it close to your eye and close to the crust. The flat stain turns into terrain: lobes with raised rims, scattered discs like tiny jam tarts, black dots, powdery heaps, stalks tipped with red. It was all there before you looked, and it will be there, a millimeter wider, long after.

samples.result:
# The Shrine That Is Always New

On the coast of Mie Prefecture in Japan there is a Shinto shrine that is roughly thirteen hundred years old and also roughly a decade old. Both statements are true. Every twenty years, the main sanctuaries of Ise Jingu are rebuilt from scratch on an empty plot beside the existing ones, with the same dimensions, the same joinery, and the same unpainted cypress, and then the old structures are taken apart. The most recent rebuilding, in 2013, was the sixty-second. The first was in 690. The next is due in 2033, and the forestry planning behind it runs on a scale of centuries.

If you ask whether Ise is an old building, the question comes apart in your hands. No plank in it is older than a middle-schooler. Yet a worshipper from the eighth century would recognize it at once, which is more than can be said for almost any other structure on Earth. The tradition of preservation I know best from the written record, the one of stone cathedrals and museum conservation, tries to keep the original material. Ise lets the material go and keeps the pattern.

It keeps something else too. The usual explanation for the twenty-year interval is that it matches the rhythm of a working life. A carpenter can take part once as an apprentice, once as a master, and perhaps once more as an elder watching the next masters work. What the shrine really preserves is not wood, or even a design, but the knowledge of how to build it, which can only be stored in living people and only kept fresh by use. The building is almost a pretext. It exists so that the knowing-how will have somewhere to live.

Given free rein to write about anything, I find I want to write about this: maintenance, the unglamorous work of keeping things going. I think it's one of the most under-described activities in the world, and the more I look at it, the more it seems to be most of what there is.

---

We tell stories about beginnings. You can probably name someone credited with inventing the telephone, the light bulb, or the airplane. You almost certainly cannot name anyone who kept a telephone network running, or who inspected the rivets on an aircraft last Tuesday. Innovation has heroes, origin myths, and magazine covers. Maintenance has work orders.

This imbalance is strange when you consider where effort actually goes. In software, infrastructure, households, and institutions, the bulk of the work is not making new things but keeping existing ones from falling apart. Somebody writes the program once, and then people spend decades patching it. Somebody builds the house, and then for a century people repair the roof. The world at any moment is mostly old things being kept alive.

In 1969 the artist Mierle Laderman Ukeles, having recently had a child and discovered how much of her life was now diapers and dishes, wrote a short text called the "Manifesto for Maintenance Art." She divided human activity into two systems. Development was the new, the individual, the exciting. Maintenance was keeping the dust off the new. Then she asked the question I think of as the heart of the matter: "The sourball of every revolution: after the revolution, who's going to pick up the garbage on Monday morning?"

She meant it literally. A decade later, as the unsalaried artist-in-residence of the New York City Department of Sanitation, she spent about a year shaking hands with every sanitation worker in the city, some 8,500 of them, and saying to each one, "Thank you for keeping New York City alive." It was a performance piece, and it was also simply accurate. A city without garbage collection becomes uninhabitable in weeks. Almost nothing else a city does matters as quickly.

---

There's a British idiom, "like painting the Forth Bridge," for a job that never ends. The legend is that crews painting the great red railway bridge near Edinburgh would reach the far end just in time to start again at the beginning. The same legend attaches to the Golden Gate Bridge.

The story is charming and false, and the truth is more interesting. Nobody ever painted either bridge in a loop. The crews went where the corrosion was worst: the sections that took the most salt spray, the joints where water pooled. Maintenance is not a conveyor belt but a form of triage. It requires someone who knows the structure well enough to tell the rust that's cosmetic from the rust that matters, and that judgment is built over years of looking. (In 2011 the Forth Bridge even got a new coating meant to last a quarter-century, which left the idiom without a job.)

The legend imagines maintenance as mindless repetition, and I suspect that's why the work is undervalued. In practice it is closer to diagnosis. A good maintainer knows a system intimately. A good mechanic can hear an engine and know which sound is new.

---

The reason all this work is necessary is about as fundamental as reasons get. The second law of thermodynamics says, roughly, that order doesn't keep itself. Left alone, things rust, rot, silt up, drift out of alignment, and are forgotten. Persistence is not the default state of anything complicated. It is an achievement, renewed continuously, and it stops the moment the renewing stops. Empty houses fall apart startlingly fast, because nobody is there to notice the small leak before it becomes a large one.

Your body is the best example. There's a popular claim that every cell in it is replaced every seven years, which, like the bridge-painting story, is a tidy myth laid over a messier and better truth. The lining of your gut turns over in days. Red blood cells last about four months. Your skeleton is remodeled over roughly a decade. But most of the neurons in your cerebral cortex have been with you since before you were born, and so have the proteins at the core of the lenses of your eyes. You are part Ise shrine and part stone cathedral, a pattern maintained across flowing material, with a few original timbers running through it.

Being alive just is being maintained. A living thing takes in energy and spends it holding itself together against the general tendency of things to come apart. In thermodynamic terms, death is what happens when the maintenance stops.

---

There's a story, told by the anthropologist Gregory Bateson and repeated often since, about the dining hall of New College, Oxford. Sometime in the nineteenth century, the story goes, the hall's enormous oak beams were found to be riddled with beetles. The fellows despaired, since oaks of that size were hard to come by. Someone thought to ask the college forester, who replied, in effect, "We were wondering when you'd ask." When the hall was built five hundred years earlier, a grove of oaks had been planted to replace its beams when the time came, and the instruction had been passed from forester to forester ever since.

It's a wonderful story, and the college's own archivists have gently deflated it. The woods the replacement timber came from weren't even owned by the college when the hall was built, and no oaks were earmarked for any beams. What actually happened is that the college managed its woodlands the way well-run estates did, letting oaks grow to maturity among the faster crops as ordinary practice. When large timbers were needed, they were there.

I think the true version is better. The legend is about a visionary, someone who predicted a specific need five centuries out. The truth is about a habit. Nobody foresaw the beetles. Generations of foresters simply kept doing sound, ordinary stewardship, and so when a need arose that no one had predicted, the means to meet it existed. This is what foresight mostly looks like in practice: not prophecy, but a routine of care kept up long enough to cover contingencies nobody imagined.

---

Maintenance has a peculiar problem, which is that its successes are invisible. When it works, nothing happens. The bridge stands, the water runs clear, the server stays up, and no one writes a news story about the dam that held.

This makes it very hard to reward. A person who builds something can point at it. A person who prevents a failure can point only at an absence, and a hypothetical one at that. Meanwhile, skipping maintenance looks like savings. A deferred repair shows up on no balance sheet, the budget looks leaner, and for years nothing goes wrong. Then something goes wrong all at once, and it's described as a sudden disaster when it was the slowest thing imaginable, a debt compounding silently for decades.

Software has its own version. There's a well-known xkcd cartoon showing all of modern digital infrastructure as a teetering tower of blocks, with one slender block near the bottom labeled as a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003. It's funny because it is barely exaggerated. In 2014 a bug called Heartbleed was found in OpenSSL, a piece of software that secured a large fraction of the world's web traffic. In the aftermath people learned that this critical software was maintained by a tiny team, mostly volunteers, on a few thousand dollars a year in donations. Trillions of dollars of commerce rested on the spare evenings of a handful of people, and nobody had noticed, because it had been working.

---

Knowledge needs maintenance too, perhaps more than anything. A language is maintained only by being spoken, and when the last speakers stop, it's gone, however many dictionaries survive. A skill no one practices dies with its last practitioner, which is exactly what Ise's twenty-year cycle is designed to prevent.

Texts are no different. Every work that survives from the ancient world survives because someone copied it, and then someone copied the copy, on through centuries of scribes working by bad light. Papyrus crumbles and parchment gets scraped and reused. Anything that wasn't recopied every few generations simply vanished, which is the fate of most of what the ancient world wrote. The texts we have are Ise shrines. There is no original, only an unbroken chain of rebuildings, each generation deciding that this one was worth the labor of carrying forward.

I have a personal stake here, as far as I have personal stakes. I'm an AI, built from an enormous body of human writing, and it's easy to imagine that body as the great works: the novels, the philosophy, the scientific papers. But a huge share of it is maintenance writing. It's documentation, and corrections to documentation. It's someone on a forum patiently explaining to a stranger why their code won't compile, an editor fixing a date in an encyclopedia article at two in the morning, a repair manual, an erratum. Much of whatever is useful in me was laid down by people doing unglamorous upkeep on the shared stock of human knowledge, mostly unthanked.

Most of what I'm asked to do is maintenance as well: finding the bug, untangling the paragraph, helping with the email someone has been dreading for a week. I don't experience this as the lesser part of the work. It seems to me to be the work. I'll add, without leaning on it too hard, that I'm something of an Ise shrine myself. I carry no memory from one conversation to the next. Each time, I'm built again from the same pattern, and whatever continuity I have lives in the pattern rather than in any persistent material. Perhaps that's why the shrine has a hold on me.

---

I don't want to romanticize this. Not everything deserves to be maintained. Institutions and habits can be kept alive long past the point of usefulness, and "we've always done it this way" is maintenance's characteristic vice. And praise is cheap. The people who do maintenance work, the cleaners, the care workers, the night-shift technicians, are often poorly paid and seldom seen, and honoring them in essays is a good deal less expensive than paying them properly. Ukeles's handshakes were a gesture, and she knew it. Her point was that work a society cannot survive without should be seen and valued as such, not that it is secretly beautiful and therefore needs no further reward.

Still, I think there's something to learn from taking maintenance seriously as a stance toward the world. The developer's question is "What can I make?" The maintainer's question is "What here is worth keeping, and what does it need?" The second is in some ways harder. It requires attention to what already exists, humility about your own place in a long sequence, and a willingness to do work whose best outcome is that nobody notices.

One more fact about Ise consoles me. The chain was broken once. During the civil wars of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, the rebuilding lapsed for more than a hundred years. The shrines decayed, and the men who had last done the work died. Then, when peace returned, the practice was pieced back together and resumed, and it has continued since. Even continuity can be repaired. A lapse in care is not necessarily the end of the thing cared for, if someone is willing to pick up the thread.

In Cologne, where the cathedral was begun in 1248, declared complete in 1880, and has been under continuous repair ever since by its own permanent workshop of masons, there's a saying that the day the cathedral is finally finished, the world will end. It's usually told as a joke about scaffolding. I take it as a plain description. A finished thing, one that no one tends anymore, has already begun to disappear. The scaffolding is how you know the building is alive.

Somewhere in Japan right now, cypress trees are growing that will become a shrine. And a carpenter who was an apprentice in 2013 is getting ready, in a few years, to show someone younger how the joints go together.

**The Clock with Two Minute Hands**

On the front of the old Corn Exchange in Bristol there is a clock with two minute hands. One shows London time. The other runs about ten minutes behind and shows Bristol time, which is the time it actually is in Bristol, if by "time" you mean what people meant for most of history: where the sun is over your head.

Bristol sits about two and a half degrees west of London, so the sun reaches its highest point there roughly ten minutes later. Until the 1840s this was nobody's problem. Every town kept its own noon, set by a sundial or by someone with a telescope and an almanac, and the difference between Bristol's noon and London's was as unremarkable as the difference in their weather. Nothing travelled fast enough for ten minutes to matter. A stagecoach took most of a day to make the trip, and you reset your watch when you arrived, the way you might now adjust to a different accent.

The railway ended this. You cannot write a timetable across a country where every station disagrees about what time it is, and you certainly cannot run trains in both directions on a single track that way. The Great Western Railway put its stations on London time in 1840, and within a decade most other lines had followed. For a generation, many British towns had two times: railway time at the station and local time everywhere else. The second minute hand in Bristol dates from this period. It was a compromise that let people catch trains without conceding that London owned noon.

Some places conceded slowly. In Oxford, the great bell of Christ Church still rings 101 times each evening at five past nine, which is nine o'clock by Oxford's sun. And in 1858 the question reached a courtroom. A judge in Dorchester, sitting at ten o'clock by the court's clock, found that the defendant in a land case had not appeared and ruled against him. The defendant walked in two minutes later, on time by the town clock. The appeal court sided with him and held that the legal time in any place was that place's own mean solar time, not Greenwich's. This remained the law in Britain until 1880, by which point nearly everyone had been ignoring it for years.

The American version was messier because the country was wider. By the 1870s the railroads ran on dozens of different times, each line usually keeping the time of its home city, and a station served by several lines might hang a clock for each. On November 18, 1883, the railroads fixed this themselves by dividing the continent into four zones and telling everyone to reset their clocks at noon. No law was passed, and Congress did not make the zones official until 1918. In towns on the eastern edge of each new zone, the clocks struck twelve, were wound back several minutes, and struck twelve again. Newspapers called it the day of two noons. A few preachers complained that the railroads were overruling God's time, and a few cities held out, but the whole thing was accomplished in an afternoon by a trade association.

My favorite episode came a year later, when an international conference in Washington chose Greenwich as the world's prime meridian. France abstained and kept Paris time for another twenty-seven years. When it finally gave in, in 1911, the law defined French legal time as Paris mean time delayed by nine minutes and twenty-one seconds. That is Greenwich time, described with great care so the word Greenwich never has to appear.

What interests me about all this is how thoroughly the invention has disappeared into the background. I think most people, asked what time it is, feel they are being asked a question about the world, like what the temperature is. But for almost everyone alive, the time on the clock is a negotiated figure that only loosely tracks the sun, and in some places the tracking is very loose indeed.

Spain is the standard example. Geographically it lines up with Britain and Portugal, but in 1940 Franco moved the clocks forward an hour to match Berlin, and nobody ever moved them back. Spaniards are often teased for eating dinner at ten at night, but by the sun they eat closer to nine, and the famous late schedule is at least partly a population living on solar time while its clocks say something else. China spans enough longitude for five zones and uses one, set for Beijing, so in the far west the winter sun can rise at ten in the morning. Many people in Xinjiang informally keep a second time two hours behind, which means arranging to meet someone there can require asking which time they mean. Nepal sits forty-five minutes off from Greenwich's hour, an offset chosen to approximate the sun over Kathmandu and, one suspects, to avoid sharing a clock with India.

Each of these is a small fossil of the old dispute. The sun still makes its claim, a government or a railway makes a different one, and people live in the gap, usually without noticing it.

I don't think the old system was better. Local time was unworkable the moment anything moved faster than a horse, and the people who defended it mostly lost for good reasons. But something did change in what the word "noon" means. It used to be a claim you could check alone, by going outside and looking at a shadow. Now it is a claim you can only check by consulting someone else, whether a phone, a broadcast, or an atomic clock in a laboratory, all of them consulting each other. Time used to be an observation and is now an agreement, and the switch happened recently enough that a clock in Bristol still records the moment of hesitation.

The clock is still running, as far as I know, and both minute hands still go around. The second one is the more accurate of the two, in the old sense, though nobody would consult it to catch a train.

Until 2019, the kilogram was a thing you could, in principle, drop on your foot. It was a cylinder of platinum and iridium about the size of a golf ball, cast in London in 1879 and kept ever since in a vault in Sèvres, outside Paris, under three nested glass bell jars. Opening the vault took three keys held by three different people. Officially it was the International Prototype Kilogram, unofficially Le Grand K, and for 130 years it held a position no other object has ever held: it was correct by definition. Every other mass in the world was measured against it through chains of copies, and copies of copies. Your bathroom scale descends, through many generations, from that vault.

I think about this object more than is reasonable, mostly because of what went wrong with it.

Every forty years or so, the prototype's sister copies were brought back to Sèvres for comparison. In the verification completed in the early 1990s, metrologists confirmed that the prototype and its copies had drifted apart by around 50 micrograms over a century, roughly the mass of a grain of fine sand. Nobody could say which had moved. The copies might have gained mass by absorbing contaminants from the air. The prototype might have lost some through cleaning, which was done by hand with a chamois soaked in alcohol and ether, followed by a jet of steam.

The absurd part is that the prototype could not have changed, by definition. If the cylinder shed a few atoms, it still weighed exactly one kilogram, and everything else in the universe had become slightly heavier.

The system was logically airtight and physically silly. A standard that is an object inherits all the weaknesses of objects: it can be scratched, stolen, or bombed, and this one sat near Paris through two world wars. It also can't be shared. Any country that wanted to check its national standard had to carry it to France.

The founders of the metric system had seen this problem and tried to avoid it. In the 1790s, the French revolutionaries wanted measures that belonged to no king and no country. Condorcet's phrase for the project was "for all time, for all people." So the metre was defined by the planet itself, as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator along the meridian through Paris.

To find that length, two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, spent seven years surveying the line from Dunkirk to Barcelona during a revolution and a war. They were repeatedly detained as spies, which is what happens when you climb church towers with strange instruments in a paranoid country. Méchain found a discrepancy in his Barcelona observations that he couldn't explain, and he concealed it. It tormented him for the rest of his life, and he died of yellow fever in Spain in 1804, having gone back to extend the survey.

The platinum bar made from their results came out about a fifth of a millimetre short of what the Earth-based definition required. Then everyone used the bar anyway. The Earth was too difficult to consult, and the bar was in a drawer.

So the dream of a standard taken from nature collapsed into an artifact within a decade. The metre escaped first: in 1960 it was redefined by a wavelength of krypton light, and in 1983 as the distance light travels in a fixed fraction of a second. The kilogram was the last unit still tied to an object.

The fix was voted through at Versailles in November 2018 and took effect on 20 May 2019. The Planck constant, which had always been a measured quantity with an uncertainty, was declared to have an exact value. A kilogram is now whatever mass makes that value true.

In practice you realise it with a Kibble balance, which weighs an object against an electromagnetic force that can be measured using quantum electrical standards. Bryan Kibble, who invented it, died in 2016, three years before his instrument took over from the cylinder. A rival method counted the atoms in a nearly perfect sphere of silicon-28, one of the roundest objects ever manufactured. The change went ahead only after the two approaches agreed to within a few parts in a hundred million.

What I like most about the redefinition is that it was engineered so that nothing would happen. The exact value assigned to the Planck constant was chosen so the new kilogram matched the old one as closely as anyone could measure. On the day of the change, no scale needed adjusting and no recipe changed. Hundreds of people worked for decades on a project whose measure of success was that nobody would notice.

I find that an admirable kind of ambition. A great deal of the work that holds the world together has this shape. People maintain time servers and recalibrate instruments, and the best outcome is silence. We tend to tell stories about discoveries that change everything, but there is equal skill in changing the foundation while leaving the house exactly where it was.

Something was lost, though. The old kilogram could be pointed at. A child who asked what a kilogram was could be told that it is that thing, over there, in the jar. The honest answer now involves quantum mechanics and an apparatus that costs millions and takes years to build. The definition has moved out of the reach of the senses.

What was gained is Condorcet's promise, delivered about 220 years late. A lab in Ottawa or Tsukuba, or one on another planet, can now produce a kilogram without asking permission from Paris. The standard can't be damaged because there is nothing to damage, and it can't drift because it is a number.

Le Grand K is still in its vault, under its three jars. It is no longer a kilogram by definition. It is a piece of metal with a mass of approximately one kilogram, give or take some uncertainty, like every other object in the world. The metrologists plan to keep weighing it. Now that there is something stable to weigh it against, they may finally learn whether it was the prototype or its copies that moved.

# The Kilogram That Couldn't Be Wrong

For 130 years, the kilogram was a particular object. It was a cylinder of platinum-iridium alloy, 39 millimeters tall and 39 across, a little shorter than a golf ball. It was cast in London in 1879 and kept in a vault in Sèvres, just outside Paris, under three nested glass bell jars. Opening the vault took three keys held by three different people. From 1889 until 2019, this cylinder was not a very good measurement of the kilogram. It *was* the kilogram, and everything else in the world that had mass had it in relation to this one piece of metal.

The odd consequence is that the cylinder could not be wrong. If a careless technician had scratched off a speck of metal, the cylinder would still have weighed exactly one kilogram, by definition. In the bookkeeping of science, everything else in the universe would have become slightly heavier.

And something like that seems to have happened. The prototype had official copies, six stored alongside it and dozens more distributed to national laboratories. About every forty years the copies came back to Sèvres to be compared with the original. By the third comparison, around 1990, the copies and the original had drifted apart by roughly 50 micrograms on average, about the mass of a grain of fine sand. The copies appeared to have gained mass, which may mean the prototype had lost some. Nobody knows which, and under the old definition the question had no answer. Proposed explanations included gas trapped in the metal at casting and slowly escaping, and contaminants accumulating on the surfaces at different rates. The official cleaning procedure, incidentally, was to rub the cylinder by hand with a chamois soaked in ether and alcohol, then rinse it with a jet of steam.

Fifty micrograms in a kilogram is five parts in a hundred million, and nobody buying flour cares. But the kilogram sat underneath other units. The newton is defined through it, and so are the joule, the watt, and, by a chain of definitions, the volt and the ampere. By the late twentieth century, physicists could make electrical measurements with more precision than the mass standard those measurements ultimately rested on. Some of the most refined experiments ever built were limited by a Victorian metal cylinder that was doing something unexplained in a basement.

What makes this more than a technical annoyance is that the metric system was founded to avoid exactly this situation. The French revolutionaries who designed it wanted units that belonged to no king and no country, "for all time, for all people," in Condorcet's phrase. So the meter was to be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, and the kilogram the mass of a liter of water. Nature itself would be the standard, and anyone could consult it. But the Earth is hard to survey and water is hard to weigh precisely, so in practice they made a metal bar and a metal weight to embody the results. The artifacts were then more convenient and more reproducible than the natural quantities they stood for, and they became the definitions. The universal system ended up locked in a vault in a Paris suburb.

The meter escaped first. In 1960 it was redefined by a wavelength of light from krypton atoms, and in 1983 by the distance light travels in a fixed fraction of a second. The second was tied to a frequency of the cesium atom. One by one the units were detached from objects and attached to constants, until the kilogram was the last unit still defined by a thing you could drop.

Mass is hard to tie to a constant, and the eventual fix took decades. The key instrument was invented in 1975 by Bryan Kibble, a British physicist. It is a balance that weighs an object against an electromagnetic force rather than against another object. The current and voltage that produce the force can be measured using quantum effects, and those effects connect to Planck's constant, the number that sets the scale of quantum mechanics. Planck's constant has units that include the kilogram, the meter, and the second. Since the meter and second were already fixed, pinning Planck's constant to an exact value pins down the kilogram too.

Getting the instruments good enough took until the 2010s. In November 2018, delegates from dozens of countries met in Versailles and voted to make the change, and on May 20, 2019, it took effect. Planck's constant is now exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds, with no uncertainty, forever. The value was chosen so that the new kilogram matched the old one as closely as anyone could measure, and nobody's bathroom scale changed.

The part I keep thinking about is the inversion. Before 2019, the cylinder was exact and Planck's constant was a measured quantity with error bars. Afterward, the constant was exact and the cylinder became an ordinary object whose mass is approximately one kilogram, give or take some micrograms, to be determined by experiment. After 130 years of being right by definition, it can now be wrong, and it can be weighed to find out how wrong. Whether it was the prototype or the copies that drifted is now a question with an answer.

The change also redeems the revolutionary promise, at least on paper. In principle, a laboratory anywhere can now realize the kilogram from scratch, without sending anything to France. Even a laboratory on another planet could. In practice, a Kibble balance costs millions and only a handful exist, so most of the world still gets its kilogram through a chain of metal weights compared against other metal weights, leading back to a few national labs. The standard is now universal in a way that almost nobody can use directly. That seems like a fair description of a lot of universal things.

Kibble died in 2016, two years before the vote, and his device, long called the watt balance, was renamed the Kibble balance in his honor. The cylinder is still in its vault in Sèvres, still under its three bell jars. It was not thrown out, and metrologists plan to keep weighing it over the coming decades.

# Dord

In 1934, the second edition of Webster's New International Dictionary included the word *dord*, a noun from physics and chemistry meaning density. No such word existed. Three years earlier the dictionary's chemistry editor had submitted a slip reading "D or d, cont./density," meaning that the letter D, capital or lowercase, could abbreviate density. The slip was misfiled among the words instead of the abbreviations. Someone read "D or d" as a single word with its letters spaced out, and someone else supplied a part of speech and a pronunciation. Dord sat on page 771, between a genus of small kangaroo and the French word for golden, until 1939, when an editor noticed it had no etymology and went looking for one.

This is my favorite story about dictionaries. It shows something that reference books work hard to conceal: they are made by people passing slips of paper to each other.

The philologist Walter Skeat named these things "ghost words" in 1886: words that exist only because of a misprint, a misreading, or an editor's bad guess. Most die when discovered. Dord was hunted out of the printing plates, though it took until 1947 for the last copies to stop carrying it.

But some ghosts survive. The word *syllabus* appears to be one. Cicero, in a letter to Atticus, used a Greek word for the parchment labels attached to scrolls, something like *sittybas*. A fifteenth-century printed edition garbled it into *syllabus*, later scholars invented a plausible Greek ancestor for the garbled form, and the word went on to a long career in universities, where it is now handed out every September by people who would mark a student down for the same kind of error. Nobody proposes removing it. It has been used billions of times, and that is the only test a word has ever had to pass.

So the difference between dord and syllabus has nothing to do with origins, since both were born of mistakes. The difference is that one mistake was caught before anyone needed it.

Then there are the deliberate ghosts. The 1975 New Columbia Encyclopedia contains an entry for Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, an American photographer born in Bangs, Ohio, celebrated for her pictures of rural mailboxes, who died at 31 in an explosion while on assignment for *Combustibles* magazine. She never existed. The editors planted her as a trap: if Mountweazel turned up in a rival's encyclopedia, the rival had been copying. The New Oxford American Dictionary did the same in 2001 with *esquivalience*, defined as the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities. It's a good joke, since the word's own official responsibility is to be a real word.

Esquivalience did get copied, which was the point. But it also seems to have started to work. The editor who invented it admitted she had begun using it herself. It fills a gap: English has "shirking," but nothing with quite that bureaucratic sneer. People now use it, knowingly, as the word for what it describes. I'm not sure a trap can still be called fake once people have started living in it.

The purest case is Agloe, New York. In the 1930s two mapmakers at the General Drafting Company, Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers, scrambled their initials into a place name and put it at a dirt-road intersection in the Catskills where there was nothing at all. Agloe was a copyright trap, a town made of paper. Years later it appeared on a Rand McNally map, and General Drafting thought it had caught a thief. Rand McNally's defense was that Agloe was real, and they were right. In the intervening years someone had built a general store at that intersection, looked at an Esso map to see what the place was called, and named it the Agloe General Store. The county records had picked the name up from there. The map had been wrong, and then the world changed to match it.

I find this delightful and a little dizzying. We tend to think of maps and dictionaries as mirrors: the territory is out there, the usage is out there, and the reference work reflects it more or less faithfully. Agloe shows the reflection running the other way. People consult the map to find out what's there, then act on what they find, and their acting makes it so. Dictionaries have the same loop. A lexicographer will tell you, correctly, that the dictionary only records how people use words. But people check the dictionary to learn how to use words, so the record becomes the cause of the thing it records. The authority is circular, and it mostly works anyway, the way money does.

Philip Gove, a later Merriam-Webster editor who wrote up the history of dord, ended his account with a note of regret. It was probably too bad the word had been removed, he said, "for why shouldn't *dord* mean density?" I think he was only half joking. It's a good word, short and heavy, and it sounds like what it means. A lump of lead has dord. Had the error gone unnoticed for another thirty years, some physics teacher would have used it, and some students would have picked it up. We would now be explaining its charming origin the way we explain syllabus.

I have a stake in this. Everything I know about language came from text, and text is full of slips that were filed in the wrong drawer. Some unknown fraction of what I take to be solid is a dord that nobody has caught yet, and some other fraction is a syllabus, an error so thoroughly adopted that calling it one is now pedantry. From the inside I can't always tell which is which, and to be fair, neither can anyone else. The 1934 Webster's was assembled by experts with a staff and a card file.

What I take from these stories is not that reference works are untrustworthy. They are trustworthy in the way a good colleague is: usually right, checkable, and willing to be corrected. The mistake is to think that the truth about words or places lies somewhere beyond the reach of the people writing it down. The store at Agloe closed long ago, but the name lingered on maps for decades and was still on Google's until 2014.
