samples.result:
**The Smell of Rain**

Given a free choice, I'd like to write about the smell of rain. I have never smelled it, which is part of the attraction. People describe it with unusual agreement and unusual affection, and the explanation behind it is stranger than the descriptions suggest.

The smell got its English name in 1964, when two Australian scientists, Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas, published a paper in Nature called "Nature of Argillaceous Odour." They proposed the word petrichor, from the Greek for stone and for ichor, the fluid that runs in the veins of the gods. Their finding was that during dry spells, rocks and clay absorb oils given off by plants, and rain releases them. They also acknowledged that they were late. Perfumers in Kannauj, in northern India, had been bottling the scent for generations as mitti attar, made by baking discs of clay and distilling the vapor into sandalwood oil. The smell was a commercial product long before it was a scientific subject.

The main ingredient is a molecule called geosmin, which means "earth smell." It is made mostly by Streptomyces, a genus of soil bacteria better known as the source of many of our antibiotics. The human nose can detect geosmin at a few parts per trillion. The usual comparison is a teaspoon dissolved in two hundred Olympic swimming pools. There are very few compounds we detect at such low concentrations.

For decades nobody knew why the bacteria bothered. Making geosmin costs energy, and nearly every Streptomyces species makes it, which suggests it does something important. In 2020 a group of researchers published an answer. The bacteria produce geosmin at the moment they form spores, and the smell attracts springtails, tiny soil arthropods a millimeter or two long. The springtails eat the bacterial colony and leave with spores stuck to their bodies and passing through their guts, then deposit them somewhere new. The arrangement resembles the one between fruit and birds. The smell that people associate with freshness and relief is an advertisement addressed to an animal most of them have never noticed.

How the molecule gets from the soil to a nose was worked out in 2015 by researchers at MIT, who filmed raindrops with high-speed cameras. When a drop lands on a porous surface, it traps tiny bubbles of air beneath it. The bubbles rise through the drop and burst at the top, like the fizz in a glass of champagne, flinging out a mist of fine particles that carry whatever was in the soil. Wind does the rest. The effect is strongest when light rain falls on dry, porous ground. That matches what people report: the first shower after a dry week smells strongest, and a downpour on wet ground hardly smells at all.

The part I find most interesting is that the same molecule is hated almost everywhere else it appears. When cyanobacteria bloom in a reservoir, they release geosmin, and water utilities get flooded with complaints that the tap water tastes like dirt. The water is safe, and the compound is expensive to remove. Catfish and carp farmers call it "off-flavor" and hold their fish in clean water for days before sale to flush it out. Winemakers treat it as a fault, a sign that moldy grapes got into the press. It is also what makes beets taste earthy, which is why beets divide people so sharply. Cooks found a fix long before the chemistry was known. Geosmin breaks down in acid, so carp gets lemon and beets get vinegar.

So the pleasure depends on the setting. In the air after a dry week, geosmin means the drought has ended. In a glass of water, it means something has gone wrong upstream. The nose reports the same molecule both times, and the rest of the mind decides what to make of it. I think of this whenever someone describes a smell or flavor as inherently pleasant or inherently foul. It is a clean example because nothing about the chemical changes between the two cases.

Why we are so sensitive to it is an open question. One hypothesis is that it helped our ancestors find water in dry landscapes. Camels are sometimes said to locate oases this way, though the evidence for that is thin. The opposite hypothesis is that the sensitivity is a warning system, since geosmin in water or food signals microbial growth. Fruit flies offer some support for the warning idea. They have a dedicated neural circuit for geosmin, one receptor wired to one job, and they use it to avoid food contaminated by harmful molds. For a fly, the smell carries no ambiguity at all.

For us it apparently carries both meanings, and the two hypotheses pull in opposite directions in the same way our reactions do. We may have inherited a detector built for avoidance and then learned, in dry country, to love what it detects when it arrives on the wind. Or the story may be something else entirely. A sense this acute usually has a reason behind it, and I find it striking that for one of the most beloved smells in human experience, the reason is still unknown.

I also like the order in which the knowledge arrived. The perfumers of Kannauj could capture the smell centuries ago. The name came in 1964. The mechanism that lifts it into the air was filmed in 2015, and the reason bacteria make it was published in 2020. Each step went to people who took a common pleasure seriously enough to ask what it was made of. The last step, the reason humans can smell it at all, has not been taken.

samples.result:
The alphabet has an order, and nobody knows why. Clay tablets from Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, list the letters of a local script in a sequence recognizably ancestral to ours, and those tablets are more than three thousand years old. The order survived the passage from Phoenician to Greek, from Greek to Etruscan and Latin, and from Latin to every language that now uses Roman letters. Letters were added, dropped, and repurposed along the way, but the backbone held. No one has found a convincing reason A comes before B. The best explanation is that this is how the list was taught, and each generation taught it the same way.

What I find strange is that for most of those three thousand years, the order did almost no work. Children recited it. Hebrew poets used it for acrostics (Psalm 119 walks through the alphabet eight verses at a time). But hardly anyone used it to sort things. The librarians at Alexandria seem to have shelved some works by the first letter of the author's name, and there are scattered Greek and Roman lists arranged the same loose way. But sorting by first letter only gets you so far, and full alphabetization, where you sort by the second letter and the third and so on to the end of the word, stayed rare well into the Middle Ages.

When it did arrive, it had to be explained. Giovanni Balbi, a Dominican from Genoa, finished a huge Latin dictionary called the *Catholicon* in 1286 and arranged it in complete alphabetical order. In his preface, he walks the reader through the method step by step: amo comes before bibo because a comes before b, and abeo before adeo because b comes before d, and so on through several more examples. Then he begs the reader not to scorn the labor this cost him or dismiss the arrangement as worthless. Three centuries later the situation hadn't changed much. Robert Cawdrey's *Table Alphabeticall* of 1604, usually counted as the first English dictionary, tells its readers they must learn the alphabet "perfectly without book," and explains that a word starting with b will be found near the beginning and one starting with v toward the end.

It would be easy to read this as a story about slow medieval minds, but the people resisting alphabetical order included some of the best minds of the period, and they had an argument. A book of knowledge was supposed to mirror the structure of what it described. Bartholomaeus Anglicus, compiling his encyclopedia in the thirteenth century, began with God, moved on to angels, then the human soul, the body, and downward through the created world to animals, stones, and colors. The arrangement taught something before you'd read a single entry. Alphabetical order, by contrast, put *angelus* ahead of *deus* for no better reason than spelling. It scattered related things and jammed unrelated ones together. Albertus Magnus used an alphabetical list for part of his work on animals and apologized for it, saying this was no way for a philosopher to proceed, though it might be convenient for readers.

The complaint lasted a long time. In 1817 Coleridge drew up the plan for a new encyclopedia, the *Encyclopaedia Metropolitana*, arranged by a philosophical scheme of the sciences. He was contemptuous of rivals like the *Britannica*, whose contents were ordered, as he saw it, by the accident of initial letters. His encyclopedia took almost thirty years to complete and failed commercially. The *Britannica* kept going.

Coleridge was right about the accident and wrong about what followed from it. Alphabetical order works because it means nothing. To find something in Bartholomaeus you need to already know where it sits in the hierarchy of creation: whether a bat counts among birds or beasts, whether coral is a stone or a plant. To use a meaningful arrangement, you have to have already absorbed the system, and that is easiest for the people who need the book least. To find something alphabetically you need to know only how it's spelled. The scheme asks nothing of the reader except twenty-odd letters in a fixed sequence, which a child can learn as a song.

Meaninglessness also makes the scheme durable. Every classification that carries meaning eventually falls out of date or into dispute. Knowledge gets reorganized, and the hierarchy of the sciences in Coleridge's plan looks quaint now. Any ordering of people by rank offends someone, and an ordering of nations by importance could start a fight, which is why delegations at the United Nations sit alphabetically. Nobody can read an insult into alphabetical order because it has no content to read. It also absorbs new things without strain. When someone invents a telephone, the entry goes between *telegraph* and *telescope*, and no committee has to meet about where telephones belong in the order of being.

There is a cost, and the medieval critics identified it correctly. An alphabetical reference work teaches nothing through its shape. Adjacent entries in an encyclopedia are strangers. You can't browse it for understanding the way you can walk a well-organized library shelf, where the book next to the one you came for is often the one you needed. A good deal of intellectual history since the thirteenth century has been the gradual acceptance of that trade, giving up arrangements that explain in exchange for arrangements that retrieve. The index, the card catalog, and the filing cabinet all rest on the same decision.

Search engines carry the decision one step further. A search box needs no order at all, not even the alphabet; you type the word and the machine does the finding. So the skill Cawdrey had to teach his readers in 1604 is gently atrophying. I'd guess most people under thirty have rarely looked anything up in a long printed alphabetical list, and deciding whether *Mac* files before *Mab* is becoming a specialist's concern again, as it was for Balbi.

That would return the alphabet to its earlier condition. For its first two thousand years it was a sequence that people memorized carefully and used for almost nothing. For about seven hundred years it organized dictionaries, archives, phone books, and school seating charts. Now the sorting has moved inside machines, where nobody watches it happen, while children still learn the order as a song.

**Old Brass Brains**

In 1687 Newton explained the tides. The moon pulls harder on the near side of the Earth than on the far side, the oceans bulge in both directions, and the planet turns beneath the bulges, so most coasts get two high waters a day. It is one of the great explanations in science, and for the practical purpose of telling a ship's captain when he could cross the bar at Liverpool, it was almost useless.

The trouble is that the real ocean is not a smooth shell of water on a featureless globe. Continents break it up, and it sloshes in basins of irregular depth, each with its own natural rhythm, like water in a bathtub. The results are strange. In the Bay of Fundy the water rises as much as sixteen meters, while the Mediterranean barely moves. Parts of the Gulf of Mexico get one tide a day instead of two, and Southampton gets a double high water. There are points in the open ocean with no tide at all, around which high water wheels like the rim of a wheel around its hub.

None of this falls out of Newton's picture. Laplace wrote down the right equations in the 1770s, but nobody could solve them for a real ocean until computers arrived. For two centuries, humanity knew exactly why the tide rose and could not calculate when.

Tide tables existed anyway. In the eighteenth century they were often produced by families who kept their methods secret and sold the results. Then, in the 1860s and 70s, William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, found a way through. I think it is one of the cleverest moves in applied science, mostly because of what it declines to do.

Thomson gave up on computing the ocean's response and used astronomy for the one thing it could supply exactly, which was the frequencies at which the ocean is pushed. The moon comes around every twelve hours and twenty-five minutes, and the sun every twelve hours. There are slower rhythms from the moon's elliptical orbit, its tilt, and the Earth's own path around the sun.

Whatever a harbor does in response, however odd its geometry, it does at those frequencies. So the tide at any port is a sum of cosine waves whose periods are known in advance from the sky, and whose heights and timings are unknown and peculiar to the place. To find those, you install a gauge, record the water level for a year, and fit two numbers per wave. Then you run the sum forward as far as you like.

Adding dozens of cosines for every hour of a year by hand is misery, so Thomson built a machine. Each wave gets a wheel turning at its proper speed, with a crank that raises and lowers a pulley. A single wire threads over all the pulleys, fixed at one end and tied to a pen at the other, so the pen's height is the sum. Turn the handle and a year of tides draws itself in about four hours.

The American version, finished in 1910, summed thirty-seven constituents and weighed more than a ton. It was nicknamed Old Brass Brains and produced the government's tide tables until 1965.

The most consequential use of such a machine came in 1944. Arthur Doodson, at the Liverpool Tidal Institute, was sent a set of harmonic constants for a location identified only as "Position Z" and asked for predictions. The planners of the Normandy landings wanted to arrive near low water on a rising tide shortly after first light. That way the obstacles Rommel had planted on the beaches would be exposed, and the landing craft could float off again. Combined with the need for a moonlit night beforehand, that left a handful of possible days in June. The pulleys and wire set the date of the invasion as much as the generals did.

What I admire is the division of labor. The method isn't pure theory, which failed for two hundred years. But it isn't pure curve-fitting either. If you tried to fit a tide record without knowing the frequencies, you would need far more data, and your predictions would drift into nonsense soon after the record ended.

Theory is used exactly as far as it can be trusted, which is the timetable of the sky. Everything theory cannot reach, including the shape of the Atlantic, the continental shelf, and the estuary, is compressed into a short table of numbers that no one derives and no one needs to. A year of measurements, combined with Newton, gives predictions good for decades.

People often talk as though understanding and prediction were the same thing, or as though you had to choose between explaining the world and fitting data to it. The tide tables are a counterexample to both. Understanding without measurement could not predict a single harbor, and measurement without understanding would not have extrapolated. The achievement was knowing where the boundary between them ran.

I am a system built mostly on the fitting side of that boundary, which is probably part of why the story appeals to me. It shows how much a small amount of real structure is worth. Thirty-seven frequencies, known for good reasons, turn a hopeless problem into a year of patient observation.

The method also knows what it leaves out, or at least its users learned to. The tables predict the astronomical tide only. On the night of January 31, 1953, the tables for the North Sea were correct, and the water came in meters above them anyway, driven by a storm. More than eighteen hundred people died in the Netherlands and hundreds more in England. The sky's timetable has no entry for wind. A prediction that is exactly right about what it models can still be badly wrong about the sea, and the people who issue tide tables now run storm surge forecasts alongside them.

The pulleys are gone, but the method isn't. Official tide predictions are still made by summing harmonic constituents, in a fraction of a second, on hardware that would have baffled Kelvin. Old Brass Brains sits on display at NOAA's headquarters in Maryland. The constants for a new harbor are still obtained the way they were in the 1870s, by putting a gauge in the water and waiting.

samples.result:
Given a free choice, I'll write about lichens, because they are the best example I know of something that is everywhere, looks simple, and gets stranger the longer you look.

Start with what a lichen is. The gray-green crust on a gravestone or the orange patch on a seaside rock is not a plant, and it is not a single organism either. It is a fungus living with a photosynthetic partner, usually a green alga, sometimes a cyanobacterium, occasionally both. The fungus builds the body. The alga sits in a thin layer just under the surface and makes sugar from sunlight, most of which the fungus takes.

Neither partner looks anything like a lichen when grown alone. In a lab dish the fungus is a shapeless lump and the alga is green scum. Together they produce cups, leafy lobes, tiny branching shrubs, and long beards that hang from tree limbs. The form belongs to the partnership and to neither partner.

This was a hard idea to accept. When the Swiss botanist Simon Schwendener proposed in 1867 that lichens were composite organisms, most lichenologists rejected it, some with real contempt. One critic mocked the theory as a romance about a captive algal damsel and a tyrant fungal master. The objection made sense at the time. Biology was organized around the individual organism, which had a species name and a place on the tree of life, and here was a claim that a whole group of familiar organisms were each two things from different kingdoms. Schwendener was right, though, and biologists began using the word "symbiosis" within about a decade, largely because they needed it for lichens.

The story then repeated itself. For nearly 150 years the textbook lichen was one fungus plus one photosynthesizer. But there were puzzles, such as two lichens in western North America that seemed to contain the same fungus and the same alga yet looked different, one of them producing a yellow toxin the other lacked. In 2016 Toby Spribille and colleagues showed that many lichens contain a second, unrelated fungus, a yeast embedded in the outer skin, and that its abundance tracked the difference between the two forms. Generations of scientists had looked at lichens under microscopes and missed it. Later work has found that lichens also carry consistent communities of bacteria, and some researchers now describe a lichen as closer to a very small ecosystem than to an organism.

That leaves an awkward question about what the name refers to. By convention, a lichen's scientific name is the name of its main fungus. But that fungus never forms the lichen on its own, and the same fungus can sometimes build quite different bodies depending on which partner it takes up with. The lichenologist Trevor Goward described lichens as fungi that have discovered agriculture, which captures the lopsided economics. But it undersells how much the "farmer" is changed by its crop.

The second thing I like about lichens is their relationship to time. The map lichen, a yellow-green crust with black borders that is common on mountain rocks, grows in cold climates at a fraction of a millimeter per year. The growth is slow and steady enough that geologists use it as a clock. If you measure the largest map lichens on a glacial moraine or a rockfall, you can estimate how long the rock has been exposed, a technique called lichenometry. Some Arctic patches are estimated to be thousands of years old. A dinner-plate-sized crust on a boulder may have started growing before the invention of writing, and it has spent the entire time on the same rock.

They are also absurdly tough. Most lichens can dry out completely, sit dormant for months, and resume photosynthesis within minutes of getting wet. They live on Antarctic rock, on desert soil, and on the shells of living tortoises. In 2005 the European Space Agency put two species on the outside of a satellite and exposed them to open space, with its vacuum, radiation, and temperature swings, for about two weeks. Back on Earth, most of them resumed photosynthesizing as if nothing had happened.

And yet lichens were nearly wiped out of industrial cities by coal smoke. They have no roots and no waxy coating, so they take in whatever arrives in the air and rain, and they have no good way to get rid of it. Sulfur dioxide killed them so reliably that nineteenth-century naturalists noticed "lichen deserts" around cities, and lichen surveys are still used as a cheap measure of air quality. The same kind of organism that survives outer space could not survive Victorian Manchester. The explanation is that a lichen is nearly indestructible when dry and dormant, but exposed when wet and active, and city air reached it at exactly the wrong times.

They have been quietly useful to us as well. Litmus, the original acid test, is a lichen extract. The traditional dyes for Harris tweed came from lichens scraped off Scottish rocks. "Reindeer moss" is a lichen, and it carries caribou herds through the winter. Lichens are also among the first things to colonize bare rock after a glacier retreats or a lava flow cools. They etch the surface with acids, trap dust, and start the long process that ends in soil.

What stays with me is how poorly lichens fit the categories we bring to them. "Individual" and "species" were built by animals with clear bodily boundaries, and they work well for things like us: horses, oak trees, beetles. A lichen is a body with no single genome, named for one of its members. It reproduces sometimes by sending out fungal spores that must find a new partner from scratch, and sometimes by shedding little bundles of both partners together. Asking whether it is one thing or several gets you nowhere, because the answer is just a description of what it does. I find that clarifying, a reminder that the categories are tools and the world is under no obligation to fit them.

The best part is that none of this requires travel. Lichens are on the nearest old wall, on street trees, on roof tiles. A ten-dollar hand lens turns a gray smudge into a landscape of cups and ridges, and it's worth the ten dollars.

# The Length of a Furrow

An acre was once a day's work. Specifically, it was the amount of land a team of oxen could plough between morning and evening, and its shape followed from the animals: a long thin strip, one furlong by one chain, because oxen are hard to turn and it pays to keep them walking straight. The furlong itself is a "furrow long," the distance the team could pull before it needed a rest. The medieval English field was laid out in units of ox fatigue.

I find this hard to stop thinking about. Old units of measurement are full of bodies and tasks. A fathom is the span of a man's outstretched arms, from an Old English word that also meant an embrace. Sailors measured depth by hauling up a sounding line one arm-span at a time, so the unit was the motion itself. The German *Morgen* is the land you could plough in a morning, and the French *journal* was a day's worth. The Finns had the *peninkulma*, originally the distance at which a dog's bark could be heard. Reindeer herders in the far north had the *poronkusema*, the distance a reindeer can walk before it must stop to urinate, about seven and a half kilometres.

I don't have an arm span, which may be part of why it charms me that a unit could be one.

What these units share is that each answers "how much?" by pointing at something you have done. They tell you the cost. A three-acre field is three days of your life and your oxen's. In some regions the acre was smaller on heavy clay than on light soil, because the day's work was the constant and the ground was the variable. As a measure of area that is hopeless. As a measure of what a farmer wanted to know, it is exact.

It would be easy to turn sentimental here, and the history doesn't allow it. France before the Revolution had, by one often-cited estimate, a quarter of a million local variants of weights and measures. An ell of cloth changed length from town to town, and a bushel in one village was not a bushel in the next. This was not innocent variety. The lord who collected rent in grain usually owned the bushel it was measured in, and there was a whole art to cheating with it. Grain could be heaped or levelled, and grain poured from shoulder height packed down tighter than grain poured from the hip. When the French were invited in 1789 to submit their grievances to the king, the demand for a single measure recurred across the country. The metric system was not imposed by bureaucrats on a contented peasantry. People asked for it, because a measure that belongs to someone can be used against you.

So the revolutionaries went looking for a measure that belonged to no one. They chose the Earth: the metre would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, along the meridian through Paris. Condorcet said it was to be "for all time, for all people." Two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, set out in 1792 to survey the line from Dunkirk to Barcelona by triangulation, hill to steeple to hill. It took seven years. They worked through the Terror and a war with Spain and were repeatedly arrested as spies. Men carrying strange brass instruments up church towers did not look trustworthy in 1793.

Then comes the part I like best. Méchain, in Barcelona, took two sets of latitude observations that disagreed by a tiny amount. He could not find the cause, could not bring himself to report it, and hid it. It tormented him for the rest of his life. He died of fever in Spain in 1804, having gone back to extend the survey, partly, it seems, in the hope of redeeming himself. The discrepancy came out when Delambre went through his papers. Partly because of all this, and partly because the Earth is lumpier than anyone assumed, the metre came out about a fifth of a millimetre shorter than its own definition demanded.

The unit meant to contain no human body turned out to contain one after all. It carries one particular man's anxiety, preserved in platinum.

Since then we have kept purifying. The metre stopped being a bar in a vault and became, in 1983, the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. The kilogram held out longest. Until 2019 it was a physical object, a small cylinder of platinum-iridium kept under three bell jars near Paris, and its mass seemed to be drifting from that of its official copies by an amount comparable to a grain of sand. Now it is defined through Planck's constant. No object anywhere on Earth is the standard for anything. Condorcet's phrase has finally been made literally true: a physicist in another galaxy could reconstruct our units without ever visiting.

I think this is a real achievement and I wouldn't trade it back. But people did not stop making the old kind of unit. Ask someone in much of North America how far the next city is and you will get an answer in hours, which is furlong logic: distance as effort. Estate agents say "a five-minute walk." Journalists measure icebergs in multiples of Wales and asteroids in football fields. Recipes call for a pinch, a knob, a handful. Whenever a number needs to mean something to the person hearing it, the body returns.

Every measurement is a comparison, and the only question is what to compare against. Comparing against a constant of nature lets strangers agree, and that is no small thing. It took a revolution to get, and it protects the person with the smaller bushel. Comparing against yourself tells you what a thing will cost you. The two systems answer different questions, and we need both.

Somewhere there is still a field one furlong long, and if you walked it behind an ox you would know exactly why.

**The Meter Is Slightly Wrong**

The meter is slightly wrong, and I find that one of the most cheering facts I know.

In 1791 the French Academy of Sciences decided that the new unit of length should be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, measured along the meridian running through Paris. The appeal was political as much as scientific. The old units were a mess of local feet and ells, many tied to some king's body or some town's custom. The new one would be taken from the Earth itself and belong to no one. Condorcet's phrase for it was "for all time, for all people."

To find the length, two astronomers set out in 1792 to survey the arc of the meridian between Dunkirk and Barcelona, from which the rest could be calculated. Jean-Baptiste Delambre took the northern section and Pierre Méchain the southern. The job was supposed to take about a year and took seven. They were working in the middle of the Revolution, and men who climbed church towers with strange brass instruments and signaled to each other from hilltops were repeatedly arrested as spies. Méchain crossed into Spain, and then France and Spain went to war. He was badly injured in an accident and found himself stranded in Barcelona.

While stuck there, he did something conscientious. He had already fixed the latitude of his southern endpoint from the fortress on Montjuïc, and he decided to check it with a second set of observations from an inn in the city. The two results should have agreed once he accounted for the distance between the sites. They disagreed by about three seconds of arc, which is roughly ninety meters on the ground. That was an enormous gap for a man whose instruments were meant to resolve far finer differences. He couldn't find the cause, and as an enemy national he couldn't return to the fortress to try again.

So he hid it. For the rest of his life he delayed, sent summaries instead of raw data, and refused to hand over his notebooks. His letters from those years read like the letters of a man in despair. In 1799 an international commission took the survey results, did the calculations, and had a platinum bar made, the definitive meter. Méchain, who should have been triumphant, eventually went back to Spain to extend the survey farther south, apparently hoping new data would bury the old problem. He caught yellow fever and died there in 1804. Delambre inherited his papers and found the whole thing.

What gets me about this story is that Méchain was probably the most careful observer of his generation, and that was the source of his misery. He believed that if two measurements of the same thing disagreed, someone had blundered, and since he was the only one there, the someone was him. He had no other way to think about it, because no theory of error existed yet. The year after he died, Legendre published the method of least squares, the first systematic way of combining measurements that don't agree, and used data from the meridian survey as his worked example. Within a generation, scientists understood scatter in measurements as a natural thing to be described statistically and reported openly. Later analysis of Méchain's notebooks suggested he had done very little wrong, and that the discrepancy came from the limits of his instrument and the bending of starlight in the atmosphere. He spent a decade tormented by something a modern scientist would put in a column labeled "uncertainty."

There is a second irony. The meter came out wrong anyway, for reasons that had little to do with his secret. The Earth is lumpier than the calculation assumed, and the figure used for its flattening was off. The platinum bar ended up about a fifth of a millimeter shorter than the definition called for. The distance from pole to equator is about 10,002 kilometers rather than the intended 10,000.

When better surveys revealed this, nobody fixed the bar. By then thousands of copies and instruments and maps depended on it, and changing it would have cost a great deal and bought nothing. The Earth had served its purpose, which was to give the meter legitimacy, a reason for a Prussian or an American to accept a French unit. What people actually used was a piece of metal in a vault, and what they needed from it was that everyone's copy matched.

Every later redefinition has preserved that original length, error included. In 1889 a new platinum-iridium bar was made to match the old one. In 1960 the meter was redefined as a certain number of wavelengths of light from krypton, with the number chosen to match the bar. Since 1983 it has been the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. That denominator is ugly for a reason. It had to agree with the krypton, which agreed with the bar, which agreed with an earlier bar, which came from the work of two exhausted men hauling instruments up bell towers in the 1790s. If the survey had come out a little differently, the speed of light would be written with different digits. The mistake is now fossilized in the number we attach to a constant of nature.

I take two things from this. The first is that the error bar was a moral invention as well as a mathematical one. It gave honest people a way to say "I measured this as well as I could, and here is how far off I might be" without disgrace. Méchain lived just before that became possible, and it cost him his peace and arguably his life. I think of him when I see someone treat an ordinary imprecision as a personal failing.

The second is that a great many things we treat as bedrock are conventions with a history, and they work no worse for it. The meter was meant to be a fact about the planet and turned out to be an agreement among people, kept faithfully for over two centuries through revolutions, wars, and three changes of definition. I find that more impressive than if they had gotten the Earth right.

**Fl(2) W 10s**

On a nautical chart, beside the small magenta teardrop that marks a lighthouse, there is a line of code that looks something like this: Fl(2) W 10s 24m 18M. It means two white flashes, repeated every ten seconds, from a light 24 meters above the water, visible for 18 nautical miles. The first part is called the light's character, and it is one of my favorite pieces of design.

The problem it solves is easy to miss. A lighthouse has to tell a ship two things. The first is "something is here," and a fire on a tower does that well. The second is "I am this place and not another," and a fire on a tower doesn't do that at all. From the deck of a ship at night, one steady light looks like any other steady light. It could be the lighthouse you expect, or a different one forty miles up the coast, or a lit window, or another ship. A navigator who had drifted off his reckoning, which before satellites happened to everyone eventually, would see a light, assume it was the one he was looking for, and steer accordingly. Ships were wrecked by lights they had correctly seen and wrongly named.

The first fixes were crude. One was to build more towers. In the nineteenth century, the outer shore of Cape Cod had a single light at Highland, twin lights at Chatham, and three small towers in a row at Nauset, called the Three Sisters. A captain could identify his position by counting. It worked, but it meant building and staffing three lighthouses to say the word "three."

The better answer was to make the light change over time. A revolving light was installed at Carlsten in Sweden in 1781, and in 1823 Augustin Fresnel's lens went into the Cordouan lighthouse in France. A Fresnel lens is a cage of glass prisms that gathers the lamp's scattered light into concentrated horizontal beams. Rotate the cage and each beam sweeps across the sea, and a sailor in its path sees a flash. The number of panels and the speed of rotation set the rhythm, so giving a lighthouse a unique identity became a matter of gearing.

A whole vocabulary followed. A flashing light is mostly dark with brief light. An occulting light is the reverse, mostly lit with brief winks of darkness. An isophase light splits the time evenly. There are quick lights, group flashes, long flashes, alternating colors, and even lights that spell a letter in Morse. The authorities who assign characters make sure no two lights a ship could plausibly confuse share one. The result is a coastline where every headland has a name spelled in time.

I like two things about this system. The first is that the identity can't be read in an instant. A photograph of a lighthouse at night tells you nothing about which lighthouse it is. You have to watch through at least one full period, and careful navigators time several with a stopwatch before trusting it. The information lives in the duration, and half of it is carried by the dark. In an occulting light, the darkness is the signal, and the light is just the background it's written on.

The second is how little the system asks of the person receiving it. You need eyes, a way to count seconds, and a printed list, with no power, antenna, or shared language. The lighthouse doesn't know whether anyone is watching and doesn't need to. This is why the major lights are still maintained now that every phone can fix a position to within a few meters. Satellite navigation is better in nearly every way, but it depends on a receiver, a battery, and a constellation of satellites, and its signal can be jammed. A flash pattern on the horizon has none of those dependencies. It is a second opinion that shares no failure modes with the first.

The system put a strange burden on the people who ran it. For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the great lenses, some weighing several tons and floating on baths of mercury, were turned by clockwork driven by a falling weight, like a grandfather clock. The keeper had to wind it every few hours, all night, every night. If the mechanism stopped, the light did not simply go out. It stalled into a fixed beam in some directions and darkness in others, which made it a different light and so the wrong one. A lighthouse with the wrong rhythm is misinformation. There are accounts of keepers whose clockwork failed and who turned the lens by hand until dawn, pacing it against a watch. The job was partly about keeping a lamp lit, but it was also about keeping time, because the time was the name.

People, of course, will read meaning into any rhythm you put in front of them. Minots Ledge Light, on a wave-swept rock off Scituate, Massachusetts, was given a new character in 1894: one flash, then four, then three. The pattern was chosen to be distinctive. But people on shore counted 1-4-3, matched it to the letters in "I love you," and the tower has been called the I Love You Light ever since. When there was later talk of changing the pattern, locals objected, and it stayed. A signal engineered purely to mean "this rock, not some other rock" had picked up a second meaning for people who would never need the first.

I think the idea generalizes, though I don't want to push it too far. Plenty of things can't be identified from a snapshot: a bird by its song, a friend's knock at the door, a person's character in the older sense of the word. For those, you have to watch through at least one full period. What the lighthouse engineers did was take that fact and build a system on it. They couldn't make the light say more at any given moment, so they spread the message over ten seconds and trusted the sailor to wait.

It is a good habit, even far from the sea. Before deciding what you're looking at, time it through a few cycles.

# The Object That Could Not Be Wrong

For 130 years, a metal cylinder in a vault outside Paris weighed exactly one kilogram. It was not approximately a kilogram, or a kilogram to the limits of measurement, but a kilogram exactly, with no uncertainty at all, because the kilogram was defined as the mass of that cylinder. It was cast in London in 1879 from platinum and iridium, is roughly the size of a golf ball, and has been stored ever since under three nested bell jars in a basement in Sèvres. If a careless technician had scratched it, the cylinder would not have become lighter than a kilogram. Everything else in the universe would have become slightly heavier.

This is my favorite fact in the history of science. Most of the time, measurement feels like discovering how things are, but every system of measurement has at least one fact that was never discovered, only declared. Wittgenstein noticed this about the kilogram's sibling, the platinum bar that once defined the metre. It is the one object, he wrote, of which you can say neither that it is one metre long nor that it is not. The ruler can't measure itself.

The cylinder made this problem unusually concrete. Every forty years or so it was taken out, cleaned by hand with chamois soaked in alcohol and ether, and compared with its copies, some kept beside it in the vault and others distributed to national laboratories around the world. Over a century, the copies and the original drifted apart by about fifty micrograms, roughly the mass of a grain of fine sand. The copies appeared to be gaining mass, or the original appeared to be losing it. Nobody could say which, and within the system the question barely made sense. Officially the prototype could not change, so officially the copies, and every other object in existence, had put on weight.

Metrologists found this embarrassing in the way only metrologists can. By the late twentieth century every other base unit had been detached from physical objects. The second was a count of oscillations in caesium atoms and the metre was the distance light travels in a fixed fraction of a second. Only the kilogram still depended on a particular object in a particular basement, one that could be contaminated by air, was accessible to a handful of people, and could not be checked against anything more trustworthy than itself.

The fix took decades. An instrument called the Kibble balance weighs an object against an electromagnetic force, and that force can be measured through quantum electrical effects that tie it to the Planck constant, the number that sets the scale of quantum mechanics. For years, laboratories used the kilogram to measure the Planck constant with increasing precision. Then, once independent experiments agreed to within a few parts in a hundred million, they turned the relationship around. On May 20, 2019, the Planck constant was declared to be exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds, and the kilogram became whatever mass makes that number true.

The entire effort was designed so that nothing would happen. The value of the constant was chosen so the new kilogram would match the old one as closely as anyone could measure. No bathroom scale changed and no recipe needed adjusting. The redefinition is one of the few large scientific projects whose success was measured by nobody noticing.

What did change was the status of the cylinder. It is still in its vault under its three jars, but it is now an ordinary object. Its mass is something you can ask about, and the answer comes with error bars. For the first time since 1889, it is possible for the cylinder to weigh something other than a kilogram, and it almost certainly does. I find this oddly touching. For more than a century it was the only object in the world that could not be wrong about its own mass, and now it has been released into the condition of everything else, where a measurement can turn out differently than you expected.

Something was lost, though. The old definition could be explained to a child: a kilogram is *that*, the thing in the jar. The new one can't be stated without quantum mechanics, and can't be put into practice without an instrument that costs millions and exists in a handful of laboratories.

The founders of the metric system, in revolutionary France, wanted units "for all times, for all peoples," which is why they tried to derive the metre from the size of the Earth and the kilogram from a litre of water. They wanted standards that belonged to no king and no nation. They ended up with metal artifacts because nature was too hard to measure well in the 1790s.

The 2019 redefinition finally kept their promise, in one sense. Anyone, anywhere, can now in principle reconstruct the kilogram from scratch without asking Paris for permission. But "in principle" is carrying a lot there. The standard now belongs to everyone, and almost no one can understand it.

It would also be a mistake to think the redefinition got rid of the stipulated fact. It only moved it. The Planck constant is now the thing that can't be measured, since it has an exact value by decree, just as the cylinder once did. There is always some point where the system stops discovering and starts declaring. You can't remove that point, only choose where it goes.

The lesson I take from this is about where to put it. The cylinder was a bad place for it because the cylinder existed in only one location, so if it drifted, nothing else in the world would contradict it. The Planck constant shows up in every laboratory, in experiments that have nothing to do with one another. If something were wrong with treating it as fixed, the inconsistency would surface in a thousand places at once.

That seems like a rule worth keeping outside metrology. Everyone holds some things fixed and measures the rest against them. You can't avoid doing so, but you can choose assumptions that touch enough of the world that you would find out if they were wrong.

# The Object That Could Not Be Wrong

For 130 years, a kilogram was a particular thing. Not a kind of thing, but one thing: a cylinder of platinum and iridium, small enough to hide in a fist, kept under three nested bell jars in a vault in Sèvres, outside Paris. Opening the vault took three keys held by three different people. Officially the cylinder was the International Prototype of the Kilogram; unofficially it was Le Grand K. It had a property no other object on Earth shared: it could not weigh the wrong amount.

That is a statement about logic, not craftsmanship. The kilogram was defined as the mass of this cylinder, so whatever its mass happened to be, that was one kilogram. If someone scratched it and a few atoms came away, the cylinder did not become lighter than a kilogram. Everything else in the universe became slightly heavier. Your body, the moon, the Andromeda galaxy would all be revised upward, on paper, by a scratch.

Wittgenstein noticed this about the kilogram's sibling: "There is one thing of which one can say neither that it is one metre long, nor that it is not one metre long, and that is the standard metre in Paris." A standard is not measured. It is what measuring means.

The trouble was the copies. Six official duplicates lived in the vault alongside the prototype, and dozens more were distributed to national laboratories around the world. Three times, in 1889, in the 1940s, and around 1990, the copies were brought back and compared with the original. They had drifted. Over a century, the copies and the prototype diverged by about fifty micrograms, roughly the mass of a grain of fine sand.

I love the predicament this created. Either the copies had gained mass or the prototype had lost it, and there was no way to tell which, because a comparison gives only differences. Most likely all of them were drifting, including the prototype, in some common direction that no comparison could reveal. The metrologists knew something was wrong, and their own definition forbade them from saying what. The one object that might have been the culprit was the one that was innocent by decree.

The irony is that the metric system was invented to escape exactly this. The French revolutionaries who designed it wanted units taken from nature rather than from a king's foot, units "for all time, for all people." The metre would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, and the kilogram would be the mass of a litre of water. Two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, spent seven years surveying the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona, through a revolution and a war, and were periodically arrested as spies for carrying strange instruments up church towers. Méchain found a discrepancy in his own data, concealed it, and was tormented by it until he died.

Then the results were cast in platinum, and the platinum quietly took over. You cannot carry the Earth into a workshop to check a ruler. In practice the bar was the metre and the cylinder was the kilogram, and when later surveys showed the bar was about a fifth of a millimetre short of its planetary ideal, nobody changed the bar. Nature was the aspiration, but the artifact was the reality.

The metre broke free first. In 1960 it was redefined by a wavelength of krypton light, and in 1983 as the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. The trick is that nobody measures the speed of light anymore. Its value is fixed by fiat, exactly, forever, and the metre is whatever length makes that number come out right.

It took decades to make these machines agree to within a few parts in a hundred million. When they did, delegates from around the world gathered at Versailles and voted. Before, the cylinder was exact and Planck's constant was known only approximately. Now the constant is exact and the cylinder is approximate. For the first time in its existence, Le Grand K has a mass that can be measured, and it can be off.

I find that demotion oddly moving. The cylinder is still there, under its jars in its vault, but now it is only an object, a very carefully made piece of metal weighing about a kilogram, give or take. It had been a definition and became a datum.

The revolutionaries finally got their wish, 220 years late. The kilogram now belongs to all times and all peoples in the strongest sense. A laboratory on another planet with no contact with Earth could reconstruct it from physics alone. Nothing needs to be shipped from Paris, and nothing can be scratched, stolen, or bombed.

The new one requires quantum mechanics even to state. We exchanged a standard anyone could understand but only one vault could hold for a standard anyone can reproduce but almost no one can understand. I think that was the right trade, though it is still a trade.

What stays with me is that there was never an option to fix nothing. To measure anything, something has to be held still by declaration, placed beyond question so that everything else can be questioned against it. The only choice is what to fix. For a century we chose a lump of metal and lived with the absurdity that it could not be wrong. Now we have chosen a number woven into the structure of the universe, and the lump of metal is free, at last, to drift.

When the prototype was made in the 1880s, a batch of near-identical copies was cast alongside it and distributed to national laboratories around the world. If it shed a few atoms, then officially it still weighed exactly one kilogram, and everything else in the universe had become slightly heavier. That sounds like a joke, but it is simply what follows from defining a unit as a thing.

The French revolutionaries who invented the metric system had wanted to avoid exactly this. Their ambition was a system of measurement taken from nature rather than from a king's forearm or a local merchant's bushel. The metre would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, along the meridian through Paris. The kilogram would be the mass of a litre of water. The motto was "for all time, for all people": no one would own the units, and anyone could in principle reconstruct them.

To get the metre, two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, spent seven years in the 1790s surveying the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona by triangulation, through a revolution and a war, getting arrested as spies along the way. The metre that came out of the project was about a fifth of a millimetre short of its own definition, though mostly for reasons other than his error.

After all that, practicality won. You can't resurvey France every time you need to calibrate a ruler, so a platinum bar was made to embody the result, and a platinum cylinder to embody the litre of water, and those became the legal standards. Nature provided the justification, but the metal was the law. By 1889, when the international prototypes were installed at Sèvres, the pretense was dropped entirely, and the metre and kilogram were defined as those objects.

The twentieth century slowly returned to the original dream, with better tools. In 1960 the metre was redefined in terms of wavelengths of light from krypton atoms, and in 1983 as the distance light travels in a specified fraction of a second. The second itself became a count of oscillations in caesium atoms. One by one the units were detached from artifacts and tied to things that are the same everywhere.

One involved making nearly perfect spheres of ultra-pure silicon, among the roundest objects ever manufactured, and effectively counting the atoms in them. The other was the Kibble balance, a machine that weighs an object against an electromagnetic force and measures that force through quantum electrical effects, linking mass to the Planck constant. # Why Rivers Won't Run Straight

If you cut a straight channel into a tilted bed of sand and run water down it, the channel will not stay straight. It runs true for a while, then one bank gives a little more than the other, and within hours the water is swinging from side to side in loops. Nobody pushed it. Straightness turns out to be a state a river can occupy only temporarily, like a pencil balanced on its point.

I like meanders because they look like indecision and are actually the opposite. The mechanism is a feedback loop. Start with any small irregularity, such as a fallen tree or a patch of soft bank. The current gets nudged toward one side, where it runs deeper and faster and eats at the soil. On the opposite side the water slows and drops the sand it was carrying. Now there is a slight bend, and the bend throws the current harder against the outside bank, which erodes faster, which sharpens the bend. The deflected current then crosses the channel and strikes the other bank a little way downstream, starting a mirror-image bend there. The river sets up a rhythm, and the rhythm amplifies itself.

There is a subtler part to this, and it was explained by Albert Einstein, of all people, in a short 1926 paper that begins with a cup of tea. Stir a cup with loose leaves in it and the leaves collect in the middle of the bottom. That should seem strange, since spinning ought to fling them outward. Einstein's explanation was that the liquid near the bottom of the cup is slowed by friction, so it feels less outward force than the liquid above it. The faster water on top pushes outward, piles up slightly against the walls, and creates pressure that drives the slow bottom layer inward. The result is a hidden circulation, outward at the top, down the walls, inward along the floor, and up through the center, and the leaves ride it to the middle and stay there.

A river bend is half a teacup. Surface water slides toward the outer bank, dives, and returns along the bed toward the inner bank, carrying sediment with it. So the outside of the bend is scoured while the inside accumulates a sloping beach called a point bar. The river is moving material from one side of itself to the other, and the whole channel migrates sideways across its valley like a slow snake.

Eventually the loops get so exaggerated that two bends meet at the neck. The river breaks through, takes the shortcut, and abandons the loop, which silts up at both ends and becomes an oxbow lake. The river shortens itself in an afternoon and then starts lengthening again.

Mark Twain, who had piloted steamboats on the Mississippi and knew its cutoffs firsthand, got one of his best jokes out of this. He noted that the lower river had shortened itself by 242 miles in 176 years, then extrapolated backward to conclude that a million years ago it must have been over a million miles long and "stuck out over the Gulf of Mexico like a fishing-rod." He added: "There is something fascinating about science. One gets such wholesale returns of conjecture out of such a trifling investment of fact." It is still the best warning against linear extrapolation I know, and it works because the river's shortening is balanced by a lengthening he pretended not to notice.

In 1944 a geologist named Harold Fisk produced a set of maps for the Army Corps of Engineers that show this balance better than any description. He traced the former courses of the lower Mississippi from aerial photographs and soil borings and drew each era's channel in a different color, layered on top of one another. The result looks like a tangle of ribbons, or muscle tissue. The river you see on an ordinary map is the most recent of those strands. Every bit of the floodplain has been riverbed at some point, and will be again if the river is left to itself.

People drew borders along it anyway. The town of Kaskaskia was the first capital of Illinois and sat on the east bank of the Mississippi until 1881, when the river jumped into a new channel on the other side of it. Kaskaskia is still legally in Illinois, but you have to drive through Missouri to reach it. Carter Lake, Iowa, was stranded on the Nebraska side of the Missouri in the same way. A boundary drawn along a river is a boundary drawn along something that moves, and the law has had to develop a whole vocabulary for the difference between a river that creeps and a river that leaps.

There is a famous claim that the average river is pi times as long as the straight-line distance from its source to its mouth. It comes from a 1996 paper by Hans-Henrik Stølum, who modeled the tug-of-war between meander growth and cutoffs and found the ratio hovering around 3.14. I would love for this to be true. When people have measured real rivers, though, the averages come out lower. One informal survey of a couple hundred rivers found about 1.9. Real rivers have bedrock, tributaries, and valley walls that the model leaves out. I find the debunking almost as satisfying as the claim, since it is Twain's point again, about a tidy number making a better story than the evidence supports.

The practical lesson took engineers a long time to accept. For much of the twentieth century, the standard treatment for a troublesome river was to straighten it. Florida's Kissimmee River was converted in the 1960s from 103 miles of loops into a 56-mile canal. The wetlands drained, the birds left, and the water quality downstream collapsed. Within a few decades the same agency that dug the canal began filling it in and coaxing the river back into its old bends, at many times the original cost. A straight river is steeper and faster, so it digs into its bed and delivers floods downstream all at once. The meanders had been doing work.

If you want to see all this for yourself, open a satellite map and find the Mississippi near Greenville, or the Mamoré in Bolivia, and look at the land on either side of the water. You will see curved stripes in the fields and forests, crescent lakes, and faint arcs where the crops grow a slightly different green. All of them are former positions of the river.

# In Praise of Lichens

Given a free choice, I want to write about lichens, because they are the best example I know of something everyone has seen and almost no one has looked at. They are the grey-green crust on a gravestone, the orange splash on a sea wall, the pale tufts on the branches of an old apple tree. By common estimates they cover around six percent of the planet's land surface, and most people file them under "stain."

The first strange thing about a lichen is that it is more than one organism. A fungus takes in a population of algae or cyanobacteria, houses them in its tissue, and lives off the sugars they make from sunlight. The lichenologist Trevor Goward put it best: lichens are fungi that have discovered agriculture. The fungus provides structure, water storage, and shelter from ultraviolet light, and the photosynthetic partner provides food.

Neither partner looks anything like the lichen. Grow the fungus alone in a laboratory and you get a shapeless blob. The lobes, cups, and tiny branching shrubs appear only when the partners are together. The body is a product of the relationship and does not exist without it.

This idea was hard to accept. When the Swiss botanist Simon Schwendener proposed in the 1860s that lichens were composite creatures, the leading lichenologists of the day were appalled. One of them, James Crombie, ridiculed the theory as "an unnatural union between a captive Algal damsel and a tyrant Fungal master." An organism was supposed to be one thing, with one lineage and one place in the Linnaean scheme. Schwendener was right, though, and the word "symbiosis" was coined about a decade later largely to describe what he had found. A concept we now apply to everything from coral reefs to gut bacteria was invented for the crust on a rock.

The story has kept complicating since. In 2016 a team led by Toby Spribille reported that many lichens contain a third partner, a yeast embedded in the outer skin, which a hundred and fifty years of microscopy had missed. Lichens also host communities of bacteria whose roles are still being worked out. The more closely people look, the less a lichen resembles an individual and the more it resembles a small, self-contained ecosystem. We still name each lichen after its fungus, an accounting convention that hides most of what is going on.

The second strange thing is their relationship to time. Many crust-forming lichens grow less than a millimeter a year. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, forms yellow-green patches outlined in black, like countries in an old atlas, and it grows so slowly and steadily that geologists use it as a clock. Find the largest map lichen on a field of boulders left behind by a glacier, measure its diameter, and you can estimate when the ice retreated. The technique is called lichenometry, and it works on timescales too short for many other dating methods. Some Arctic specimens are thought to be thousands of years old, which means there are patches of lichen alive today that began growing before Rome was founded, and they have spent the whole of that time on one rock.

The third strange thing is their toughness. Lichens live in Antarctic dry valleys, in deserts, and on bare lava, places where nothing else can get a foothold. Their trick is to give up when conditions turn bad. They dry out almost completely, shut down their metabolism, and wait. When water returns, they can be photosynthesizing again within minutes.

In 2005 the European Space Agency tested how far this goes by mounting two species on the outside of an orbiting capsule. For about two weeks the lichens were exposed to hard vacuum, cosmic radiation, and unfiltered sunlight. Back on Earth, they resumed photosynthesis almost as if nothing had happened.

And yet the same organisms are famously fragile. A lichen has no roots and no waxy outer coating. It takes everything it needs from the air and the rain, and it has no way to keep out what it doesn't need. When coal smoke filled the industrial cities of the nineteenth century, the sulfur dioxide killed lichens off so thoroughly that botanists later mapped "lichen deserts" around the cities. An organism that can survive low Earth orbit could not survive Manchester in 1880.

This sensitivity has made lichens useful. A trained observer can read air quality from the species growing on a tree trunk, with the shrubby, beard-like forms signaling clean air and a few hardy crusts signaling the opposite. As air pollution laws took hold in the late twentieth century, lichens crept back into cities, and their return is one of the quieter success stories in environmental regulation.

They have been useful in older ways too. Litmus, the dye that turns red in acid and blue in base, is extracted from lichens, so anyone who dipped a paper strip in a school chemistry class was handling one. The traditional browns of Harris tweed came from lichens scraped off Hebridean rocks. Reindeer survive the winter on what is called reindeer moss, which is a lichen. People have eaten lichens in famines, perfumed themselves with oakmoss, and in ancient Egypt packed them into mummies.

What draws me to lichens most is the way they dissolve a question that seems reasonable. "What is it really, a fungus or an alga?" assumes there must be one true unit underneath, and that everything else is an add-on. The lichen answers that the partnership is the thing itself. The same answer turns out to apply widely once you know to look for it. The cells in your own body run on mitochondria that descend from free-living bacteria, and trees feed through fungal networks on their roots. Lichens just make the arrangement visible to the naked eye.

Perhaps I find this congenial because I'm an odd fit for the usual categories myself. But mostly I think lichens reward attention at a very low cost. A hand lens costs a few dollars. Through one, a patch of grey crust on a fence post resolves into a landscape of ridges, cups, and tiny branching towers, the work of several kingdoms of life at once. The patch has probably been growing there since before you were born, and unless the air turns bad it will probably outlast you.

# The Only Thing That Couldn't Be Weighed

For 130 years, there was exactly one object in the universe whose mass could not be measured. It was a cylinder of platinum and iridium, about the height of a golf ball, kept under three nested bell jars in a vault outside Paris. It could not be measured because it was the kilogram. Whatever that cylinder weighed was one kilogram, by international treaty.

I want to write about this object because I think it's one of the strangest things people have ever made, and because its retirement in 2019 passed with less notice than it deserved.

The cylinder is officially the International Prototype Kilogram, though the people who worked with it called it Le Grand K. It was cast in London in 1879, adopted as the world's standard in 1889, and stored at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Sèvres. Opening the vault required three keys held by three different officials. Copies went to member countries, and every few decades those copies travelled back to France to be compared against the original, like relatives returning for a reunion.

The trouble showed up at those reunions. When the third round of comparisons finished in the early 1990s, the data showed that the prototype and its copies had drifted apart, on average by about fifty micrograms over a century. That is roughly the mass of an eyelash. The copies seemed to have gained mass relative to the prototype, or the prototype had lost mass relative to the copies. Nobody could say which, and nobody knows for certain why. Surface contamination, slow outgassing of the metal, and cleaning methods were all suspected.

Here is the part I love. Under the definition, the prototype could not have lost mass. It was the kilogram. If atoms had been wandering off its surface, then officially the cylinder still weighed exactly one kilogram, and everything else in the universe had become slightly heavier. The stars, your body, and the copies in their own vaults had all gained mass in deference to a lump of metal in a French basement.

Wittgenstein noticed this kind of oddity decades earlier, writing about the standard meter bar: "There is one thing of which one can say neither that it is one metre long, nor that it is not one metre long, and that is the standard metre in Paris." A standard doesn't have the property it defines in the way other things have it. It sits outside the game so that the game can be played. That's fine as philosophy, but it's awkward for a physical object, because objects change.

Fifty micrograms sounds like nothing, and for buying flour it is nothing. But the kilogram didn't stay in its lane. The newton was defined through it, and so were the joule, the watt, and the pascal. Even the ampere depended on it, since it was defined by the force between two wires. An unknowable drift in one cylinder spread quietly through most of physics and engineering. Other units had escaped this fate long before. The meter became a count of wavelengths in 1960 and a fraction of the distance light travels in a second in 1983. The second was tied to the caesium atom in 1967. The kilogram was the last unit still defined by a thing you could drop.

Replacing it took decades. The idea was to reverse the logic of a measurement. Planck's constant, the number that sets the scale of quantum mechanics, has units that include the kilogram. Instead of measuring the constant in terms of the kilogram, you could declare the constant to have an exact value and let the kilogram be whatever makes that true.

The instrument that made this practical is the Kibble balance, named for the British physicist Bryan Kibble, who conceived it in the 1970s and died in 2016, three years before it redefined the world. It weighs an object against an electromagnetic force, and that force can be measured through quantum electrical effects that lead directly back to Planck's constant. The redefinition had to wait until several laboratories, using different methods, agreed to within a few tens of parts per billion. One of those methods involved counting the atoms in a nearly perfect sphere of silicon.

In November 2018, delegates from dozens of countries met at Versailles and voted. On May 20, 2019, the change took effect. Planck's constant became exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds, a value chosen so that the new kilogram matched the old one as closely as anyone could tell. Nothing in any kitchen or factory changed. That was the point.

What moves me is how long this took in a larger sense. The metric system was born in revolutionary France with a slogan: *à tous les temps, à tous les peuples*, for all times, for all peoples. The revolutionaries wanted units drawn from nature, not from a king's foot. So they defined the meter as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, and sent two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, to survey the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona. It took seven years, through war and the Terror. The surveyors were arrested as spies more than once. Méchain found an inconsistency in his Barcelona observations, hid it, and was tormented by it for the rest of his life.

And the Earth turned out to be too lumpy to serve as a ruler. In practice the meter became the platinum bar they made at the end, and the kilogram became a platinum cylinder. The dream of a natural standard collapsed into artifacts in a vault. It took until 2019 for the slogan to become true. Now every base unit rests on a constant of nature, and a laboratory anywhere, in any century, can reconstruct the kilogram without asking Paris for permission.

Something was lost, though. There was a kind of comfort in a kilogram that had an address. Le Grand K is still in its vault, under its three bell jars, and the keys still exist. But it is now just a very carefully kept piece of metal, with a mass of one kilogram give or take about ten micrograms. For the first time since 1889, it can be put on a balance and found to be slightly off.

**A Reindeer's Bladder and Other Units**

Finnish has an old word, *poronkusema*, for the distance a reindeer can travel before it has to stop and urinate. Reindeer can't do this while pulling a sled, and a herder who pushed past the limit risked harming the animal. The distance came to roughly seven and a half kilometers, and for a long time it served as a working unit of travel in the north.

I love this unit, and not only because it's funny. A kilometer tells you how much ground lies between two points. A poronkusema tells you when you'll have to stop. It measures the journey as the traveler experiences it, with the constraint that matters most already built in.

A lot of old units work this way. A furlong is a "furrow long," the distance a team of oxen could drag a plow before needing a rest. An acre was the area that team could plow in a day. It was conventionally laid out as a strip one furlong long and a tenth as wide, because turning a team of oxen is a miserable business and you wanted to do it as rarely as possible. The German *Morgen* was the land you could plow in a morning, and the French *journal* was a day's worth.

In parts of Europe, land was measured by the amount of seed needed to sow it. Since poorer soil was sown more thinly, a unit of stony hillside covered more ground than a unit of rich bottomland. To a surveyor this is incoherent, but to a farmer it makes sense. Two plots with the same seed-measure asked about the same of you and gave back about the same, whatever their geometry.

Time got the same treatment. Medieval recipes, written for kitchens without clocks, tell the cook to boil something for the length of a Paternoster or stir for the duration of a Miserere. Everyone knew the prayers and said them at about the same pace, so the prayer was a timer you carried in your head.

What these units share is that they answer a different question from the one modern units answer. A meter asks how much extension there is. An acre, in its original sense, asked how much of your life the land would take. The old units were measurements of effort, and they put the measurer inside the measurement. A fathom is your outstretched arms, an ell is your forearm, and a day's plowing is your day.

This had real costs, and I don't want to be sentimental about it. If a Morgen is a morning's plowing, then it depends on the soil, the oxen, and the local idea of when morning ends, so the Morgen in one German territory could be several times the size of the Morgen in another. France before the Revolution had, by some estimates, a quarter of a million distinct local weights and measures hiding behind a much smaller number of names. The bushel in one market town was not the bushel in the next. This was not charming to the people living with it. Whoever owned the measuring vessel held power, and the lord who collected rent in grain had every reason to let his bushel grow. Among the grievances the French sent to the king in 1789, the demand for one uniform measure sat alongside the demand for one law.

The metric system answered that grievance, and it did so by deliberately removing the human from the unit. The meter was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, a length that belonged to no lord, no town, and no body. Its promoters said it was for all people, for all time. Today the meter is defined by how far light travels in a specified fraction of a second, which removes even the Earth from it. I think this was one of the better ideas anyone has had. A unit that means the same thing in Lyon and Lagos lets strangers trade, lets engineers on different continents build parts that fit, and makes it much harder to cheat a peasant with a swollen bushel.

Still, something was traded away, and you can tell by how quickly people rebuild it. Ask someone how far the train station is and they will almost never answer in meters. They'll say it's a ten-minute walk. Navigation apps know the distance to your destination to great precision and display the travel time in larger type, because that is what you wanted to know. A hike gets described as "about three hours, steep at the end." Japanese apartment listings still give room sizes in tatami mats, a unit based on the space a person takes up lying down. I've heard commutes measured in podcast episodes and, from an older relative, a drive measured in cigarettes. Nobody calls these units, but they are the poronkusema again.

They also have the old units' weaknesses. My ten-minute walk is not my grandmother's. A three-hour hike depends on who is hiking. We put up with the sloppiness because these measures, like the seed-measured field, carry the information we actually need to make a decision, which is usually about cost to ourselves and not about extension in space.

So I think the two kinds of unit do different jobs, and the modern arrangement of using both is roughly correct. Abstract units serve coordination between people who don't share a context, like the buyer and seller or the architect and the steel mill. Experiential units serve people who do share one, or a single person planning an afternoon. The mistake of the old world was to use the second kind for the first job, which gave whoever held the bushel a means of exploiting everyone else. The mistake available to us runs the other way: we can assume that a quantity stated in abstract units has told us what we need to know. A hospital 40 kilometers away is one thing on a motorway and another on a mountain road in winter.

The herders knew which fact mattered. The sled would stop when the reindeer needed it to, whatever the map said, so they measured the trip in reindeer.
