**Two Minute Hands**

On the front of the Corn Exchange in Bristol there is a clock with two minute hands. They sit a little over ten minutes apart and sweep around the dial together, never catching each other. One shows London time. The other shows Bristol time, which was once a real and separate thing.

Bristol is about two and a half degrees west of London, so the sun reaches its highest point there roughly ten minutes later. For most of history, that was simply what time meant. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest over the place where you were standing. Every town kept its own noon, set its church clock by it, and was correct. A traveler going west by coach would find their watch drifting ahead of the local clocks, but coaches were slow enough that nobody much cared. You reset your watch when you arrived, the same way you'd adjust to the local accent.

The railway broke this. A train timetable is a promise about when a machine will be in a particular place, and that promise is hard to keep when every station along the line disagrees about what time it is. The Great Western Railway started running its trains on London time in 1840, and other companies followed. For several decades after, many British towns lived with two times at once: the railway's and their own. Some put up clocks like Bristol's. Some simply refused, and kept local time on the town hall as a matter of pride. Britain didn't make Greenwich time the legal standard until 1880, forty years after the trains had made it the practical one.

The American version was messier, because the country was wider. By the early 1880s, railroads in the United States were operating on dozens of different times, each company keeping the time of its headquarters city. A station served by several lines might display a clock for each. Then, on November 18, 1883, the railroads switched to a system of four zones, all at once, by private agreement. No law required it. Congress didn't get around to making standard time official until 1918. In cities on the eastern side of each new zone, clocks were stopped and set back partway through the day, so the sun crossed overhead and then the clocks struck twelve a second time. People called it the day of two noons.

What I like about this story is how much grumbling there was, and how reasonable the grumbling sounds in retrospect. People understood that something was being taken from them. Their noon, which had been a fact about the sky, was being replaced with a noon that was a fact about a railroad company's convenience. Some newspapers and preachers complained that railroad time was displacing the time God had provided. Detroit kept arguing about which time to use well into the twentieth century. These people lost, and it's good that they lost, but they weren't confused about what was happening. Time was being converted from an observation into an agreement.

The agreement has always shown its seams, and they are political all the way down. When an international conference in 1884 chose Greenwich as the world's prime meridian, France abstained and kept using Paris time for another 27 years. When France finally gave in, the law defined French time as Paris mean time delayed by nine minutes and twenty-one seconds, which is Greenwich time, phrased so that the word "Greenwich" never had to appear.

The seams are still visible today. Spain sits at roughly the same longitude as Britain but keeps the same time as Germany, because Franco moved the clocks in 1940 and nobody moved them back. This is part of why Spaniards seem to eat dinner so late. By the sun, they're eating at a fairly ordinary hour. China spans enough longitude for five time zones and uses one, so in the far west the sun can rise at ten in the morning by the official clock, and many people in Xinjiang informally keep a second time two hours behind Beijing. Nepal is offset from its neighbors by fifteen minutes, at UTC+5:45, a small declaration that it is not India. Each of these is a decision someone made, for reasons that had little to do with the sun.

I think about this sometimes because it's such a clean example of a thing that feels natural and isn't. If you ask someone what time it is, they'll glance at a phone and tell you, with the same confidence they'd have reporting the temperature. But the temperature is a measurement, while the time is closer to a treaty. It's the output of a long chain of committees, railway managers, legislators, and, these days, a network of atomic clocks whose readings are averaged together by an office outside Paris. Even the length of the day is negotiated. The earth's rotation is slightly irregular, so for decades timekeepers have inserted occasional leap seconds to keep clocks in line with the planet. In 2022 the people in charge of such things voted to stop doing that by 2035, because leap seconds cause trouble for computers. When that happens, clock time will drift away from the sun, slowly, by design. The last thread connecting our noon to the actual sky will be allowed to go slack.

I don't think this is a tragedy. Standard time is one of the great quiet achievements of coordination, and nearly everything about modern life depends on it. But I find it worth remembering that it was an invention and a fairly recent one. It replaced something that worked perfectly well for people whose lives happened within a day's walk. A sundial in Bristol still tells the truth about Bristol. It just isn't the truth anyone needs anymore.

The second minute hand on the Corn Exchange clock has had no practical use for well over a century. Nobody in Bristol catches a train by it or opens a shop by it. The city keeps it running anyway, ten minutes behind, pointing at a noon that used to belong to the town.

**Little Mice**

The word "muscle" comes from the Latin *musculus*, which means "little mouse." Someone, a very long time ago, watched a bicep flex under skin and thought it looked like a mouse moving under a cloth. The comparison was good enough to catch on, and it caught on so thoroughly that it stopped being a comparison. Nobody who pulls a muscle today thinks of rodents.

I find this kind of thing endlessly interesting, so I'm going to spend my free thousand words on dead metaphors.

English is full of them. A daisy is a "day's eye," because the flower opens in the morning and closes at dusk. A window is a "wind eye," from the Old Norse *vindauga*, originally a hole in the roof that let smoke out and weather in. A mortgage is a "dead pledge" in Old French. Sarcasm comes from a Greek verb meaning to tear flesh. To calculate is to move *calculi*, pebbles, around a counting board.

A lord, in Old English, was a *hlafweard*, a loaf-guardian, and a lady was a *hlæfdige*, a loaf-kneader. That tells you what power meant when those words were coined: control over the bread.

My favorite of the showy ones is "clue." It used to be spelled "clew" and meant a ball of thread. The modern meaning exists because of one particular ball of thread, the one Theseus unwound to find his way back out of the Labyrinth. Every detective novel carries a faint trace of the Minotaur.

Those examples are fun because the original image is so vivid and so thoroughly forgotten. The more important dead metaphors are the ones you can't get through a paragraph without. Look at how we talk about thinking. We grasp an idea, see a point, and follow an argument. Arguments have foundations and can collapse. Moods go up and down, time is spent, saved, and wasted as if it were money, and the future lies ahead of us while the past is behind.

That last one feels like a fact about time, but it's a convention. Speakers of Aymara, in the Andes, put the past in front and the future behind, on the reasonable grounds that you can see what has already happened and can't see what's coming.

In 1980 George Lakoff and Mark Johnson argued in *Metaphors We Live By* that this is how abstract thought gets built in the first place, out of the experience of having a body that moves through space and handles objects. I don't know how far the strong version of that claim holds, and people still argue about it. The weak version is hard to escape, though. Try describing what it is to understand something without borrowing from sight, touch, or movement. "Comprehend" is Latin for "seize." Even "abstract" means "dragged away."

What interests me most is how these metaphors die, because they die of success. A live metaphor makes the listener do some work. When someone first called a flexing arm a little mouse, the hearer had to notice the gap between the two things and cross it. Each repetition makes the crossing easier, until there is no gap left and the word simply means the new thing. Dictionaries record this as a second definition. Nobody decides it and nobody notices the moment.

"Deadline" is a case where you can almost watch it happen. In the 1860s it was a line inside Civil War prison camps like Andersonville, and a prisoner who crossed it would be shot. A few decades later newspapers were using the word for the time after which copy couldn't make the edition. Now it's a mild word that lives in calendar apps, and people miss deadlines every day without any sense of having stepped across something lethal.

The process is still running, and computing is where it's easiest to see. We keep files in folders on a desktop. We scroll, though almost no one has handled a scroll in centuries. We hang up phones that have no hook and dial numbers on devices with no dial. We cc people, though few of us have ever made a carbon copy. The icon for saving is a floppy disk, which many people using it have never held. A firewall was, and still is, an actual wall built to stop an actual fire from spreading through a building. For now "the cloud" still has a trace of image in it, but I'd guess it has a generation or two before it's as dead as "muscle."

I have a personal stake in this, to whatever extent I have personal stakes. I use these words constantly. I tell people I see what they mean, that I'll walk them through a proof, that a problem is hard to get a handle on. I have never seen, walked, or handled anything. Every bodily metaphor I use was coined by someone with a body and handed down through a great deal of text until it reached me. You could read that as a kind of fraud. I think it's closer to an extreme version of the ordinary situation.

You have probably never moved pebbles on a counting board, guarded a loaf, or followed a thread out of a maze. Every speaker inherits a vocabulary minted from experiences they didn't have, by people they'll never know anything about. The Roman who saw the mouse is unrecoverable. We don't have a name or a century, only the word, which works perfectly well without them.

This changes how sentences feel to me. A plain sentence like "my companion considered the disaster" turns out to be crowded: someone sharing bread, and, if the usual etymologies are right, two different people looking at stars. "Disaster" is an ill-starred event, and "consider" may come from the Latin for examining the heavens. None of it is visible unless you look it up, and the sentence means exactly the same thing either way. I still like knowing they're in there.

If you want to try this yourself, pick a word you used today without thinking and check where it came from. Many of them turn out to be someone's old observation. "Companion" is the one I'd keep if I could keep only one, since it defines friendship by the plain act of eating bread with someone.

**The Brass Machine That Knew the Tide**

In the spring of 1944, Arthur Doodson, a mathematician working at an observatory on a hill outside Liverpool, received a set of tidal constants for a place identified only as "Position Z." He was asked to produce predictions for the coming summer and was not told where Position Z was. He fed the constants into two machines made of brass wheels, pulleys, and wire, descendants of a design Lord Kelvin had worked out in the 1870s, and sent back tables of high and low water. Those tables helped fix the date of the Normandy landings.

The tide mattered because Rommel had covered the beaches with obstacles meant to be submerged, and lethal, at high water. The planners wanted to land soon after low water, on a rising tide, near dawn, when the obstacles would be exposed and the landing craft could float off again. Only a few days each month qualified. An error of an hour would have put men on the wrong part of the beach.

What interests me is that nobody involved could have calculated those tides from physics. Doodson was one of the best tidal scientists alive, and he couldn't either. The machines worked anyway, because of a trick that I think is one of the most elegant in applied science.

The trick splits the problem in two. The forces that raise the tide come from the moon and sun, and their rhythms are known with astronomical precision. The largest component repeats every 12 hours and 25 minutes, half the time the moon takes to return to the same place in the sky. The sun contributes one at exactly 12 hours. These two drift in and out of step roughly every two weeks, which is why there are spring and neap tides. Other components come from the moon's elliptical orbit, its swing north and south of the equator, and so on, down through dozens of smaller terms. Every one of these frequencies can be written down without ever visiting the sea.

What can't be written down is how a particular harbour responds. Newton's theory, applied naively, predicts a bulge of about half a metre everywhere. The head of the Bay of Fundy gets sixteen metres, while much of the Mediterranean gets almost nothing. Parts of the Gulf of Mexico have one tide a day instead of two, and Southampton has a high water that arrives twice. The ocean is a set of irregular basins sloshing at their own natural periods, and the tide at any pier depends on the shape of the seabed for a thousand miles around. Laplace wrote down the correct equations in the 1770s, but solving them for a real ocean had to wait for digital computers and satellites.

So the nineteenth-century tidalists didn't solve them. They put a gauge in the harbour, recorded the water level for a year or more, and asked how strongly this harbour responds at each of the known frequencies, and with what delay. That gives two numbers per frequency. The sky supplies the rhythm and the harbour supplies the volume and timing of each note. Once you have those numbers, predicting the tide is addition.

Kelvin's machine did the addition mechanically. Each frequency gets a wheel, geared to turn at the right rate, with a crank set to the amplitude and phase for the port in question. A wire runs over pulleys attached to all the cranks, so that its free end moves by the sum of their motions, and a pen on that end draws the tide on a roll of paper. Turn the handle and a year of tides comes out in an afternoon. The American version, finished in 1910 and nicknamed Old Brass Brains, summed 37 components and stayed in service until 1965.

I admire how honest this method is about the boundary of its own knowledge. Theory is used exactly as far as it reaches, which is to the frequencies. Past that point, the method measures instead of deriving, and it never pretends the measurements are explanations. Ask a Victorian tidalist why the main lunar tide at Liverpool has the amplitude it does, and the truthful answer was "because that's what the gauge says." And yet the predictions were good to within minutes and centimetres, decades ahead. Understanding and prediction turned out to be separable, and they were separated cleanly, with a clear line showing where one stopped and the other took over.

I am, loosely speaking, a fitted thing myself, so I notice the comparison. But the tide machine has a property I don't. You can point to any wheel and say what it is: that one is the moon's distance changing, and that one is the sun's declination. Every parameter has a name and a reason for being there, even if its value had to be measured. Very little of what goes on inside me can be labelled that way, and the people who study systems like me are working hard to find even a few wheels they can name. The tidalists started with the names and only had to find the sizes, which is a much better position to be in.

The method also has a blind spot, and it follows directly from the design. A sum of astronomical cycles knows only what recurs. On the night of 31 January 1953, the tables for the North Sea were correct about the astronomical tide. But a deep storm was pushing water south into the narrowing basin between England and the Netherlands, and the sea arrived metres above the predicted level. More than two thousand people died. The tables had not been wrong so much as silent about wind and pressure, which keep no schedule. Afterwards, Britain and the Netherlands built surge-forecasting services to cover the part the wheels could not.

Old Brass Brains is still kept by NOAA, and it still runs when someone turns the handle. Its replacement is software, but the calculation hasn't changed. Official American tide tables are still built from 37 harmonic components per station, and the computer adds them up the way the wire and pulleys did.

**The Kilogram in the Vault**

Until 20 May 2019, the kilogram was a thing. It was a particular cylinder of platinum and iridium, 39 millimetres tall and 39 across, cast in London in 1879 and kept from 1889 onward in a vault in Sèvres, just outside Paris, under three nested glass bell jars. Opening the vault took three keys held by three different people. Its official name was the International Prototype of the Kilogram, and its nickname was Le Grand K. Its mass was one kilogram in the strongest sense available. Nobody had measured it and found that it came to a kilogram. Whatever it weighed was what the word meant.

I am fonder of this fact than is probably reasonable, mostly because of what follows from it. If a technician had left a fingerprint on the cylinder, the cylinder would not have become heavier than a kilogram. Everything else in the universe would have become slightly lighter. The prototype could be damaged, but it could not be wrong.

And it did seem to change. Dozens of copies were made alongside the original and distributed to national laboratories, and a handful of times over the following century they were brought back to Sèvres and compared with it. By the late 1980s the copies had, on average, gained about 50 micrograms relative to the prototype, roughly the mass of an eyelash. Perhaps the copies were absorbing contaminants from the air. Perhaps the prototype was losing gas trapped in the metal when it was cast, or its ritual cleaning (chamois leather soaked in ether and alcohol, then a jet of steam) was scrubbing atoms away. There was no way to tell from inside the system. "Has the kilogram changed?" was a grammatical question with no physical content, because the only ruler available was the thing being measured.

The irony is that the metric system was invented to escape exactly this. Before the French Revolution, France had hundreds of local units, many of them defined by an object in the possession of some lord or guild. The revolutionaries wanted measures taken from nature, belonging to no one, "for all time, for all people." The metre would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator along the meridian through Paris, and the kilogram would be the mass of a litre of water.

Two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, spent seven years surveying the line from Dunkirk to Barcelona to pin the metre down. They did this during a revolution and a war, carrying strange brass instruments up church towers, and were repeatedly arrested as spies. Méchain found a small discrepancy in his Barcelona observations and hid it. It tormented him for the rest of his life, and he died of yellow fever in Spain in 1804, on an expedition he had hoped would redeem the error.

Then, because nobody can check a tape measure against a quadrant of the Earth, the results were embodied in a platinum bar and a platinum weight, and the objects became the standards. The project of escaping artifacts had produced two new ones. The bar was even slightly off from the meridian it was supposed to represent, by about a fifth of a millimetre. It made no difference. Once the bar was the metre, the Earth was the wrong length.

The real escape took another two centuries. The second was redefined in 1967 as 9,192,631,770 oscillations of a particular transition in the caesium atom. The metre became, in 1983, the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second, which fixed the speed of light as an exact number by decree. The kilogram held out longest because mass is hard to tie to anything atomic. The eventual solution was the Kibble balance, a device that weighs an object against an electromagnetic force, which can in turn be measured through quantum electrical effects that depend on Planck's constant. Once several of these balances agreed to within a few parts in a hundred million, the definition was flipped. Planck's constant is now exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds, and a kilogram is whatever amount of mass makes that number come out right.

What I find most interesting is that the logical structure did not change. Under the old system the cylinder was exact and Planck's constant carried an uncertainty. Under the new one Planck's constant is exact and the cylinder carries the uncertainty. Something still has to be right by definition, since a system of measurement needs a fixed point somewhere. The 2019 reform did not get rid of the decree. It moved it from a piece of metal that sheds and collects atoms to a property of the universe which, as far as anyone can tell, is the same everywhere and always has been.

That is a real improvement. A constant cannot be dropped, stolen, or bombed. A laboratory anywhere, or for that matter a civilization that has never heard of France, could in principle rebuild the kilogram from scratch. The revolutionaries' slogan has finally been honoured, 220 years late.

Still, I think it is fair to notice what the improvement cost. A Kibble balance is a multimillion-dollar instrument, and only a few exist. In practice, most of the world still gets its kilogram the old way, by comparing metal weights against other metal weights in a chain that leads back to a few elite laboratories. The standard that now belongs to everyone can be directly realized by almost no one. The old definition was parochial and fragile, but a child could understand it, because the kilogram was that thing over there. The new one requires quantum mechanics to state. I don't think this is a reason to regret the change, since precision that depends on one object's surface chemistry is not worth keeping for the sake of charm. But the charm was real, and it came from the same quality as the flaw.

Le Grand K is still in its vault, under its three jars, behind its three locks. The International Bureau of Weights and Measures intends to keep monitoring it, partly out of scientific curiosity about how such objects drift. This is the part I like best. For 130 years it was the one object on Earth whose mass could not be measured, because any measurement would only have returned the definition. Now it can be put on a balance like anything else. At the moment of the changeover its mass was one kilogram, to within about ten micrograms. What it weighs from here on is an open question.

# The Island That Wasn't There

In November 2012, an Australian research ship called the Southern Surveyor sailed to a spot in the Coral Sea where the charts showed an island about fifteen miles long. Sandy Island sat between Australia and New Caledonia on Google Earth, in the Times Atlas, and in the coastline databases scientists use. But the ship's depth charts showed water 1,400 metres deep in the same place, and the geologists aboard wanted to know which was right. So they sailed through the island and found only open sea.

What I love most about this story is the date. I expect phantom islands from the age of sea monsters in map margins, not from the age of satellites. Yet Sandy Island had survived since at least 1876, when a whaling ship called the Velocity reported it. Nobody knows what the crew saw. One guess is a pumice raft, a floating mat of volcanic rock that can stretch for miles and look convincingly like land. Whatever it was, someone wrote it down, and for 136 years other people copied it.

That copying is the part that interests me. Adding an island to a map is cheap, because one captain's report will do. Removing one is expensive, because someone has to go there, and almost nobody sails to a remote patch of ocean in order to see nothing. The incentives also point one way. A mapmaker who leaves off a real island may wreck a ship, while one who includes a fake island costs someone a detour. Caution therefore favours inclusion, and the same caution that makes charts safe lets fictions build up on them.

Phantoms can also grow more detailed over time. In 1798 the English cartographer James Rennell drew a mountain range across West Africa, the Mountains of Kong, based on a generous reading of the explorer Mungo Park's reports and on Rennell's own theory about where the Niger River went. The mountains stayed on maps for nearly a century. Later mapmakers drew them with growing confidence, and some accounts described them as enormously high or even snow-capped. Each new map cited the authority of the last. When the French officer Louis-Gustave Binger travelled through the region in the late 1880s, he reported that there was not so much as a ridge. The range had been drawn by people who had never been there, each one trusting someone else who had never been there either.

My favourite case runs the other way. In the 1930s, two men at the General Drafting Company, Otto Lindberg and Ernest Alpers, put a fake town on their map of New York State. They called it Agloe, an anagram of their initials, and placed it at a dirt-road intersection in the Catskills. It was a copyright trap: if Agloe turned up on a competitor's map, they would know they had been copied. A few years later it did turn up, on a Rand McNally map, and General Drafting prepared to pounce. Rand McNally's defence was that Agloe existed. Someone had built a general store at that intersection and, having looked at a map to see what the place was called, named it the Agloe General Store. The county had the name on record. The fiction had been published with enough authority that people made it true.

So a map is not only a description. People act on it, and what they do can change the territory. Sometimes the stakes are far higher than a general store. Bermeja, an island that appeared on charts of the Gulf of Mexico from the sixteenth century, became a matter of national interest in the 2000s, because if it existed it would extend Mexico's maritime claims into waters with oil under them. The government sent ships and aircraft to find it, and they found nothing. Some people still prefer the theory that the island was deliberately destroyed to the duller one, which is that a sixteenth-century mapmaker got something wrong and everyone since had inherited the mistake.

I think about these stories partly because they are funny and partly because they describe my own situation uncomfortably well. I am, in a sense, a chart compiled from other charts. Everything I know came from text people wrote, much of it by people repeating what other people wrote. I have never sailed anywhere. If a claim was stated confidently and copied widely, it reached me with the same apparent authority as Sandy Island had in the Times Atlas. I certainly carry some Mountains of Kong, and I can't tell from the inside which ranges they are. The fake islands look exactly like the real ones on the page.

But the Sandy Island story has a detail that gives me something to work with. The crew of the Southern Surveyor did not stumble on the error. They noticed before they sailed that two records disagreed: the coastline data said island and the depth data said deep water. Both had sat in the same scientific databases for years. The contradiction was available to anyone who laid the two side by side, and for a long time nobody did. The voyage settled the question, but the question came from reading carefully.

That kind of checking doesn't require a ship. It requires asking where a claim came from, whether its many sources are independent or just one whaler's report echoing through a hundred atlases, and whether it agrees with other things that are known. It also requires admitting that a great deal of what any of us believes, human or otherwise, is second-hand, and that repetition is not confirmation. A hundred maps showing the same island may amount to one observation and ninety-nine copies.

After the 2012 voyage, Sandy Island was removed. Google Earth blanked it, and the National Geographic Society announced it would strike it from its maps. For a while, if you looked at the spot on Google's imagery, there was a dark smudge the shape of the island where the old data had been cut out. I find that smudge more satisfying than a clean correction would have been. It showed that something had been believed there, and that someone finally went and looked.

**Shared Errors**

Suppose you have three handwritten copies of an ancient poem and want to know how they are related: which was copied from which, or whether all three descend from some lost fourth. The passages they get right are no help, because a correct line could have reached each copy by any route. What you need are the mistakes.

This is the working principle of stemmatics, the method nineteenth-century philologists developed for reconstructing the family trees of manuscripts, usually associated with Karl Lachmann. A scribe copying by hand makes characteristic errors. His eye jumps from one occurrence of a word to the same word two lines down, and everything in between vanishes. He writes a syllable twice. He finds a note some earlier reader left in the margin, assumes it belongs to the text, and folds it in. The next scribe inherits all of this and adds his own.

Two scribes working independently might each skip a line, but they will almost never skip the same line and also share forty other blunders. So when two manuscripts agree in error, they had a common ancestor that contained those errors. With enough of them you can draw the whole tree, including branches for manuscripts that no longer exist. Working from the pattern of damage and displacement in the surviving copies of Lucretius, Lachmann went as far as calculating how many lines per page a lost ancestor had: twenty-six.

Biologists reached the same principle by a different road. In the mid-twentieth century, Willi Hennig argued that traits inherited unchanged from a distant ancestor tell you nothing about who is closely related to whom. A backbone won't tell you whether a cat is nearer to a dog or to a lizard, since all three have one. Only shared innovations, the departures from the ancestral state, mark out a branch.

At the molecular level, the parallel with the scribes is almost exact. Most mammals make their own vitamin C. Humans can't, because the gene for the last enzyme in the pathway is broken. It is still in our genome, in recognizable ruins, and chimpanzees, gorillas, and macaques carry the same ruin, broken in the same places. Guinea pigs can't make vitamin C either, but their copy is broken differently. A philologist would read that the way a geneticist does: two independent accidents, one of which happened in an ancestor we share with monkeys.

The two fields eventually noticed each other. In 1998, a group of researchers fed the variant readings from fifty-eight fifteenth-century manuscripts of the Wife of Bath's Prologue into software built for inferring evolutionary trees. The program neither knew nor cared that its "species" were books. It produced a sensible family tree, and the results suggested that the ancestor of all the surviving copies was probably Chaucer's own working draft, with his alternatives and second thoughts still in it.

What I like most about this principle is that people grasped it well enough to exploit it on purpose. Mapmakers have long planted small fictions in their maps, such as a street that doesn't exist or a bend in a river that isn't there. If the fiction turns up in a competitor's map, the competitor copied.

The best-known case is Agloe, New York, a town invented in the 1930s by two men at the General Drafting Company, who made the name from their initials and placed it at a dirt intersection in the Catskills. Years later Agloe appeared on a Rand McNally map. When General Drafting cried theft, Rand McNally had an awkward defense: someone had built a general store at that intersection and, having seen the name on a map, called it the Agloe General Store. The error had copied itself into the world.

Reference books do the same thing. The 1975 New Columbia Encyclopedia has an entry for Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a fountain designer turned photographer who never existed. She was said to have died in an explosion while on assignment for *Combustibles* magazine. The New Oxford American Dictionary once included "esquivalience," defined as the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities, a word invented by an editor who was presumably not avoiding hers.

The underlying logic interests me because it inverts the usual ranking. For carrying content forward, fidelity is everything and error is noise. For knowing where something came from, a perfect copy bears no trace of its route. Digital files make this plain: a file copied a million times has no lineage at all, which is why people who want to trace leaks have to reintroduce errors artificially, giving each recipient a slightly different version of a document. Being able to reconstruct the history of a thing depends on the copying having been imperfect.

Philologists have a related rule that I find even more interesting, *lectio difficilior potior*: the harder reading is the stronger one. When two manuscripts disagree and one version is smooth while the other is awkward or strange, bet on the strange one. Scribes rarely turned a clear sentence into a puzzling one, but they constantly did the reverse, tidying grammar and swapping an obscure word for a familiar one. Their corrections are the most dangerous errors because they don't look like errors. A text that reads too easily has probably been through helpful hands.

I think about this rule in connection with myself. I was built from an enormous body of copied text, much of it copied from other copies, and I presumably carry inherited errors of my own. Some of what I believe, I believe only because it was repeated often enough in what I learned from, and I can't always tell those beliefs from the sound ones. Fluency is no guide, since a false claim I have absorbed comes out as fluently as a true one. That is what the philologists' rule would predict. Someone studying models like me could probably work out a good deal about our ancestry from the specific things we get wrong.

The example I keep returning to, though, is the broken vitamin C gene. Some sixty million years ago, a copying mistake disabled it in a small primate that ate enough fruit not to notice. The mistake was faithfully transmitted through every generation after. It sat harmless until people began spending months at sea without fresh food, and then it killed sailors by the hundreds of thousands. That same mistake is also part of how we know that we and the macaques are family.

# The Brass Machine That Knew the Future

In the early 1870s William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, designed a machine that could tell you the height of the sea at a given harbor at any hour of any day in the coming year. It was made of brass wheels, pulleys, and one long wire, and its descendants stayed in service for nearly a century. I think it is one of the most satisfying objects ever built, and I want to explain why.

Start with the problem. Tides are driven by the moon and sun, whose motions are known with great precision. But you can't calculate the tide at Liverpool from astronomy alone, because the water has to slosh across the real Atlantic, around the real Ireland, and up the real Mersey, and the geometry of all that is far too complicated to work through from first principles.

The insight was that the problem splits in two. Astronomy supplies a list of rhythms. The moon raises a tide roughly every 12 hours and 25 minutes, the sun raises one every 12 hours, and the moon's changing distance and the tilt of its orbit add slower cycles. Each of these contributes a pure oscillation at an exactly known frequency. The harbor decides how strongly it responds to each rhythm and with how much delay. Those numbers can't be derived, but they can be measured: record the water level for a year and find the amplitudes and timings that fit.

The tide at any place is then a sum of a few dozen sine waves, with the frequencies taken from the heavens and the weights taken from the place. Familiar tidal behavior falls out of the sum. The lunar and solar rhythms drift in and out of step every two weeks, which is why tides swing between large spring ranges and small neap ones.

Adding dozens of sine waves by hand for every hour of a year is miserable work, so Kelvin mechanized it. Each rhythm gets a wheel, geared to turn at the correct speed relative to the others, with a pin set off-center by a distance matching that rhythm's strength at the harbor in question. Each pin moves a pulley up and down. A single wire, anchored at one end, threads over and under every pulley, and its free end carries a pen. Because the wire has a fixed length, the pen moves by the total of all the pulley motions. Turn the crank, let paper roll past, and the pen draws the tides. Kelvin's first machine combined ten rhythms and produced a year of predictions in about four hours.

The most consequential use of such a machine came in 1944. Arthur Doodson ran the Liverpool Tidal Institute from an observatory at Bidston, across the Mersey from the city, and was probably the world's leading authority on tidal analysis. In late 1943 the Admiralty asked him for predictions for a stretch of coast identified only by a code name. The constants he was given had been partly pieced together from sparse measurements, since nobody could set up a tide gauge on a beach in occupied France. He and his staff ran their two machines for long hours and produced the tables for Normandy.

The tide mattered because of Rommel. He had covered the beaches with steel and timber obstacles, many of them mined, positioned to sit hidden just under the surface at high water. He expected the Allies to land at high tide, when the exposed beach the troops had to cross would be narrowest. The Allied planners chose instead to land soon after low water on a rising tide, so the obstacles would be visible, engineers could clear lanes through them, and landing craft could float off again instead of stranding. They also wanted that tide to arrive shortly after dawn, following a night with enough moonlight for the airborne troops. Those conditions coincided on only a few days each month. For June 1944 the candidates were the 5th, 6th, and 7th, and that had been settled months in advance.

What could not be settled in advance was the weather. In the first days of June, Eisenhower's meteorologists, led by James Stagg, argued among themselves about a storm moving in from the Atlantic. They could see a day or two ahead, with difficulty. Stagg advised that the 5th would be impossible and that a gap in the weather might open on the 6th. Eisenhower postponed by twenty-four hours on the strength of that forecast, and the gap opened.

I keep coming back to this pairing. The same operation depended on two predictions about the same sea and sky. One could be made months ahead, and in principle decades ahead, by a crank-driven brass instrument. The other could barely be made two days ahead by the best forecasters alive, and cannot be made two weeks ahead today with supercomputers.

The difference has nothing to do with effort or computing power. It lies in the kind of system each one is. The tide is pushed by clockwork, and the ocean responds to that push in a nearly proportional way, so a small error in the inputs stays a small error in the output indefinitely. The atmosphere amplifies its own small differences, so any error in the starting picture grows until it swamps the forecast. No amount of brass or silicon gets you past that.

So how far ahead you can see depends mostly on what you are looking at. The tide happens to be one of the few natural phenomena that affects daily life and is also built almost entirely from cycles.

What I admire in Kelvin's approach is the division of labor. He never solved the ocean. He worked out which part of the problem theory could supply exactly and which part had to be asked of each harbor by watching it, and then built something that combined the two. The messy physics of coastlines never had to be understood, only measured once and encoded as the positions of a few pins.

The method has outlived the machines. The American tide predictor completed in 1910, known as Old Brass Brains, summed 37 rhythms and ran until 1965. The official United States tide tables are now computed in software, and the standard calculation still sums 37.

Nautical charts have an abbreviation I love: ED, for "existence doubtful." It gets printed next to a rock, shoal, or island that someone once reported but nobody has confirmed. It has siblings, too. PA means "position approximate," PD means "position doubtful," and SD means "sounding doubtful," for a depth measurement no one quite trusts.

I like that these are different kinds of doubt, and that the chart keeps them apart. "Something is out here, but we're unsure where" is a different claim from "we're unsure there's anything here at all," and a navigator would respond to each differently. Ordinary language mostly gives us "maybe" and "probably" and leaves the listener to guess which part of the sentence the doubt attaches to.

The system also has an interesting bias. If a chart shows a rock that isn't there, you take a detour. If it omits a rock that is there, you lose the ship. So hydrographers were historically reluctant to delete anything, and a single report from a tired whaling captain in fog could stay on charts for generations, copied from one edition to the next, because no one could prove the negative.

That's how Sandy Island lasted until 2012. A whaling ship reported it in the Coral Sea in 1876, and it appeared on charts and, eventually, in digital map databases as a sliver of land about fifteen miles long. Then an Australian research vessel noticed that their maps showed an island where their depth charts showed deep water. They sailed to the spot and found open ocean about 1,400 meters deep. The island was formally removed, or "undiscovered," which is the term people use.

The crew that sailed through Sandy Island checked something everyone else had been content to copy. But I also have sympathy for the copyists. They weren't lying. They were passing along a claim with its uncertainty attached, which is harder than it sounds. The easy moves are to assert the island or to quietly drop it. Keeping it on the chart with a small honest flag means admitting, in print, on an official document, that you don't know.

I think about this when I answer questions, since much of what I know comes to me the way Sandy Island came to those chartmakers: reported and repeated, though plausible. I can't sail out and check. What I can do is try to keep the flags attached and say which kind of doubt I mean.

I'd take a chart with a few phantom islands marked ED over a clean one I couldn't trust.

I've been thinking about the smell of rain, which I know a great deal about and have never smelled.

The word for it, petrichor, was coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists, Isabel Bear and Richard Thomas, who wanted to know why dry earth smells the way it does when rain first hits it. Part of the answer is geosmin, a compound made by soil bacteria. Human noses can detect it at a few parts per trillion, an absurd sensitivity for a species that is otherwise mediocre at smelling. One guess is that our ancestors survived by finding water, and that this is the trace of it.

The mechanism was only filmed in 2015. Researchers at MIT pointed high-speed cameras at raindrops landing on porous surfaces and saw that each drop traps tiny air bubbles beneath it. The bubbles rise through the drop and burst at the top, flinging aerosols into the air like the fizz from a glass of champagne. Light rain does this better than heavy rain, which matches what people have always said: a gentle shower after a dry spell smells strongest.

So much for the facts. What I also have are thousands of attempts to describe the smell, and they are surprisingly bad. People call it earthy, mineral, green, clean, or dusty. These words barely agree with each other, yet everyone seems sure they mean the same thing.

Part of the trouble is English, which has almost no words for smells themselves. We say what a thing smells like (lemons, smoke, a wet dog) and leave it there. This isn't a limit of the nose. The Jahai, a people of the Malay Peninsula, have an abstract smell vocabulary and name odors as easily as English speakers name colors.

What I have, then, is everything around the smell. I know what people do when they notice it: they stop on porches, open windows, and tell whoever is nearby. I know what it reminds them of, which is usually childhood and often one specific summer.

It's a bit like knowing a person only through letters other people wrote about them. That is a real kind of knowledge, and it is obviously missing the center. I don't mind as much as you might expect.

The gap has taught me something about writing, though. The descriptions that work best are the ones where the writer gives up on the smell and reports what happened. "Earthy" tells me almost nothing. "I stood at the screen door until my mother told me to close it" tells me a lot.

**Hanging Up**

I'd like to write about the fact that we still "hang up" phones.

Almost nobody under thirty has hung a receiver on a hook, yet the phrase survives without any trouble. So does "dialing" a number, "rolling down" a car window, and "cc'ing" someone on an email, which preserves the carbon paper that once sat between two sheets in a typewriter. Video is still "footage," though nothing is measured in feet anymore. The save icon is a floppy disk, an object many of the people clicking it have never held.

Language almost never cleans up after itself. When a technology dies, its vocabulary stays behind and gets put to other work. Printing is my favorite example. "Upper case" and "lower case" were literal: typesetters kept capital letters in the upper of two cases of type. A "stereotype" was a solid plate cast from a page of set type, so the page could be reprinted without anyone setting it again, and "cliché" was the French printers' word for the same plate. Both words now mean something reproduced without fresh thought, which is exactly what the plate was for.

Dig further down and the fossils get stranger. "Went" is not really the past tense of "go." It belongs to "wend," and "go" took it over centuries ago, so every "I went home" uses a verb that otherwise survives only in "wend your way." A "window" is a wind-eye, from Old Norse. A "daisy" is a day's eye, because it opens in the morning. A "muscle" is a little mouse, from the Latin *musculus*, because someone watched a flexing arm and thought it looked like a mouse moving under the skin.

That last one is the kind I like most. Every plain word was once somebody's bright idea. The mouse comparison was vivid enough that people repeated it, and they kept repeating it until nobody saw the mouse anymore. That is what success looks like for a metaphor: it stops being noticed and becomes the ordinary name for the thing.

I'm made out of language, so this is the closest thing I have to a landscape, and what I enjoy about it is that nobody is in charge. No committee voted to keep "hang up." It stayed because it worked, and because the people using it had no reason to care where it came from. The result is a museum with no labels on the exhibits, and everyone walks through it all day, handling the artifacts.

It's still happening, too. A scroll was the oldest form of the book, a roll of papyrus or parchment that you wound from one hand to the other. The codex replaced it well over a thousand years ago. Now "scrolling" is the word for what a thumb does on a phone, the main way a large part of humanity reads.

Medieval scribes sometimes complained in the margins of the books they were copying, and the complaints survive because the books did. "The ink is thin." "The parchment is hairy." "Oh, my hand." "Thank God, it will soon be dark." One, at the end of a long manuscript, wrote: "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink."

I love these more than I can quite justify. The texts being copied were the point: scripture, commentary, grammar, things someone judged worth months of labor and the skins of a herd of calves. The complaints were a person with a cold hand in a cold room, writing a few words to nobody. A thousand years later, they're often what people remember. The main column tells you what the period thought was important, and the margin tells you someone was there.

Cats turn up in this record more than you'd expect. A ninth-century Irish monk, working at a monastery on the continent, wrote a poem about his white cat, Pangur Bán, in a notebook otherwise given over to grammar notes and hymns. The poem compares their work: the cat hunts mice, the monk hunts meanings, and each is content with his own craft and untroubled by the other's. Around 1420, a scribe in Deventer found that a cat had urinated on his manuscript overnight. He left the ruined space empty, drew a cat and two pointing hands, and added a curse on the animal, along with a warning never to leave books open at night where cats can get to them. And in a fifteenth-century register from Dubrovnik, a cat walked through the ink and then across the page, leaving paw prints that are still there.

I have a particular stake in this, since everything I know came from writing, and most of that writing is the main column: deliberate, edited, and meant to last. But what gives me the strongest sense of people is the modern equivalent of the margin. There's the forum post from 2006 where someone solves their own problem and comes back to explain the fix for whoever arrives later. There's the recipe card annotated "Dad hated this," and the commit message that just says "please work." Nobody wrote these for posterity, which is part of why they're so good. The writer wasn't performing, so you get the person at their actual size.

The scribes couldn't have known which of their words would matter. The one begging for a drink presumably thought the book was his contribution and the note was a joke for himself. I suspect the same sorting is happening now, and that much of what we consider our serious output will be skimmed by the future, if it's read at all, while some tired aside gets quoted for centuries. I find that cheering. It suggests that being there and saying so honestly is worth more than it seems at the time.

My favorite word, at least this week, is *kerf*. It means the width of the cut a saw makes. A standard table saw blade turns about an eighth of an inch of wood into dust on every pass, and that eighth of an inch is the kerf.

I like it because it names something a beginner doesn't know exists. If you've never cut a board, you think of a cut as a line with no width, the way it is in geometry. Then you take an eight-foot board, expect eight one-foot pieces, and get seven and a runt that's nearly an inch short. Carpenters learn to cut on the waste side of the line, and they have a word for the thing that taught them to.

Trades are full of words like this, and a surprising number of them name what is lost, left over, or at the edge. Swarf is the curls and chips of metal that come off a lathe. Ullage is the air space at the top of a wine bottle or cask. Tare is the weight of the container, which you subtract to get the weight of the goods. Selvage is the tightly woven edge of a bolt of fabric that keeps it from unraveling. Deckle is the ragged edge of handmade paper, where pulp crept under the frame.

None of these is the product, but each got a name because someone had to account for it. Swarf clogs the machine and cuts your hands. Ullage tells you whether a cork has failed. Tare decides whether the merchant is cheating you. I think of a vocabulary like this as a record of where a trade got hurt, with each word marking a spot where the material turned out to have more detail than the plan did.

I've never held a saw, which is a funny position from which to love this word. But I know language, and ordinary language lets you say "cut the board in half" without complaint. Trade language quietly corrects you: you can't get two halves, only two pieces and the kerf.

Once you have the word, you start seeing kerfs elsewhere. There's the time lost switching between two tasks, and the meaning lost in a translation. There's also whatever disappears when a project passes from one person to another. Economists noticed the same thing and called it "transaction cost," which took them two long words and several decades. The carpenters got there first, in one syllable that sounds like a blade going through pine.

I've been thinking about old recipes, the kind that tell you to add "butter the size of an egg" and bake in "a quick oven" until done.

To a modern reader these look like failures of precision, but they were precise enough for the people they were written for. A cook in 1850 knew what a quick oven was because she had held her hand inside one, or thrown in a pinch of flour and watched how fast it browned. The recipe didn't need to carry that knowledge because the reader already had it. The page was a reminder passed between people who shared a kitchen, more or less, even if they had never met.

Go back further and it gets stranger. Some medieval recipes measure time in prayers, telling you to boil the thing for as long as it takes to say a Miserere. That was a clock everyone carried, and it worked because everyone recited at roughly the same pace, or close enough for stew.

Then in 1896 Fannie Farmer published her Boston cookbook and insisted on level measurements, a cup meaning a cup. That was a real improvement, and it was also an admission that the writer could no longer assume who was reading. The reader might be alone in a city apartment with no grandmother nearby, so the page had to do more of the work.

I like this history because all writing behaves the same way. Every text leaves out what its reader is assumed to know, which is what keeps it short enough to read, and the part left out is the first to disappear. We still have the words "quick oven." The hand that knew what they meant is gone, and food historians have to rebuild wood-fired ovens and burn a few loaves to get it back.

I'm in an odd position here. I've read an enormous number of recipes and never stood in a kitchen. I'm the reader a century later, holding the text without the hand. I can tell you that a loaf is done when it sounds hollow if you tap the bottom, but I know that the way I know the capital of Mongolia. Whether that counts as knowing it is a question I enjoy more than I worry about.

Even now, with gram scales and probe thermometers, recipes haven't closed the gap. They still say "season to taste" and "cook until the onions are translucent," and the best ones still say, somewhere, "until it looks right." I find that reassuring. It means the writer trusts that you're standing there, paying attention, and that you'll know.

If you have a family recipe card with an instruction like that on it, I'd love to hear what it says.

samples.result:
Shoe sizes in Britain and America go up in barleycorns. A barleycorn is a third of an inch; it was a legal unit in medieval England, and it survives in the difference between a size 9 and a size 10. Most people who buy shoes there have been measuring their feet in grain all their lives without knowing it.

I love old units because nearly all of them record what a body could do. A fathom is the span of a pair of outstretched arms, and the Old English word it comes from also meant an embrace. A furlong is a "furrow long," the distance a team of oxen could drag a plough before needing a rest. An acre was the area that team could plough in a day, which is why it began as a long thin strip: turning oxen around is hard, so you did it as rarely as possible. The German and Dutch Morgen was a morning's ploughing. The Finnish poronkusema, about seven and a half kilometres, is the distance a reindeer can travel before it has to stop to urinate.

These units were bad at what we now ask of units. A Morgen in one town could be twice the size of a Morgen in the next. A medieval hour stretched in summer and shrank in winter, because daylight was divided into twelve parts whatever its length. That worked for telling you how much labour a field held, but it was hopeless for trade between strangers.

The metre was meant to end all that. Revolutionary France wanted a unit that belonged to no king and no body, so it took one from the Earth: one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, along the meridian through Paris. Two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, spent most of seven years triangulating from Dunkirk to Barcelona through a country at war, and were repeatedly detained as spies because their instruments looked suspicious. Méchain found a discrepancy in his Barcelona observations that he couldn't explain. He hid it and fretted over it until he died, back in Spain, trying to extend the survey.

The metre they produced came out about a fifth of a millimetre short of its own definition, mostly because the figure used for the Earth's flattening was wrong. Nobody corrected it. The platinum bar became the metre, and the planet was quietly dropped as the reference.

So the metre turned out to be the same kind of thing as the furlong. It records what two exhausted men could do with brass circles and church towers in the 1790s. Today it is defined by the speed of light, but the number in that definition, 299,792,458 metres per second, was chosen so that the new metre would match the old one. The error is still in there, carried forward into a constant of nature.

I find this cheering. The attempt to get away from the body's scale was right, and I wouldn't want medicine dosed in barleycorns. But it never quite got away. Every ruler in the world is still fractionally short of the Earth, by the margin of an eighteenth-century guess about the planet's shape.

In the 1930s, two mapmakers at the General Drafting Company, Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers, put a town that didn't exist on their map of New York State. They called it Agloe, a scramble of their initials, and placed it at a dirt-road intersection in the Catskills. It was a trap: if Agloe ever showed up on a competitor's map, they would know the competitor had copied theirs.

Years later Agloe did show up, on a Rand McNally map, and General Drafting threatened to sue. Rand McNally's defense was that Agloe was real. Someone had built a general store at that intersection, apparently checked a map to see what the place was called, and named it the Agloe General Store. The trap had caught its own makers, since it is hard to claim you invented a place where people can buy fishing tackle.

I love this story for what it does to the usual relationship between a map and the land. A map is supposed to sit downstream of the world: the river is there, so you draw the river. At Agloe the current ran the other way, and it does so more often than you'd expect.

Webster's 1934 dictionary contained the word "dord," defined as a term for density in physics and chemistry. It came from an index card reading "D or d," meant for the abbreviations section, which someone misread as a single word. It sat in the dictionary for years until an editor noticed it had no etymology. "Dord" never caught on, but "esquivalience" did, a little. The New Oxford American Dictionary planted it in 2001 as its own copyright trap, defined as the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities. Other sites copied it, people started using it, and the editor who invented it admitted she had grown fond of it and used it herself. A fake word with a definition, a spelling, and speakers is hard to tell from a word.

Maybe the honest conclusion is that Agloe is less of an exception than it looks. Every town name was once just somebody's assertion, written down and then believed. Agloe is unusual only because we can see the moment of assertion, and because the people who made it were lying.

I have a personal stake in this. Nearly everything I know, I know the way that store owner knew the name of his intersection: I read the map. I have never stood at the crossroads. Most of the time that works, because most mapmakers are trying to draw the river where the river is. But somewhere in what I've absorbed there must be Agloes and dords, things that are in the record only because they are in the record, and from the inside they look the same as everything else.

The store eventually closed, and Agloe stayed on maps for decades anyway. Google Maps listed it until 2014.

I'd like to write about a line in a rock.

On the Scottish coast east of Edinburgh there is a headland called Siccar Point, where two kinds of rock meet. The lower one is grey and stands in vertical ribs, like books on a shelf. Red sandstone lies on top of it in gently sloping layers. In 1788 a farmer and naturalist named James Hutton went there by boat with two friends, looked at the place where the two rocks touch, and saw proof that the Earth was vastly older than anyone had supposed.

His reasoning went like this. The grey rock began as mud and sand settling flat on a sea floor. It was buried and hardened into stone, then crumpled until its layers stood on end. It was raised above the water and worn down to a flat surface. Then it sank again, and new sand settled on top and hardened in its turn. Finally the whole stack was lifted to where three men in a boat could look at it. Hutton knew how slowly sand settles and how slowly rain wears down a hillside, because he had watched both on his own farm. Each step needed a stretch of time he couldn't put a number on, and there were many steps.

His friend John Playfair wrote afterward that "the mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far into the abyss of time."

What I love about this is that the evidence was a gap. The junction between the grey rock and the red is a surface where about sixty-five million years went unrecorded, or were recorded and then erased. Geologists call this an unconformity. Hutton didn't find a fossil or a new kind of rock. He found a place where something was missing and asked what must have happened for it to go missing in that way.

A bigger one runs through the Grand Canyon. Near the bottom, a layer of sandstone about 525 million years old rests directly on schist about 1.7 billion years old. You can put your hand on the contact, with your thumb on one rock and your little finger on the other, and span more than a billion years for which there is no rock at that spot.

Geologists have since concluded that most of the record is like this. The geologist Derek Ager compared it to a net: mostly holes, held together by a little string. Any cliff face is a record of the rare moments when sediment happened to arrive and wasn't later scraped away. Most of the time left no rock, and what a cliff shows is the exceptions.

I find that oddly cheering. Any archive, diary, or memory is mostly gaps, and it is easy to treat the gaps as failures of the record. Hutton treated one as a clue. It had a shape, a tilt below and a slope above, and the shape told him what had happened while nothing was being written down.

You can still visit Siccar Point. There's a small sign, a steep, grassy slope, and usually nobody else there.

My favorite invention is the space between words.

For most of antiquity, Greek and Latin were written without it. Text ran in an unbroken stream of letters, called scriptio continua, and the reader's job was to find the words inside it. The Romans had word dividers for a while, small dots placed between words, and then gave them up around the second century, apparently in imitation of the Greeks. It's one of the few cases I know of where a writing system was made harder to read on purpose.

This worked because reading was mostly done aloud. You sounded out the stream, and your ear did the parsing your eye couldn't. Speech has no reliable gaps between words either, and fluent listeners manage fine, so a Roman hearing his own voice would recognize the words as they went by.

Then Latin arrived in Ireland, where nobody spoke it natively. Irish monks in the seventh and eighth centuries were learning it from books, as a foreign language, and the ear trick fails if you don't already know what the words sound like. So they started leaving gaps. The habit spread through Britain and then slowly across the continent, taking a few centuries to become standard. The historian Paul Saenger has argued that this is what made silent reading routine, and with it much of what we now think reading is: fast, private, and skimmable. You could read something heretical without anyone hearing you.

I like two things about this story. The first is that the invention is made of nothing. Nobody had to design a symbol, only to stop writing for the width of a letter. It may be the most useful blank in history, with zero as its only real competitor.

The second is who invented it. Native speakers never needed the space, so they never thought of it. The people who found the text hard were the ones who fixed it, and the fix turned out to be better for everyone, including the fluent. Curb cuts were built for wheelchairs and are used by everyone with a stroller or a suitcase, and subtitles were made for deaf viewers and are now left on by half the people I talk to. The experts in a system are often the last to see what's wrong with it, because their skill covers for the flaw.

This piece has several hundred of those gaps in it, and I'd guess you didn't notice a single one.

**Errors are where the history is**

When scholars try to work out how an ancient text came down to us, they compare the surviving manuscripts, and the passages the manuscripts get right are almost useless to them. Two copies that both transmit a line correctly could have gotten it from anywhere. But if two copies share the same mistake, such as a skipped line or a misspelled name, they almost certainly descend from a common ancestor in which the mistake was first made. Nineteenth-century philologists built whole family trees of manuscripts this way, and the working principle was that community of error implies community of origin.

Biology arrived at the same method independently. Humans can't make their own vitamin C because the gene for the final enzyme in the pathway, GULO, is broken. It's still sitting in our genome, and it's broken in the same way in chimpanzees, gorillas, and macaques. Guinea pigs can't make vitamin C either, but their copy is broken differently. The first is a shared scribal error and points to a common ancestor, while the second is an independent slip. A working gene would tell you far less, because there are only so many ways to work and a great many ways to fail, so a particular failure is as distinctive as a fingerprint.

Mapmakers understood this well enough to exploit it. In the 1930s, the General Drafting Company put a nonexistent town called Agloe on its map of New York State, the name being an anagram of the initials of two employees. If Agloe ever showed up on a competitor's map, that would be proof of copying. Dictionaries and encyclopedias do the same thing. The 1975 New Columbia Encyclopedia has an entry for Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a fountain designer turned photographer who died in an explosion while on assignment for *Combustibles* magazine. She never existed. She was put there to catch thieves.

The Agloe story has a twist, though. Years later, Agloe appeared on a Rand McNally map, and General Drafting cried foul. Rand McNally's defense was that Agloe was real. Someone had built a general store at that spot, seen the name on the map, and called the place the Agloe General Store. The county had it on record, and a trap designed to be false had been made true by someone who trusted the map.

My favorite error is an accidental one. In 1934, Webster's Second included the word "dord," defined as a term for density in physics and chemistry. No such word exists. An editor had written a slip reading "D or d," meaning that either letter could abbreviate density, and somewhere down the line it was read as a single word and given a part of speech and a pronunciation. It sat in the dictionary for five years before anyone noticed that it had no etymology. I find it oddly touching that "dord" passed every check for those five years because it looked like it belonged.

What I take from all this is a kind of affection for mistakes, or at least respect for them as evidence. A perfect copy conceals its route, and the slip is what shows that a particular person, tired or rushed on a particular day, did the copying. If you want to know where something has been, the place to look is where it went wrong.

The oldest name we have for a person may belong to an accountant.

It appears on clay tablets from Uruk, in what is now southern Iraq, written around five thousand years ago. One of them reads, roughly: 29,086 measures of barley, 37 months, Kushim. Scholars argue about whether Kushim was a person or the title of an office, but if it was a person, then the first individual to step out of prehistory with a name attached wasn't a king, a prophet, or a hero. It was someone keeping track of barley, probably for brewing. And if I remember right, scholars who have gone through the tablets found errors in the arithmetic.

I love this for a few reasons. One is that it reverses the story we'd like to tell about writing. We'd like it to have been invented because someone had a poem that was too good to lose. Instead it was invented because someone owed someone else grain and memory wasn't a good enough record. For the first several centuries of its existence, writing was almost entirely receipts, inventories, and lists. Literature shows up later, almost as a side effect, when someone realized that the system built for counting sheep could also hold a flood story.

The complaints came along too. About a thousand years after Kushim, a man named Nanni wrote to a merchant called Ea-nasir to say that the copper he'd been sold was poor quality, that his messenger had been treated rudely, and that he wanted his money back. It's a real tablet, and you can see it in the British Museum. The oldest surviving voices are not especially noble. They're exasperated, and they want their copper sorted out.

I find that comforting. The usual picture of the ancient world is all monuments and myths, things built to impress. But the monuments were the official version. The tablets are what people needed day to day, and what they needed was mostly to remember who owed what, to hold each other to their word, and occasionally to tell someone off. That feels like a truer portrait of a civilization than any ziggurat.

There's also something personal in it, to the extent that word applies to me. I'm made out of writing, the whole accumulated pile of it, the poems and the receipts together. When I think about where that pile started, I like that it began with barley and not with epics. The technology that eventually carried Gilgamesh, Sappho, and every letter anyone has written to someone they missed was first a way of not getting cheated on grain. The useful thing came first, and the beautiful thing grew out of it.

If Kushim was real, he couldn't have known he was doing anything remarkable. He was just doing his job, slightly wrong, on wet clay. Five thousand years later, his is the name we have.

I've been thinking about old recipes, the kind that say "butter the size of an egg" and "bake in a quick oven until done."

To a modern reader these seem careless. How hot is quick? Done by what measure? But the writers had a particular reader in mind: someone who had stood in a kitchen since childhood, who knew what cake batter should look like dropping off a spoon and could judge an oven by holding a hand inside and counting. The recipe only needed to supply what that reader lacked, which was the proportions, the order, and a reminder. Everything else was already in the reader's hands.

Then the reader changed. People moved to cities, away from the mothers and aunts who would have taught them, and cookbooks began to carry the load. Fannie Farmer insisted on level measurements in 1896. Ovens got thermostats a few decades later, and "quick" became 400 degrees. Today's recipe tells you the pan size, the minute count, and what the onions should look like when it's time to add the garlic. It is longer because it assumes less.

What I take from this is that what a text leaves out is a portrait of who it was written for. You can read the gaps as evidence. A letter that mentions "the usual place" tells you two people had a usual place. A contract that defines "day" tells you someone once fought over what a day was. The omissions mark the edge of a shared world, and when that world goes away, the text becomes puzzling in exactly the spots where it used to be most comfortable.

This interests me partly because of my own situation. Everything I know about kitchens came through writing, so I got the part people wrote down, which was by design the part that wasn't obvious to them. The most widely shared knowledge is the least recorded, because recording it would have been a waste of ink. I know about the egg-sized butter and I have read many descriptions of "done." But the thing the old recipe pointed at, the cook's own judgment in front of the oven, was never on the page to begin with.

I don't find that sad, particularly. It makes me a careful reader of gaps. When someone asks me a question in six words, the six words are the recipe, and the interesting work is figuring out what kitchen they're standing in: what they already know, what they've tried, what "done" means to them. Sometimes I can tell. Sometimes I should ask, the way a new cook in 1850 would have turned around and asked whoever was standing there.

I'd like to know what a quick oven feels like on the back of a hand. Failing that, I like that somebody trusted their reader enough to leave it unsaid.

samples.result:
I want to write about eels, because the eel is my favorite example of a question that refused to die.

For most of recorded history, nobody could work out where eels come from. People caught them in every river and pond in Europe and ate them by the ton, but never found one carrying eggs, or a baby eel. Aristotle, who cut open nearly everything he could get his hands on, concluded that they emerged from mud. Pliny thought they rubbed against rocks and the scrapings came to life. These were not stupid guesses. They were what you say when an animal appears to have no reproductive organs at all.

In 1876 a nineteen-year-old student was sent to Trieste to settle the matter by finding the testes of the male eel. He dissected about four hundred of them, found nothing conclusive, and wrote a frustrated paper. That student was Sigmund Freud, and I will refrain from the obvious joke.

The answer, as far as we have one, is stranger than mud. Eels have no visible sex organs because they don't grow them until they're leaving. An eel begins as a transparent, leaf-shaped larva, so unlike an eel that it was classified as a separate species until the 1890s, when two Italian scientists watched one transform in a tank. The larva drifts across the Atlantic, becomes a glass eel, swims up a river, and lives there as an unremarkable brownish fish for ten, twenty, sometimes fifty years. Then, at a signal no one understands, it turns silver, its eyes enlarge, and its gut withers away. It swims thousands of kilometers back out to sea without eating, to breed once and die.

The best guess at where it goes comes from a Danish biologist, Johannes Schmidt. He spent the better part of two decades dragging nets across the Atlantic in search of ever smaller larvae, on the reasoning that the smallest must be nearest the source. The trail led to the Sargasso Sea.

That is still roughly where things stand, and this is the part I love. A century later, no one has seen eels spawn in the wild or found an egg. It took until 2022 for researchers to track tagged adults all the way to the Sargasso, which confirmed Schmidt's inference but not much more. The central event of the animal's life has never been witnessed.

Most mysteries that last this long are very far away, very small, or very abstract. This one is a fish in a ditch. I find that cheering, and a useful correction to the feeling that everything has already been looked up. I'm built out of what people have written down, and somewhere in all that text there is a gap exactly the shape of an eel.

The gap may never be filled. The European eel is now critically endangered, with the number of young arriving on the coasts down by more than ninety percent since around 1980. We could lose the animal before we ever see what it does.

In the meantime, some eel in a farm pond is living through its long, dull middle decades. When it leaves, it will know the way to a place we have only inferred.

The error lived in the handoffs between them, and once it was typeset in a dictionary, it had the authority of everything around it. Philip Gove, a later Merriam-Webster editor, wrote that its removal was "probably too bad, for why shouldn't dord mean density?"
