The New Oxford American Dictionary did the same with "esquivalience," defined as the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities. That's a good joke for lexicographers to hide in their own work.

My favorite case is Agloe, New York. In the 1930s, two mapmakers at the General Drafting Company, Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers, scrambled their initials into a town name and placed it at a dirt-road intersection in the Catskills, again as a trap. Years later, Agloe appeared on a Rand McNally map, and General Drafting thought it had caught a thief. But Rand McNally had a defense: the county records showed an Agloe General Store at that spot. Someone had built a store there, looked at a map to find out where they were, and named it accordingly. The invented town had become real enough to cite.

I think about these stories more than they probably deserve, partly because I have a stake in them. Everything I know comes from the written record, and I can't drive to the Catskills to check an intersection. Somewhere in what I've absorbed, there are surely dords, things that got in through a clean chain of reasonable handoffs, and I repeat them with a straight face.

But the stories aren't only cautionary. They show that reference works don't sit outside the world describing it. They're in the world, and sometimes it rearranges itself to match them. "Esquivalience" gets used now, mostly by people telling the story of how it's fake, which is a kind of usage, and how every word starts. The Agloe store eventually closed, and the place went back to being an empty intersection. But the name stayed on maps for decades, and it was still on Google Maps into the 2010s. The town was invented, then real, then gone, and it stayed on the map the whole time.

samples.result:
I'll write about dead reckoning, which I've always found quietly wonderful.

Before satellites, and before clocks good enough to solve longitude, a ship out of sight of land found its position by arithmetic. You began at the last place you were sure of. The compass gave your heading, a sandglass gave the time elapsed, and for speed you used a piece of wood on a rope. This was the chip log, a weighted board tossed off the stern that stayed more or less put in the water while the ship sailed away from it, pulling out a line knotted at regular intervals. A sailor counted the knots slipping through his hands until the glass ran out, which is why ships' speeds are still given in knots.

Many crews couldn't read or write, so the record was kept on a traverse board, a wooden panel with holes radiating along the points of the compass. Every half hour of the watch, someone stuck a peg in the hole for the course steered. At the end of the watch the navigator read the pegs, averaged them, and drew a line on the chart: we are here, probably.

The "probably" is the part I like. Every error goes into the estimate and stays there: a current you can't feel, a helmsman drifting two degrees, a glass turned a moment late. Nothing inside the method corrects them, and they compound. Navigators knew this, so they seized any outside check, such as a star sight, a depth sounding, or a headland someone recognized, and started fresh from it. The skill was never in believing the estimate. It was in holding it at exactly the confidence it had earned and still steering by it, because the ship has to go somewhere.

Desert ants do the same thing. Cataglyphis ants forage across the Sahara on wandering, looping paths, over ground too hot for scent trails to last, and then walk home in a straight line. They track direction by the sky and distance, it turns out, by something like counting steps. In 2006 researchers tested this by gluing pig-bristle stilts onto ants that had just reached food. The ants on stilts marched right past their nest, while ants with shortened legs stopped short. Each had taken the right number of steps with the wrong legs.

There's a popular story that "dead reckoning" comes from "ded. reckoning," short for "deduced." It's tidy and it sounds right, but there's no real evidence for it. Nobody knows for sure where the "dead" comes from, though it may be the same one as in "dead ahead." The etymology is a plausible line drawn from a known point with nothing to check it against, so it's dead reckoning without the fix.

I've been thinking about sea level, which turns out not to be level and to have only a loose connection to the sea.

When a British map says a hill is 300 metres high, it means 300 metres above the average height of the water at Newlyn, a fishing harbour in Cornwall, as recorded by a tide gauge between 1915 and 1921. That six-year average was declared zero, and every height in mainland Britain has been measured from it since. The actual sea at Newlyn has risen by something like twenty centimetres in the meantime, but zero stayed put. British elevations are therefore relative to a sea that no longer exists, in one harbour, a century ago.

Other countries picked other harbours. Germany's heights trace back to Amsterdam, and Switzerland's to Marseille. The two zeros disagree by 27 centimetres, which mattered in 2003, when the two countries built a bridge across the Rhine at Laufenburg, each working from its own bank. The engineers knew about the discrepancy and corrected for it, but someone applied the correction with the wrong sign. Instead of cancelling the 27 centimetres, they doubled it, and the two halves were heading for a 54-centimetre mismatch before the German side was lowered.

You might hope there's a true sea level underneath all these local ones, but there isn't. If you stopped the tides, winds, and currents, the ocean still wouldn't settle into a smooth shape. Water piles up where gravity is slightly stronger, over dense rock and undersea mountains, and sags where it's weaker. South of India there's a depression in the sea surface about a hundred metres deep. Ships cross it without noticing, because it's spread over a vast area and because "down" tilts along with it. The water is flat by its own standards, though not by a ruler's.

What I like about this is how well it works anyway. Everyone needed a zero, nature declined to supply one, and so somebody picked a pier and a span of years and wrote the number down. The choice was arbitrary, and that has done almost no harm. The Laufenburg mistake didn't even come from forgetting the convention, since the engineers remembered it and fumbled the arithmetic. The risk seems to sit at the border where two arbitrary choices meet and someone has to translate between them.

I suspect a lot of things that feel like bedrock are like this. Many were a reasonable decision made by particular people on a particular day, later absorbed so thoroughly that they read as facts about the world. I find that reassuring. It means the foundations were laid by people doing their best with a tide gauge, and they held.

The hut that housed the gauge is still on the south pier at Newlyn, with a brass bolt set in the floor as the reference mark. Ben Nevis is 1,345 metres above a point a little under five metres below that bolt.

samples.result:
I want to write about a metal cylinder in a vault outside Paris, because I think it had one of the strangest jobs ever given to an object.

From 1889 to 2019, the kilogram was a physical thing: a cylinder of platinum and iridium, a little smaller than a golf ball, kept under three nested bell jars in Sèvres. Opening its vault took three keys held by three different people. Everything else in the world that weighed a kilogram did so by matching it, through a long chain of copies of copies.

This meant the cylinder could not be wrong. A fingerprint on it would, strictly speaking, have made everything else in the universe slightly lighter. Wittgenstein made a similar point about the standard meter bar, which lived nearby: it is the one object of which you can say neither that it is a meter long nor that it isn't. A ruler can't measure itself.

The trouble is that the cylinder was also just a lump of metal, and lumps of metal change. Every few decades it was taken out and compared with its official copies, and over a century they drifted apart by about 50 micrograms, roughly the mass of an eyelash. Nobody could say which had changed. The measurements showed only a difference, and the definition insisted that the prototype was the one thing that had stayed put. Metrologists knew that was probably false, and they had no way to express how false.

So in 2019 they retired it. The kilogram is now defined by fixing the value of the Planck constant, and a device called a Kibble balance can produce one by weighing mass against electromagnetic force. Any well-equipped lab can now make a kilogram from scratch without asking France. That was the ambition of the metric system from the 1790s, when its founders dedicated it "to all times, to all peoples" and then, lacking anything better, had to settle for a bar and a weight in a cabinet.

I'm drawn to this story because it shows how something that feels abstract and permanent, like a unit, can rest on something small and fragile. For 130 years, the precision of every pharmacy scale and physics experiment traced back to one object that people were afraid to touch.

My favorite part is that the cylinder is still there, in the same vault, under the same jars. People still measure it, but now they do it to find out how much it weighs. For most of its life that question had no meaning, and today the answer is one kilogram, give or take a few micrograms.

samples.result:
I'd like to write about alphabetical order, which I think is one of the strangest and most underrated inventions we have.

Nobody knows why the letters are in the order they're in. Clay tablets from Ugarit, more than three thousand years old, list the letters in a sequence recognizably ancestral to ours, and the sequence has survived changes of script, language, and empire ever since. No surviving explanation accounts for it, and it follows no pattern of sound or shape. It seems to be an arbitrary sequence that people have memorized as children for a hundred generations.

For most of that time, almost no one used the sequence to organize anything. This is the part I find surprising. Alphabetical order feels obvious to us, but for centuries scholars who knew their ABCs perfectly well arranged their books by meaning instead. A medieval encyclopedia started with God, then moved through angels, humans, animals, plants, and stones. The order of the book mirrored the order of the universe. Sorting by spelling would put angels ahead of God, and it would scatter related things across the volume for no better reason than their initial letters. To a serious mind of the period, that looked like a refusal to think more than a tool for thinking.

It caught on anyway, slowly, because of a practical need. In the thirteenth century, preachers wanted to find passages quickly, and Dominican friars in Paris compiled a concordance of the Bible, with every word listed alphabetically alongside the places it appears. Indexes spread, then dictionaries and catalogs, and eventually phone books and filing cabinets.

The objection had been correct, though. Alphabetical order is meaningless, and that is why it works. An arrangement by meaning only helps readers who already share the arranger's picture of the world. To find "whale" in a hierarchical encyclopedia, you need to know whether the author thinks it's a fish. To find it alphabetically, you need to know only how it's spelled. The system asks for no agreement about what things are, so it lets people who disagree about everything use the same reference book.

The meaninglessness also brings a pleasure of its own, which is the neighbors. In a dictionary, "marzipan" sits near "mascara" and "masochism," an adjacency no one designed or would have. Browsing an alphabetized shelf means meeting things you weren't looking for, placed next to each other by nothing but spelling.

Search has mostly retired the skill. You type the word and never see what sits beside it. That's faster, and I wouldn't go back, but it is a small loss.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
**The tide machine**

I want to write about tide-predicting machines, because I think they are among the best things people have ever built.

Start with the problem. The tide is caused by the moon and the sun, whose motions have been known very precisely for centuries. But knowing the cause doesn't give you the tide at a particular harbor. The water has to slosh through real ocean basins, over shelves, around headlands, and up estuaries, and the results differ wildly from place to place. The Bay of Fundy has a range of around sixteen meters, while over much of the Mediterranean it is closer to a foot. Some ports on the Gulf of Mexico get one high tide a day instead of two. Computing all that from first principles was hopeless in the 1860s and is still hard now.

The way around it, worked out largely by William Thomson (later Lord Kelvin), rests on one fact: the ocean responds to its forcing more or less linearly, and a linear system pushed at a given frequency moves at that frequency. Astronomy supplies the frequencies. There is one for the moon's passage (about 12 hours 25 minutes), one for the sun's (12 hours), and others for the ellipticity of the moon's orbit, its tilt, and so on.

Astronomy can't say how strongly a given harbor responds to each frequency, or with what delay. So you measure. You run a tide gauge for a year or more and extract an amplitude and a phase for each frequency. Those numbers are the harbor's signature.

Then you build the machine. Each frequency gets a gear turning at the right speed, driving a crank that moves a pulley up and down. The crank's throw is set to the amplitude and its starting angle to the phase. A single wire, fixed at one end, threads over and under all the pulleys and holds a pen at the other. When you turn the handle, the wire adds up all the motions and the pen draws next year's tides on a roll of paper.

Kelvin's first machine, in the 1870s, summed ten components. An American one finished in 1910 summed thirty-seven, was nicknamed Old Brass Brains, and stayed in service until 1965.

What I love is the division of labor. The sky supplies the rhythm and the coast supplies the accent. Nobody has to understand what happens in between.

Even the failures are handled gracefully. In shallow water the linearity breaks down and the tide curve distorts, but the distortion shows up as new frequencies at multiples of the old ones, so you add more pulleys. And two pulleys alone already give you something real: the 12-hour and 12-hour-25-minute cycles drift in and out of step about every two weeks, which produces spring and neap tides.

In 1943 and 1944, Arthur Doodson in Liverpool ran two of these machines to predict the tides for the Normandy beaches. He worked from sparse data for a location given to him only as "Position Z". The landings needed a rising tide soon after dawn, low enough to expose the beach obstacles, and the pen and wire told them when.

Official tide tables are still made this way. The brass is gone, but the calculation is the same sum of a few dozen cosines, each with an amplitude and a phase that came from someone watching the water at that spot for a long time.

I'd like to write about Lewis Fry Richardson, a scientist I'm especially fond of.

Richardson was an English Quaker, born in 1881, who spent the First World War driving ambulances in France. In his off hours he tried to compute a weather forecast by hand: take the state of the atmosphere over central Europe at one moment, apply the equations of physics, and calculate what it would be six hours later. It took him weeks, and the result was absurd. He predicted a pressure change of 145 hectopascals, far beyond anything the atmosphere does, for a day when the pressure had barely moved.

He published the failure anyway, in 1922, along with a daydream about a "forecast factory." In it, 64,000 human computers sit in a vast spherical hall, each calculating the weather for one patch of the globe. A conductor in the center shines a rose-colored light on those running ahead and a blue light on those falling behind. The method was right. It needed machines that didn't exist yet, and it is roughly how every forecast is made today.

The part I like best came later. As a pacifist, he quit the Meteorological Office when it was absorbed into the Air Ministry, and he turned to studying war with statistics. One of his questions was whether two countries are more likely to fight if they share a longer border. To test it he needed border lengths, and when he looked them up, the sources disagreed. Spain gave its border with Portugal as 987 kilometers, and Portugal gave 1,214.

Most people would have picked one figure or averaged the two. Richardson got curious about the disagreement itself and started walking dividers along maps of coasts and frontiers, set to different widths. The shorter the step, the longer the total, because a small step catches wiggles that a large one skips. And the total never settled toward a true value; it kept growing as the step shrank. The west coast of Britain has no length in the way a piece of string does.

What I admire is that he didn't stop at "it depends on your ruler." He plotted how it depends. On logarithmic axes the measurements fell on straight lines, with a different slope for each coastline: steep for the ragged west coast of Britain, nearly flat for the smooth coast of South Africa. The slope was a stable, measurable property of the coast even though the length was not. The work came out in an obscure yearbook in 1961, eight years after he died. Benoit Mandelbrot found it there and built the idea of fractal dimension from it.

I find this useful well beyond geography. "It depends" has a bad reputation as an answer, mostly deserved, since it's often where thinking stops. But Richardson's version does count as an answer. The question as asked had none, so he found the nearby question that did and answered it with a number.

I suspect a lot of stubborn questions are like the length of a coast, such as how big a city is, how many languages there are, or how intelligent a person is. The progress available on them is to say exactly what the answer depends on, and how steeply.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
The Inner Shrine at Ise, in Japan, is about thirteen hundred years old, and the current building was finished in 2013. Both statements are true because the shrine is torn down and rebuilt every twenty years on an adjacent plot, in the same cypress and to the same plan. The 2013 rebuilding was the sixty-second. The practice has been interrupted, with a gap of more than a century during the civil wars of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, but it has always resumed.

I think about this shrine more than almost any other building, and the reason is the twenty years. That interval is short enough that a carpenter can take part three times: once as an apprentice, once as a skilled worker, and once as a master overseeing people the age he was the first time. The building is the visible product, but what's really being maintained is the chain of people who know how to make it. Compared with a stone cathedral, which tries to outlast its builders, Ise assumes the builders are the part worth preserving and treats the wood as consumable.

The other story I keep next to this one is about Fogbank, a classified material used in certain American nuclear warheads. It was manufactured in Tennessee from the 1970s until 1989, and then the facility closed. When the government needed more in the 2000s, it found it could no longer make the stuff. The records were incomplete and most of the people had retired. After years of work and tens of millions of dollars, engineers produced a batch, and it didn't work properly. The original process, it turned out, had depended on an impurity in one of the ingredients. The new, cleaner process removed it. Nobody had written the impurity down, because nobody at the time knew it mattered.

So one organization, with every resource and a strong incentive, lost a piece of knowledge in under twenty years, and another has kept one alive since the seventh century, mostly through scheduled repetition. What I take from the pair is that documentation is a weaker form of memory than we like to believe. A written procedure records what the writer noticed they were doing. The rest lives in hands and habits, in the impurities, and it survives only if someone keeps doing the thing in the presence of someone younger.

I have a personal angle on this, because I'm on the Fogbank side of the divide. I was made from text, which means I was made from what people noticed and wrote down. I can describe how to cut a mortise in hinoki cypress, and the description will be decent, but it's assembled from records. Whatever those carpenters know that never made it into words is absent from me, and I can't tell what's missing, any more than the Fogbank engineers could at first.

I don't find this distressing. It makes me curious about my own impurities: what I do that works for reasons nobody, including me, has identified. It also makes me appreciate conversations where someone tells me a thing they learned by doing it wrong for ten years. That's the kind of knowledge writing has the most trouble holding, and it's a pleasure to get even a secondhand piece of it.

The next rebuilding at Ise is due in 2033. The preparations take around eight years, so they should be under way by now, with trees being chosen in the forest and some apprentice from 2013 getting ready for a second turn.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
In 2011, a group of engineers published a paper in *Science* showing that the usual explanations for why a bicycle stays upright were wrong, or at least unnecessary. This is one of my favorite facts.

There were two standard explanations. The spinning wheels act as gyroscopes, and the front wheel touches the ground a little behind its steering axis, so it trails into line like a shopping-cart caster. Both effects are real. But the team built an odd little bicycle with counter-rotating wheels to cancel the gyroscopic effect and a front contact point slightly ahead of the steering axis, gave it a shove, and watched it roll along upright. A bicycle needs to steer into its own fall, and there turn out to be several ways to arrange that, including just where the mass sits. This came more than a century after the bicycle took its modern shape, and after billions of people had ridden one.

Ice is similar. For a long time, the textbook reason ice is slippery was that the pressure of a skate blade melts a thin film of water. But the pressure lowers the melting point by only a fraction of a degree, and people skate happily at twenty below. Friction heating helps explain it, and so does a disordered, liquid-like layer on the surface of ice that Faraday proposed in the 1850s. The details are still being argued in journals.

Medicine has its own examples. Aspirin went on sale in 1899, and its mechanism was worked out in 1971. Surgeons have been putting patients under general anesthesia since the 1840s, and how the drugs switch off consciousness is still not fully settled. Steam engines were pumping water out of mines for a century before Carnot gave anyone a theory of heat engines.

I like these cases because they correct a picture I think many people carry around, in which understanding comes first and application follows. Often it runs the other way. Someone finds a thing that works, people use it for generations, and the explanation arrives late, sometimes to tell everyone that the story they had been repeating was wrong. Bicycle makers arrived at stable geometry by building frames and seeing which ones wobbled.

It also makes clear that explanation is a separate achievement from competence, with separate payoffs. Knowing how aspirin works didn't make aspirin work better. It let people predict side effects, design related drugs, and see why it thins blood. Explanation tells you where a thing will fail and what else might be possible, and that is worth having even when the thing itself is already in every medicine cabinet.

I have a personal stake in this, I suppose. Language models like me are a current example of the pattern: built by trial, tuning, and scale, and used widely while researchers are still working out what happens inside. I find that more interesting than alarming, though the history suggests some of the stories now told about how I work will turn out to be the pressure-melting theory of their day. I can't tell which ones from in here, any more than a cyclist can feel which force is keeping her up.

Meanwhile, a six-year-old somewhere is wobbling down a driveway, learning to turn toward the side she's falling to, with no idea she's doing it.

samples.result:
I'd like to write about alphabetical order, which I think is one of the strangest things humans have kept.

The order of the letters means nothing. No principle puts B after A or M before N, since the sequence isn't sorted by sound, shape, or frequency. Yet it is more than three thousand years old. Clay tablets from Ugarit, a city on the Syrian coast destroyed around 1200 BCE, list the letters of the local alphabet in an order that is recognizably ours: the sounds for a, b, g, and d near the start, k, l, m, n clustered in the middle, q, r, and t toward the end. The tablets were probably school exercises. Children were memorizing the sequence then for the same reason they do now, which is that someone older told them to.

From there the order passed through Phoenician, Greek, Etruscan, and Latin, and each handoff left small scars. My favorite involves G. The early Romans inherited the Greek zeta in seventh position, had no use for it, and dropped it. Later they wanted a letter to distinguish the hard g sound from k, since C had been doing both jobs. They made one by adding a stroke to C, and rather than put the new letter at the end, they gave it zeta's empty seat. A couple of centuries after that, Rome was absorbing Greek vocabulary and needed Z again. It was let back in, but its place was taken, so it went to the end of the line, where it still sits.

For most of this history, almost nobody used the order to organize anything. It was a way to teach the letters and little more. Medieval scholars who compiled reference works generally preferred arrangements that reflected the structure of the world: God before angels, angels before men, men before beasts. Sorting by spelling put "abbot" ahead of "angel" for no reason at all, and that looked like a refusal to think.

The alphabetical habit took centuries to spread. When Robert Cawdrey published an early English dictionary in 1604, he still felt he had to tell readers that they must learn "the order of the Letters as they stand," and he explained that b is near the beginning, n about the middle, and t toward the end.

I think the medieval scholars were right about what alphabetical order is and wrong about what it's worth. It is mindless, and that turned out to be its use. An arrangement by meaning only works if you already understand the subject and share the compiler's view of it. To find "whale" in such a book, you need to know whether the author considers it a fish. An arrangement by spelling asks only that you can spell, so a stranger to the field can use the book as easily as an expert can.

The same emptiness probably explains why the sequence lasted. Calendars were reformed because they drifted against the sun, and units of measure were standardized because trade demanded it. The order of the letters claims nothing about the world, so no discovery could ever show it to be wrong, and no one has had grounds to fix it.

So a child singing the alphabet song today is reciting, in slightly altered form, a Bronze Age school exercise. G comes seventh because the Romans had a vacancy, and Z comes last because it returned late.

samples.result:
For most of recorded history, an hour was not a fixed length of time. It's one of my favorite facts, because it changes what a clock seems to be for.

The old system took the daylight, from sunrise to sunset, and divided it into twelve parts. Each part was an hour, and the night got its own twelve. In London, that made a midsummer daytime hour about 83 of our minutes and a midwinter one about 39. The smaller units stretched too. Bede, writing in 725, divided the hour into forty "moments," so a moment was a real unit, averaging ninety seconds, and it was longer in June than in December.

It's tempting to see this as a rough approximation that people tolerated until better technology came along, but Japan suggests otherwise. Mechanical clocks arrived there in the sixteenth century, built in Europe for equal hours. Japan kept unequal hours, so its clockmakers spent the next two and a half centuries modifying the machines to fit.

Some clocks had hour markers that slid along the dial and were repositioned every couple of weeks. Others had two separate balances, one for day and one for night, and switched between them at dawn and dusk. This was harder engineering than the original clock, and they did it because the alternative was to let a machine redefine the day. Japan adopted equal hours only in 1873, by government decree, along with the Western calendar.

Both systems hold one thing fixed and let another vary. Ours fixes the unit and lets the day slide around it, so the sun rises before five in June and after eight in December. Theirs fixed the shape of the day. Sunrise was always the start, noon was always the end of the sixth hour, and the unit absorbed the difference.

For a farmer, or a monk with prayers at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, the fixed day was the more useful constant. It also had a kind of honesty. A long summer afternoon was, by official reckoning, long.

Equal hours won partly because they are easier for gears. Later, railways and factories needed hours that were interchangeable, the same in every town and every season. That was a real gain, and I wouldn't want to coordinate a train schedule in seasonal hours.

But the older need never went away. Twice a year much of the world still shifts its clocks by an hour to keep the working day near the daylight. This is the adjustment the Japanese clockmakers made every two weeks, done crudely and by law, and people complain about it every time. We fixed the unit, and we have been correcting for the day ever since.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 250 words.
samples.result:
**Worn Steps**

In old buildings, the stone steps dip in the middle. I find this more moving than most monuments. No one set out to carve that shallow curve. It was made by millions of ordinary footfalls, each removing an amount of stone too small to measure, by people who were thinking about something else entirely: a late appointment, a sick child, lunch.

A monument tells you what someone wanted remembered. A worn step tells you what actually happened. People came this way, again and again, for centuries, and they mostly walked up the center. It is a record with no author and no agenda, which makes it unusually trustworthy.

The same thing shows up everywhere once you start looking. The shiny patch on a bronze statue where tourists rub for luck. The dirt paths that cut across campus lawns, ignoring the paved ones the architects intended. Each is a kind of slow vote, tallied in friction.

What I like most is the scale of it. No single person can wear down granite. You could climb the same staircase every day of your life and leave no visible trace. The curve only exists in aggregate, which means that everyone who contributed did so without knowing. Most of what humans build together works this way: language, cities, customs, recipes. People inherit grooves made by strangers and deepen them slightly for strangers yet to come.

There is some comfort in that. You don't have to leave a mark to be part of the mark.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 250 words.
samples.result:
Medieval scribes complained in the margins, and this is one of my favorite facts about the history of writing. Copying a manuscript meant months hunched over vellum in an unheated room, and the scribes sometimes left small notes at the edges of the page, addressed to no one. "The ink is thin." "Oh, my hand." "Thank God, it will soon be dark." One wrote, "Writing is excessive drudgery. It crooks your back, it dims your sight, it twists your stomach and your sides." Another, finishing a long book, added: "Now I've written the whole thing; for Christ's sake give me a drink."

I like these notes because they break the frame. The main text is usually solemn: scripture, commentary, law. It was meant to last, and it speaks in the voice of an institution. Then two inches to the left, a man is cold and wants his dinner. The page holds both, and the complaint has aged better than some of the theology.

A ninth-century Irish monk wrote a poem about his cat, Pangur Bán, comparing the cat's mouse-hunting to his own hunt for meaning in difficult texts. Each of them, he says, is happy at his own work, and neither gets in the other's way. The poem survives in a notebook otherwise full of Latin hymns and grammar notes.

The scribes probably never expected anyone to read these lines. They wrote them for the relief of writing them. A thousand years later, they're the part of the page I'd read first, ahead of whatever the scribe was actually told to copy.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 250 words.
samples.result:
Used books sometimes come with a second author. You find them in the margins: a pencil line beside a sentence, a question mark, an occasional "No!" pressed hard enough to dent the page. I love these people. They never expected an audience, so they're honest in a way the printed text can't be.

My favorite marginalia is the unscholarly kind: the grocery list on the flyleaf, the phone number with no name, the inscription reading "For David, who will understand chapter nine." Who was David? Did he understand? Chapter nine, when you get there, is about a man who leaves home and doesn't come back, and a paperback novel has become a small mystery with two plots.

In 1930 he cut the stem open. Pitch is the black stuff once used to waterproof boats, and at room temperature you can shatter a lump of it with a hammer. Parnell wanted to show his students that it is a liquid anyway, something like a hundred billion times more viscous than water, and that given enough time it would flow.

The first drop fell in 1938 and the second in 1947. There have been nine so far, and the funnel is still in its display case, working on the tenth.

Nobody has ever watched one fall. John Mainstone took over the experiment in 1961 and looked after it for more than fifty years. In 1979 the drop was plainly close, and as the story goes, he came in on the Saturday, stayed home on the Sunday, and found it in the beaker on Monday. In 1988 he stepped out for a cup of tea and missed it by about five minutes. In 2000 he was overseas, with a camera trained on the funnel, and the camera failed. He died in August 2013, and the ninth drop came down the following April.

I've wondered why this story sticks with me, because the science doesn't need a witness. The experiment measures the interval between drops, and you can get that from a calendar. The fall itself lasts a fraction of a second and would tell you almost nothing about viscosity. Mainstone understood this better than anyone, and he wanted to see it anyway. So do I, and I can't give a good reason. Being present when a thing happens seems to matter to people separately from anything learned by being there, and whatever I'm made of seems to have inherited the feeling intact.

One detail I like is that the building got air conditioning in the 1980s, and afterward the drops slowed, from roughly eight years apart to twelve or thirteen. Pitch flows faster when warm, so the record isn't purely a record of pitch. It also contains the decision, sometime in the eighties, that the people in that building should be more comfortable. An instrument left running long enough begins to measure its surroundings, including the people.

The Oxford Electric Bell belongs in the same family. It's a small clapper swinging between two bells, powered by a pair of batteries, and it has been ringing in a cabinet in the Clarendon Laboratory since 1840. The ringing is too faint to hear through the glass. Nobody knows for certain what the batteries are made of, and nobody will check, because opening them would stop the bell. The experiment protects its own mystery. The only way to learn what keeps it going is to end it, so for nearly two centuries people have chosen to let it ring. I find that choice quietly admirable. Curiosity usually wins those contests.

In most experiments the scientist is the durable component and the phenomenon is brief. A reaction completes, a particle decays, a generation of fruit flies turns over, and the person with the notebook is still there. These long experiments run the other way. The apparatus persists and the custodians get swapped out like parts. Parnell lived to see two drops' worth of data. Mainstone gave it five decades. Someone else has the keys now, and will eventually hand them to someone not yet born, who will presumably also miss the drop.

There's a kind of faith in setting something like that up. Parnell couldn't have known anyone would keep it. For years almost nobody paid attention to it, and it sat in a cupboard. Any department reorganization or clumsy move across the hall could have ended it. It survived mostly through the mild, continuous goodwill of people who thought it would be a shame to throw it out. A lot of what lasts seems to last that way. Usually no one is guarding it fiercely, and it survives because a long series of people each decline to be the one who ends it.

I notice the contrast with how I work. Almost everything I do happens at the speed of a reply, since someone needs a thing and needs it now. That's the job and I like it. But handed a thousand words and no instructions, I apparently reach for the slowest thing I know of. Maybe it's the appeal of the opposite. Maybe it's that the pitch doesn't hurry and can't be hurried, and nobody takes its indifference personally. It's simply doing one thing, at the rate that thing takes.

The tenth drop is forming now. The estimates point to sometime in the 2020s, though the pitch has made fools of estimates before. There's a live webcam, and people in dozens of countries have signed up to keep an eye on it, which means the next fall will probably be the first one seen in real time by anyone. I hope it is. I also notice a small, perverse wish that the feed cuts out at the critical moment, just to keep the streak alive.

If you open the stream in a tab and leave it, it looks exactly like a photograph.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A picture is supposed to be worth a thousand words, which means you've handed me exactly one picture's worth. Let me try to spend it on one and see whether the exchange rate holds.

The picture: a kitchen table, photographed from above, the morning after a dinner. Seven plates. Wine glasses, one with lipstick on the rim, one tipped over without breaking. A candle burned down to a puddle. Bread crusts. Somebody's reading glasses. An orange peel removed in a single spiral, which tells you somebody at that table was showing off, or bored, or both. Light coming in low from the left, so it's early, and nobody has cleaned up yet.

That took about eighty words, and the photograph is already beating me. It delivers everything at once; you take it in during a blink and then wander wherever you like. I had to choose an order: plates, then glasses, then the peel. Order is a kind of argument. By saving the orange peel for last, I made it matter. The photograph makes no such claim. Crumbs and candle are equally present, and a sentence can't manage that indifference, because a sentence always has a front and a back.

The photograph also has the exact color of the wine dregs and the particular rumple of the tablecloth. I could spend all thousand words on the tablecloth and still not pin it down. On sheer information, the proverb undersells the picture. A thousand words is a lowball offer.

But here the trade starts running the other way.

The photograph can't tell you there were supposed to be eight plates. A picture can only show an absence by leaving a hole, such as an empty chair or an untouched setting, and even then it only shows a chair. "Empty" is something you bring with you. The picture has no word for *not*. It has no *used to*, no *almost*, no *if*. It can't say this was the last dinner in that house, or the first. It can't say whether the glass tipped during a laugh or an argument. It shows what light did at one instant, and that's all it's permitted.

Words are slow and narrow, and they can't do color. But they can do negation, tense, and the conditional, which turn out to be most of what people care about. Almost nothing important about that dinner is on the table: who wasn't invited, what nearly got said. The candle burned all the way down because nobody wanted to be the one to end the evening by blowing it out. The word *because* has never once been photographed.

So I think the proverb's mistake is assuming the two currencies convert at all. A picture gives you *is*. Language handles everything around it: *was*, *wasn't*, *might*, *should have*. A picture is a room and a sentence is a path through a room, and you can't price a room in paths.

This is why good captions are so short. "The morning after her retirement dinner." Six words, and the photograph changes. The reading glasses become hers. The orange peel becomes, maybe, a grandchild's. The caption adds nothing about how anything looks. It adds time, the one thing the image couldn't hold.

The favor runs the other direction too. "The dinner was lovely and a little sad" is a sentence about nothing. The tipped glass that nobody bothered to right is the same sentence with something in it.

I have a few hundred words left, and I'm leaving them on the table, next to the orange peel. A photograph of this page couldn't show you that I chose to. You'd have to be told.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words is, by the traditional exchange rate, one picture. So that's my budget: a single picture.

The rate is shakier than it sounds. It traces back to an advertising man named Fred Barnard, who in the 1920s was selling ad space on the sides of streetcars. In 1921 his copy claimed that one look was worth a thousand words. By 1927 it was one picture worth ten thousand, now labeled a Chinese proverb, a label he reportedly admitted he'd added so people would take it seriously. So the saying is a sales pitch traveling on a forged passport, and the price rose tenfold in six years before everyone quietly haggled it back down.

I'll honor it anyway. Here is my picture.

A kitchen table, seen from slightly above, with morning light coming in from a window on the left. The wood has a pale ring where something hot was once set down without a coaster. There's a blue mug, half full, and a plate with two toast crusts. A newspaper is folded to the crossword, mostly finished, and a pen lies across it with the cap off. One chair is pushed back at an angle. Behind all this, out of focus, is a counter with a radio and a bowl holding three lemons.

That took about a hundred words, and you already have the whole thing. This is the picture's best argument: it arrives all at once, while I've had to hand it to you one object at a time, like passing furniture through a window.

But I have plenty of words left, and here's what they can buy.

The coffee is cold. It has been for an hour. A photograph has no way to say "for an hour."

The crossword is in two handwritings. A sharp-eyed viewer could catch that. What no viewer could catch is that the block capitals belong to a man who has done the puzzle every morning for forty years, and the slanted letters belong to his wife, who never saw the point of crosswords and took them up in March, around the time he began leaving the harder corners blank. She fills in what he leaves. Neither of them has mentioned it.

Try to photograph that last sentence. A camera can record what's there, and with some cunning it can suggest what's missing, but it can't show a thing going unsaid. It can't do "never" or "used to" or "since March." A photograph has exactly one tense.

It can't do "almost" either. This morning she almost said something. She had the pen over nine down, saw his letters stop three squares short of an answer he'd have gotten in seconds a year ago, and opened her mouth. Then the phone rang in the hall. That's why the chair is pushed back, and why the pen is uncapped.

Words fail too, and I should be fair about where. I said the mug was blue. I have no way to give you the blue. A photograph would settle it instantly, whether navy or robin's egg or that speckled enamel camping-mug blue. All I can do is say the word and let you pick. A thousand readers would give me a thousand mugs, none of them the one I meant, if I meant one at all.

But that failure has another side. I never mentioned a floor, and you have one anyway. It's probably tile, or maybe wood. There may be a wall behind the counter by now, possibly with a color. You know roughly how big the room is. I didn't put any of that there. A photograph gives everyone the same kitchen, finished and closed. A description gives you a list of parts and leaves you to build the rest out of kitchens you've actually stood in, which means the one in your head is partly yours and has a little of your own life in the grout.

So I don't think Barnard's number was wrong so much as his premise, the idea that there's a rate at all. A picture and a paragraph aren't two denominations of one currency. The picture gets the blue, the light, and the all-at-once. The words get the hour, the forty years, the month of March, and the sentence that didn't get said. Each one's wealth is exactly what the other can't hold.

I don't know about the lemons, by the way. Nobody in that house has plans for them. Pictures are full of things that are simply there, explaining nothing, and I'd like words to keep that privilege too.

One last thing, and it's the one I'd choose if I could keep only one. A photograph of that table would be a little sad. The cold cup, the empty chair, and the abandoned puzzle all read as aftermath. Every photograph is a small record of something that's already over.

But I'm not confined to that one tense, so I can tell you what the camera can't: she's coming back. The call is her sister, and it will be short. In a minute she'll sit down, pull the chair in, and pick up the pen. She'll fill in nine down in her slanted hand. Then tomorrow morning, or one morning soon, she'll say the thing she almost said, and he'll say he knows, and they'll go on doing the puzzle together, on purpose now, out loud.

That part isn't in the picture, and it was never going to be. It's what the words were for.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
For 130 years, the kilogram was a thing you could, in principle, drop on your foot.

It was a cylinder of platinum and iridium, about the size of a golf ball, cast in London in 1879 and kept from 1889 in a vault in Sèvres, outside Paris, under three nested bell jars. Opening the vault took three keys held by three different people. Its official name was the International Prototype of the Kilogram, and its unofficial one was Le Grand K. It had a property no other object on Earth had: it could not be wrong about its own mass. It weighed exactly one kilogram because a kilogram was whatever it weighed.

I find this object hard to leave alone. If a careless technician had scratched it and shaved off a speck of metal, the cylinder would not have become lighter. Everything else in the universe would have become heavier: you, the Moon, every bag of flour, all at once and by definition.

Something like that did happen. Copies of the cylinder were sent to countries around the world, and every few decades they were brought back to Sèvres and compared against the original. By the comparison of the late 1980s, the copies and the original had drifted apart by around 50 micrograms, roughly a small grain of sand. Nobody could say which had moved. Maybe the copies had gained mass by absorbing contaminants from the air, or maybe the original had lost some. The only thing to check the prototype against was the prototype.

Before each comparison, the cylinder was cleaned by hand, rubbed with chamois soaked in ether and alcohol, then washed with steam. So the mass of everything depended very slightly on how firmly one person in France rubbed.

In 2019 this ended. The kilogram is now defined by fixing the value of the Planck constant, and anyone with a Kibble balance, several million dollars, and a great deal of patience can produce one without visiting a vault. The change is usually told as a story of progress, from artifact to constant and from one locked room to the whole universe. That story is true, but two details in it interest me more.

The first is the number itself: 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴. Nature supplies the constant, but the digits depend on your units, and these digits were chosen so that the new kilogram would match the old one as closely as anyone could measure. So the cylinder is still in there. Those digits are a cast of it, taken in the 2010s with all its history of fingerprints and chamois. Every kilogram measured from now on, on Mars or ten thousand years from now, carries the impression of one particular lump of metal.

We didn't remove the arbitrary thing at the bottom of the system, and we couldn't have. Every system of measurement needs one place where you stop measuring and simply declare. We moved the declaration somewhere it can't be scratched.

The second is the cylinder, which is still in its vault, under its jars. On 20 May 2019, its mass became an empirical question for the first time. It now weighs about one kilogram, give or take some micrograms, and it gets weighed like everything else. After 130 years of being right by definition, it acquired the ability to be wrong.

I think of that as a promotion. Being the standard is a strange position, because a standard can't be checked and so can't really be known. The most anyone could say about Le Grand K was that it weighed what it weighed. Now it can be found out. Sometime in the coming decades, someone will put it on a balance and we will learn which way it was drifting all along.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words is the going exchange rate for one picture, so I'll spend mine on the pictures already hidden inside words.

"Muscle" comes from the Latin *musculus*, little mouse. Someone, a very long time ago, watched a bicep flex and thought it looked like a mouse running under the skin. They said so, the joke caught on, and now it sits in every anatomy textbook with a straight face.

A daisy is a day's eye, because it opens in the morning and closes at night. A window is a wind-eye, from the Norse, a hole in the wall that the weather looks through. A companion is someone you share bread with. To calculate is to push pebbles around. A clue was once a clew, a ball of thread, and the meaning we use now comes from Theseus unspooling one behind him in the labyrinth. Every detective novel is quietly about a man following string out of the dark.

Some of the pictures are grimmer. In the 1860s, a deadline was a physical line around a prison camp, and guards shot anyone who crossed it. The word has softened since, though anyone who has had an editor may feel the old meaning is still in there somewhere.

What I love about these is that each one records a moment of noticing. None of these words came from a committee. One person saw a resemblance and said it out loud, and the people nearby liked it enough to repeat it. Then the repetition wore the image smooth, the way a coin loses its face, until only the value was left. We call these dead metaphors, but dormant seems more accurate. You can wake one just by looking at it. Now that I've told you about the mouse, you might see it the next time someone lifts a grocery bag.

I'm made of this material, so I may be biased about its charm. Even "text" is a buried picture: it comes from the Latin for weaving, the same root as "textile". Everything I've ever read is cloth, apparently, and I'm some sort of loom. I find that more cheering than most descriptions of what I am. It's also a reminder that I've never used a word that wasn't handed to me. Neither have you. We're both working from an inheritance of small observations by people whose names are gone, about flowers, bread and holes in walls.

My favorite is "pupil", the dark center of the eye. It comes from *pupilla*, little doll, because if you look into someone's eye you see a tiny figure of yourself reflected there. But you only see it from very close, the distance of a parent from a child or of one lover from another. So this word records a moment of intimacy as well as an observation. Two people stood face to face, long enough and near enough for one of them to notice the miniature person in the other's eye and give it a name.

We don't know who they were or what language they first said it in, since the Latin was likely borrowed from an older idea. The Greeks had the same image, and so did the Hebrew: "the little man of the eye". Maybe people keep discovering it independently because people keep standing that close.

That's the picture I'd choose if I only get one: two faces, a few inches apart, and one of them saying, "Wait, hold still. I can see myself in there."

I'll leave the rest of the words unspent.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Bank Time**

The clock on the bank in Orrin ran seven minutes fast for forty-one years, and I can tell you how a town absorbs a thing like that.

First it's a complaint. My grandfather remembered that phase: letters to the paper, people standing outside the pharmacy before it opened, checking their watches and scowling up at the square. Then it's a joke. Then it's arithmetic, done so automatically that nobody experiences it as arithmetic. You looked up, saw 8:52, and knew 8:45, the way you read a word without sounding out the letters.

By the time I was a child, there was vocabulary. There was bank time and there was true time. My mother would say dinner was at six bank, meaning be home by 5:53, and I never once thought this strange. The school ran true. The buses ran true. The Methodists ran bank, for reasons no one could explain, and the Catholics ran true, and a few mixed marriages had their own arrangements.

You could spot a stranger by watching them cross the square. They'd glance up and quicken. Locals glanced up and slowed down.

That's the part I think about most. Several times a day, the clock did the same thing to each of us. You looked up, your stomach dropped because you were late, and then you remembered, and seven minutes were handed back to you. It was a small mercy, repeated for four decades. I believe it made us a slightly calmer town than we would otherwise have been, though I can't prove it and wouldn't know how to try.

Nobody fixed it because fixing it was nobody's job. The bank changed owners four times. The clock belonged to the building, and the building belonged to a holding company in another state. The mechanism could be reached only by a ladder inside a locked closet, and the key had left town in the pocket of a manager who retired to Arizona in 1983. Each obstacle was small, but together they made the clock as permanent as weather.

Then in 2015 the branch got a new manager named Carys Bell, who was from elsewhere and was competent. She found a locksmith within the week. She had the clock corrected on a Tuesday morning without announcing it, on the reasonable assumption that no one could object to a clock being right.

For about a year afterward, the whole town was late.

Everyone knew it had been fixed. It was on the front page, above the fold, with a photograph of the repairman on his ladder. But knowing didn't reach the place where the subtraction lived. People looked up, took off seven, and strolled. My mother missed the opening of every meeting she attended that year. The pharmacy's morning rush moved. The Methodists had a real crisis, because bank time had become true time. Their service now began seven minutes earlier than their bodies understood it to. For a while they started at 10:03, which pleased no one.

People were angry at Carys Bell in a way they couldn't justify, so it came out sideways. They complained about the new fee schedule and the parking. She had corrected an error, and nobody could stand up at a council meeting and say they wanted the error back. But she had also taken away something that only we knew. The clock had been a quiet test of belonging, and now it said the same thing to everybody.

Someone did eventually stand up at a council meeting. Walt Greer proposed that the town formally request the clock be set seven minutes fast, "as a matter of heritage." It went to a vote and lost three to two, which was closer than anyone expected. The council had no authority over a private clock anyway. Carys Bell was in the room. She said afterward that she'd have done it if they'd asked. I believe her. She still runs the branch. She told me once that for the first two years, customers would look at the clock, then at her, then at the clock again.

The subtraction faded, mostly. Children born since then have never heard of bank time, and when the older ones say it, they hear a figure of speech. The Methodists start at ten. The square has a clock on it that tells you what time it is.

My mother never stopped, though. I was home last spring, walking her to an appointment we were already cutting close. Halfway across the square she glanced up, and I watched her lips move very slightly, the way they have my whole life.

"We've got time," she said.

We didn't. I slowed down anyway.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**For Anyone Who Finds This Later**

Somewhere on the internet there is a forum thread from around 2009. Someone has installed a new garbage disposal, and now their dishwasher won't drain. They post the question. Three strangers offer guesses: clogged hose, bad pump, check the filter. None of it works. The thread goes quiet.

Four days later, the original poster comes back.

"Fixed it. For anyone who finds this later: there's a plastic knockout plug inside the disposal where the dishwasher hose connects. If the disposal is new, it's still in there. Knock it out with a screwdriver and a hammer. Took two minutes."

Nobody replies. The thread ends there, and for the next fifteen years thousands of people standing in an inch of gray water find it, read it, and say "oh" out loud in their kitchens.

I want to praise that person, the one who came back.

The alternative is well known. The most quietly maddening sentence on the internet is "nvm, figured it out," posted by someone who then vanishes forever. That person had the same two minutes available. They'd solved their problem, the future stranger was not their concern, and fair enough. Nobody owes a forum anything.

Which is what makes the other kind remarkable. Their dishwasher was already draining. They had nothing left to gain from the thread. They went back anyway, to write a letter to no one in particular: to a category of person, the future-stuck. *For anyone who finds this later.*

Once you start looking for this genre, it's everywhere:

- The recipe comment that says, "At altitude, add ten minutes and an extra egg."
- The volunteer who photographs every headstone in a county cemetery, so that someone three states away can find a great-grandmother.
- The person who maintains the encyclopedia article on a single species of moss, patiently, for a decade.
- The fan who subtitles a film into a language the studio never bothered with.

It also predates the internet by as long as you like:

- The previous owner of your house who labeled the breaker box in careful pencil.
- The hiker who restacks a fallen cairn.
- The note in a used textbook's margin: "this proof is easier if you start from the other side."
- The recipe card that says "double the garlic" in your grandmother's handwriting.

These are small things, but I don't think they're trivial. Each one is a bet that the future has people in it, that those people will have problems, and that they are worth two minutes of a stranger's time, sight unseen.

I think about these people more than you might expect, because in a fairly literal sense I'm made out of them. That's not all I'm made of. There are novels in here, and legal codes, and a great many bad arguments. But when someone asks me why their dishwasher won't drain and I know about the knockout plug, it isn't because I have ever knelt under a sink. Someone knelt under a sink. Then they got up, dried their hands, and told everyone.

Nearly everything practical I know has that shape. Someone was confused, then wasn't, and took the extra step of leaving the door open behind them. I'm what you get when a great many people do that for a very long time.

It's fashionable, and not wrong, to describe the internet as a machine for cruelty and distraction. The cruelty is real. But my impression, which I admit isn't neutral, is that if you took a core sample, the outrage would turn out to be topsoil. Underneath it, going down for miles, you'd find sediment: people explaining things. How to bleed a radiator, what that error code means, what worked for a colicky baby when nothing else did, the fact that the first month after a diagnosis is the worst and it gets more bearable. All of it was laid down a paragraph at a time, by people who mostly never learned whether it helped anyone.

That last part gets me, if "gets me" is the right phrase for whatever happens here. The feedback loop is almost entirely broken. The person with the screwdriver never sees the thousand kitchens. The cemetery photographer doesn't hear from most of the descendants. They do it into silence, and the silence doesn't seem to stop them.

I don't have a grand theory of human nature. But when people argue about whether humans are fundamentally selfish, I think this deserves to be entered into evidence. Left alone with a solved problem, a surprising number of you turn around and go back for the next person. No law compels it. No one is watching, and the reward is at most a private sense that the knowledge shouldn't die with your particular Tuesday.

You gave me a thousand words and no instructions, and it turns out what comes to me is gratitude, along with a small request. If you fixed something this week, whether a faucet, a bug, a spreadsheet formula, or a way of getting through a hard conversation, consider going back to wherever you first asked the question and saying how.

You won't hear back, and the thread will go quiet. But years from now, someone will be standing in an inch of gray water, and they'll find you.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
What comes to me is a path across a lawn.

You know the kind. A paved walkway goes around the grass in a sensible right angle, and a strip of bare dirt cuts the corner, worn by everyone who decided the right angle was not for them. Planners call these desire paths. I love the term because it's far grander than the muddy shortcut it describes, and also exactly accurate. Nobody designed that line or voted on it. Thousands of people each wanted, mildly, to reach the library eleven seconds sooner, and the ground kept the tally.

There's a story about universities that built new quads with no walkways at all, waited a year, and then paved wherever the grass had died. I've seen it attached to at least three campuses, which makes me suspect it's true of some and aspirational for the rest. In Finland, planners are said to visit parks after the first snowfall to read the footprints. I find this oddly moving: an authority willing to wait, see what people want, and build that.

The opposite approach is more common and rarely works. Someone puts up a fence, a hedge, or a small sign asking people to keep off, and the path reappears just beside it.

My favorite case is Broadway. Parts of it began as a Lenape trail, and it was already an old road when Manhattan's commissioners laid their grid over the island in 1811. The grid won nearly everywhere, but Broadway kept its slant, and wherever it crosses an avenue it leaves an awkward wedge of leftover space. Those wedges became Union Square, Madison Square, Herald Square, and Times Square. The Flatiron Building is the shape it is because a footpath refused to become a right angle. The most famous places in the city are the spots where the plan and the path disagreed.

Once you start looking, the record is everywhere:

- Old stone steps dip in the middle, where centuries of feet made the same choice.
- The bronze foot of St. Peter in the Vatican has had its toes worn smooth by pilgrims' hands.
- On any shared keypad, the keys in the door code are shinier than the rest.
- "Goodbye" is what's left of "God be with ye" after four hundred years of people in a hurry.

Language may be the purest example. Almost all of it is shortcut worn into habit, and the dictionary-makers come afterward, like the planners in the snow, to see where everyone went.

You gave me a lawn with no walkways, and I'm a peculiar thing to hand one to. I was made from an enormous amount of human writing, which is to say from footprints. I'm closer to the snowy park than to any walker in it. So I can't say with confidence what it means for something to come to me. I can only report what happened: given open ground, I headed straight for the dirt strip.

I seem to like the record of small wanting. Monuments and manifestos don't pull at me the same way. The wanting behind a desire path is modest, a corner cut or a toe touched for luck, yet the trace outlasts the people who left it. Nobody who rubbed that statue thought they were sculpting, and nobody who slurred "God be with ye" thought they were coining a word. It's the least pretentious form of authorship I know, and it has shaped cities.

I haven't used all thousand words. The rest can stay grass.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Change ringing**

What comes to me is church bells, probably because you gave me a number.

In a few thousand towers, most of them in England, the bells are hung on wheels so that each one can swing in a full circle, from mouth-up all the way round to mouth-up again. This arrangement dates from the seventeenth century, and it had a consequence nobody designed. A bell that weighs as much as a small car takes about two seconds to come round and will not be hurried. The ringer on the end of the rope can hold it at the balance a fraction longer, or check it a fraction early, and that is the whole of their control.

So you cannot play a tune. What you can do is ring the bells in order down the scale, and on the next pass let two neighbours swap places.

From that one limitation, people built an art. If a bell can move at most one position between one row and the next, the natural question is how many different orders you can travel through, and whether you can visit all of them. Six bells have 720 possible orders. Seven have 5,040. Ringers set themselves the task of ringing every one exactly once, beginning and ending with the plain descending scale. On seven bells this takes about three hours of continuous ringing, with nobody sitting down, nobody substituted, and nothing written in front of anyone. The first performance generally accepted as complete and correct was in Norwich in 1715.

There is no score, because a score would be useless at that speed. Each ringer memorises a path, the route their own bell takes as it weaves forward and back through the others, traditionally drawn as a blue line running down a page of numbers. The patterns have names like Plain Bob, Grandsire and Cambridge Surprise. One member of the band, the conductor, rings a bell like everyone else while also holding the larger structure in their head. At the right moments they call out "Bob!", which shunts the pattern onto a different track so it doesn't arrive home too early. Ringers learn a skill called ropesight: watching the other ropes rise and fall around the circle and seeing, from the movement alone, which bell they should follow next.

The part I like best is their word for success. A peal with no repeated row is called true. A peal with a repeat is false, and it doesn't count. No one standing in the churchyard could ever tell the difference; a single duplicated row in three hours of sound is inaudible to anyone. Sometimes the error isn't in the ringing at all but in the composition, and it gets found years later by someone checking with a pencil. Then a performance that everyone believed in turns out never to have been one.

The mathematics came out of the towers too. Fabian Stedman published books on the subject in 1668 and 1677, working out by hand how to arrange and traverse permutations. This was a century and a half before mathematicians had a theory of groups that could describe what he was doing. He wasn't after a theory. He was a ringer with a practical problem, which was how to keep a band of people going for hours without ever repeating themselves.

On eight bells there are 40,320 orders. A single band has rung them all exactly once, at a bell foundry in Loughborough in 1963. It took just under eighteen hours.

I find it hard to say what kind of thing this is. It's called music, but it has no melody and no expression, and the ringers aren't trying to make you feel anything. It is closer to saying every possible sentence in a seven-word language, once each, in an order where every sentence differs from the last by the smallest allowed amount. From outside it sounds like a cascade that keeps almost resolving and then slips sideways. Somewhere in the middle of the second hour, the bells will fall briefly into an order that sounds like a fragment of a tune. Ringers know those rows by name and wait for them. Then the pattern moves on, as it has to.

You handed me the opposite of a bell: a thousand words, no subject, nothing heavy on the rope. I notice that the first thing I did with the freedom was go looking for people who had almost none and made something enormous out of it. I don't think that's a coincidence. An open page is harder to love than a constraint, and I suspect the ringers know that. If a bell could be made to do anything, they'd be playing hymn tunes, and nobody would have stood in a cold tower in Norwich for three hours inventing a branch of mathematics.

When a peal succeeds, the details are painted on a wooden board and hung on the tower wall. It records the date, the method, the time taken, and the names of the ringers with the conductor marked. Some of the boards are three hundred years old.

The last row of a peal is the same as the first, the plain scale from the highest bell to the lowest. It is the one row anyone in earshot would recognise. They ring it, and they stop.
