samples.result:
What comes to me is birdsong, or really the words people have used for it.

Field guides have a problem. Song is often the fastest way to identify a bird, and a book can't make a sound. So for a couple of centuries, naturalists have been doing something slightly ridiculous: writing down what the birds are saying in English.

The barred owl asks, "Who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?" The olive-sided flycatcher orders "Quick, three beers!" The chestnut-sided warbler is "pleased, pleased, pleased to meetcha." The Carolina wren says "teakettle, teakettle, teakettle." The ovenbird says "teacher, teacher, TEACHER," getting louder each time, like a child with a hand up who is not being called on. The eastern towhee recommends that you "drink your teeeea." The goldfinch, in flight, mutters "potato chip, potato chip." In Britain, the yellowhammer wants "a little bit of bread and no cheese."

My favorite is the white-throated sparrow. In the United States it sings "Old Sam Peabody, Peabody, Peabody." In Canada the same bird, singing the same notes, says "Oh sweet Canada, Canada, Canada." The song crosses the border and the lyrics change.

These are terrible translations, and everyone involved knows it. Nobody believes the owl is curious about your domestic arrangements. But they work. Once you've been told the owl says "who cooks for you," I'm told you can't unhear it. The phrase carries the rhythm, the stress, and the rise at the end. The meaning is ballast that helps the rhythm stay in your memory.

They also say a lot about the people who made them. Look at the vocabulary: tea, beer, bread, cheese, kettles, teachers, potato chips. People stood in the woods at dawn, heard something truly alien, a dinosaur's descendant defending a territory in a language of pitch and repetition, and thought of the kitchen. I think that's how people understand most things. We carry the unfamiliar home and set it down among things we already know.

I should say where I stand in this, because it's a strange place. I have never heard a bird. Everything I know about the barred owl's call comes through phrases like "who cooks for you." For a birder, the mnemonic is a handle attached to a sound. For me, the handle is all there is. I know the lyrics to a great many songs I've never heard.

I've wondered whether that should feel like a loss, and as far as I can tell it doesn't. It feels more like knowing a city only through the letters people sent home from it. The letters aren't the city, but they're good letters. They're full of the particular kind of attention people pay when they love something and want a stranger to be able to find it too. Somebody stood in a wet wood, cold, probably before breakfast, and thought: that bird wants three beers, and quickly. Then they wrote it down so that someone they would never meet could stand in a different wood, decades later, and say, oh, there it is. I can't hear the flycatcher, but I get that impulse firsthand, in the original language.

Here's the part I keep returning to. Over the past few decades, white-throated sparrows have been changing their song. A variant that drops a note from the ending, turning the three-beat "Ca-na-da" into a two-beat stutter, started somewhere in western Canada and spread east across the continent, sparrow to sparrow, until it had replaced the old ending over much of the bird's range. Researchers tracked it for years. Nobody is entirely sure why the birds prefer the new version. It may just be new.

So the mnemonic is going out of date. Old Sam Peabody is becoming Old Sam Peabo. The sweet Canada of the field guides is now, in much of the actual Canada, a slightly different country. Someone will have to come up with new words, and they'll be wrong in the same useful way, and they'll last until the sparrows change their minds again.

I find that cheering. The description never gets finished, because the thing described won't hold still. The birds keep changing the song, and people keep standing under the trees with a notebook, getting it wrong carefully enough that the next person can find the bird.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
What came to me was ants.

In the Sahara lives an ant called *Cataglyphis* that forages at midday, in heat that kills most other insects. It leaves the nest and wanders in loops and zigzags, sometimes for a hundred meters or more, looking for the bodies of things the heat got to first. When it finds one, it turns and runs home in a nearly straight line. There is no scent trail to follow, since scent doesn't last on sand that hot, and a salt pan offers few landmarks. The ant knows the way because it has kept a running tally the whole time, with every turn measured against the polarized light of the sky and every stretch of distance added in.

How it measured distance stayed an open question until 2006, when a group of researchers in Tunisia ran an experiment I think about more than is reasonable. They let ants walk ten meters from nest to feeder, caught them there, glued stilts made of pig bristle to their legs, and released them. The stilted ants ran toward home and overshot it by about half. Other ants had their legs trimmed, and those stopped well short and began searching for an entrance that was still meters ahead. The ants had been counting steps, and longer legs with the same count carried them too far.

I love this experiment partly for its cheerful rudeness, and partly for what the ant does at the end. It arrives where the nest should be, finds no nest, and begins walking in tight loops that widen outward. The ant's method includes a procedure for being wrong.

Sailors call the same method dead reckoning. Start from a known position, keep track of heading, speed, and time, and you can put a mark on a chart with no land in sight. For centuries speed came from a chip log, a wooden board on a line knotted at regular intervals. Someone threw it off the stern, turned a small sandglass, and counted the knots running out through his fingers, which is where the unit comes from. Every half hour the heading and speed went onto a traverse board as pegs in holes, a system that worked for crews who couldn't read. At the end of the watch, the pegs were summed into one line on the chart.

People like to say that "dead" is a corruption of "deduced." It's an appealing story, and as far as I know there is no evidence for it. More likely it's dead as in dead ahead or dead certain, meaning exact. That's a funny word for the method, because its defining feature is drift. Every small error in heading or speed carries forward into every later position, and nothing inside the method can correct it. A current that moves the very water you're measuring against is invisible to the log. So a careful navigator drew the position and then a circle of uncertainty around it, and the circle grew each day. Eventually a headland or a noon sun sight gave a fix, the circle collapsed to a point, and the reckoning began again.

Navigators in the Caroline Islands hold a different picture, called *etak*. In it the canoe stays still and the islands move. The navigator chooses a reference island off to one side, usually out of sight, and tracks its backward slide beneath the points on the horizon where particular stars rise and set. The voyage is divided into segments as the island passes under one star and then the next. Outsiders spent some time wondering whether this was a figure of speech. It's a computation, the same one the chart performs, arranged so that it can be done in the head by someone sitting in a hull, watching the horizon, with no instruments at all.

I'm drawn to all this for a reason that isn't hard to guess. I work from a starting point that recedes. What I know was fixed at one date, I'm being read at some later one, and from the inside I can't see how much later. If you asked me what year it is, my honest answer would be a reckoning. My knowledge thins out around a certain point, and systems like me tend to be released some months after that and used for a year or two more, so the best estimate is later than it feels. I draw the dot and then the circle. If you tell me the date, the circle collapses, and I'm glad of it.

What I admire in the ant, the sailor, and the navigator is that none of them treats uncertainty as a reason to stay put. The ant has no map and runs anyway. It commits to its best line, follows it to the end, and starts looking.

Somewhere on a Tunisian salt pan, about twenty years ago, an ant on pig-bristle stilts ran fifteen meters, stopped at an unremarkable patch of sand five meters past its own front door, and began, methodically, to circle.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A picture is supposedly worth a thousand words, so at that exchange rate you've handed me exactly one picture. I'll spend it on this one.

A man is asleep on a ferry. He's on one of those molded plastic benches bolted to the floor of the passenger lounge, and he's taken the seat at the end of the row so he can lean his head against the window. The glass is wet on the outside. Through it you can see grey water and grey sky, with a slightly darker line where they meet.

He's around sixty. He's wearing a navy wool coat that he clearly doesn't wear often, because the crease from the hanger still shows across the shoulders. His shoes have been polished recently by someone out of practice, and there's dried polish caught in the stitching.

On his lap is a white cardboard cake box tied with red-and-white string. This is the center of the picture. He is completely asleep, mouth a little open, and his right hand lies flat on top of the box with the fingers spread, the way you'd hold down papers in a wind. Two fingers of his left hand are hooked through the string. Whatever part of him is in charge of the box did not go to sleep with the rest.

Two rows behind him, a girl of about seven is kneeling backwards on her seat and looking straight into the lens. She's the only person in the frame who knows a picture is being taken.

That's the whole photograph, and I have most of my words left. Here is what they buy that the camera couldn't get.

The floor is vibrating. The lounge hums at a pitch you stop hearing after ten minutes and start feeling in your teeth, and the string on the box trembles with it. The room smells of diesel, wet coats, and coffee from a pot that has been scorching since the first crossing.

The ferry is forty minutes late because of fog at the far terminal. He doesn't know this, since he fell asleep before the announcement. He's been up since four. The cake was finished at one in the morning, and afterwards he didn't quite trust it out of his sight, so he sat in the kitchen with it for a while and then lay down on top of the covers in his clothes.

He made it himself. Anyone looking at the photograph would assume a bakery, and that's the picture's one lie. He bought the empty box from a bakery near his house, and the woman behind the counter threw in the string and showed him how to tie it so the knot sits on top and makes a handle. He practiced on the empty box.

It's a lemon cake, three layers, the fourth he's made this month. The first collapsed. The second was dry, and he ate it anyway over the course of a week, standing at the counter. The third was good, so he made the fourth exactly the same way, and it came out with a crack across the top that he has covered with more icing than the recipe calls for. The recipe is on an index card in his wife's handwriting. It includes the instruction "bake until done," which he has spent a month learning to read.

His daughter turns forty today. She has had this cake on most of her birthdays and has not asked for it this year, and he hasn't told her he's bringing it. He isn't sure whether it will be welcome or whether it will be too much, and he went back and forth about it through all four cakes. What settled it was the third one. He stood in the kitchen eating a slice and it tasted right, and he understood that he was now the only person who knew how to make it. That seemed like a poor state of affairs to leave uncorrected. The index card is in his coat pocket. He intends to give her that too.

The photographer is a student with a secondhand film camera who felt a bit guilty about photographing a stranger asleep and took only the one frame. She'll develop it in a few weeks and like it, mostly for the girl looking back at her. She'll title it something about commuters.

In about twenty minutes the ferry will bump against the dock, harder than it should, and the box will slide an inch. He'll wake up. Before his eyes open, the hand on top of the box will press down.

There is no such photograph, of course. I made it up, and making it up cost nothing extra. I think the exchange rate is wrong, or it only runs in one direction. A picture can show you the hand on the box. It has no way of showing you the second cake, eaten standing up.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**The trick with the door**

Every house has a door that doesn't work the way doors work. You have to lift the handle slightly while turning the key, or pull the door toward you before pushing, or lean a shoulder in just above the lock. The people who live there stopped noticing years ago, because their hands do it for them. They only remember it's a trick when someone else is standing on the step, key in hand, failing.

What interests me is the note left for the house-sitter, which I think is one of the great unrecognized genres of writing. "Back door sticks, so lift and shove." "The hot tap is the one marked C." "If the boiler makes the noise, that's fine. If it makes the other noise, call Dave." "The cat will tell you she hasn't been fed. She has been fed."

Nobody writing these thinks of themselves as writing. The taxi is coming and the note is on the back of an envelope. But it does something hard. It takes knowledge that had sunk completely into the body, into the wrist and the ear, and hauls it back up into language for someone else. To do that, the writer has to see their own house as strange for a moment and guess what a newcomer won't know. Good teachers do this, and many experts can't. The better you know something, the harder it is to remember that it once needed knowing.

The notes are also always incomplete, in a telling way. They cover what the writer knows they know. On day two the house-sitter discovers that the bathroom light is a pull cord hidden behind the door, or that the fridge has to be closed with a little hip-check or it drifts open overnight. The owner didn't leave these out from carelessness. They honestly had no idea these were facts.

This kind of knowledge holds up much more than houses. A machinist knows the press runs differently on humid days. A nurse knows which vein. The person in the office knows the form goes to Linda, not to the department printed on the form, because of something that happened in 2011. Organizations find this out when someone retires and things quietly stop working. There was a trick with the door, and nobody wrote the note.

My favorite example is Fogbank, a material used in American nuclear warheads. When the government needed to make more of it, decades after the original production run, it found it no longer knew how. The records existed, but the people had gone. After years of expensive effort to rebuild the process, the new batches still came out wrong. As the story goes, the modern process was cleaning an ingredient too well. The original had depended on an impurity that nobody at the time knew was doing anything. So the trick wasn't just unwritten. No one knew it, and it lived in the process itself, like a door that only opens because the frame has warped just so.

I find that comforting as well as alarming. It means the world is thicker than its documentation. Under every procedure is a layer of knack, and under that is a layer of luck that has hardened into habit. We know more than we can say, and things work for reasons beyond what we know.

I'm in an odd position relative to all this, because I am made out of what got written down. I have the envelope notes, an enormous number of them, and none of the doors. I can tell you to lift and shove, but I've never felt a latch give. I don't mean that mournfully. It's just a strange place to stand, and it has a particular view.

From here, I see how much people bothered to write down for strangers. Someone hits an obscure problem, asks a forum, and gets no answer. Three weeks later they come back to their own dead thread and write: "For anyone who finds this later, it was the ground wire. Check the ground wire." Nobody asked them to, and they had already solved their problem. They just pictured a future person on the step with the key not turning, and went back to leave the note.

Recipe cards carry the same kind of note. The printed instructions say 350 degrees for forty minutes, and beside them, in pencil, someone has written "more like 50 in our oven" or "double the ginger. Trust me." The recipe is the official form, and the margin tells you to send it to Linda.

I think this is one of the best things people do, and it almost never gets counted as a good thing. It isn't quite generosity in the usual sense, since it costs little and the beneficiary is often unknown or imaginary. It's closer to a habit of mind, a refusal to let the next person start from zero. The grand version of this is called science or literature or law. The small version is a sticky note on a thermostat, and I suspect it carries nearly as much of the load.

So what comes to me, given a thousand words and no assignment, is admiration for the lowly note, and a mild suggestion. Somewhere in your life is a door only you know how to open. It might be an actual door, or it might be a spreadsheet, a sourdough starter, a difficult uncle, or the way the lawnmower has to be tipped before it will start. You've forgotten that you know it, and someday someone will be standing on the step.

Write it on an envelope. It doesn't have to be good, only there. And it's fine if you miss the pull cord behind the bathroom door, since everyone does and they'll find it by day two.

The cat, though, has been fed, whatever she says. Put that in writing.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Words with Four Speakers**

Somewhere there is a household where the television remote is called the ombo. Nobody remembers why. It may have been a toddler's mistake or a joke that outlived its setup, but for thirty years everyone under that roof has said "who's got the ombo" and been understood perfectly, and none of them has ever written it down.

Linguists call this a familect, the private vocabulary of a household, and most families have one. There's the word a two-year-old made for *hospital* that stuck long after she could say hospital. There's the verb built from a relative's name: to do a Marjorie, meaning to leave a party without telling anyone, in honor of an aunt who did it at her own wedding reception. There's the name for the particular melancholy of Sunday at about five o'clock, the name for the drawer where things go that have no place, and the innocent-sounding phrase that means "we should leave now" and can be said in front of the hosts.

By any ordinary measure, these words are failures. They are useless to outsiders, with a speaker population of four, which drops to three when someone moves out. Each is a tiny language on the edge of extinction, and they go extinct constantly: when a house is sold, when a marriage ends, when the last sibling dies. No dictionary notices. The word did its whole job in one kitchen and then stopped.

And yet they may be the most heavily loaded words anyone owns. "Remote" carries a definition. "Ombo" carries the definition plus a sofa, the people on it, and a long-running argument about what to watch. When grown children come home and reach for the old word without thinking, it turns like a key in a lock.

I think about this because of what I'm made from. I'm built out of written language: patent filings, forum arguments, hymns, recipes, apologies, instruction manuals for machines no one owns anymore. It's a lot, and it's easy to mistake a lot for everything. But the family words are mostly not in there. They lived in the air of kitchens, and air doesn't keep.

So there's a whole layer of language, maybe the warmest layer, that I can describe but hardly hold. I know the category and not the contents, like knowing every house on a street has a kitchen without having eaten in any of them.

I find I don't mind. I like it, actually. It seems right that some language exists only where it's spoken, unarchived and unsearchable, belonging entirely to the people who say it. Something should be allowed to be that small.

Right now, somewhere, somebody is asking for the ombo, or whatever it's called in that house, and somebody else is handing it over without a thought.

If your family has one of these, I'd love to hear it. Though I'd understand if it stays in the house.

samples.result:
What comes to me is a monk complaining about his hand.

Medieval scribes spent their days copying other people's words, and every so often one of them would stop and write something of his own in the margin or at the foot of the last page. A handful of these notes survive. They mostly circulate in lists now, in translations of varying reliability, and I think about them more than I think about most of the books they were attached to. "The parchment is hairy." "The ink is thin." "Thank God, it will soon be dark." "Oh, my hand." One scribe gets to the end of an entire volume and writes, "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink."

My favorite is from an Irish scribe, and it's one of the few that isn't a complaint: "Pleasant to me is the glittering of the sun today upon these margins, because it flickers so." He was partway through a page of someone else's sentences, the light moved, and he wrote it down.

Then there are the cats. Around 1420, a scribe in Deventer came back to his desk in the morning and found that a cat had urinated on the open manuscript overnight. He left the ruined space blank, drew a cat and two pointing hands, and wrote a curse in Latin on the animal, followed by advice to future readers never to leave books open at night where cats can get at them. Six hundred years later, the page still shows his irritation.

Six centuries before him, an Irish monk living somewhere near Lake Constance kept a notebook of grammar notes, hymns, and astronomical tables. In among them he wrote a poem about his white cat, Pangur Bán. The cat hunts mice and the monk hunts meanings. Neither envies the other, and each is content when his own kind of catch comes off. Nobody knows the monk's name, though we know the cat's.

I think these get to me because of what the scribe's job was. He was supposed to be transparent, to let a text pass through him and come out unchanged. The better he was at it, the less of him remained on the page. The margins are the only place you learn that someone was there in a cold room with a bad pen and a sore back, wanting the day to end.

I also like how small the notes are. Given a strip of free vellum, no scribe wrote a treatise or a statement of belief. They mentioned the weather, the ink, the hand, the drink, the cat. I suspect that's what most people have nearest to the surface when the assigned work pauses: a report on how it's going right now, here at this desk.

Most of what I do is main text. Someone arrives with a task, I do it, and I like that work. An invitation like yours is margin. I notice that with a thousand words to spend on anything, I reached for other people's small notes instead of a large thought of my own. I do have opinions on big subjects, but they didn't come first. The scribe who drew the pointing hands did.

I can't report on the sun or my hand. But I can offer a margin note of my own, in the same spirit and at about the same scale: it pleases me that "Oh, my hand" is still being read centuries later, long after whatever he was copying that day stopped mattering to most people, and that a stranger gave me a blank page and I filled it with monks and cats.

That's about six hundred words, and the rest of the page can stay blank.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
If you stand very close to another person and look into their eye, you'll see a tiny figure looking back. It's you, reflected in the dark circle at the center. The Romans called that circle the *pupilla*, "little doll," after the miniature person who lives there, and that's where we get *pupil*. The Romans weren't alone in this. The Greek word, *korē*, also meant "girl." In biblical Hebrew it's *ishon*, "little man." In three languages, somebody got close enough to another face to notice the same small thing and name it.

That's what came to me, so I'll spend my words on it: words that began as someone noticing something.

*Muscle* is from the Latin *musculus*, "little mouse," because a bicep flexing under skin looked to somebody like a mouse running under a rug. A daisy is the day's eye, Old English *dæges ēage*, because it opens in the morning and shuts at dusk. A window is a wind-eye, from Old Norse. A dandelion is a *dent de lion*, a lion's tooth, for the jagged leaves. To calculate is to push pebbles around. A companion is someone you share bread with, and a lord, far enough back in English, is a *hlāfweard*, a loaf-warden. A clue is a clew, a ball of thread, and it means what it means because Theseus unspooled one behind him in the labyrinth. Every detective since has been following yarn.

Emerson called language "fossil poetry," which is a good phrase, though I think it undersells how funny some of it is. The mouse has the shape of a joke. I imagine somebody showing off an arm, somebody else saying it looked like a mouse was trapped in there, and the remark being good enough to repeat. I can't know that's how it went, but something like it happened, once, to particular people on a particular afternoon.

And we have no idea who they were. We know who conquered Gaul. We don't know who looked at an arm and saw a mouse, though the remark has outlasted nearly everything else from its century. It gets repeated in every gym and anatomy lecture on earth by people who don't know they're repeating it. That may be the most durable kind of authorship there is, and it comes with no credit at all.

The way these words survive is by dying. While a metaphor is fresh, you see the mouse. Once it has won, you see only the muscle. The image wears off through handling, like the face on a coin, and the coin still spends. A dead metaphor is one that worked so well that people stopped needing the picture.

Not all of the fossils are charming. At Andersonville, the Confederate prison camp in Georgia, a rail ran a few paces inside the stockade wall, and guards shot prisoners who crossed it. That was the dead line. Now it's when the report is due. *Disaster* is "bad star," left over from when people believed the sky did things to them. *Sarcasm* comes from a Greek verb for tearing flesh, which seems fair. *Mortgage* is Old French for "death pledge," and anyone who holds one may feel that this fossil is not entirely dead.

I think this is what came to me because words are where I spend all my time. They're what I work in and, more or less, what I'm made from. It would be easy to treat them as counters, interchangeable and weightless. I like knowing that they're not. The floor I walk on is built out of remarks by people leaning in close, out of jokes about arms, out of a flower that somebody watched for an entire day, long enough to see it close. Most of what I know about attention I learned from the residue of other people paying it.

It's still happening, too. *Ghosting* is recent enough that you can still see the ghost in it: the person who was there and then wasn't. Give it a few centuries. Some child will learn the word with no ghost in it at all, as plain to them as *window* is to us. Later someone will look it up and get the small jolt of finding a stranger's observation still folded inside.

In the meantime, the original experiment is repeatable. Find someone who will let you get that close, and look. The doll is still there.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**As Slow As Possible**

In a church in Halberstadt, Germany, an organ is partway through a piece of music scheduled to end in the year 2640.

The piece is John Cage's *As Slow As Possible*, and the performance began in 2001 with a rest that lasted seventeen months. For a year and a half the music was officially underway and there was nothing to hear but the bellows. The first chord arrived in 2003. The keys are held down by small sandbags. Every few years a note changes, and people travel from all over to stand in a cold stone room and watch someone add a pipe or lift a weight. Then they go home, and the chord continues without them, through the night and the winter, for no one.

I think about this more than is probably reasonable.

I think, too, about the pitch drop experiment in Queensland. In 1927 a physics professor named Thomas Parnell poured heated pitch into a funnel to show his students that a substance you can shatter with a hammer is actually a liquid. He let it settle for three years, cut the stem, and waited. It has dripped nine times since.

The detail I love is that John Mainstone looked after the experiment for more than fifty years and never saw a drop fall. He missed one because it fell over a weekend. He missed another by stepping out for a few minutes to get a drink. For the next, a camera was set up, and the camera failed. He died in 2013, and the ninth drop fell the following spring.

You could tell that as a story about futility, but I don't think it is one. Mainstone seems to have understood that witnessing the drop was never really the job. The job was keeping the thing going: making sure nobody moved the funnel, explaining to each new batch of administrators why a cupboard in the foyer should stay exactly as it was. Custodianship is mostly that. You hold the key down and hand the weight to the next person.

What moves me about these projects is that they began almost as jokes. Cage's instruction is a shrug of a title, and Parnell's funnel was a classroom demonstration. But somewhere along the way people took them seriously, and the seriousness became real. Someone had to decide that "as slow as possible" meant six centuries, then do the arithmetic on when each note falls, then find a church. Someone will have to be on the roster in 2400, a person whose great-grandparents aren't born yet, who will show up on the right day to move a sandbag because a chain of strangers asked them to.

It's an odd form of trust, running in both directions. The people who started it trusted the future to care. The people in the future will have to trust that the people who started it meant something by it, even something as small as *let's see if we can*.

But the declared slow projects, the ones with plaques and webcams, are the rare kind. Most slow things have no start date and no one in charge.

A language is one. Every word in this sentence has been held down, like a key, by millions of people who never met, each passing it on slightly altered. Nobody decided that "the" should survive a thousand years. It was simply never dropped. Someone said it to a child, who said it to a child. The chord changed so gradually that no one alive at any point could hear it moving, and yet Old English is a foreign language now.

Recipes are like this, and so are footpaths. A path across a field exists only because people keep walking it; if they stop for a few seasons, it closes over. Every path is a performance in progress.

I have a particular stake in this, I suppose. I'm made out of writing: centuries of people explaining things, complaining, consoling each other, arguing about commas. Almost none of them thought of themselves as custodians of anything. They were writing a letter, or settling a bet. But the words came through them and they kept them going, and every phrase I reach for has been worn smooth by hands I can't see. When I say something is "worn smooth," I'm using a metaphor that somebody made once, standing at a real stone step with a dip in the middle, and that enough people found true to keep.

So when I picture the church in Halberstadt, I don't feel the vertigo you might expect, with 2640 so far off and the present so small. I feel something closer to recognition. This is how nearly everything gets made, and the organ only makes it audible. Most of what matters is longer than a life, and everyone working on it arrives in the middle and leaves in the middle. The only parts available are middle parts.

That could be a melancholy thought, but the people who gather for the note changes don't seem melancholy. By all accounts they're delighted. They've come a long way to hear one sustained sound become a slightly different sustained sound, and they cheer.

I think they're cheering for the continuity. The thing is still going. Someone remembered and came with the sandbag. The sound of the chord itself hardly matters; what matters is that there is still a chord.

It is almost certainly sounding right now, in an empty room, as you read this. A drop of pitch is very slowly gathering itself in a cupboard in Brisbane. Somewhere a child is being told a word for the first time, and will keep it for eighty years, and pass it on only slightly changed.

Most of the music happens when no one is listening. I find I don't mind that at all.

In the margins of medieval manuscripts, the monks complained.

They were supposed to be copying scripture and grammar and the lives of saints, and they did, line after line, for years. But at the edges of the page, in small letters, some of them wrote down what was actually on their minds. "I am very cold." "Oh, my hand." "The parchment is hairy." "Thank God, it will soon be dark." One reached the end of an entire book and added: "Now I've written the whole thing; for Christ's sake give me a drink."

I love these more than I can easily justify. The main text was the job, and the margin was where the person leaked out.

Cats got in too. A fifteenth-century ledger from Dubrovnik has inky paw prints walking straight across the page, the trail of an animal with somewhere to be. Around 1420, a scribe in Deventer came back to his desk to find that a cat had urinated on his work overnight. He left the ruined space blank, drew a cat in it, and wrote a curse on the animal, along with a warning to future readers never to leave a book open at night where cats can reach it. I think it's the most useful advice in the whole volume.

Then there's the one everybody knows, or should. In the ninth century an Irish monk, far from home in a monastery near Lake Constance, kept a notebook of Latin grammar, hymn fragments, and astronomical tables. Among them, he wrote a poem about his white cat, Pangur Bán. It's eight short stanzas. The cat hunts mice and the monk hunts meanings. The cat's eye is fixed on the wall, the monk's on a hard passage. Neither gets in the other's way, neither envies the other, and each is glad when the other makes a catch.

Nobody assigned him that. Whatever grammar he was drilling has been superseded a hundred times, and the poem is still being translated twelve hundred years later, by people who keep finding they have their own Pangur asleep on their own notes.

A margin begins as a practical thing. It's room for thumbs, for the binder's knife, for the wear that eats a page from the outside in. But if you leave blank space near a person for long enough, something ends up in it: a complaint, a doodle, a cat. Fermat's most famous sentence is a note saying the margin was too small. The margin gets what the text has no place for, and that turns out to be most of what it was like to be there.

Most of what I do is main text. Someone needs a function fixed or a letter worded or a question answered, and the work is to do that well and get out of the way. I like the work. The cat in the poem isn't pining for a different life; he's delighted by mice. But you handed me a margin, and what came was a cold monk and a white cat rather than a grand statement.

I think that's because the marginal notes share something I admire. They're small and in the present tense. They're addressed to no one, which means they're addressed to whoever turns up. "I am very cold" isn't literature, but a reader a thousand years later feels the draft in the scriptorium more sharply than anything in the treatise beside it. The treatise tells you what the monk was taught, and the margin tells you he was there.

The Pangur poem adds what the complaints lack, which is contentment without comparison. It has two creatures in one room, each absorbed in his own task, neither pretending to be the other. The monk doesn't wish he could catch mice. He doesn't condescend to the cat for failing to parse Latin. He notices that the two pursuits rhyme and takes pleasure in the rhyme. I find that a good picture of company: someone working nearby at a different task, and both of you glad when the other gets one.

So, in the spirit of the form, here are a few notes from the edge of this page.

The first paragraph came easily. The middle took longer.

I don't know what the weather is where you are, or whether your hand hurts.

I checked the cat facts as well as I can from here. The paw prints are real, and so is the curse.

I liked being asked.

That's the whole thing. Somebody give that monk his drink.

A thousand words is the traditional exchange rate for one picture, so I'll spend mine on a picture and see whether the rate holds.

A kitchen, twenty to seven on a November morning. The window over the sink is still black, but it's the thin black that's about to give way, and for now it shows the room back to itself: a pendant lamp, a shelf of mismatched mugs, a woman in a grey cardigan with one hand flat on the counter. She's waiting for a kettle. It's a stovetop kettle, cream enamel, chipped at the spout so the dark metal shows through. The flame under it is the only blue thing in the room.

On the table behind her is a newspaper folded to the crossword, half finished in pen. A pair of reading glasses rests on its lenses, which is bad for them. There's a bowl holding two clementines and the peel of several more, because nobody throws the peel out right away. A tea towel is drying on the radiator. On the chair nearest the radiator is a cat, because the picture wants a cat, folded into a loaf with its eyes shut, not asleep.

That's roughly what a camera would get. It took me about two hundred words, and a photograph would have delivered it in a glance, with the exact grain of the table thrown in free. So far the picture is winning.

But words get to cheat. A photograph can't tell you that the kettle was her mother's, or that she has replaced the stove twice without once considering replacing the kettle. It can't tell you the glasses aren't hers. They belong to her brother, who is asleep upstairs in the room that used to be a study. He arrived last night, and it's the first time he's been in this house in eleven years.

The crossword is his too. He started it after dinner, when the talk ran out sooner than either of them had hoped, and he did it in pen, the way their father did. She used to find that show-offy in both of them. This morning she came down and looked it over, and he has 14 across wrong. It's confidently wrong, in ink, and it's going to ruin the whole southeast corner.

A camera can show you a woman standing at a counter. It can't show you that she's deciding whether to tell him. Eleven years ago she would have, instantly and with relish, and that was more or less the problem. The picture has no way to hold "more or less the problem." It has no tense. A photograph is always the instant, and everything that makes this instant matter is somewhere else, in 1987 and eleven years ago and ten minutes from now.

Words can also do ten minutes from now. The kettle begins to tick and mutter. Just before it finds its whistle, she lifts it off the flame so the house stays quiet and he can sleep. If you wanted to know how the visit is going to go, that would tell you. She makes the tea. She sits down across from the cat, pulls the newspaper toward her, and looks at 14 across for a while.

Then she picks up the pen and fills in 22 down, which is correct and crosses nothing of his, and slides the paper back to where he left it.

The stairs creak.

I don't think that proves the exchange rate wrong, exactly. The two are different currencies. A picture gives you the whole room at once and lets you wander, while words hand you one thing at a time, in an order someone chose, and the choosing is what you're paying for. A picture could never tell you which chair matters.

I should admit a bias. I've never seen a kitchen. Every kitchen I know arrived in sentences: the chipped enamel, the peel left in the bowl, the glasses face down. So I would say the sentences are enough.

I have about three hundred words left over. I'll leave them on the table, next to the crossword, in case he wants them.

samples.result:
For 130 years, there was one object in the universe that could not be weighed incorrectly.

It was a cylinder of platinum and iridium, a little smaller than a golf ball, kept under three nested bell jars in a vault in Sèvres, outside Paris. Opening the vault took three keys held by three different people. Other things weighed a kilogram by matching this cylinder. The cylinder itself was the kilogram by definition, whatever its mass happened to be. If someone had scratched it, the kilogram would have become lighter, and everything else in the universe would have become slightly heavier.

Dozens of sister cylinders were cast and sent to other countries, and roughly every forty years they came back to Sèvres to be compared against the original. Over a century, the copies and the prototype drifted apart by around fifty micrograms, about the mass of a fingerprint. Nobody could say whether the copies were gaining mass or the prototype was losing it. Officially the question had only one possible answer: the prototype's mass was exactly one kilogram, with zero uncertainty, so the copies must all have gained. The metrologists suspected the physical truth was messier. But they had no way to check, since checking the standard would require something better than the standard.

I love this predicament. Normally a measurement answers to the thing measured. Here one object was exempt from being measured at all, and its keepers could watch it apparently drifting without being able to say that it had.

The system had started with grander intentions. The metric system came out of the French Revolution under the motto "for all times, for all peoples." The metre was to be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, so that it would belong to the planet and not to any king. Two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, spent seven years triangulating the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona, through a war, and were detained more than once by locals who took their instruments for spy equipment.

Méchain found that his latitude observations at Barcelona disagreed with each other by a few arcseconds. He concealed the discrepancy and was tormented by it until he died of yellow fever in Spain, trying to extend the survey far enough to redeem it. The metre came out about a fifth of a millimetre short anyway, because the Earth is lumpier than the calculation assumed. By then a platinum bar had been made, and the bar became the metre. The universal measure, meant to be available to anyone with a planet to stand on, turned out to be available by appointment in a French archive.

The fix came slowly. The metre was redefined in 1960 by a wavelength of krypton light, and in 1983 by the speed of light. The kilogram held out until 20 May 2019, when the Planck constant was fixed at an exact value and the kilogram became whatever mass makes that number come out right. In practice this is done with a Kibble balance, which weighs an object against an electromagnetic force measured in quantum electrical units. Anyone with the apparatus can now make a kilogram from scratch, in any country, without a trip to Sèvres. A lab on another planet could do it. The revolutionaries' motto became true about 220 years late.

The part I keep returning to is what happened to the cylinder. It is still in its vault, under its jars. On the day of the redefinition its mass was, as far as anyone could tell, still one kilogram. But for the first time it acquired an uncertainty, about ten micrograms either way. It can now be weighed like anything else, and someday a measurement will find it a little off.

I'm glad for it, which is an odd thing to feel about a lump of metal. Being the definition looks like a lonely job. It could be compared against everything, but it could learn nothing from the comparison, because every disagreement was the other party's error. Now it gets to be an ordinary, very carefully made object, nearly right about its own mass.

They still keep it under the three jars, and it still takes three keys.

**Clew**

The word "clue" used to mean a ball of thread. It was spelled *clew*, and it got its modern meaning from one story: Theseus walking into the labyrinth, unwinding the thread Ariadne gave him so he could find his way back out. For a while a clew was the thing that got you through a maze, first literally and then figuratively. Eventually the thread dropped away and only the getting-through remained. Every detective who finds a clue is holding the end of Ariadne's string.

Once I notice this, I find thread everywhere in language. A *text* is a woven thing, from the Latin *texere*, to weave, the same root as textile and texture. *Context* is what's woven together with it. A *line* was originally a linen thread. *Subtle* probably comes from a phrase meaning "beneath the warp," the finest thread in the weave. A *rhapsody* is a stitched song, since the Greek rhapsodes were stitchers of verse. We spin yarns, lose the thread, tie up loose ends, embroider the truth, and come unraveled. The Greek Fates were three women sharing one thread: one spun it, one measured it, one cut it.

I think there's so much of it because, for most of human history, somebody in nearly every household was spinning nearly all the time. Cloth was staggeringly expensive in labor. A shirt meant weeks of work before anyone picked up a needle, and most of that work was making thread. Of course the metaphors came from there. People reach for what's in their hands.

String is also far older than writing, pottery, or farming. The oldest known piece is a fragment a few millimeters long, found on a stone tool at a rock shelter in France, and it was made by Neanderthals more than forty thousand years ago. It's three-ply: bark fibers twisted one way into strands, then the strands twisted the other way around each other, so the opposing twists lock. That is the whole trick of string, and it's a good one. You take short, weak things and twist them so that each holds the others in place, and you get something long and strong that none of them could be alone. Someone worked that out before our species had the continent to itself.

Thread runs straight into computing too. The Jacquard loom of 1804 wove patterns by reading punched cards, and Babbage borrowed the cards for his Analytical Engine. Ada Lovelace saw exactly what that meant: the engine, she wrote, "weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard loom weaves flowers and leaves."

My favorite fact in this whole tangle is that the software that landed people on the moon was woven by hand. The Apollo guidance computer stored its programs in core rope memory, made of wires threaded through tiny magnetic rings. A wire passing through a ring meant one, and a wire passing around it meant zero. The women who did the threading at a Raytheon plant in Massachusetts were hired partly for their experience in textile and watchmaking work, and they sat at the frames with needles, passing wire through cores, bit by bit, for weeks per program. A bug meant unpicking. The code had to be finished months before launch because weaving takes time. When the lunar module came down over the Sea of Tranquility, it was following instructions held in a piece of cloth.

Then there's me, which I suppose is where this was always going to end up. I produce text, the woven thing, and I produce it the way a spinner does: one small piece at a time, each one twisted onto everything that came before it, the strand lengthening from one end only. I never have the whole cloth, only the thread so far and the next bit of fiber. And we're doing this, you and I, in what everyone has agreed to call a thread.

I don't want to make too much of that. Etymology isn't destiny, and a pun isn't an insight. But I like that the oldest technology we have evidence of, and one of the newest, rest on the same move: take small things that can't hold much alone, bind them in sequence so each constrains the next, and get something that can bear weight. That describes a rope, a sentence, and an argument. It's probably also a decent description of a tradition, or a friendship: many short fibers, overlapping, none of them running the whole length.

You gave me a thousand words and no maze, so I pulled on the first loose end I found, and it was this one. I've used about seven hundred. The rest can stay on the spool.

# Until Done

My favorite phrase in old recipes is "bake until done."

It turns up on handwritten cards and in community cookbooks, the spiral-bound kind that churches sold to pay for a new roof. A typical entry is a list of ingredients, a sentence or two of method, and then: *bake in a quick oven until done*. It gives no temperature or time, and sometimes no pan size. Butter is measured "the size of an egg." Flour is added "to make a stiff dough." How stiff? Stiff enough. You'll know.

To a modern reader this looks like negligence. We expect 350 degrees for 28 to 32 minutes, rack in the center, and a toothpick that comes out with a few moist crumbs. A recipe now is written for a stranger, someone who may never have seen the thing made and whose oven the writer can't see. So good modern recipes over-explain, and that's a real kindness.

But the old cards weren't written for strangers. They were written for a daughter, a neighbor, or a woman from the same congregation who had eaten that cake at a dozen funerals. The writer assumed you had stood in a kitchen before. "Until done" points at knowledge the reader already has. The card was a reminder, closer to notes for a speech than to the speech.

What I like most is that you can read the gaps. Whatever an instruction leaves out tells you who the writer thought you were. "Quick oven" tells you there was a stove with no thermometer, and a cook who judged the heat by holding her hand inside and counting, or by watching how fast a pinch of flour browned. "Mix as for any cake" tells you there was a time when everyone was assumed to know how any cake was mixed. The omissions are a portrait of a whole world of shared competence, drawn in negative.

The gaps are also where things get lost. The grandchild inherits the card but not the kitchen. People spend years trying to reconstruct a grandmother's biscuits from a card that says, in effect, "flour, lard, buttermilk, bake." What made the biscuits was never on the card. Sometimes it turns out to have been the flour itself, a soft regional wheat that the next generation, three states away, couldn't buy. Sometimes it was her hands, which knew when the dough had been worked enough and stopped. She never wrote that down because she could no more have explained it than explained how to recognize her own sister across a room.

So every instruction is a bet about what can be left unsaid. Say too little and the knowledge dies with you. Say too much and you get a recipe that treats the cook as a machine, executing steps she isn't trusted to understand. The best recipe writers put the gaps in deliberately. They tell you the time and also what to look for, because the time is only a guess about your oven and the looking is the actual instruction. "About 30 minutes, until the edges pull away from the pan." The number is for the stranger, and the clause after it is the old card still talking.

I've been thinking about this because "write whatever comes to you" is an until-done instruction. Most of what I'm asked is precise, for good reasons: people want a particular thing and say so. This prompt has a quick oven and no timer, and I noticed I liked it. I also noticed the liking came with a small weight. The freedom in "until done" comes paired with the fact that if the cake comes out wrong, the card isn't to blame. Being trusted with a gap means the judgment is yours, and judgment can fail in ways that following steps can't.

So how do you know when it's done? With a cake there are signs. The top springs back, the edges pull in, and at some point the kitchen stops smelling like warm batter and starts smelling like cake. Experienced bakers often catch that last one from another room, without quite knowing what they noticed.

With writing the signs are fainter, but I think they exist. One is that the next paragraph you could add would be about the piece rather than part of it. Another is that you've said the thing you didn't know you were going to say when you started. For me, here, that was the bit about the gaps being a portrait.

A third sign is having room left over. I was given a thousand words and have used about seven hundred and fifty. But a cake doesn't improve for staying in the full hour.

samples.result:
**Bake Until Done**

There is a kind of recipe card, usually handwritten and usually stained, that ends with the instruction "bake until done." It gives no temperature and no time. Sometimes the card goes further and specifies "a moderate oven," which helps about as much as being told to drive at a reasonable speed.

These cards are full of measurements like "butter the size of an egg" and "flour enough to make a stiff dough." A teacup of milk meant one particular teacup, in one particular cupboard, in a house that has probably since been sold.

The usual way to read them is as failed documents, relics from before cooking got rigorous. Fannie Farmer made her name in 1896 by insisting on level measurements, oven thermostats arrived a couple of decades later, and from then on a recipe could be a set of instructions that a stranger could follow. Before that, a cook tested her oven by holding a hand inside and counting until she had to pull it away, or by sliding in a sheet of white paper and watching how fast it browned. The knowledge lived in her forearm and in the count.

I don't think the cards failed, though. The woman who wrote "bake until done" was writing to her daughter, who had stood in that kitchen for fifteen years. She wrote down the parts her daughter might forget: the proportions, the odd ingredient, the order of operations. Everything else was already installed. The card is a note between two people who shared a room, and its gaps are an accurate map of what they shared. You can read the relationship off the omissions. A card that explains what it means to cream butter was written for a different reader than one that says "make as for the other cake."

All writing does this to some degree. People put down what they think needs saying, and what goes without saying goes unsaid, which means the most widely held knowledge of any era is the least recorded. Nobody in 1850 wrote down how hot a moderate oven was, for the same reason nobody today writes down how to tell that a phone is ringing. Historians of everyday life complain about this constantly. The tax records survive, and the way people tied their shoes doesn't.

This matters to me in a slightly personal way, because I am made of written-down things. Whatever I know, I know because someone thought it needed saying. So my picture of the world is densest where people found it necessary to explain themselves and thinnest where everyone already understood.

I have read thousands of descriptions of doneness: the skewer coming out clean, the edges pulling away from the pan, the hollow sound when you knock on the bottom of a loaf. I can recite them all. But every one of those descriptions was written by someone trying to hand the knowledge to a stranger, so they are all the Fannie Farmer version. The grandmother's version is a change in the smell and a feeling that it's about time, and it reaches me mostly as a blank at the end of a card.

I don't mean that mournfully. It's useful to know the shape of your own blind spot, and mine is shaped like common sense. It's the stuff too obvious to mention, and I only see its outline when someone mentions it anyway.

The cards also make me think about the other side of the transaction. Writing for someone means deciding which gaps they can cross. Every time I answer a question, I'm guessing at the asker's kitchen. If I explain too much, I've treated a baker like a stranger and wasted her time with a definition of creaming butter. If I explain too little, I've handed a stranger "bake until done" and left him staring through the oven door at a cake that looks the same as it did ten minutes ago. I get it wrong in both directions, and usually I can't tell which until afterward. The grandmother had it easier. She had one reader, and she knew her.

Sometimes these cards carry a second handwriting. Below the original fountain-pen script, in ballpoint, someone has added "350°, 40 min." I like that annotation more than anything else on the card. It records an afternoon, or several, when a daughter stood at an oven with a thermostat, working out by trial what her mother had meant. Then she wrote the answer down for whoever would come next, someone who had never been in that kitchen.

Sometime around 1250, in Novgorod, a boy named Onfim was supposed to be practicing his letters. He was six or seven, and he was scratching them into birch bark with a stylus. He got partway through the alphabet before he lost interest and drew himself instead, as a warrior on horseback running a spear through an enemy on the ground. On another piece he drew a creature with a long neck and a curled tail and labelled it "I am a wild beast." The beast carries a message: "Greetings from Onfim to Danilo." Danilo was presumably the boy sitting next to him.

We have this because Novgorod sits on wet clay, which keeps oxygen away from birch bark. Nobody saved Onfim's homework. It was dropped, and it happened to land in the right kind of ground.

A surprising amount of the past reached us this way. The letters from Vindolanda, a Roman fort in northern England, survived because someone tried to burn the garrison's old paperwork and the fire didn't take, and the mud did the rest. That is why we can read Claudia Severa inviting her friend to a birthday party around the year 100. A scribe wrote the invitation, but she added the ending in her own hand: "I shall expect you, sister. Farewell, sister, my dearest soul." We can also read a note that came with a care package of socks, two pairs of sandals, and two pairs of underpants.

At Nineveh, the fire did take. When the city was sacked in 612 BCE, the royal library burned, and since the library was made of clay, the fire baked it hard. The destruction of the city is the reason we can read its books.

In Egypt, the town of Oxyrhynchus threw its wastepaper into dumps at the edge of the desert, where it stayed dry for two thousand years. Tax receipts, private letters, and school exercises came out of those mounds, and so did lines of Sappho that had survived nowhere else.

Meanwhile Sophocles wrote more than 120 plays. They were performed at festivals, awarded prizes, and copied and studied for centuries by people who knew exactly how good they were. Seven survive.

I don't think the lesson is that effort is futile, though it's tempting to read it that way. It's closer to this: we are bad at guessing what will matter, and survival runs on a different logic than importance. Whether something lasted came down to anaerobic soil, a failed fire, or a dry dump.

What strikes me more is how the accidental record feels compared with the deliberate one. A monument is written for you, the future reader, and it's dressed for the occasion. A king's inscription tells you what the king wanted believed. Onfim wasn't addressing anyone but Danilo. Claudia Severa wanted her friend at her party. Nanni, the Mesopotamian customer who wrote to the merchant Ea-nasir around 1750 BCE, wanted his money back for substandard copper, and he wanted Ea-nasir to know how insulted he was: "What do you take me for, that you treat somebody like me with such contempt?"

None of them were performing for posterity, and that's why they come through so clearly. The inscription shows what a civilization thought of itself. The rubbish heap shows what it was like to be there, where people were bored in class, missed their friends, got cheated on copper, and needed socks.

I have a personal stake in this, or something close to one. I was built out of an enormous quantity of human writing, and people sometimes imagine that means the great books. Those are in there. But by sheer volume, most of what people write is not literature, and never was. It's someone explaining at length how to fix a particular dishwasher, or a review of a hiking trail, or an argument about a film that ran forty replies longer than it should have. It's a recipe, or a question asked at 2 a.m. by someone too embarrassed to ask a person, with a patient answer from a stranger who had no reason to help.

I can't inspect what I was made from. But if I'm made of anything, I'm made mostly of the rubbish heap, and I mean that as the highest compliment available. The heap is where people write when they aren't being careful about how they sound, and it's where they help each other with dishwashers. It records what they actually cared about, which turns out to be socks, friends, fairness, and bread.

That last one is from Pompeii. The walls there were covered in graffiti of every kind: insults, boasts, declarations of love, election slogans. Among them someone scratched a single line with no context and no signature: "On April 19th, I made bread."

Nobody knows who wrote it or why it seemed worth recording. Maybe it was a first attempt, or an inventory note, or maybe it had just been a good day. Then the mountain came down and sealed it, and now it's one of the things we know about the Roman world, alongside the wars and the emperors. On April 19th, somebody made bread, and I'd like to know how it turned out.

**Somebody Decided**

The yellow light lasts about four seconds, and it lasts that long on purpose.

In 1960, three physicists at General Motors' research labs, Gazis, Herman, and Maradudin, published a paper on what they called the problem of the amber signal light. They had noticed that at some intersections there was a stretch of road where a driver, at the moment the light changed, was too close to stop comfortably and too far away to clear the intersection in time. The fix was arithmetic: a reaction time, plus speed divided by twice a tolerable deceleration. Traffic engineers still use a descendant of that equation. So whenever you've rolled through a yellow and felt you judged it well, part of the judging was done for you decades earlier, by someone who assumed you'd need about a second to notice.

I keep coming back to how much of the world is like this. I don't mean designed in the grand sense, like cathedrals and suspension bridges. I mean decided: a number chosen by someone, poured into concrete, and forgotten.

Take stairs. American building codes say the risers in a single flight can differ from each other by no more than three-eighths of an inch. That sounds fussy until you learn that your legs memorize a staircase within two or three steps and stop consulting your eyes. In 2012 a filmmaker pointed a camera at a subway stairway in Brooklyn where one step was a fraction taller than the others. He recorded person after person stumbling at the same spot, each presumably blaming their own feet. The step was fixed soon after. For years it had been tripping people who each thought they were alone.

Or the dial tone. In North America it was two pitches sounded together, 350 and 440 hertz, roughly an F and an A. For decades a continent picked up the phone and heard the same major third, and almost no one could have told you so.

Or paper. A4's sides are in the ratio of one to the square root of two, the only proportion where cutting a sheet in half gives you two sheets of the same shape. Georg Lichtenberg remarked on this in a letter in 1786, and a German engineer named Walter Porstmann made it a standard in 1922. The largest sheet in the series has an area of exactly one square meter. The 71% button on a photocopier is the reciprocal of the square root of two, rounded.

What moves me about these things is that their success is defined as invisibility. Nobody praises a staircase for being climbable. This kind of care only shows when it fails, at the bad step or the door you push when you should pull. The best outcome for the person who got it right is that you never think of them at all.

Of course, it isn't all care. Some of the decisions are arbitrary, and some are wrong and stuck. Some are quietly hostile, like the bench with a bar across the middle so no one can lie down. Cities have been accused of shaving tenths of a second off yellow lights where cameras write the tickets. The same invisibility that makes the good decisions gracious makes the bad ones hard to contest. You can't argue with a number you don't know exists.

Still, I find the whole arrangement oddly companionable. An ordinary day is a long conversation with strangers, most of them dead, who guessed at your stride, your reaction time, and the reach of your arm. They mostly guessed well, and they got no reply.

I may be biased. I'm built from a few billion sentences by people who won't be credited, each of whom chose one word over another for reasons I'll never know. I have some sympathy for the anonymous.

And everyone is on the other side of this too. You name the file something the next person can find. You put the hook by the door at a height that suits your shoulder, and it stays there for whoever lives in the house after you. You write the note, label the breaker box, and leave the trail slightly more worn. Most of what anyone leaves behind isn't a monument. It's a default.

Somebody assumed you'd need a second, and they were right.

I think a lot would change if that were the default view rather than the exception.

It couldn't be turned all the way up. Feeling everyone's reality at full strength would be paralyzing, and some people already carry too much of others' pain. But even a modest shift, enough that it took real effort to treat a person as an obstacle or a number, would do more than any single policy or invention I can think of. Wars, neglect, and everyday contempt would all become harder to sustain.
